artigo.texto: BYD Atto 3 Gets New Atlantis Gray Colour Option in India BYD has replaced Surf Blue with Atlantis Gray on the Atto 3, which continues to offer two battery options, up to 521km of claimed range, and the same equipment list. BYD has introduced a new colour option for the Atto 3 electric SUV in India, with Atlantis Gray replacing the previously available Surf Blue. The change is limited to the exterior colour palette, with no reported updates to the SUV's features, battery packs, or performance. The Atto 3 continues to be offered in multiple variants. Also Read: BYD Denza India Entry Confirmed; Here's What to Expect BYD Atto 3: What's Changed? With Surf Blue discontinued, the BYD Atto 3 is now available in four colours: Atlantis Gray, Cosmos Black, Ski White and Harbour Grey. The SUV retains its existing design, including full-LED lighting, chrome and black exterior elements, a panoramic sunroof and either 17-inch or 18-inch wheels, depending on the variant. BYD Atto 3: Battery The electric SUV is available with 49.92kWh and 60.48kWh battery packs. Both use an electric motor that develops 201bhp and 300Nm of torque. The smaller battery offers an ARAI-certified range of 468km, while the larger unit has a claimed range of 521km. BYD claims a 0-100km/h acceleration time of 7.3 seconds. For charging, the smaller battery supports DC fast charging at up to 70kW, while the larger pack supports up to 80kW. The cabin features a 12.8-inch rotating touchscreen, wireless smartphone connectivity, wireless charging and a six-speaker audio system. Other equipment includes a powered tailgate, a 360-degree camera, an NFC key card, tyre pressure monitoring and auto-hold. The front seats are electrically adjustable, with six-way adjustment for the driver and four-way adjustment for the front passenger. Safety equipment comprises seven airbags, Level 2 advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and disc brakes on all four wheels, with ventilated discs at the front. The BYD Atto 3 is priced from Rs 24.99 lakh to Rs 34.49 lakh (ex-showroom), depending on the variant. The new colour has not brought a price increase, and the SUV's existing specifications remain unchanged.

Malásia vira polo global de IA ao atrair EUA e China ao mesmo tempo
País do Sudeste Asiático recebe bilhões de empresas americanas e chinesas em data centers de IA, explorando posição neutra na guerra tecnológica entre as potências.
Enquanto Estados Unidos e China travam uma guerra tecnológica cada vez mais intensa, um país de 35 milhões de habitantes encontrou uma forma de lucrar com os dois lados. A Malásia se transformou em um dos maiores polos globais de data centers voltados para inteligência artificial, recebendo investimentos bilionários tanto de gigantes americanas quanto de empresas chinesas que buscam acesso a chips avançados fora do alcance das sanções de Washington.
No estado de Johor, no sul do país, 65 projetos de data centers estão em operação, construção ou em diferentes fases de aprovação. As instalações já consomem mais de 2 gigawatts de eletricidade, o suficiente para abastecer mais de um terço das residências do país. Se todos os projetos planejados forem concluídos, a demanda pode superar 10 gigawatts, o que transformaria a região em uma das maiores concentrações de poder computacional do planeta.
Por que a Malásia e não outro país do Sudeste Asiático
A combinação é difícil de replicar: terrenos baratos, energia relativamente acessível e proximidade estratégica dos cabos submarinos que conectam a China ao restante do mundo. Mas o fator decisivo é político. A Malásia optou deliberadamente por uma posição neutra na disputa entre as duas potências, recebendo investimentos de ambos os lados sem alinhar-se a nenhum.
Microsoft, Google e Oracle investem pesadamente no país para se aproximar de clientes asiáticos. Do outro lado, ByteDance, Tencent e Alibaba construíram infraestrutura de processamento de dados na mesma região. Em alguns parques industriais de Johor, instalações voltadas para empresas americanas e chinesas estão sendo erguidas praticamente lado a lado. Como descreveu um integrante do governo local envolvido na aprovação dos projetos: “Este é o único lugar do mundo onde estamos vendo isso acontecer.”
O movimento teve origem por volta de 2021, quando Singapura proibiu novos projetos de data centers por conta de restrições energéticas. A demanda migrou para o outro lado da fronteira. Empresas chinesas chegaram primeiro, seguidas pelas americanas, e a dinâmica se retroalimentou desde então. A corrida global por infraestrutura de IA encontrou no estado de Johor uma válvula de escape para as tensões geopolíticas.
O papel dos chips da Nvidia na equação geopolítica
No coração dessa história estão os semicondutores mais avançados da Nvidia, amplamente proibidos de serem exportados diretamente para a China desde 2022. As restrições impostas por Washington impediram a venda dos chips mais sofisticados ao território chinês, mas não regularam o uso desses mesmos processadores em data centers localizados em outros países.
Essa distinção regulatória criou uma brecha. Empresas chinesas como a ByteDance, controladora do TikTok, passara

Gestora global de investimentos registra US$ 65,2 bilhões em ativos sob gestão, além de um ritmo forte de investimentos e captação de recursos durante os primeiros nove meses de 2026
2 de novembro de 2026, às 09:27
MANAMA, Bahrein, 2 de novembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A Investcorp, gestora global líder em investimentos alternativos, anunciou hoje que registrou US$ 11,1 bilhões em atividades agregadas em captação de recursos, alocação de capital e desinvestimentos durante os primeiros nove meses de 2026, evidenciando a força e o crescimento contínuos de sua plataforma global.
O anúncio, feito durante o fórum internacional Gateway Gulf 2026 no Bahrein, destaca o dinamismo da Investcorp em seus investimentos globais e seu compromisso contínuo com o Reino, onde a empresa foi fundada em 1982.
Entre janeiro e setembro de 2026, a Investcorp captou US$ 4,8 bilhões de sua base global de investidores, alocou US$ 3,7 bilhões em novos investimentos e registrou US$ 2,6 bilhões em desinvestimentos por meio de suas frentes de negócios. Em setembro de 2026, o total de ativos sob gestão da Investcorp era de US$ 65,2 bilhões.
Durante o mesmo período, a Investcorp alcançou marcos significativos na captação de recursos em suas plataformas de Private Equity e Capital Estratégico na América do Norte, garantindo mais de US$ 2,3 bilhões em compromissos agregados.
Mohammed Alardhi, presidente-executivo da Investcorp, disse: “A Investcorp foi fundada no Bahrein há mais de quatro décadas, e o Reino continua sendo fundamental para o nosso crescimento e ambições globais. Nosso ritmo contínuo de avanço reflete a força de nossa plataforma internacional e a confiança de nossos investidores e parceiros. Com o olhar voltado para o futuro, reafirmamos nosso compromisso de conectar o capital global a oportunidades de investimento alternativas, abraçando a inovação e contribuindo para a posição do Bahrein como um dos principais centros financeiros internacionais”.
Principais destaques de investimento e inovação
A Investcorp continuou a expandir suas atividades de investimento internacional durante 2026, com transações e marcos significativos em suas diversas áreas de atuação:
Essas conquistas refletem a capacidade da Investcorp de conectar investidores a oportunidades na América do Norte, Europa, Oriente Médio e Ásia. A participação da Investcorp no Gateway Gulf 2026 reforça seu compromisso de longa data com o Bahrein e o papel do Reino como porta de entrada para o capital global e a inovação financeira.

Google inaugura centro de dados no espaço e testa inteligência artificial em órbita
O protótipo Suncatcher, equipado com uma Unidade de Processamento Tensorial (TPU) e o modelo Gemma 4 de inteligência artificial, já está online e realizando tarefas experimentais, marcando um passo inicial para a computação espacial
A Google deu um passo significativo na exploração da computação em órbita com a ativação de seu primeiro satélite protótipo de centro de dados, o Suncatcher. Lançado no início de outubro a bordo de um foguete Falcon 9 da SpaceX, o satélite, que carrega uma Unidade de Processamento Tensorial (TPU) da Google e gera até 1 kW de eletricidade, tem como objetivo pavimentar o caminho para futuras redes de satélites que realizarão grandes cargas de trabalho de inferência diretamente no espaço. Após um período de comissionamento de cerca de três semanas, o Suncatcher iniciou suas operações, testando a capacidade de processamento de inteligência artificial em um ambiente orbital.
Inteligência artificial em órbita: poesia e condições espaciais
A primeira tarefa do modelo de inteligência artificial pré-carregado no satélite, o Gemma 4 do Google DeepMind, foi criativa e funcional. Na última terça-feira (27), engenheiros em terra enviaram um comando pedindo ao modelo que escrevesse um haicai sobre a experiência de estar no espaço. A resposta poética do Gemma 4 foi: “Mármore azul abaixo / Dados fluem em graça silenciosa / Luz estelar alimenta meu núcleo”. Além da poesia, a Google também solicitou ao satélite relatórios sobre as condições orbitais ao seu redor, confirmando que a operação estava ocorrendo de forma nominal.
Leia também:
A Unidade de Processamento Tensorial (TPU) é um chip desenvolvido pela Google especificamente para acelerar cargas de trabalho de inteligência artificial, como o aprendizado de máquina. No contexto do Suncatcher, a TPU é utilizada para inferência, que é o processo de usar um modelo de IA já treinado para fazer previsões ou tomar decisões a partir de novos dados. Este tipo de processamento é menos exigente em termos de recursos do que o treinamento de modelos, mas ainda assim requer capacidade computacional considerável.
Desafios do ambiente espacial e próximos passos
Um dos principais desafios para a operação de hardware de computação no espaço é a radiação. Embora a Google tenha testado extensivamente suas TPUs em aceleradores de partículas na Terra, o ambiente espacial apresenta condições únicas que podem afetar o desempenho dos chips. A radiação pode causar “bit flips”, alterações indesejadas nos valores armazenados na memória do computador, o que pode corromper dados sem que as ferramentas de monitoramento usuais detectem o problema. Os testes em solo sugeriram que o impacto da radiação seria mínimo para cargas de trabalho de inferência, sendo mais problemático para o treinamento de modelos. Agora, a equipe da Google poderá avaliar essas dinâmicas na realidade, e não apenas em simulações.

artigo.texto: We're selling 58 shares of DuPont at roughly $143 each. Following Monday's trade, Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust will own 450 shares of DD, reducing its weight in the portfolio to 1.65% from 1.85%. We're offsetting our Boeing purchase from earlier Monday with a small trim of DuPont. Shares of the diversified industrial are up about 10% since the end of September, benefiting from the rotation out of heavily exposed data center buildout names. The rebound puts shares within a few dollars of their August highs, though the stock remains about $12 below its 2026 peak. DuPont shares are up about 18% for the year. DD YTD mountain DuPont YTD DuPont reports earnings before Tuesday's opening bell. While not making a call on the results, we wouldn't be surprised to see some noise like last quarter due to disruptions in the Middle East impacting the timing of a few large clean water technology projects. Another factor for this trim is that the simplification story has mostly been played out now that it's been almost exactly one year since it completed the separation of its electronics business, Qnity Electronics . DuPont shares have rallied about 36% since the breakup. We will be looking for the next catalyst with Tuesday morning's earnings. From this sale, we will realize a gain of roughly 48% on stock purchased in August 2023. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long DD, Q, BA. See here for a full list of the stocks.) As a subscriber to the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer, you will receive a trade alert before Jim makes a trade. Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. If Jim has talked about a stock on CNBC TV, he waits 72 hours after issuing the trade alert before executing the trade. artigo.texto: Anatel vai ao Governo e pede R$ 30,76 milhões para quitar contas básicas A crise orçamentária tem origem no bloqueio de R$ 51,83 milhões determinado pelo governo em maio. Agência estaria devendo ao data center. A Anatel alertou o governo federal sobre risco de não conseguir quitar contas básicas de funcionamento. A agência acumula R$ 30,76 milhões em notas fiscais pendentes referentes à aquisição de seu próprio data center, em Brasília. Na semana passada, o presidente da Anatel, Carlos Baigorri, pediu ao Ministério do Planejamento o desbloqueio de R$ 30 milhões para cobrir os compromissos. A informação foi dada pelo jornal Folha de São Paulo, nesta segunda-feira, 3/11. A estrutura em questão sustenta serviços digitais oferecidos a cidadãos e a empresas de telecomunicações, além dos sistemas internos usados pela agência em suas atividades de fiscalização. Os R$ 30,76 milhões estão classificados como “restos a pagar”, categoria que reúne despesas do ano anterior ainda não quitadas. A crise orçamentária tem origem no bloqueio de R$ 51,83 milhões determinado pelo governo em maio. A restrição reduziu o orçamento discricionário da Anatel, destinado a custeio e investimentos, de R$ 275,37 milhões para R$ 223,54 milhões; queda de 19%. Em dezembro de 2025, a Anatel assinou contrato de R$ 44,95 milhões com prestadores de produtos e software de tecnologia. O acordo envolve equipamentos, programas de gerenciamento, conectividade e serviços de implantação, migração, suporte, manutenção e garantia, com vigência até dezembro de 2030. A dificuldade vem sendo relatada desde agosto, quando a Anatel solicitou a antecipação de R$ 23,3 milhões originalmente previstos para dezembro. A agência diz que já revisou contratos, projetos e despesas para se adequar ao corte e que busca evitar a cobrança de “multas, juros e outros encargos contratuais”.

artigo.texto: Cloud Revenue Hits $168B as AI Capacity Expands Cloud infrastructure revenue reached $168 billion in the third quarter as providers brought higher-priced AI capacity online, reinforcing demand for new data centers even as power constraints slow delivery. Cloud providers are bringing data center capacity online for higher-priced AI services as enterprise cloud infrastructure spending accelerates, reinforcing demand for construction even as power constraints complicate delivery. Worldwide spending on cloud infrastructure services reached $168 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up 55% from a year earlier, according to a Synergy Research Group report. The market has doubled in eight quarters, and AI-specific services now account for roughly one-third of total revenue. John Dinsdale, chief analyst at Synergy, told Data Center Knowledge that three factors are driving the surge: additional capacity coming online, higher pricing, and a continued shift toward more expensive AI services. “A lot of the additional capacity that is coming online is specifically targeting more valuable, higher-priced AI services,” he said. That shift in pricing and service mix helps explain how cloud revenue can grow faster than the data center capacity supporting it. JLL’s August midyear report illustrated the construction demand behind that expansion. Hyperscalers accounted for 59% of North American data center tenant demand, while 28 GW of owner-occupied capacity was under construction, according to JLL. Neoclouds – specialized cloud providers offering GPU-as-a-Service to enterprise customers – represented another 11% of demand, while AI companies accounted for 7%, broadening the customer base competing for facilities. The buildout is expected to continue. Global data center capital spending is projected to exceed $3 trillion by 2030 as hyperscalers, sovereign AI programs, and specialized cloud providers expand their infrastructure to support growing AI workloads, according to an August report from Dell’Oro Group. AI Changes the Cloud Customer Mix The cloud market’s expansion is also reshaping which companies need infrastructure and how they compete. Amazon retained the largest share of worldwide cloud infrastructure revenue at 26%, followed by Microsoft at 19%, and Google at 16%, Synergy reported. “AI has totally transformed the cloud market in terms of service capabilities, customer demand, and growth opportunities,” Dinsdale said. Microsoft and Google grew faster than Amazon, while Oracle and neocloud providers, including CoreWeave, Crusoe, and Nebius, were among the fastest-growing companies outside the top three. Synergy said neocloud expansion is eroding the market shares of some established providers. For data center operators, that changing mix raises questions about tenant durability and contract stability, particularly if some fast-growing providers consolidate. Dinsdale said he expects the underlying infrastructure to retain value even if an individual neocloud’s prospects change. Construction Demand Persists Despite Power and Tenant Risks CBRE’s August report on North American data center trends found 7,481 MW under construction across eight primary markets in the first half of 2026, up 24.8% from a year earlier. More than 80% was preleased, up from 74.3% a year earlier. Power constraints continued to extend completion schedules, leaving customers competing for capacity that has yet to be delivered. Those commitments mean operators evaluating expansion must weigh construction schedules and tenant stability alongside cloud revenue growth. Dinsdale said he expects data centers, installed equipment, and existing customer contracts to find new owners if neocloud providers consolidate or fail. That suggests consolidation would redistribute infrastructure rather than leave large amounts of it unused, though the financial outcome would vary significantly by asset. “Whatever happens to a neocloud company and its prospects for carrying on as an independent entity, there will be valuable assets that will not go to waste,” he said. “Valuations will vary greatly, but I don’t imagine too many stranded assets being trashed.”

artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Liquid Cooling Is Changing What Data Centers Need to Measure Liquid cooling changes data center operations by making precise, real-time measurement across both liquid and air environments essential. For high-density AI environments, the data center industry has made its decision on liquid cooling. Facilities running dense AI workloads have led the way, and direct-to-chip cooling, in which liquid is routed through cold plates directly onto the processors, is becoming increasingly important in AI-optimized environments. The question is no longer whether liquid cooling will become more widely deployed. The more important operational question is what accurate, reliable measurement looks like in this new scenario. Liquid cooling solves a thermal problem. But operating these systems reliably over time introduces a different set of requirements, and the measurement infrastructure that supports reliable operation is part of that shift. From One Domain to Two Running a liquid-cooled facility is not a straightforward extension of running an air-cooled one. It is a categorically different operational environment, demanding new expertise across power, structural and mechanical engineering, fluid dynamics and chemistry, and instrumentation. And across all of these disciplines, measurement is the layer that makes the environment controllable. In a traditional air-cooled facility, the management of controlled environments is well understood. Temperature, relative humidity, and differential pressure have decades of industry practice behind them, supported by mature sensor technology and standardized guidance such as that published by ASHRAE, the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers. Operators know what they are measuring, why they are measuring it, how the information feeds into controls, and what the numbers mean. Liquid cooling extends that domain significantly. Pipes carrying cold water have always been part of data center infrastructure. What changes when cooling is brought all the way to the chips through CDUs and cold plates is the scope and criticality of liquid-side measurement. The parameters that now require dedicated instrumentation include liquid temperature, pressure, flow rate, and level, as well as leak detection and coolant health indicators such as pH, turbidity, conductivity, and refractive index. Each carries its own failure modes and must be understood in the context of cooling-loop performance and liquid quality. Liquid cooling takes over where air-side cooling runs out of headroom, but air-side management remains essential for everything else. Direct-to-chip cooling removes heat from the hottest components, but residual heat still needs to be managed with air. That is why operators need to understand both environments together. Measurements in a Liquid-Cooled Environment Alongside the liquid-side parameters, ambient conditions in the data hall and in the critical parts of the cooling system must be actively managed. Dew point is one area where the risk concentrates. Liquid cooling improves efficiency by circulating cold liquid over the cold plates. However, colder piping in an air-conditioned space also poses a risk of condensation. When pipe surface temperature drops below the ambient dew point, water can form near equipment, where the consequences of a failure event can far exceed any maintenance budget. A common practice is to maintain coolant supply temperatures at least 2°C above the measured ambient dew point. The coolant distribution unit is responsible for maintaining that margin, but only if it has a continuous and accurate picture of the actual dew point. The measurement challenge across all these parameters is not exotic. It draws on well-established sensor physics. The greater challenge is applying that physics correctly by understanding where to measure and how sensor data should feed into control decisions. Dynamic Facilities Demand Dynamic Measurements AI workloads fundamentally differ from traditional data center workloads in ways that matter for cooling. AI training jobs are intensive, and AI inferencing is intermittent. A cluster can move from idle to full load in minutes, generating a sharp change in thermal output that the cooling system must respond to in real time. The CDU managing that cluster needs to continuously control the cooling loop, ensuring supply and return temperatures stay within limits, pressure and flow rates remain within tolerance, and the ambient dew point near the cold manifolds stays within tolerance as conditions change. Reliable measurement is what makes that dynamic control possible. Without accurate, real-time data on critical parameters across the facility, control systems may be operating on delayed or inaccurate information. The consequences can cascade. Inefficient cooling wastes energy. Inadequate cooling puts hardware at risk. Overcorrection can waste energy and reduce operational efficiency. What the Next Generation Will Require Rack densities will continue to increase, and each step in that progression adds measurement requirements that do not yet benefit from decades of established industry practice. Reliable measurements give operators confidence that both the cooling infrastructure and the compute hardware it supports are operating within safe parameters. They enable more precise control, help facilities pursue efficiency targets, and provide early warning when conditions begin to drift. Without trustworthy measurements, a liquid-cooled data center is operating on assumptions. As cooling architectures become more complex and air-side and liquid-side environments increasingly need to work together, understanding what rigorous measurement looks like in this environment is where the hard work of the next phase begins.

artigo.texto: AI’s Expansion Hits the Limits of Local Power Power shortages and local opposition are delaying data center projects, making AI expansion harder, costlier, and more dependent on scarce grid access. Grid connection delays and local resistance are extending development timelines as operators race to add AI-related capacity, though analysts differ on whether those constraints are already limiting AI development. Data center projects are taking longer to reach construction as developers struggle to secure electricity connections and local approval, complicating expansion plans intended to meet growing AI demand. Projects that broke ground between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026 waited an average of just over two years after being announced, according to GlobalData. That compares with about 18 months for projects that started construction between early 2020 and mid-2025. Martina Raveni, senior analyst on GlobalData’s Strategic Intelligence team, told Data Center Knowledge that grid access and public opposition are the two biggest constraints. “The grid is the hardest to fix because it is structural: new grid infrastructure takes five to 15 years to build, while a data center takes one to three,” she said. GlobalData forecasts annual data center electricity consumption will rise from 590 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 1,520 TWh in 2030. Meeting that demand will require developers to address power, permitting, and construction bottlenecks that investment alone cannot quickly overcome. Grid Access Determines What Can Move Forward A project’s other development challenges can become secondary when there is no available electricity connection. Luis Fernandes, IDC senior research manager for cloud and data centers within enterprise infrastructure, told Data Center Knowledge that discussions with developers, designers, and large operators consistently point to grid access as the dominant obstacle. “It is by a long shot the biggest cause for delay in projects, to the point that we haven't seen delays in projects for any other reason, given that the lack of grid connection halts the entire exercise,” Fernandes said. Raveni said developers in Europe’s main data center hubs can wait up to a decade for a connection. Skilled labor shortages add another constraint, with insufficient electricians and other trades pushing some delivery schedules back by around a year. Delays are expected to be more common than cancellations, with Fernandes suggesting some stalled projects could change hands as other operators seek opportunities to acquire and complete them. “Speed in construction [comes at] a premium, and a paused construction site is still bleeding cash,” he said. Raveni cautioned that it remains too early to quantify eventual cancellations, although projects in grid-constrained locations or facing strong local opposition are particularly exposed. Community Pushback Makes Timelines Harder to Predict Community resistance can disrupt projects even when developers have customers and funding. Concerns about electricity bills, water consumption, noise, and land use can affect permitting and construction schedules. Ya-Han Brownlee-Chen, DP World’s vice president of data center strategy in the Americas, told Data Center Knowledge that local acceptance is becoming one of the sector’s most significant barriers to development. “There's a growing tension between the demand for AI infrastructure and communities' willingness to accommodate the physical facilities required to support it,” she said. That tension complicates site selection and makes construction timelines harder to predict. Brownlee-Chen also pointed to rising costs for land, equipment, and other resources, with owners seeking premiums for sites that could accommodate data centers. Those pressures can affect whether a delayed project remains financially viable. She said outcomes will depend on developers’ ability to resolve local objections, obtain infrastructure, and execute within a workable schedule, rather than on demand alone. On-Site Power Can Reduce Delays but Add New Risks Developers seeking alternatives to delayed grid connections can face additional environmental and permitting challenges. Raveni said on-site gas generation can bridge a power gap, but redundancy requirements may necessitate generating capacity substantially greater than the data center’s normal needs. Air pollution and water concerns can then intensify the same local resistance developers are trying to resolve. “The real risk is that a temporary fix becomes permanent and pushes emissions up just as grids are decarbonizing,” she explained. Power and cooling decisions also need to account for their combined demands on local resources. Joe Johnston, executive vice president and president of applied water at Xylem, said the infrastructure challenges need to be addressed together. “Some of the biggest barriers to data center growth are tied to physical infrastructure, particularly power availability, water resources, and cooling capacity,” Johnston told Data Center Knowledge. Johnston called for more efficient and resilient water and cooling infrastructure to support expansion while reducing pressure on community resources. GlobalData, for example, identified closed-loop cooling, water stewardship, and diversified power supplies among operators’ responses, although it describes progress as uneven. The Effect on AI Remains Unclear Longer development schedules raise questions about when infrastructure constraints will limit AI deployment, beyond increasing the cost of new capacity. Raveni said access restrictions are already emerging, citing cloud providers rationing capacity, customers needing to reserve further ahead, and usage caps affecting large AI companies. Fernandes, however, offered a more measured conclusion. “In terms of compute capacity, there is no hard evidence that we can point to [showing] that being a limitation to AI development,” he said. artigo.texto: Trump Onsite Power Push Meets AI Data Center Reality Trump’s onsite power push highlights a hard reality: most AI data centers will likely need hybrid energy strategies rather than fully off-grid designs. With data centers dominating industry and policy discussions, it was only a matter of time before President Donald Trump weighed in. In an Oct. 21 Truth Social post, Trump said new, large-scale data centers should generate their own electricity and return excess power to the local community or grid. He also suggested that developers make financial arrangements with host communities, including payments to residents: “As the President of the United States, I have been watching Data Centers very closely, and have come to a very strong conclusion. New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data Centers are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid, and therefore there is electric price increase. In fact, there could be a substantial decrease. Other elements likewise! If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend.’ I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck. MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A. President DJT” The comments are likely to intensify debate across the sector. Many projects already under construction have secured grid connections, signed power purchase agreements (PPAs), or otherwise locked in their energy strategy. If Trump’s position were translated into formal policy, developers would face difficult questions about whether those plans would need to change. Equipment availability would be another major challenge. Many of the components required for gas-fired, nuclear, and battery-backed onsite power systems are already in tight supply, with some turbine models effectively sold out through 2031. That would present a serious challenge for data center designers, engineers, developers, and operators, said Patrick Hughes, senior vice president of strategy, technical, and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA). Hughes was involved in developing the AI Data Center Energy Performance Framework,co-developed by NEMA, the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE), and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL). “It’s possible for a standalone AI data center to provide sufficient onsite power to fuel its own operations – whether it’s a combined-cycle plant or solar plus storage, we have the technology,” Hughes said. “But that doesn’t mean it’s feasible for a single AI data center – let alone the whole fleet of AI data centers – to supply 100% of their own power and operate reliably 24/7; that requires significant operational management and maintenance.” Permitting timelines, fuel and equipment supply chains, interconnection rules, and community considerations vary widely by location, Hughes added. Those factors will shape what is practical at any given site. For many facilities, the most likely outcome may be a hybrid approach that combines onsite generation and storage with a grid connection. Why AI Data Centers Can’t Easily Go Off-Grid There are substantial technical and logistical barriers to any broad requirement that AI data centers supply all of their own power. AI training and inference facilities have power densities and load profiles that differ sharply from those of traditional data centers and from facilities that have historically relied on co-located generation and storage. At the same time, the AI infrastructure buildout is grappling with enormous demand for electrical equipment and skilled labor across utilities, buildings, transportation, and industrial manufacturing. Whether or not developers are pushed toward a bring-your-own-power model, they are already competing with other sectors for turbines, switchgear, transformers, batteries, and specialized labor. Regardless of the onsite resource selected, the AI Data Center Energy Performance Framework offers technical standards and guiding principles for safety, resilience, and grid interaction. Data center designers, engineers, developers, and operators can use it to improve energy and water efficiency while supporting grid reliability and resilience through load flexibility and other grid-interactive operations. Existing Power Deals and Renewable Commitments Complicate the Shift A blanket onsite power requirement would also have to contend with existing clean-energy mandates, corporate sustainability goals, and regional differences in the availability of renewable resources. Many AI data centers already have agreements in place to draw power from solar and wind projects. The Stargate site in Abilene, Texas, offers one example. The project is already using natural gas, fuel cells, and gas engines during the construction phase and to power the first data centers now operating there. Developers are also planning to incorporate solar and wind, and the area’s solar generation potential was one of the reasons the location was selected. Abilene offers strong irradiance, abundant undeveloped land, and no major urban loads nearby. With developers scrambling to find 1.2 GW once all phases are complete, wind and solar are expected to supplement other power sources. Applied Digital’s AI data center project in North Dakota provides another example. The company has arranged for 400 MW of stranded wind power to serve its Ellendale campus and continues to emphasize renewables in its energy strategy. It also recently signed a deal with data center developer Soluna to use output from Soluna’s 150 MW Briscoe wind farm for a new data center in Texas. artigo.texto: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers September 4, 2026 Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land. Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily. AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University. From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. An insatiable appetite for power Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that. And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. How the AI boom could slow climate progress All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels. One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal. Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries. Hidden water demand Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume. In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023. There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%. Data centers are making cities hotter Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy. Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%. Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts. First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities. On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants. O Brasil pode ter um integrante na direção da União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT), agência especializada da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU). O presidente da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel), Carlos Baigorri, é o candidato oficial do País ao cargo de secretário-geral adjunto, o número dois na hierarquia do organismo internacional.
A UIT tem sede em Genebra e membros de 194 países. Ela surgiu em 1865 para administrar as redes de telégrafos, equipamentos antigos usados para envio de mensagens, uma espécie de tataravô dos smartphones. Hoje, a UIT gerencia o espectro de radiofrequências, as órbitas de satélites e define os parâmetros para as novas gerações de internet, como o 5G e o 6G.
Ou seja, a UIT é quem pavimenta o caminho para a evolução tecnológica das telecomunicações no mundo todo. E, vale lembrar: sem protocolos de internet bem estruturados, não há inteligência artificial, computação na nuvem, data centers, redes sociais ou veículos autônomos. Portanto, são protocolos com importância econômica e geopolítica.
No banco do motorista
“Queremos estar no banco do motorista nas grandes discussões, não no banco do passageiro”, disse Baigorri, em entrevista à Coluna. “Hoje, telecom é um pedaço de algo maior, da economia digital”, reforçou. Para o Brasil, conquistar um assento na diretoria da UIT seria fundamental para consolidar o seu papel como uma liderança técnica no setor e para exercitar as suas habilidades diplomáticas.
O Brasil já ocupou o cargo de vice-secretário-geral da UIT (equivalente ao atual posto de secretário-adjunto) com o engenheiro Roberto Blois, entre 1999 e 2006.
Na parte técnica, o Brasil é visto como referência lá fora devido ao grau elevado de desenvolvimento da internet por aqui. O País tem a quinta internet mais veloz do mundo, e um dos maiores porcentuais de população coberta (acima de 90%). Um dos responsáveis por esse sucesso foi o edital para licitação do 5G, que priorizou compromissos de investimentos das empresas na expansão da cobertura nas escolas, rodovias e região Amazônica, em vez de pagamento de outorga.
Já nas licitações anteriores, o foco foi maximizar a arrecadação. “Em vários eventos internacionais, o Brasil é citado como uma referência positiva. Dia sim, dia não a Anatel recebe delegações da Europa, Ásia e da América Latina para entender o que fizemos para ter essa cobertura. O edital está sendo copiado lá fora”, contou Baigorri.
Neutralidade brasileira ajuda
Na parte diplomática, a neutralidade histórica do Brasil é um facilitador para atuar como um intermediador dentro da UIT. “O Brasil conversa com a China e com os Estados Unidos. Além do conhecimento técnico, sabemos lidar com a diversidade. Muitos não sabem como fazer isso, ou não têm essa credibilidade”, avaliou.
Baigorri iniciou a carreira na antiga associação de operadoras móveis, que mais tarde se tornou a Conexis. Em 2009, passou no concurso para especialista em regulação na Anatel. O servidor de carreira cresceu na agênc

João Paulo Costa Pereira, CEO da Solo Network: “Nossa intenção é transformar essa estrutura em uma das principais operações do país no segmento de data centers de pequeno e médio porte.” (Divulgação)
Freelancer em Negócios
Publicado em 1 de novembro de 2026 às 09h01.
A integradora de tecnologia Solo Network anunciou a aquisição de 80% da Planeje, empresa de engenharia, infraestrutura e construção de data centers, para executar projetos completos no Brasil. O grupo prevê R$ 10 milhões para capital de giro e expansão comercial e pode disponibilizar mais R$ 50 milhões a partir de 2027, quando pretende dobrar o faturamento da Planeje.
A Solo Network, integradora de tecnologia e provedora de serviços gerenciados, acaba de anunciar a aquisição de participação majoritária na Planeje, empresa especializada em engenharia, infraestrutura e construção de data centers.
A operação chega para ampliar a atuação da empresa, que passa a executar projetos completos de data centers de pequeno e médio porte em todo o país. “Estamos vendo uma mudança na demanda por capacidade computacional. Nossa decisão foi participar de forma direta da cadeia de infraestrutura e trazer para dentro do grupo a engenharia e a construção de data centers”, afirma João Paulo Costa Pereira, CEO da Solo Network.
Na primeira etapa, a Solo Network prevê destinar cerca de R$ 10 milhões ao capital de giro e à expansão comercial da Planeje. A partir de 2027, o grupo pode colocar à disposição da operação até R$ 50 milhões, ao longo de três anos, para executar novos projetos à medida que a demanda crescer e os clientes contratarem os empreendimentos. A meta inicial é dobrar o faturamento da Planeje em 2027.
Com a compra de 80% das cotas da Planeje pelos sócios da Solo Network, por meio de suas holdings, o grupo passa a atuar em diferentes etapas da construção de data centers. A estratégia é combinar a engenharia e a execução de projetos da Planeje com a capacidade industrial da Envolve Ambientes Seguros, que já tem sócios em comum com a integradora, e a experiência da Solo em tecnologia, nuvem e cibersegurança.
A aproximação entre as empresas foi precedida por uma experiência conjunta. A Planeje e a Envolve trabalharam no data center modular do Exército Brasileiro, inaugurado em 2025 após as companhias vencerem um edital. No projeto, a Envolve instalou uma sala segura modular de 112 m², com proteções contra incêndio, arrombamento, jatos d'água e impactos, além de blindagem eletromagnética.
A Planeje, por sua vez, ficou responsável pela integração dos sistemas críticos, incluindo subestações de média e baixa tensão, climatização, geradores com até 12 horas de autonomia, no-breaks e mais de mil pontos de cabeamento estruturado em fibra óptica e metálico. A estrutura atende ao 3º Centro de Telemática de Área (3º CTA), dedicado à gestão de informações críticas da defesa nacional.
A experiência evidenciou, segundo Pereira, como as duas empresas podem atuar de forma complementar. A Planeje responde pel

Principais destaques
- O preço da computação orbital: a chefe de energia dos data centers do Google alerta que instalações no espaço podem custar até 100 vezes mais do que as terrestres.
- A IA já chegou à órbita: o Google executou um modelo Gemma em uma TPU de classe data center instalada em um satélite, em um teste experimental.
- A Terra continua sendo prioridade: a empresa quer avançar em energia nuclear, geotérmica e armazenamento de longa duração antes de apostar em infraestrutura espacial em grande escala.
Construir data centers no espaço pode parecer uma solução elegante para alimentar a próxima geração de inteligência artificial. Afinal, a energia solar está disponível em abundância fora da atmosfera, e a computação orbital poderia abrir novas possibilidades para a infraestrutura digital.
Mas existe um problema que não desaparece nem quando os servidores deixam o planeta: a conta.
Amanda Peterson Corio, responsável global pela estratégia de energia dos data centers do Google, alertou que instalações espaciais podem custar até 100 vezes mais do que as construídas na Terra. A declaração, divulgada pelo The Information, expõe a distância entre a ambição tecnológica da empresa e a viabilidade econômica dessa ideia.
A observação ganha relevância porque o próprio Google está testando processadores de inteligência artificial no espaço.
🚀 O Google já colocou a IA em órbita
O alerta sobre os custos chegou poucos dias depois de a empresa divulgar um avanço experimental do Projeto Suncatcher, iniciativa que investiga a possibilidade de executar cargas de trabalho de inteligência artificial em satélites.
Em um teste divulgado em 30 de outubro, engenheiros do Google conseguiram executar um modelo Gemma em uma unidade de processamento tensorial, conhecida como TPU, instalada em um satélite construído pela Planet Labs.
O experimento demonstrou que é possível enviar instruções a um modelo de IA embarcado em uma plataforma orbital e receber uma resposta.
🛰️ O teste teve até um toque poético: os engenheiros pediram ao modelo que escrevesse um haicai sobre estar no espaço. A resposta foi recebida enquanto o satélite sobrevoava Svalbard, na Noruega.
Bola azul lá embaixo
Dados fluem em silenciosa graça
A luz das estrelas alimenta meu núcleo
O Google descreveu o resultado como a primeira resposta de IA produzida por uma TPU de classe data center em órbita.
O sistema também foi testado com limeriques e instruções para gerar relatórios sobre o estado dos sistemas da carga útil.
É um avanço técnico importante, mas ainda está muito distante de colocar um data center completo em funcionamento no espaço.

artigo.texto: A Anatel apresentou problemas de solvência para pagar as suas contas básicas o que pode impactar um dos seus projetos mais importantes, o de um data center próprio. De acordo com reportagem da Folha de S. Paulo veiculada nesta terça-feira, 3, a agência precisa de R$ 30 milhões para honrar compromissos. Desde maio deste ano, a entidade está com um contingenciamento de R$ 52 milhões por restrição orçamentária. Essa restrição afeta também outros órgãos do governo que buscam se adaptar aos cortes na máquina pública. Porém, isso gera impacto em suas operações. É o caso do centro de dados, um contrato assinado em dezembro de 2025 e que dura até 2030 por R$ 45 milhões. Esse data center é crucial para o armazenamento e acesso a dados do ecossistema de telecomunicações nacional, com informações de operadoras e usuários, por exemplo. Vale lembrar que grande parte dos dados da Anatel são abertos e podem ser acessados via painéis e outros sistemas na nuvem. Em resposta ao Mobile Time, a Anatel informou que até o momento, “as medidas adotadas têm buscado mitigar os impactos decorrentes de restrição orçamentária imposta à agência”. No entanto, o órgão regulador afirmou que “a persistência das restrições orçamentárias e financeiras poderá exigir novas medidas de reprogramação de despesas”.

artigo.texto: A migração para a inteligência artificial exige uma infraestrutura redesenhada, segundo especialistas que participaram de um painel do Roadshow Embrapii, realizado nesta terça-feira, 4, em Campinas/SP. Um dos pontos que precisam passar por mudança, segundo Gerson Freire, enterprise architect da Dell, é a estrutura de fornecimento de energia elétrica, que precisará ser dimensionada para atender à alta demanda das GPUs. De acordo com Waldir Campos, head de operação da TERRANOVA, houve uma explosão no consumo de energia pelos racks. Atualmente, cada um precisa de algo em torno de 300 Kw. Campos e Freire avaliam que o mercado enfrenta o desafio de manter esses ambientes críticos em pleno funcionamento sem interrupções no fornecimento de energia ou falhas térmicas. O executivo da Dell explicou que, no Brasil, o modelo de refrigeração mais comum é o a ar. No entanto, racks de alta densidade costumam utilizar refrigeração líquida, tecnologia que, segundo ele, tende a se tornar o padrão. Além disso, Freire considera necessário desenvolver redes especializadas para atender às demandas da IA, com altíssima capacidade de transmissão de dados (throughput) e latência mínima. Além dos desafios de infraestrutura, há outro obstáculo: a mão de obra. Para Campos, a escassez de profissionais qualificados pode dificultar a expansão dos data centers na América Latina. Nesse contexto, parcerias com instituições de ensino locais podem ser uma alternativa, já que muitas instalações estão situadas em regiões do interior dos países. “De forma geral, precisamos planejar a infraestrutura de IA como um projeto integrado, que deve entregar resultado”, afirmou Freire.

artigo.texto: FT: Nvidia orienta clientes de centros de dados a reduzir exposição à China Nos últimos meses, a maior fabricante de chips do mundo informou a clientes de serviços de computação em nuvem que eles deverão destinar pelo menos 51% de seus serviços a empresas de fora da China, segundo cinco fontes a par do assunto. Até então, não havia restrições desse tipo Atualizado A Nvidia está orientando seus parceiros de centros de dados a reduzir sua exposição a clientes chineses, em uma medida que restringe ainda mais a capacidade da China de acompanhar seus concorrentes americanos, em meio à intensificação da disputa entre as duas superpotências mundiais em inteligência artificial. Nos últimos meses, a maior fabricante de chips do mundo informou a clientes de serviços de computação em nuvem que eles deverão destinar pelo menos 51% de seus serviços a empresas de fora da China, segundo cinco fontes a par do assunto. Até então, não havia restrições desse tipo. As instruções foram transmitidas verbalmente e implementadas pelas equipes de vendas e pelos representantes regionais da Nvidia, em vez de serem formalizadas em documentos, segundo as fontes. A medida representa uma nova ameaça às ambições das empresas chinesas de tecnologia no campo da IA, num momento em que Washington tenta restringir ainda mais o acesso dessas empresas a chips americanos avançados por meio de contratos de serviços de computação em nuvem no exterior. Muitos grupos chineses já recorreram a esse tipo de locação para realizar tarefas avançadas de IA, inclusive o treinamento de modelos. Regras para novos contratos As novas regras de conformidade se aplicam aos clientes da Nvidia em todo o mundo, e não apenas aos centros de dados na Ásia, disseram duas das fontes. As exigências, porém, afetam apenas novos contratos, não os acordos de locação já existentes. A Nvidia disse: “Os centros de dados e serviços de computação em nuvem construídos com chips americanos são a base de que os desenvolvedores americanos de modelos e aplicativos precisam para competir em escala global. A política de longa data dos EUA incentiva todos os provedores de serviços em nuvem a utilizar infraestrutura americana e conquistar clientes onde quer que possam. Essa política sempre apoiou a expansão da infraestrutura americana em todo o mundo, trazendo prosperidade, influência e empregos de volta ao país”. A Nvidia implementou a nova exigência no terceiro trimestre, em uma tentativa preventiva de reduzir as críticas que costuma receber de parlamentares americanos e de outros que não gostam de sua postura em relação à China, segundo disseram duas fontes. Os EUA estão tentando reprimir tanto os intermediários que ajudaram a criar um próspero mercado clandestino de chips da Nvidia na China, como o acesso de empresas chinesas a chips avançados no exterior, por meio de contratos de locação firmados fora do país. Os provedores de serviços de computação em nuvem estão tendo dificuldades para cumprir as novas exigências porque “é difícil encontrar clientes não chineses em número suficiente fora dos EUA”, segundo disse um grupo sediado em Cingapura. “Se forem aplicadas rigorosamente, as regras certamente prejudicarão os negócios.” As medidas restritivas adotadas pela Nvidia também vêm agravando a escassez de capacidade computacional avançada para as empresas chinesas de tecnologia. Escassez Um conjunto de chips B300 da Nvidia, que no mercado internacional é vendido a cerca de US$ 600 mil, foi negociado na China, no mês passado, a 18,5 milhões de yuans (US$ 2,8 milhões) devido à sua escassez, segundo diz uma fonte com conhecimento direto da transação. O B300, cuja venda na China é proibida pelas restrições americanas à exportação, é um dos produtos mais avançados da Nvidia e é utilizado por importantes empresas americanas de inteligência artificial, como Anthropic e OpenAI. A Nvidia já reduziu em mais da metade o número de clientes asiáticos autorizados a comprar seus chips de IA, após estabelecer, este ano, uma “lista branca” de empresas que passaram por verificações mais rigorosas – medidas destinadas a impedir que os produtos cheguem à China. Isso resultou em uma diminuição na entrada de chips avançados da Nvidia na China via contrabando, forçando grupos de tecnologia chineses a buscar contratos de locação com provedores de computação em nuvem sediados no exterior. Os EUA e a China são, de longe, as duas maiores fontes de demanda por poder computacional, enquanto os grupos chineses de tecnologia têm sido os maiores clientes de centros de dados em mercados como o do Sudeste Asiático. A decisão da Nvidia também levou centros de dados de fora dos EUA a buscarem, com urgência, clientes que não sejam chineses. Caso não consigam, essas instalações poderão ser forçadas a reduzir a escala de suas operações. As ações da Nvidia caíram mais de 13% no último mês, mas ainda acumulam uma valorização de 7% no ano. Com a queda recente da ação, o grupo liderado por Jensen Huang foi superado pela Apple, que assumiu o posto de companhia de capital aberta mais valiosa do mundo.(Tradução de Mario Zamarian)

artigo.texto: WEST RICHLAND, Wash. - The City of West Richland said Monday that Amazon purchased land within the city and is looking to develop a data center campus. The land is in the Lewis and Clark Ranch area north of Ruppert Road and was originally bought by data center developer Trammel Crow. As of now, the City has yet to approve development of a data center according to its website. No development applications have been submitted so far. Amazon estimated a three-building phase would add 120 to 150 full-time jobs and bring in millions of dollars in local taxes. Amazon will host a community open house on Nov. 19 at Enterprise Middle School from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. where they say subject matter experts will be available. The City says more information will be available soon. Previous city council meetings on the initial sale to Trammel Crow featured dozens of speakers that brought common concerns with data centers like environmental damage, utility prices, noise pollution and more. An Amazon spokesperson provided the following statement: “Amazon is hosting an Open House on November 19th to share more about our proposed plans in West Richland. When we consider investing in a community, we think residents deserve a chance to learn what we're doing and ask our team questions directly. Think of it like a science fair—residents can visit different booths and talk to our experts about the topics people care about most, like water, energy, sound, jobs, and the environment. Washington has been our home for over 30 years, so we’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area.”

artigo.texto: The federal government has announced $6.77 million in funding for Melbourne-based Clutch Industries to help manufacture batteries that can be used at home or taken on the road. Melbourne-based Clutch Industries will use the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) funding to design, construct and commission a scalable manufacturing line in Coburg North, Victoria, supporting Australian capability in an emerging battery technology. The $19.35 million project is expected to create at least 16 ongoing skilled jobs and strengthen Australia’s battery manufacturing capability. The new facility will incorporate automated assembly, testing, quality assurance and traceable supply chains, helping to establish advanced manufacturing capability in Australia. The project will focus on Clutch Industries’ PowerNet – a 20-kilogram portable 4kWh battery pack that can operate independently or be combined with multiple units to create a home battery system. Units can also be detached and used as portable power sources. “We don’t want Australia to simply export the raw materials needed for the industries of the future. We want to build more things here, create more skilled jobs here and capture more of the economic opportunities created by the global energy transition,” Minister for Industry and Innovation and Minister for Science Tim Ayres said. “Australia has a growing demand for home batteries and off-grid power solutions. This project can demonstrate how the next generation of modular battery technology can meet this requirement. “This investment will help grow Australian manufacturing capability, support skilled jobs in Victoria and strengthen our ability to produce advanced battery technologies here in Australia.” The project will also test the batteries’ safety and performance across different uses, helping refine the product and meet the requirements needed to bring it to a wider market. “Batteries are critical to Australia’s energy future, and we want to see more of this technology designed, manufactured and developed here at home,” member for Wills Peter Khalil said. “By supporting Clutch Industries to establish a scalable manufacturing line right here in Coburg North, we’re backing local industry, creating opportunities for skilled Australian workers and building our advanced manufacturing capability. “It’s great to hear this $19.35 million project is expected to create at least 16 ongoing skilled jobs, which demonstrates how Australian innovation can translate into real economic opportunities.” Want to see more stories from trusted news sources? artigo.texto: Rule requires 600 large companies to report emissions Finance Ministry sets rules and timetable for phased implementation Atualizado 03/11/2026 The Finance Ministry issued an ordinance Thursday (29) defining the industries covered by Brazil’s regulated carbon market. The measure identifies the sectors subject to greenhouse-gas emissions monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) requirements and establishes a timetable for phased implementation. The rules will begin applying in 2027 to companies emitting more than 10,000 tonnes annually. The Special Secretariat for the Carbon Market estimates that fewer than 600 large companies will have to begin reporting emissions, meaning they must provide precise information on how much carbon dioxide they release. The government aims to build an official database before Brazil’s regulated carbon market begins operating in 2030. The final text differs from the proposal submitted for public consultation on July 28 after several industries requested changes to the allocation of activities among the three implementation stages. In an interview with Valor, Special Secretary for the Carbon Market Cristina Reis described the public consultation outcome as positive. The plan retains 17 sectors, without adding any new ones, but redistributes some activities among the timetable’s stages. Reis argued that retaining the scope validates the federal government’s original proposal. The decision to move some industries into the first phase demonstrates that “the sectors already consider themselves mature and prepared and understand the value of regulation,” she noted. Under the regulated market, greenhouse-gas emissions will be measured, reported, and limited by law. Companies emitting more than 10,000 tonnes a year will be required to monitor and report their emissions. Those emitting more than 25,000 tonnes annually will be subject to emissions caps. The policy seeks to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and encourage the development of low-carbon technologies. The overall emissions cap and rules for distributing Brazilian Emission Allowances (CBEs) are scheduled for 2030, when the National Allocation Plan (PNA) begins. The ordinance does not require immediate report submission, establish emissions caps, or impose costs on companies. Until the PNA takes effect, the Finance Ministry recommends monitoring regulatory developments. Deputy Secretary José Pedro Bastos Neves believes the regulations could also create opportunities for Brazilian decarbonization solutions. The initiative offers a chance to promote technologies and decarbonization pathways developed in Brazil, he observed. The first MRV stage begins in 2027 and covers aluminum, iron, and steel production at integrated mills; cement; oil and natural-gas exploration and production; pulp and paper; glass; selected chemical-industry activities; and iron-ore and bauxite mining. Compared with the preliminary proposal, glass, iron-ore and bauxite mining, and some chemical-industry activities were moved forward to the initial stage. Oil refining and air transportation were removed from this phase. The second stage, scheduled to begin by 2029, will cover ceramics, iron and steel production at semi-integrated mills, chemical-industry activities not included in the first stage, food and beverage manufacturing, mining of other mineral resources, oil refining, and the electric-power sector. Recycled aluminum, glass, solid waste, and sewage treatment are no longer included in the second phase. The third stage remains scheduled for 2031 and includes road, rail, and water transportation, unchanged from the original proposal. Each stage provides a four-year preparation and adjustment period before the data is consolidated. During the first year, companies must prepare a monitoring plan and submit it to the governing body of the Brazilian Emissions Trading System (SBCE) for approval. Effective monitoring begins in the second and third years, when companies measure and collect data on greenhouse-gas emissions and removals. In the fourth year, they will consolidate the data and submit an emissions report under the PNA. According to Reis, removing solid-waste and sewage-treatment activities from the general timetable reflects the understanding that the law itself exempts activities proven to have sustainable-production attributes from direct obligations. “To encourage decarbonization—and here we are talking mainly about methane emissions from the waste sector—the best approach is for these activities to operate in the voluntary market by generating carbon credits,” she explained. Reis added that the mechanism could also help expand waste treatment and encourage the elimination of open-air dumps. The Finance Ministry also granted an aviation-industry request to align its MRV timetable. “Instead of placing air transportation in stage one, we determined that the requirement will take effect when ProBioQAV, a program focused on the sustainable aviation fuel market, is regulated,” she summarized. Taciana Stec, an expert at the Talanoa Institute, considers the change to the first-stage timetable positive. She cautioned, however, that it remains unclear how forest carbon credits will be integrated into the regulated market. Marta Salomon, a senior expert at Talanoa, argued that once emissions caps take effect, the system will begin fulfilling its goal of reducing emissions from carbon-intensive industries. artigo.texto: Emet e B.Real captam R$ 120 mi no exterior para fundo de data centers no Brasil Expectativa é levantar outros R$ 100 milhões até o primeiro trimestre de 2027 para ampliar os investimentos A Emet Capital e a B.Real Capital anunciaram nesta terça-feira (3) a captação de R$ 120 milhões junto a investidores estrangeiros para o Data Brasil Infra FIP, fundo de investimento em participações voltado ao desenvolvimento de terrenos com infraestrutura de energia para instalação de data centers. O veículo tem uma carteira de nove projetos e prevê investimentos de R$ 2,5 bilhões nos próximos três anos. A expectativa é levantar outros R$ 100 milhões até o primeiro trimestre de 2027 para ampliar os investimentos. A iniciativa busca aproveitar o crescimento da demanda por infraestrutura de processamento de dados, impulsionada pela expansão da inteligência artificial e dos serviços de computação em nuvem. Os projetos estão distribuídos por São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, Centro-Oeste e Nordeste, com capacidade energética projetada de 3,5 gigawatts (GW). A estratégia consiste em desenvolver terrenos com acesso à rede elétrica de alta potência, licenciamento e infraestrutura necessária para receber os centros de processamento de dados. Os imóveis poderão ser alugados por contratos de longo prazo ou vendidos a operadores de data centers e empresas de tecnologia. “A grande chave de valor e oportunidade no mercado de data centers hoje está na infraestrutura de energia e na localização do terreno”, afirma Raffael Faustino, diretor da Emet Capital. Segundo ele, a construção de uma subestação elétrica ou a obtenção de autorizações para conexão à rede pode levar mais de dois anos, tornando os terrenos com disponibilidade de energia um ativo estratégico para o setor. Alison Takano, CEO da B.Real Capital, explica que o FIP antecipará etapas críticas de desenvolvimento, licenciamento, estruturação regulatória e conexão elétrica. O fundo tem administração fiduciária da Horizon Trust e já destinou os R$ 120 milhões captados à carteira de projetos em desenvolvimento, segundo as gestoras.

artigo.texto: OCP 2026: Cooler Master Scales Liquid Cooling from Cold Plates to 2.5 MW CDUs Key Highlights - Cooler Master's new 2.5 MW in-row CDU separates facility water from the IT coolant loop, with centralized management supporting up to 32 interconnected units. - The 300 kW air-assisted liquid cooling system targets facilities without dedicated water infrastructure, featuring modular radiator racks and hot-swappable components. - The portfolio extends liquid cooling beyond CPUs and GPUs to optical modules, networking hardware, and other rack-level components. - Specialized filling, flushing, and leak-testing tools support liquid cooling deployment and maintenance, while factory equipment handles cold-plate drying and validation. - Manufacturing operations in China and expanding production capacity in Vietnam support Cooler Master's growing portfolio of data center cooling equipment. Cooler Master used the OCP Global Summit 2026 to introduce a 2.5-megawatt coolant distribution unit (CDU), extending a growing portfolio of liquid cooling technologies aimed at the increasingly demanding thermal requirements of AI infrastructure. The new 2,500 kW liquid-to-liquid in-row CDU anchors a product lineup that now spans facility-level heat transfer, rack-level coolant distribution, direct-to-chip cold plates, manifolds, and the specialized equipment needed to fill, test, and commission liquid cooling systems. For a company long associated with PC cooling and enthusiast hardware, the breadth of the offering reflects a substantial evolution. Cooler Master began developing data center products for hyperscale customers in 2018, building on its experience with liquid cooling in consumer and server markets. Its own branded data center infrastructure products have emerged more recently. During a guided showroom tour conducted in conjunction with OCP 2026, Data Center Frontier examined an assortment of the company's cooling systems, including modular liquid-to-air CDUs designed for existing data centers, rack-level cooling hardware, and equipment intended to streamline manufacturing and deployment. The most revealing aspect of the tour was the attention given to the practical requirements of operating liquid-cooled infrastructure. Alongside increasing thermal capacity, Cooler Master is emphasizing modular equipment, replaceable components, redundant systems, and the processes needed to prepare liquid cooling loops for service. The resulting product strategy addresses two distinct challenges facing data center operators: scaling liquid cooling for new AI deployments while finding ways to accommodate increasingly dense computing systems in facilities originally designed around air cooling. That integrated approach reflects the shift from scaling to coordination identified in DCF's OCP 2026 reporting, as computing, power, cooling, and operations become increasingly interdependent. A 2.5 MW CDU Anchors the Portfolio At the upper end of the lineup, Cooler Master's 2.5 MW liquid-to-liquid in-row CDU is designed to manage heat loads approaching 2,500 kW through a heat exchanger that separates facility water from the secondary coolant loop serving IT equipment. The system is rated for a 4–5°C approach temperature difference at its advertised cooling capacity. Its architecture incorporates redundant pumping, fluid monitoring, and centralized management intended to support deployments involving multiple cooling units. Cooler Master says the management architecture can coordinate as many as 32 interconnected CDUs, allowing operators to monitor and manage coolant distribution across larger installations. The system also incorporates remote management capabilities, including support for standard data center communications protocols. Mass production was targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. The significance of the new platform lies partly in its scale. As AI infrastructure moves toward increasingly dense rack-level configurations, CDU capacity has become a critical consideration in the design of liquid cooling distribution systems. Larger cooling units can serve multiple racks or computing clusters, but their integration also places greater demands on pumping capacity, filtration, monitoring, redundancy, and facility piping. Cooler Master's approach extends beyond simply increasing the size of the heat exchanger. Its product strategy encompasses the supporting equipment needed to move coolant reliably through the system and maintain operating conditions as thermal loads change. The company also offers smaller liquid-to-liquid CDU configurations, including in-rack equipment for applications that do not require a multi-megawatt installation. In its OCP announcement, Cooler Master CEO Thomas Chen emphasized deployment flexibility as a priority, particularly for customers balancing new construction with the need to expand AI capacity inside existing facilities. That distinction becomes especially relevant in the company's liquid-to-air product lineup. Modular Air-Assisted Cooling Targets Existing Data Centers One of the most instructive systems examined during the tour was Cooler Master's 300 kW Air-Assisted Liquid Cooling (AALC) CDU, a modular liquid-to-air design intended for data centers without an existing facility water distribution system. Rather than transferring server heat into a building's chilled-water or facility-water loop, the AALC system circulates coolant through the IT equipment and rejects the captured heat through fan-driven radiators. The distinction matters for operators seeking to introduce liquid-cooled AI racks into facilities that were not built with dedicated liquid cooling infrastructure. Although air-assisted systems still require sufficient facility airflow and heat rejection capacity, they offer an alternative to extending a new water distribution network throughout the data hall. In September alone, installations hit 145.1 GWh, a record monthly high, up 15.8% YoY. Amid continued global market expansion, the competitive landscape of the power battery industry is undergoing sharp differentiation, with Chinese battery makers continuing to gain ground while Japanese and South Korean giants are collectively under pressure.

artigo.texto: It’s been a big year for anti-data center activism in North Carolina. WFDD’s April Laissle has had a front-row seat, attending packed public meetings across the Piedmont and listening to hours of testimony from concerned residents. With Election Day imminent, she wanted to know: how is the debate carrying over to the midterms? For this week’s Carolina Curious, we brought the question to Western Carolina University political science professor Chris Cooper. Interview Highlights On the debate becoming a major campaign issue: “I think we could have predicted that the economy would matter. We could have predicted that prices and affordability and all that would matter. Healthcare, sure, but I think the data centers issue is really the one new one that seems to be defining this election season.” On politicians following the public's lead: “It's very clear that candidates want to make known their stance on data centers, their stance that they are against data centers, or at least for more restrictions on data centers. So I think this is definitely a case where the leaders are following the people. Some folks in office, particularly some Republicans, might have seen this as economic development just six months ago, but now the way public opinion has changed, they are a bit on their heels.” On the role the issue could play in future elections: “I expect this cycle the data center issue is going to probably be the number one issue for some of these municipal off-year elections coming up in 2027. So after this election, don't feel like we're done with this issue for two more years."
