artigo.texto: Crea-PE promove debate sobre consumo de energia por inteligência artificial e data centers O encontro será realizado das 14h30 às 18h, no auditório da Federação das Indústrias do Estado de Pernambuco (Fiepe), no bairro de Santo Amaro Clique aqui e escute a matéria O avanço da inteligência artificial (IA) e a expansão dos data centers têm ampliado a demanda por energia elétrica e levantado discussões sobre a capacidade de abastecimento e a sustentabilidade do setor. Para debater os desafios e as perspectivas da matriz energética, o Conselho Regional de Engenharia e Agronomia de Pernambuco (Crea-PE) realiza, na próxima terça-feira (10), o seminário “Perspectivas da Energia Elétrica para o Nordeste e o Brasil”. O encontro será realizado das 14h30 às 18h, no auditório da Federação das Indústrias do Estado de Pernambuco (Fiepe), no bairro de Santo Amaro, no Recife. A programação é gratuita e aberta ao público, mediante inscrição prévia pela internet. O Nordeste se destaca na produção de energia eólica e solar no Brasil, mas o crescimento do consumo exige investimentos em infraestrutura para garantir o fornecimento contínuo de eletricidade. Entre os principais desafios estão a capacidade de armazenamento, a ampliação das linhas de transmissão e a instalação de subestações. Segundo projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), a demanda por energia dos data centers no Brasil deve crescer, em média, 13,7% ao ano até 2036. Essas estruturas funcionam continuamente e consomem grandes volumes de eletricidade para manter o processamento e o armazenamento de dados. “O Crea-PE, através do Comitê Tecnológico Permanente, será o catalisador deste debate. Nossa contribuição apontará soluções técnicas viáveis para assegurar a segurança energética necessária para o desenvolvimento do País”, afirma o presidente do conselho, Adriano Lucena. De acordo com o coordenador técnico do seminário, José Carlos Miranda, o encontro pretende discutir a evolução do setor elétrico e apresentar alternativas para garantir o abastecimento de forma segura e sustentável. Programação do seminário A programação será dividida em quatro palestras, com especialistas do setor elétrico e ambiental. Os temas abordados serão: - “Evolução da Matriz de Energia Elétrica do Brasil e do Nordeste” – com o engenheiro eletricista e ex-secretário de Planejamento e Desenvolvimento Energético do Ministério de Minas e Energia, Altino Ventura Filho; - “Oportunidades e Riscos das Fontes Renováveis no Nordeste e em Pernambuco” – com o presidente da Associação Nacional de Entidades Representativas de Energias Renováveis, Rudinei Miranda; - “Desafios da Energia de Pernambuco para Atender as Demandas Crescentes” – com o engenheiro civil e presidente do Sindicato das Indústrias de Energia e de Serviços do Setor Elétrico de Pernambuco (Sindienergia-PE), Bruno Câmara; - “Riscos Ambientais dos Novos Grandes Consumidores das Fontes Renováveis” – com o engenheiro eletricista Ricardo Furtado, ex-superintendente de Meio Ambiente da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) e da Companhia Hidro Elétrica do São Francisco (Chesf). O último tema vai abordar os impactos ambientais relacionados à instalação de grandes consumidores de energia, como os data centers, cuja expansão acompanha o desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial e de outras tecnologias digitais. Debates e participação do público A mediação será conduzida pelo engenheiro eletricista José Carlos Miranda, integrante do Comitê Tecnológico Permanente (CTP) do Crea-PE. Após as palestras, haverá um debate com a participação da engenheira ambiental Emmanoelle Lira e do engenheiro eletricista João Bosco de Almeida, também integrantes do comitê. O público presente poderá participar da discussão e apresentar questionamentos aos especialistas. artigo.texto: All politics is local, as the adage goes. In Arkansas, this year’s midterm campaigns are revealing that data center politics is primarily local too. The concern over data centers has prompted a local backlash in Arkansas, with several communities enacting measures to block their construction or impose new restrictions. But unlike in states like Ohio and Texas where data centers have become one of the leading issues in the midterm election, the political fallout in Arkansas hasn’t been as prominent in top races for governor, Congress or the Legislature. Data centers and artificial intelligence have mostly come up in local races. The lack of campaign resources for Democrats has likely played a role, said Jay Barth, a professor emeritus of politics at Hendrix College. “It is interesting that there has not been more engagement on that issue,” Barth said. “I think that is an issue that I think would have probably popped up more assertively if there had been more expansive campaigns.” Data center construction has accelerated amid a race by major technology companies to develop AI models and products. That data center blitz has run into local worries about energy and water use, and suspicions about the promises of large numbers of jobs or tax revenue for local schools. That’s not to say that opposition to the data centers has lessened. Polling of likely voters in the 2nd Congressional District conducted by Talk Business & Politics and Hendrix College in August found that more than half of Arkansans are strongly opposed to a data center being built in their community, with nearly 19% somewhat opposed. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. The sentiment in Arkansas has largely mirrored national trends, said Robert Coon, a strategist and consultant for Republican campaigns. When data centers come up on the campaign trail, Democrats have mostly been on the attack — though opposition to data centers is bipartisan. Democratic challenger Hallie Shoffner has gone after Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton on the topic, and said she wants to be on the Senate Energy Committee in response to the concerns about data centers. Shoffner’s campaign stops have included Clarksville, where a $6.6 billion data center project is under construction. It’s also come up in at least one race for the state legislature. Former Republican Rep. Debra Hobbs, who is running to represent Clarksville as an independent, has taken aim at data centers too — as well as her opponent’s support of tax incentives for building the projects. Incumbent Republican Rep. Aaron Pilkington of Knoxville is a prominent supporter of the data centers, becoming the executive director of the Arkansas Connected Communities Association, a pro-data center and pro-AI advocacy nonprofit, earlier this year. Data centers have resonated more at the local level. Former circuit and appeals court Judge Wendell Griffen, the Democratic nominee for Pulaski County’s top executive office, spearheaded a monthslong fight to pass land-use regulations for the centers in unincorporated Pulaski County. The regulations were spurred by community anger over a planned data center. In Conway, residents have been pushing for the ouster of some city council members in part due to anger over a data center proposal in the area. Griffen was a regular presence at quorum court meetings, speaking forcefully and at length during public comment about his belief that the regulations were necessary. His Facebook posts on the topic were equally detailed. At one point, Griffen posted on Facebook an “independent transparent analysis” of the proposed regulations that he said was generated by ChatGPT, an AI model — the development of which by companies like Google, Anthropic and OpenAI is a primary driver of the rapid data center buildout nationwide. “Judge Griffen did a good job of becoming an advocate for (regulations) in a very visible way, and that kind of elevated the issue in the midst of that campaign,” said Barth. But overall, data centers aren’t having the campaign impact here that they’re having in states like Ohio and Texas, he added. Griffen’s opponent, Republican Michael Rushin, said he was neither “for nor against” data centers “as a category” when weighing in on the debate recently. He took issue with the regulations authored by Griffen because he believed it would get the county sued — which happened two days after the quorum court overrode the current county judge’s veto on them. Other AI-related issues have also been playing out at the local level, sometimes in unusual ways. In the Little Rock mayor’s race, City Director B.J. Wyrick appeared to make Flock cameras an issue in her bid to unseat incumbent Frank Scott. A 40-second video Wyrick posted on social media depicts floating eyeballs as a parody of the Rockwell song “Somebody’s Watching Me” plays and refers to thousands of Little Rock cameras. According to the Little Rock Police Department’s Flock transparency portal, it operates 114 Flock cameras. Coon said candidates who support the centers likely aren’t bringing them up on the campaign trail. When the centers do come up, he said, it’s likely not the facilities themselves that move the needle. “I think that, from a messaging standpoint, I think it’s probably easier for people to leverage impacts rather than just saying, you know, a candidate is pro-data center versus anti-data center,” Coon said. He pointed to Cotton’s proposed DATA Act, which would make it easier for data centers to produce their own electricity, as an example. “I think Sen. Cotton in particular has a really interesting proposal that he’s put out, which probably has helped insulate him from some criticism over data centers,” Coon said. “For someone who likes the idea of data centers, you’re taking away a large chunk of controversy when you’re talking about, ‘Why can’t data centers bring their own power to the grid,’ right?” Republican Gov. artigo.texto: We hear almost constantly about the downsides of data centers, but there are those encouraging Americans to look into the benefits that they can offer to the communities that wind up playing host to them. In a recent op-ed for Fox News, Chris Johnson with the American Energy Leadership Institute pointed out that in a number of communities—namely, towns like Ellendale, North Dakota—small, struggling municipalities are getting a much-needed boost from the data centers. One such example is Richland Parish, Louisiana, which saw massive investment from Meta. “Places like this in Louisiana, where a data center comes in from Meta, and then each of the teachers there gets an individual $50,000 bonus,” he said. He pointed out that nothing other than the investment from Meta in the community changed. Johnson went on to point out that there are plenty of benefits to the job market on top of that. He pointed out that: “All the construction jobs, the facilities and industries that are providing the facilities for these developments—all of these are high-paying jobs.” Of course, that hasn’t led to an overnight surge in support for data centers. As a recent U of H poll shows, concerns remain high, and voters want the data centers to pay their own way. Johnson says that’s something data centers appear to be largely on board with. According to him: “Now they’re going even a step further and saying, ‘We’ll pay even more than our fair share for this electricity, so that we can ensure that the benefits are felt by the ratepayers, and not the cost.’”

artigo.texto: Dongwha Electrolyte joins $95 mil. next-generation battery research initiative Dongwha Electrolyte is joining a major national research initiative to develop sodium-ion batteries, as Korea seeks to advance alternatives to lithium-based energy storage and strengthen its position in the next generation of battery technology. The company, an affiliate of Dongwha Enterprise, said Tuesday that it would participate in the Market-Leading Next-Generation Secondary Battery Innovation Strategic Research Group, known as K-BIC, under the government's Global TOP Strategic Research Group support program. The initiative has a total budget of 130 billion won ($95 million) and brings together major players from industry, academia, research institutions and government to overcome technical barriers, secure foundational technologies and build a collaborative research platform. Dongwha Electrolyte is currently the only electrolyte manufacturer among the participating institutions, according to the company. The company will join the second phase of a project aimed at developing low-cost, long-life, nonlithium secondary batteries, targeting sodium-ion technology with production costs below $50 per kilowatt-hour. Research will expand beyond materials development to include battery cell development, commercial-scale manufacturing processes and safety verification, with an emphasis on practical demonstration. Dongwha Electrolyte will focus on manufacturing and supplying standard electrolytes, identifying their critical quality characteristics and establishing quality standards. The research project is led by the Korea Institute of Energy Research. "By joining K-BIC, we will be able to secure sodium-ion battery materials technology ahead of market demand, reflecting the needs of the energy storage system industry, while establishing a market-oriented demonstration research framework," Dongwha Electrolyte co-CEO Kim Jong-hoon said. He added, "By expanding our next-generation portfolio in preparation for future markets, we will further strengthen the business foundation of Dongwha Electrolyte." The initiative is overseen by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National Research Council of Science and Technology, with the Korea Research Institute of Chemical Technology coordinating the overall battery research program. This article was published with the assistance of generative AI and edited by The Korea Times.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de cabos de baixa tensão: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de cabos de baixa tensão até 2035: crescimento impulsionado por energias renováveis e expansão de data centers Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Cabos de Baixa Tensão, o setor inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de cabos de baixa tensão é um segmento fundamental da cadeia de valor da infraestrutura elétrica, abrangendo cabos isolados de potência, controle, instrumentação, comunicação e especiais com tensão de até 1 kV. Em 2025, o mercado se caracteriza pela demanda estável da construção civil, da automação industrial, das instalações de energia renovável e da infraestrutura digital. O período de previsão 2026-2035 aponta para uma expansão sustentada, com o valor global de mercado projetado para crescer a uma CAGR de 5,2%, alcançando um índice de mercado IndexBox de 166 até 2035 (2025=100). O crescimento é sustentado pela aceleração da eletrificação, pela urbanização nas economias emergentes e pela transição para sistemas energéticos de baixo carbono. No entanto, a volatilidade dos preços do cobre e do alumínio, somada ao endurecimento das regulamentações ambientais sobre isolamentos poliméricos, representa obstáculos. O cenário competitivo é moderadamente fragmentado, com os principais fabricantes investindo em expansão de capacidade e inovação em produtos sustentáveis. Este relatório oferece uma perspectiva baseada em dados sobre tamanho de mercado, segmentação, dinâmica regional e as principais tendências que moldam o setor até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado global de cabos de baixa tensão projeta uma CAGR de 5,2% entre 2026 e 2035, com o valor de mercado subindo de cerca de US$ 95 bilhões em 2025 para aproximadamente US$ 158 bilhões até 2035. Espera-se um crescimento robusto em volume, impulsionado pelos gastos em infraestrutura e pela eletrificação industrial. O índice de mercado deve chegar a 166 até 2035 (2025=100). A Ásia-Pacífico continuará sendo a maior e mais dinâmica região, apoiada por projetos de construção e de energia renovável na China, na Índia e no Sudeste Asiático. América do Norte e Europa terão crescimento moderado, com a demanda cada vez mais moldada pela modernização das redes e pela expansão dos data centers. A América Latina e o Oriente Médio e África oferecem potencial ainda inexplorado, mas enfrentam desafios econômicos e regulatórios. As principais premissas incluem crescimento estável do PIB global, manutenção do apoio político às energias renováveis e ausência de grandes rupturas nas cadeias de suprimentos. Entre os riscos de baixa estão uma desaceleração na China mais acentuada do que o esperado e a volatilidade prolongada dos preços das matérias-primas. Vetores e restrições da demanda Principais vetores de demanda - Expansão acelerada da capacidade de energia renovável, sobretudo solar e eólica, que exige ampla cablagem de baixa tensão para coleta e distribuição - Aumento da construção e modernização de data centers para sustentar computação em nuvem e IA, impulsionando a demanda por cabos de comunicação e de energia de alta velocidade - Urbanização e desenvolvimento de infraestrutura em escala global, especialmente nas economias emergentes, elevando o consumo de fiação predial e de cabos para máquinas industriais - Eletrificação dos transportes, incluindo infraestrutura de recarga de veículos elétricos e modernização ferroviária, criando nova demanda por cabos de baixa tensão especializados - Modernização das redes e iniciativas de redes inteligentes, que exigem a substituição de cabos envelhecidos e a instalação de cabos avançados de controle e instrumentação - Automação industrial e adoção da Indústria 4.0, ampliando a necessidade de cabos de controle e instrumentação nas plantas fabris Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - Volatilidade dos preços do cobre e do alumínio, que afeta diretamente os custos de produção de cabos e as margens dos fabricantes - Endurecimento das regulamentações ambientais sobre materiais de isolamento poliméricos, exigindo reformulações dispendiosas e adequação às normas - Desaceleração da atividade de construção nas principais economias devido a juros altos e incerteza econômica - Concorrência intensa de fabricantes regionais de baixo custo, sobretudo na Ásia, pressionando os preços para baixo - Rupturas nas cadeias de suprimentos e desafios logísticos que afetam a disponibilidade de matérias-primas e os prazos de entrega Estrutura da demanda por indústria de uso final Fiação predial (participação estimada: 32%) A fiação predial é o maior segmento de uso final dos cabos de baixa tensão, abrangendo distribuição de energia, iluminação e cabeamento de comunicação em edificações residenciais, comerciais e institucionais. A demanda está intimamente ligada à atividade de construção, com novos projetos residenciais e comerciais impulsionando o volume. Nos mercados desenvolvidos, as reformas e retrofits ganham importância crescente, sobretudo para ganhos de eficiência energética e instalações de prédios inteligentes. Até 2035, o segmento se beneficiará da rápida urbanização na Ásia-Pacífico e na África, onde os déficits de infraestrutura habitacional e comercial são substanciais. No entanto, o crescimento nos mercados maduros será moderado, compensado pela migração para cabos de maior valor agregado, resistentes ao fogo e sustentáveis. artigo.texto: HUBBARD - Voters in the City of Hubbard passed the first city wide ban of data centers. The ordinances passed 76% to 23% by Hubbard voters. Those results were clear from the beginning of votes being counted. “I’m not surprised. I mean based on social media and people I've talked to around town, I'm not surprised that it passed. Good. I mean, people put a lot of work into that, and they got what they deserved,” said Mike Mogg, Hubbard City Council President. As the results came in, the Hubbard committee against data centers celebrated, saying it puts the power into their hands. “Thank you Hubbard City thank you,” said Katie Costello, data center petition organizer. “The ability to use the democracy as it was meant to be used. It's something that I wouldn't have believed until I went through it, and I think everybody on this committee feels that way. It's an incredible moment to be able to say we were able to change this.” “We now have the power to say no. Let's put the brakes on. Let's wait to see if you know if environmental changes, if technology changes, make something like this possible in the future. Then we can reconsider it,” said Jenny Goldberg, data center petition organizer. The ban stops any size data center project from coming into city limits. While happy the people's voices were heard, council president Mike Mogg said he wishes the ban did not include smaller facilities. His next steps are to put the city's data center committee on hold and talk to the community. “Until we talk with the public and see what their feelings are, if they want us to proceed and see if we can get the public to work with us to regulate data centers so that we can alter this, and we'd be happy to work with them do it. But our next steps are the law director will drop the the ordinance to ban the data centers. It'll come before council, and council will approve it,” said Mogg. Mayor Ben Kyle told 21 News voters made a clear decision and the administration will respect it. Moving forward, Kyles said the city will continue to look at regulations that protect the community and residents. The data center ban can be reversed with another vote. Ohio voters decided on 20 other data center issues, more than any other state in the nation. They voted on bans, certain regulations and zoning changes.

artigo.texto: Workshop debate proposta sobre rateio de custos da reserva de capacidade com baterias Evento virtual reunirá representantes da ANEEL, EPE, ONS e CCEE para discutir proposta que define a forma de custeio e divisão do encargo associado à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL) realizará, nesta quinta-feira (5/11), das 9h às 12h, workshop para discutir temas relacionados à Consulta Pública nº 37/2026, que busca obter subsídios para o aprimoramento da proposta que disciplina a base de custeio e a metodologia de rateio do Encargo de Potência para Reserva de Capacidade (ERCAP) associado à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. O encontro será realizado de forma virtual, por meio da plataforma Microsoft Teams. Os interessados deverão se inscrever neste formulário para acompanhar as apresentações e os debates por meio da sala virtual do evento. A programação contará com a participação de representantes da ANEEL, da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) e da Câmara de Comercialização de Energia (CCEE). Durante o workshop, serão apresentados aspectos relacionados às propostas da ANEEL e do ONS, à adesão ao Contrato de Uso de Potência para Reserva de Capacidade (COPCAP), ao mecanismo de repasse do ERCAP a contratos regulados e à discussão de metodologias de aferição de flexibilidade operativa, com espaço para esclarecimentos e debate entre os participantes. As perguntas poderão ser encaminhadas pelo chat durante as apresentações e serão respondidas nos momentos destinados ao debate. A ANEEL destaca que o workshop tem caráter informativo e não substitui o envio formal de contribuições à Consulta Pública nº 37/2026. As manifestações poderão ser encaminhadas, conforme modelo de contribuição, até 6 de novembro de 2026 para o e-mail cp037_2026@aneel.gov.br.

But just like this year, some unknowns could really change the economic picture the way the conflict in the Middle East and the spike in energy prices have done this year. Let’s look at all the key variables to help you develop a picture that can inform your short-term plans for 2027. Key Predictions – Overall Economic Picture “Generally speaking, outside of data centers and related energy projects, it’s going to remain a sluggish construction environment for many contractors,” said Anirban Basu, chairman and CEO of Sage Policy Group (sagepolicy.com). “Warehouse, office and housing construction has dwindled.” Manufacturers can look forward to a fairly benign operating environment in 2027. “We look for a moderate acceleration in growth,” said Bernard Yaros Jr., lead U.S. economist at Oxford Economics (oxfordeconomics.com). But the biggest story of 2026 may not drive the economy in 2027. Yaros commented, “The worst of the energy price spike is tentatively over, federal spending on defense will increase, and businesses will spend money rebuilding their inventories.” Oxford Economics expects real GDP to grow by 2.5% in 2027, a small increase from the 2.2% expected when 2026 numbers are finally tallied. While the economy will likely avoid a recession, its growth rate remains among the most sluggish of the past 10 years. Even so, it is sufficiently strong to provide businesses with a solid springboard for generating profits. (Gross domestic product, the total value of the nation’s goods and services, is the most commonly utilized measure of economic growth. “Real” GDP subtracts the effects of inflation. Economists say an increase of 2% to 3% in real GDP reflects the nation’s “natural growth rate,” which supports business activity and maintains full employment while avoiding inflation). Support for the favorable GDP numbers is coming from the consumer and business quarters, noted Yaros: “Gains in financial wealth are powering the spending of well-to-do households, while the AI infrastructure buildout has turbocharged business investment.” Housing Angst High interest rates make mortgages more expensive and thus dampen the housing industry, a significant driver of the nation’s economic health and of demand for pallets. For house shoppers, competition for available funds is keeping borrowing rates high. Mortgage rates are closing in on 7% toward the end of 2026. “Global demand for credit is coming from places like China and the U.S. to support their budget deficits as well as from the private sector to support the rollout for artificial intelligence,” said Bill Conerly, principal of his own consulting firm in Lake Oswego, Oregon (conerlyconsulting.com). “Families shopping for mortgages are competing for loans with companies like SpaceX and Anthropic, as well as the U.S. and Chinese Treasuries, while the global supply of savings has not increased much.” Additional downward pressure on sales is coming from the increasing price tags on available homes. “We are looking for median prices of existing homes to increase 3.7% in 2027 after increasing 1.7% in 2026 and 1.9% in 2025,” said Yaros. Little wonder that for the second year running, single-family homebuilders are contending with a significant inventory of unsold homes, which needs to be worked down before too many new ones come on the market. “I continue to be not too optimistic about residential construction,” said Conerly. “We’re not going to see mortgage rates coming down. People say we need more housing, but the fact is our population is hardly growing, and with restrictions on immigration population growth will stay fairly low.” Forecasts from Oxford Economics put numbers on the phenomenon. “We look for housing starts to fall by 2.4% in 2027, after falling 1.4% in 2026 and 1% in 2025,” said Yaros. Multifamily builders are also facing slow rental growth and high rental vacancy rates. Meanwhile, labor constraints continue to affect builders, especially amid the crackdown on unauthorized immigration. Commercial Construction Manufacturers also create products for the commercial side of construction, and there the story is much happier, at least for the burgeoning sector that serves the growth of AI. “On the commercial side, I think we will continue to see strong demand for data centers,” said Conerly. “Despite the political opposition, there will be plenty of communities around the country that will look favorably on the tax revenue they can get from having data centers in their community.” A further positive impetus is that the hyperscalers who are driving the investment—the Amazons and Metas and Microsofts of the world—do not seem to be sensitive to interest rates or material costs. What’s good for the data center world, though, does not seem to be helping the rest of the non-residential sector. “The economy is just not growing so quickly that we need a lot more retail stores,” said Conerly. “We’re also a bit overbuilt in industrial and warehouse space. We’ll build some offices in the suburbs but not much in the downtowns with exceptions like New York and San Francisco.” The overall construction sector will need to deal efficiently with the current soft construction market. “Backlog may shrink and payments may be delayed,” warned Basu. “All the more reason to have a talk with one’s banker about extending lines of credit to ensure sufficient financial flexibility to get through the year.” There’s going to be a lot more work for those professionals in construction firms who provide estimating and marketing services, added Basu. “Because each project will attract more competition, prudent contractors will be wise to send out more bids.” This trend may also hold true in the new pallet market where there is excess capacity chasing constrained volumes. artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- On October 29, IM Motors kicked off pre-sales for the LS8 NEO, the first full steer-by-wire, large five-seat flagship SUV under its NEXT·2028 strategy. Two trims—the 93 Max+ and 103 Max+—are available with a pre-sale price starting from 249,800 yuan. The official launch is set for November 5. A standout moment of the event was the joint appearance of IM Motors and CATL. "The LS8 NEO comes standard across the lineup with CATL-customized, high-quality batteries," said Xu Yin, vice president of IM Motors. "By leveraging the quality assurance of two industry giants, we ensure consumers can buy with confidence." Xu Yin, Vice President of IM Motors Gao Huan, chief technology officer of CATL, noted: "In new energy vehicles, the battery is a focal point for both cost and safety. We and IM Motors share the philosophy that 'professional matters should be left to professionals,' allowing each side to leverage its strengths. With the LS8 NEO—whether in safety, low-temperature efficiency, or fast charging—we have achieved exceptional performance." Gao Huan, CTO of CATL The LS8 NEO offers two battery options: a 93 kWh golden high-efficiency unit and a 103 kWh single-crystal ultra-energy unit, delivering CLTC ranges of 684 km and 752 km, respectively. Paired with SAIC's latest NEO electrification architecture and a full-domain 800V high-voltage platform, the vehicle can add 529 km of range in just 15 minutes. Even at a 20% state of charge, it can unleash over 370 kW of peak power, while energy consumption is as low as 15.2 kWh per 100 km under CLTC conditions. Beyond the rigorous battery selection, the new model comes standard with a full steer-by-wire Digital Chassis. It features an ultra-small turning radius of 4.85 meters and rear-wheel steering of up to 24 degrees in both directions. It also features full-domain physical AI powered by Momenta's world model, along with flagship amenities like 4D mechanical massage seats, B&O premium audio, and an intelligent refrigerator. Essentially, the vehicle brings features typically found in luxury cars down to the 250,000-yuan pure-electric segment, offering a comprehensive leap in class. Following the pre-sale conference, IM Motors Vice President Xu Yin, IM Motors CTO Xiang Jiao, and CATL CTO Gao Huan participated in a group media interview. They discussed the logic behind the collaboration between two giants, battery technology adaptation, the strategy of standardizing steer-by-wire chassis, product cadence, and the outlook for next year's auto market. The following is an edited transcript of the conversation for industry reference. From left to right: IM Motors CTO Xiang Jiao, IM Motors Vice President Xu Yin, CATL CTO Gao Huan Q: Why did IM Motors choose to launch a pure electric version at this juncture? Xu Yin: In April, we launched the LS8 extended-range variant equipped with our "Super Star" large battery. In the nearly six months since its debut, the vehicle has earned a solid market reputation and user acceptance. During the sales process, we received significant feedback from users asking if a pure electric version would be released. Driven by this direct market demand, we introduced the electric version to answer user calls while adapting to shifts in market structure. As everyone knows, the extended-range market has seen considerable volatility this year, while the pure electric market has experienced modest growth. (Note: Data from the China Passenger Car Association shows that from January to September 2026, cumulative retail sales of domestic extended-range passenger vehicles stood at approximately 694,000 units. This represents a year-on-year decline of about 19%, indicating the extended-range market is undergoing structural adjustment. During the same period, retail sales of pure electric passenger vehicles fell by about 4.6% year-on-year, demonstrating stronger resilience against the backdrop of a 12.8% overall decline in new energy passenger vehicle retail sales.) Q: R&D investment in batteries is massive, and there are constant calls within the industry for automakers to develop batteries in-house. Why does IM insist on deep collaboration with CATL instead of pursuing self-development? Xiang Jiao: Our philosophy is clear: deliver the most solid and reliable experience to users. That's why we choose to "let professionals handle professional matters." There are two layers to our decision to partner with CATL. First, from the user's perspective, the battery is the core component they care about most in a pure EV. We must rely on the quality of a major manufacturer to build confidence in safety. CATL has held the global market share lead for nine consecutive years, with cumulative shipments exceeding 10 billion cells used in approximately 30 million vehicles. Its defect rate is at the parts-per-billion (PPB) level, meaning single-digit defects appear only per billion cells. At the launch, we displayed a battery that had completed extreme road tests covering the Sichuan-Tibet line and Mohe—totaling 250,000 km. After disassembly, the capacity retention rate remained at 90%, and it passed all rigorous safety tests. That is the value of choosing a top-tier supplier. Second, our collaboration with CATL aims to achieve a synergy where "one plus one is greater than two." Since 2017, we have jointly established two battery factories—SAIC CATL and CATL SAIC—to supply both battery packs and cells. CATL possesses top-tier battery chemistry systems and manufacturing processes. SAIC brings 70 years of automotive heritage, resulting in vehicle integration capabilities. These include full-domain thermal management, structural safety design, and energy efficiency management. A battery cannot truly deliver its value without system-level integration at the vehicle stage. artigo.texto: Energy Storage Stock Climbs as U.S. Partner Doubles Order For industrial operators, backup power is becoming more than a safeguard against outages. Battery storage can also cut electricity costs during periods of peak demand, while increasingly connected equipment creates new requirements for securing power controls and communications. Those needs are opening opportunities for suppliers that serve critical infrastructure. Shares of Aegis Critical Energy Defence Corp. (CSE: QESS) (OTCQB: QESSF) are climbing Tuesday after the company announced a second U.S. order through channel partner GGV Energy. The order covers 14 PWR Flex 261Q energy storage units valued at approximately C$1.35 million, placed on behalf of a large private infrastructure support group. The units have a combined capacity of approximately 3.65 megawatt-hours. The order is twice the size of Aegis’s first U.S. order, announced May 26, and comes from the same partner less than six months later. Together, the two orders bring the number of units committed to U.S. customers to 21, with combined capacity of about 5.5 megawatt-hours. Deliveries are scheduled for the first quarter of 2027 across multiple U.S. states. The systems will provide backup power and peak shaving, allowing the customer to draw on stored electricity during periods of high demand. Aegis expects the installations to serve as reference sites for future industrial and infrastructure sales. The PWR Flex 261Q is an outdoor-rated, all-in-one energy storage system manufactured by SEETEL New Energy in Taiwan. It combines battery storage with an energy management system designed by Aegis and Quantum eMotion’s Quantum Random Number Generator, which secures the unit’s control and data communications. Each unit ships with built-in quick connects so it can be placed and energized without extensive site work. Aegis has also upgraded the cabinet for oil and gas, defense and mining applications, where equipment must operate in demanding environments. “This is the order that establishes Aegis in the United States,” said Ramtin Rasoulinezhad of Aegis. He described the repeat purchase, at twice the size of the first order and within six months, as evidence of growing customer demand for the system. Aegis and GGV Energy are pursuing additional U.S. opportunities, and the company expects deployments from both orders to support further sales through 2027. Based in Vancouver, Aegis develops secure and resilient energy systems for critical infrastructure, combining energy storage, hybrid and distributed generation, intelligent control and cybersecurity for defense, marine, remote and industrial applications. What we do Overview: how the EBRD operates Across three continents, the EBRD supports the transition to successful market economies. Work with us Overview: how you can work with the EBRD We draw on three decades of regional knowledge and financial expertise to tailor our products and approaches to each client's needs. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) is providing a €30 million loan to Tenevo Solar Technologies for the development of a major battery energy storage project in south-eastern Bulgaria. The financing is being complemented by €30 million in parallel funding from Raiffeisen Bank International AG (RBI). The €60 million package will finance the construction and operation of a battery energy storage system (BESS) at Tenevo, one of the largest battery storage projects in Bulgaria. The new facility will have a power capacity of 246 MW and be able to store 512.5 MWh of electricity. The BESS facility will be co-located with an existing 242 MWp solar photovoltaic (PV) plant (also financed by the EBRD and RBI), and a 65 MW battery installation capable of storing 260 MWh of electricity. It will increase energy storage capacity at the site, enhancing grid stability and supporting the integration of additional clean energy into Bulgaria’s power system. Tenevo Solar Technologies is a long-standing client of the EBRD. Previously the Bank provided €50 million to build and operate the fully merchant Tenevo solar PV plant. The project was supported by first loss risk cover deployed under the EBRD’s InvestEU Framework for Sustainable Transition. As Bulgaria accelerates its energy transition and reduces its reliance on fossil fuels, renewable energy generation and battery storage are becoming increasingly important for the decarbonisation of the power sector, improving flexibility and strengthening energy security. The rapid growth of battery storage capacity, which is exceeding 6.2 GW / 19 GWh according to latest estimates, is one of the country’s most significant energy transition achievements, positioning Bulgaria among the regional leaders in terms of renewable energy integration and decarbonisation. From 2023, the EBRD worked with Bulgaria’s Ministry of Energy on the design of grant schemes, competitive allocation and technical verification to support renewable energy and electricity storage projects under the country’s Recovery and Resilience Plan. September 2026 marked the successful completion of these crucial schemes, which have transformed Bulgaria’s renewable energy market. Manuela Naessl, EBRD Head of Bulgaria, said: “Bulgaria has made remarkable progress in deploying battery storage, and this project is another important step in that journey. By increasing the system’s flexibility and helping to integrate more renewable energy, Tenevo will contribute to a more resilient, secure and sustainable power sector. Supporting investments of this kind is central to the EBRD’s commitment to Bulgaria’s green transition.” The EBRD is a leading institutional investor in Bulgaria, having invested almost €5.3 billion in the country through 330 projects to date, with a strong focus on private sector development, competitiveness and the green economy transition. artigo.texto: JDEnergy Named BNEF Tier 1 Energy Storage Manufacturer for Seventh Consecutive Quarter XI'AN, China, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- JDEnergy has retained its place on BloombergNEF's (BNEF) Tier 1 Energy Storage Manufacturer list for Q4 2026, marking its seventh consecutive appearance. With BNEF raising its assessment standards and placing greater emphasis on project bankability and proven delivery records, JDEnergy's continued inclusion reflects its established project track record in the international energy storage market. JDEnergy specialises in string PCS technology, with a product portfolio spanning modular eBlock energy storage systems and prefabricated BESS solutions featuring string PCS architecture. This architecture enables independent control of individual battery strings, helping improve energy utilisation, system efficiency and availability while simplifying maintenance. The solutions serve a range of applications, including utility-scale energy storage, commercial and industrial (C&I) facilities, and solar-plus-storage projects. JDEnergy has obtained multiple international certifications covering product safety, grid code compliance and technical performance. Its systems are designed to comply with local grid codes and regulatory requirements and operate under different environmental conditions across Europe, the Americas and Asia-Pacific. JDEnergy has delivered energy storage products to more than 15 countries and regions, supporting applications such as grid flexibility, renewable energy integration and industrial energy management. Its growing international project portfolio reflects the company's experience in meeting diverse technical requirements and customer needs. Local technical support is an important part of JDEnergy's international operations. Working with regional partners, JDEnergy provides technical coordination, commissioning support and after-sales services to help customers navigate local grid requirements and maintain reliable system operation. This combination of standardised products and local expertise supports project delivery and long-term operation. As energy storage markets mature, developers and investors are placing greater emphasis on system reliability, operational performance, lifecycle costs and long-term returns. JDEnergy plans to further expand its presence in key international markets, working with local partners to deliver commercially viable energy storage projects and support the integration of renewable energy into power systems. About JDEnergy JDEnergy is a leader in smart energy storage across the value chain, offering integrated products and services for utility-scale and C&I applications. With capabilities spanning R&D, manufacturing, system integration, project delivery and intelligent operation, JDEnergy is committed to accelerating the deployment of energy storage and supporting the global transition toward a cleaner, more reliable and more sustainable power system. artigo.texto: HUBBARD - Voters in the City of Hubbard have decided to ban data centers. A decision to approve or reject the data center ban in Hubbard was placed on the ballot after public discourse over the city leaders’ conduct. The ordinance passed by a vote of 2,622 for to 802 against. The community effort to put the ordinance on the ballot started after discovering Hubbard Mayor Ben Kyle signed a non-disclosure agreement in 2024, and had over a year's worth of conversations with a data center company. Those organizing the petition spent a majority of the summer collecting signatures, saying it takes the decision out of the city's hands and into the voters’. “There were perceived transparency issues, and it felt like we weren't really 100% informed in terms of what the plans were from Hubbard City, and that kind of put us in a knee-jerk reaction. So we had to do something immediately,” said Jim Frederick, petition organizer. The committee was formed to help the city learn more about how a facility would affect the community, and it has paused meetings ahead of the election. “Nothing that we said at city council meetings. I felt like it was all falling on deaf ears,” said Petition Organizer Katie Costello. “It was just then that we said, okay, well, we have this way that we can take this out of their hands and say this is what the city of Hubbard wants. Katie Costello, who helped form a citizen-led data center committee, was one resident who helped gather hundreds of signatures for the petition, alongside Frederick. Before the petition efforts, there were weeks of packed city council meetings and, eventually, a 12-month moratorium on data centers in June. While applauding the effort, Hubbard Council president Mike Mogg feels the action is extreme as written. “If it passes, it's just a matter of doing the zoning, the correct zoning to ban data centers in the city. If it doesn't pass, then the committee will get back together to work to make it so that mega centers can't come into town, but make it open so that smaller data centers could have the possibility of coming to town,” Mogg previously stated. artigo.texto: Data centers are the digital steel of the AI century. America can't stop building them. COMMENTARY | In defense of the industry that will power America's next century. I grew up in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, a steel town that knows what losing an industry costs. When the mill closed, the jobs and the tax base went with it. Families watched storefronts empty and kids move away. Data centers sound far from the kitchen table. They are not. They are where artificial intelligence lives, and every advance below runs on one. Start with science. The Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, launched in November 2025, connects DOE's 17 national laboratories and their supercomputers into one AI discovery platform, aiming to double the productivity of American science within a decade. The order behind it says America is "in a race for global technology dominance." Then the taxpayer. Through ATARC, I hear firsthand how government officials are using AI to serve the American people. Our fraud working group brings oversight officials and industry together to stop improper payments in Medicare, Medicaid, SNAP and Social Security before the money goes out the door. At our October forum in Reston, inspectors general also focused on how AI and shared data can spot risks faster. Then cancer, which touches nearly every family. In Sweden's MASAI trial of more than 105,000 women, AI-supported mammography found 29% more cancers than standard screening. Sybil, built at MIT and Massachusetts General Hospital, predicts lung cancer risk up to six years out from a single CT scan. This is the space race of our time, and America is canceling launches. The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, citing Heatmap data, reports that at least $260 billion in planned U.S. data center investment has been canceled after local opposition this year, costing more than 2 million construction jobs, while China keeps building. Loudoun County, Virginia, shows what is at stake. It is the world's largest data center market and has the nation's highest median household income. Its roughly 233 data center buildings generated $1.2 billion in property taxes in fiscal 2026 — 39% of the county budget — which has helped cut homeowners' rates. Replacing that revenue would take roughly 63 more cents on today's 80.5-cent rate. Just as Silicon Valley grew up around the chip, a data center ecosystem has grown up in Loudoun: electricians, construction crews, network and cybersecurity professionals, suppliers and a community college degree in data center operations. Not every voice against this industry is a neighbor. In August, X reported roughly 200 accounts tied to a suspected Chinese bot farm pushing Americans to oppose data centers. Most opposition is homegrown, but Beijing knows what is at stake, and so should we. So let me be blunt: local zoning is paramount. If a community does not want a data center next to its homes, it does not go there. Period. The race will be won by building where communities welcome the investment, not by steamrolling neighborhoods. The administration's job is to make those projects possible, and the biggest barrier is power. Speed permitting for generation and transmission, clear the way for advanced nuclear and make the biggest users pay the full cost of their power so households never subsidize hyperscalers. Which brings me home. The Wall Street Journal has reported on a $2 billion plan to turn Aliquippa's long-closed mill site into a power plant and AI data centers. For towns like mine, the bigger risk is another generation of empty mill sites. Aliquippa's mills made the steel that built America's century. Data centers are the digital steel that will build the next one. Respect the neighbors. Power the grid. Keep making digital steel. Tom Suder is the founder and president of the Advanced Technology Academic Research Center (ATARC), a GovExec company.

artigo.texto: The Glendale City Council recently considered a 160-acre land annexation for Project Eagle, located west of the northwest corner of Litchfield Road and Olive Avenue — approximately 1 mile north of Luke Air Force Base. The proposed land use for the property includes three data centers, totaling 1.1 million square feet, and a gas generation plant. Amid the discussion, multiple speakers voiced their thoughts on the proposed annexation. “This project has been before so many different boards and each time it has passed — it has the Luke Air Force Base approval, otherwise the board of supervisors would’ve said no,” Surprise resident Lisa Everett said. “The people who are concerned about this, I hear them and I understand their concerns — but if not this project, what would they accept? “Change is hard and it’s different — but the reality is the sky is not falling.” “I’m not opposed to economic development — my concern is that the proposed protections for the nearby neighborhoods are simply not adequate for a development of this size,” said Troy Mortensen, a Waddell resident who said he lives 2,000 feet from the project site. “The proposed PAD relies primarily on 75-foot setbacks, 6-foot-high walls and limited landscaping as a transition for this massive industrial campus. “Growth and neighborhood protection are not mutually exclusive — we can have both.” As the purpose of the public hearing was to give the public an opportunity to provide feedback, the City Council did not make any final decision with regard to the land annexation. Senior Planner Sydney Tirella explained that the adoption of the annexation application and rezoning is expected to return to the dais on Oct. 27 for further consideration. According to Tirella, the project is organized in phases, with the data centers and turbines being constructed in phases one and two. Phase three will include an APS substation in the northeastern corner of the site. The proposed access points for the project site include Hatcher Road to the west and Olive Avenue to the south. Tirella said that in its future phases, the site will also include access to the north via the extension of the 143rd Avenue alignment to Peoria Avenue. As it stands, the Maricopa County jurisdiction zoning for the 160-acre land package is IND-3, for heavy industrial with an approved military compatibility permit — which would become M-2 once the annexation is complete. To accommodate the proposed data centers and gas generation plant, the city would need to rezone the property to Planned Area Development (PAD). The property sits within Luke Air Force Base’s noise contours and is designated for Luke-compatible land use under Glendale’s General Plan. Following the staff presentation and public comment section, Councilmember Leandro Baldenegro asked whether the taller walls, berms, trees and other protections Mortenson noted in his argument could be added. Project attorney Edwin “Ed” Bull clarified that the proposal did include some of the protections, including a block wall at least 8 feet high along portions of the site, as well as “landscaping where it’s appropriate.” “Maybe not to the degree they’re requesting them — but what was deemed appropriate setbacks, appropriate walls, appropriate landscaping, other screening mechanisms and so on is all part of what’s included in the County approval, and as part of what’s being brought forward in your design review analysis,” Bull said. Additionally, Mayor Jerry Weiers asked Bull to clarify whether Luke Air Force Base had any issues with the project. Bull explained that the base issued a letter that lists certain conditions of approval that his client, the applicant, agreed to. Vice Mayor Ray Malnar also asked about the distance between the project and land available for future residential development — noting that “there’s a pretty big distance between the property and the next available property that can be developed for residential.” The attorney confirmed and explained that statutory, General Plan and zoning limitations exist to regulate what development can exist around the project site. Councilmember Lupe Conchas asked whether similar developments combining large-scale data centers and on-site power generation have been successfully developed elsewhere in the country. Bull described the configuration as an “evolving trend,” but said he could not cite a completed example during the meeting and would provide additional information when the project returns to council.

artigo.texto: - The VCM is tracking more than 30 local and international project developers focusing on emissions reduction projects, including methane capture and nature-based solutions. - Saudi Arabia's aim to achieve net-zero emissions by 2060 is supported by its Circular Carbon Economy framework and a developing voluntary carbon market. - Challenges for the carbon market include ensuring liquidity, transparency, and maintaining credit quality amidst varying prices for different projects. RIYADH: Saudi Arabia’s carbon market is evolving from a platform supporting climate action into a channel for financing projects and reducing emissions, with the Voluntary Carbon Market Co. having traded more than 15 million carbon credits over three years, equivalent to SR350 million ($93.3 million) in financing directed toward climate projects worldwide. This comes as demand for carbon credits in the domestic market exceeds supply, according to the company’s CEO, Fadi Saadeh, who spoke to Al-Eqtisadiah. Saadeh said the platform facilitated trades of more than 2.5 million carbon credits in 2024 at a price of SR37.5 per tonne, adding that the market is working to stimulate domestic demand and attract developers and investors to projects that generate credits through emissions reduction or removal. Saadeh said in a 30-minute interview via Microsoft Teams that the company is tracking more than 30 project developers locally and internationally, whose projects range from methane capture and waste treatment to nature-based solutions, direct air capture and the use of low-carbon concrete. With domestic demand for carbon credits exceeding supply, he said the market needs to expand its project pipeline and diversify credit sources to meet the needs of Saudi companies seeking to manage their emissions. This expansion comes as Saudi Arabia seeks to translate its target of achieving net-zero emissions by 2060 into practical tools for financing and emissions management through its Circular Carbon Economy, or CCE, framework and the development of a voluntary carbon market. The company operates with the support of the Public Investment Fund and Saudi Tadawul Group, aiming to link financing with climate projects and develop market infrastructure for carbon trading. The challenge extends beyond supplying sufficient carbon credits to building a market that is credible and capable of attracting investment, supported by clear standards for measuring actual emissions reductions and verifying the climate impact of projects. The Kingdom is pursuing this agenda amid broader changes in global climate markets, with growth in energy-related emissions worldwide slowing to around 0.4 percent, while countries in the Middle East have begun developing regulatory frameworks to address emissions, according to the CEO. Against this backdrop, the carbon market is emerging as a potential channel for directing financing toward climate projects, although its growth will depend on expanding supply, maintaining credit quality, and sustaining corporate demand. Interview with Saadeh Q: How do you assess the Middle East and Saudi Arabia’s position in global carbon emissions, and what competitive advantage does Riyadh have in carbon markets? Globally, we are seeing some progress in carbon markets. For example, growth in energy-related carbon emissions slowed to around 0.4 percent this year. In the Middle East, however, progress remains relatively slow, although countries in the region are beginning to introduce regulations to support these efforts. In Saudi Arabia, the Voluntary Carbon Market Co. was established to help develop the market and establish its standards. Over the three years since the company was established, we have successfully traded more than 15 million tonnes of carbon credits, equivalent to approximately SR350 million directed toward financing climate projects worldwide. In Saudi Arabia, we focused first on building demand for carbon credits. We are now seeing growing interest, alongside an increase in the number of projects and developers that could become suppliers of credits in the Saudi market. We are tracking more than 30 project developers locally and internationally. Their projects span different sectors and environments, from waste landfills to nature-based solutions and advanced technologies such as direct air capture. These projects are spread across different parts of the country, giving Saudi Arabia a significant opportunity to become a major hub in the Middle East and a leading market for carbon credits and investment in them globally. Q: To what extent have voluntary carbon markets demonstrated their economic effectiveness in reducing emissions? How are carbon credit prices determined in Saudi Arabia compared with global markets? Carbon credits are a tool for strengthening corporate climate action. Companies need to develop sustainability strategies aimed at reducing their emissions, and we at VCM help companies in Saudi Arabia and the Middle East develop these strategies. There will always be emissions that are difficult to reduce or avoid. Carbon credits can therefore be one of the tools that help companies progress toward net zero by investing in climate projects through the purchase of credits. Globally, a significant part of the impact on carbon markets comes from direct carbon-pricing mechanisms, such as compliance markets, which currently cover more than 29 percent of emissions. Saudi Arabia has announced plans to launch a carbon compliance market. Globally, carbon credit retirements exceeded issuances for the first time in the first half of 2026, with retired credits exceeding 100 million tonnes. One of the main differences between global and regional markets is the expansion of forward carbon credit purchase agreements in global markets. We are seeing strong interest in these transactions from major companies such as Google and Microsoft, while this trend is developing more slowly in regional and domestic markets. Q

artigo.texto: Jaipur Discom and GEAPP Launch Sodium-Ion Battery Pilot 02 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share Jaipur Discom and global not-for-profit organisation GEAPP have launched a pilot project to assess sodium-ion battery storage for renewable power at the distribution transformer level in Jaipur. The initiative aims to help manage peak electricity demand and improve the use of energy generated by rooftop solar installations in Rajasthan. The entities have invited industry proposals to develop a 250 kilowatt-hour (kWh) battery energy storage system at KL Saini Stadium in the Mansarovar area of Jaipur. The request for proposal was issued during the second day of a national conference of electricity distribution companies being held in the city. The project will examine whether storing electricity closer to consumers can help maintain supply during periods of high demand and reduce pressure on local transformers. It will also assess sodium-ion batteries as an alternative to lithium-ion technology, including their performance under Rajasthan’s climatic conditions. Jaipur Discom will provide the project site, technical personnel and operational data. GEAPP will support system design, performance monitoring and technical work, while also training engineers from the distribution company. The pilot is intended to generate operational evidence from a working electricity network rather than relying solely on estimates. Rajasthan Energy Secretary and Discoms Chairperson Arti Dogra said the impact of rising demand during peak hours was first experienced at the distribution transformer level. She said the project would assess the ability of battery storage to ease transformer loads, store rooftop solar power and improve distribution network performance. GEAPP India Country Head Tanya Singhal said energy storage would become increasingly important to India’s electricity grid and that distribution companies needed dependable technology options beyond lithium-ion batteries. The organisations will share the pilot’s findings with electricity distribution companies across the country to support future decisions on energy storage systems. artigo.texto: MARCY, N.Y. -- A proposed battery energy storage facility has sparked strong opposition from residents at a public hearing held by the Town of Marcy Zoning Board of Appeals. The meeting took place at the Marcy Municipal Building, where many residents voiced concerns about the project. The proposed facility would be located at 9318 Cavanaugh Rd., across from the Marcy Beverage Center on River Road. Gridi Marcy Cavanaugh, the company behind the project, would need a use variance to build three separate battery energy storage systems at the site. Each system would have a capacity of 5 megawatts. Company representatives attended the hearing to answer questions from the board, local first responders and residents who oppose the project. "I've gotten a lot of contact from constituents in the Marcy area. They have concerns over this battery storage facility, whether it's going to devalue their property, safety concerns for our fire department. I have not received one phone call or contact in favor of this," said Oneida County Legislator Victoria Celia. Maynard assistant fire chief Randy Caldwell said, "Anytime we're dealing with lithium batteries. There's always concerns. The extinguishment of those it's not easily done. Sometime. Sometimes you just have to let them burn out. There are some agents that you can apply, but those are difficult fires." The board voted to accept the application for the use variance, but it will be at least 62 days before any decision is made.

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Mercado de carbono vai redefinir competitividade das empresas brasileiras, diz Érica Perin, sócia da EY Brasil Publicado 03/11/2026 • 18:34 | Atualizado há 14 horas ALERTA DE MERCADO: Dow Jones sobe após vitória histórica dos democratas nos EUA; dólar e petróleo recuam KEY POINTS O avanço do mercado regulado de carbono no Brasil deve transformar a agenda de sustentabilidade em um fator direto de competitividade para empresas, com efeitos sobre custos, financiamento, tributação e comércio internacional. É o que afirmou Érica Perin, sócia e líder de impostos diretos da EY Brasil e líder de Tax Sustainability para a EY América Latina, em entrevista ao Times Brasil — Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC. Segundo a executiva, o mercado regulado começa a exigir que companhias preparem inventários de emissões, estruturas de governança e mecanismos de controle capazes de medir o impacto do carbono sobre seus negócios. “No final do dia, a gente vai precificar o carbono, precificar as emissões”, afirmou. Perin destacou que a implementação será gradual. De acordo com ela, uma regulamentação publicada em outubro estabeleceu etapas para a entrada dos diferentes setores no sistema. Segundo a executiva, empresas de papel e celulose, ferro e aço, cimento, alumínio, mineração e exploração e produção de petróleo e gás estarão entre as primeiras a avançar na nova fase de adequação, a partir de 2027. Essas companhias terão de preparar inventários de emissões, estabelecer processos de governança e avaliar os impactos do cumprimento das novas regras sobre suas operações. “Já tem que fazer os seus inventários das emissões, tem que colocar a governança de como vão ser as emissões e, inclusive, verificar qual vai ser o impacto desse compliance nos seus negócios”, afirmou. Em etapas posteriores, outros segmentos, como setor elétrico, alimentos e bebidas, indústria química e transportes, também deverão ser incorporados. Para Perin, a preparação não pode ficar restrita às áreas de sustentabilidade. “Não é só área de sustentabilidade. É a área financeira, porque isso vai impactar o caixa, é a área jurídica, tributária. Vai ter inúmeras discussões”, disse. A executiva também destacou o impacto das regras europeias sobre empresas brasileiras que exportam produtos intensivos em carbono. Segundo Perin, o mecanismo europeu de ajuste de carbono exige que importadores apresentem informações sobre as emissões associadas à produção de determinados bens, como aço, alumínio e fertilizantes. “A Europa já vai exigir que você comprove o quanto de emissões você teve para produzir aquele aço brasileiro”, afirmou. Na avaliação da executiva, o Brasil pode transformar essa exigência em vantagem competitiva devido à participação elevada de fontes renováveis na matriz energética. Ela citou o aço brasileiro como exemplo de produto que pode apresentar pegada de carbono menor do que a de concorrentes de outros países. “A gente é mais competitivo. Só que a gente está num momento em que tem que trazer isso para a mesa”, afirmou. Para Perin, possuir uma matriz energética mais limpa ou uma agricultura de menor emissão não será suficiente para assegurar vantagem comercial. Empresas brasileiras terão de desenvolver métricas, controles e padrões capazes de comprovar essas características de forma comparável internacionalmente. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC É nesse contexto, segundo ela, que a taxonomia sustentável brasileira ganha importância. A padronização pode ajudar empresas a demonstrar ao mercado internacional atributos ambientais de seus produtos e projetos. “A gente tem muitos ativos no Brasil, por ter uma agricultura de baixo carbono, por ter uma matriz energética verde”, disse. Para Perin, esse processo será cada vez mais relevante para determinar a competitividade dos produtos brasileiros. “Buscar esses inventários, buscar controles de governança, principalmente para mostrar isso, vai ser o ponteiro da competitividade dos nossos produtos e serviços brasileiros”, afirmou. A executiva destacou ainda o potencial brasileiro na produção de combustíveis sustentáveis de aviação, conhecidos como SAF. Segundo ela, a expansão das exigências ambientais no setor aéreo pode ampliar a demanda por biocombustíveis, área em que o Brasil possui vantagens competitivas. “O que a gente tem aqui no Brasil, e que acho que é a joia que deve ser muito bem explorada, é a questão do biocombustível”, afirmou. Na avaliação de Perin, o mercado brasileiro de carbono deve ser entendido não apenas como uma obrigação regulatória doméstica, mas como instrumento de inserção do país na economia global de baixo carbono. “O mercado regulado não vai só impactar a questão local, mas principalmente está sendo desenvolvido por uma questão de competitividade mundial”, disse. Perin afirmou que a reforma tributária do consumo também terá impacto sobre a agenda de descarbonização. Um dos principais instrumentos será o Imposto Seletivo, criado para incidir sobre produtos e atividades considerados prejudiciais à saúde ou ao meio ambiente. A executiva alertou, porém, que a calibragem do tributo será decisiva para evitar distorções. “A forma de como vai ser implementado esse Imposto Seletivo é crucial”, afirmou. Segundo ela, a reforma também preserva espaço para incentivos voltados à sustentabilidade, principalmente em investimentos relacionados a equipamentos, energia renovável e inovação tecnológica. “A boa notícia é que, em termos de incentivos, os incentivos que vão remanescer estarão mais buscando a questão da sustentabilidade”, disse. Para Perin, a combinação entre mercado de carbono, taxonomia sustentável, reforma tributária e exigências internacionais transforma a sustentabilidade em uma agenda cada vez mais ligada à estratégia financeira das empresas. “É um momento em que os setores estão se juntando com o governo para demonstrar isso e trabalhar em cima disso”, af

artigo.texto: Tamil Nadu Approves 100 Per Cent Charge Waiver for BESS 02 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share The Tamil Nadu state cabinet has approved the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Policy 2026 after detailed discussions, with the policy aimed at accelerating the installation of battery storage across power generation and transmission networks. It covers projects with a capacity of 1 MW and above and seeks to improve renewable energy utilisation while reducing the curtailment of electricity generated from renewable sources. The policy recognises two categories of battery storage systems: standalone BESS and co-located BESS. Standalone BESS refers to independent systems with a capacity of more than 1 MW, which can be connected to transmission or distribution networks or to private consumer networks. Standalone projects will be eligible for a 100 per cent waiver of applicable transmission and wheeling charges. The systems can be used to meet peak-hour demand, support grid operations and provide other services approved under the policy. Co-located BESS refers to storage systems integrated with solar, solar-hybrid or other renewable energy projects with a capacity of more than 1 MW. These systems will store electricity produced by associated renewable energy plants and supply it during peak-demand periods or whenever required. Co-located BESS projects linked to existing or new solar, wind or hybrid projects will also receive a 100 per cent waiver of applicable transmission and wheeling charges. The policy will apply to all BESS projects for which applications are submitted on or after the date of notification, as well as projects commissioned on or after April 1, 2027. By covering both independent storage installations and systems paired with renewable energy projects, the policy establishes a common framework for deploying BESS across the state’s electricity network. The incentives are intended to support storage use during periods of peak demand and help renewable power reach the grid when it is needed. artigo.texto: From Readiness to Investment: Global Article 6 Forum Connects Host and Buyer Countries to Strengthen Carbon Market Cooperation November 3, 2026 Category The Global Article 6 Forum concluded in Seoul after four days of exchange among governments from eight buyer and enabler countries, and sixteen host countries, alongside carbon project developers, financiers, donors and academia. From 20 to 23 October 2026, the Forum gave actors across the carbon market landscape a shared platform to work through practical questions of international cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as countries move from readiness to results. Hosted by the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) as part of Global Green Growth Week (GGGW) 2026, the Forum marked an evolution of the Community of Practice for Article 6 Implementing Countries (CoP-ASIC). Established under the Supporting Preparedness for Article 6 Cooperation (SPAR6C) program, CoP-ASIC has convened country practitioners annually since 2023. In Seoul, collaboration with GGGI’s Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF) helped extend the community from four to more than twenty countries actively pursuing Article 6 cooperation. Strengthening International Cooperation The expansion of CoP-ASIC reflects a central lesson: carbon markets are not only about rules and systems, but also about the relationships and trust that allow host countries, buyers, investors and project developers to cooperate to achieve climate targets. Building those relationships, through honest exchange about practical challenges, shared learning and a clearer understanding of country priorities, is essential to turning climate ambition into credible projects and benefits. More than twenty sessions translated country experience and insights into dialogue with market actors on actionable co-created solutions towards Article 6 readiness and implementation. Participants discussed practical challenges of moving towards carbon project pipeline development, including host-country strategies regarding additionality and corresponding adjustments, market interoperability, credit demand, and upfront financing. The sessions identified where stronger coordination and financing approaches are needed, and were complemented by interactive trainings on Article 6 operationalization. In his final day remarks, GGGI Executive Director Sang-Hyup Kim placed the Forum within the wider theme of GGGW 2026, “Powering Green Transformation: Technology, Finance and Global Cooperation at Scale.” He said: “Carbon markets, when built on integrity and effective governance, can mobilize finance where it is needed most, raise climate ambition, and support sustainable development across our member countries. They are a vital instrument of green growth, which lies at the heart of GGGI’s mandate.” Fenella Aouane, GGGI’s Managing Director and Head of Carbon Finance, highlighted the value of bringing the wider Article 6 community together. “Some of the most insightful moments of this Forum have been during conversations off this stage. I especially value the questions and discussions about getting funding on the ground – because that is where the most impact is and why we are all here to exchange ideas and solutions towards our shared challenges. We have supported host countries so they can lead the way to setting their own rules and translate Article 6 to how best it works for them, so barriers to carbon finance can be tackled effectively and transparently in each country.” Four Days of Learning and Exchange Day 1: CoP-ASIC Annual Meeting The fourth CoP-ASIC Annual Meeting brought together SPAR6C countries (Colombia, Thailand, Zambia and Pakistan) to discuss implementation experience, including progress on readiness, emerging strategic approaches and operational challenges. A highlight was the session “Sustaining SPAR6C Results Beyond 2027,” where participants discussed how capacities, networks and institutional arrangements can continue beyond the program’s end and shape a lasting legacy in partner countries and beyond. The SPAR6C 2025 achievement video was also screened and can be viewed here. Day 2: Capacity Development and Practical Exchange The second day was devoted to interactive learning and peer exchange, with workshops and applied discussions on the strategic and financial dimensions of Article 6. Highlights included workshops for host countries on corresponding adjustments, and on financing and contracting Article 6 activities featured in SPAR6C Toolbox’s Guide Six. The day also featured the research poster exhibition and award ceremony for third and final cohort of the SPAR6C Research Mentoring Program, where Masters and PhD students gained thesis support, networking and career opportunities as well as hands-on mentoring. Days 3 and 4: Conference, Market Dialogue and Knowledge Exchange On the third and fourth days of the Forum, participation opened to a wider group of carbon market stakeholders including governments, private sector actors, financiers and partners who met to discuss strategic choices, up-front financing challenges, blending of carbon and climate finance and broader market developments under Article 6. Sessions addressed emerging and cross-cutting themes and future collaboration across CoP-ASIC and the wider Article 6 community, including “Advancing Blue Carbon and Marine-Based Article 6 Cooperation,” “Advancing Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) in Mitigation Activities” and “Leveraging Carbon Finance for Adaptation Goals in Climate-Vulnerable Countries.” The conference closed with Buyer, Enabler and Host Countries Roundtables, that were a candid exchange among the three groups on the opportunities and challenges shaping Article 6 implementation, particularly for safeguarding and promoting benefit-sharing between countries. Together with country partners and the broader ecosystem, GGGI continues to support transparent and effective carbon market cooperation aligned with the Paris Agreement
