artigo.texto: LG CNS, a South Korean digital transformation and information technology services company, has completed construction of a 30 MW AI data center in Jakarta, Indonesia. The project was commissioned by Kuningan Mas Gemilang (KMG), a joint venture between Indonesia’s Cinarmas Group and South Korea’s Tuzarial Asset Management. According to an LG CNS press release, the facility is designed to support high performance computing (HPC) using next generation graphics processing units (GPUs) and marks the first time a South Korean company has directly built an AI data center overseas for a local customer. Hyun Shin-kyun, CEO, LG CNS, said, “Completion of the construction of the Indonesian AI data center will provide LG CNS’s domestically accumulated data center capabilities to overseas customers. It is a meaningful achievement that has proven business competitiveness in the global market. We will use this as a bridgehead to expand our AI data center and AI factory business in global markets, including the Asia-Pacific region, where demand for AI computing is rapidly increasing.” The data center’s power infrastructure can support loads exceeding 300 KW per rack, allowing it to accommodate multiple GPUs within a single rack. Redundant power systems, including backup supplies, are designed to maintain operations around the clock in the event of a disruption to the main electricity supply. Its cooling infrastructure combines air cooling with provisions for liquid cooling, which will be introduced in a subsequent construction phase to manage the heat generated by high density AI servers. Once completed, the data center’s total capacity is expected to reach 400 MW, positioning it among Indonesia’s largest AI data center facilities. The project also brought together capabilities from across the LG Group, including LG Electronics’ air conditioning systems and LG Energy Solution’s batteries, alongside LG CNS’ data center design, construction and operation expertise. LG CNS is also pursuing AI data center projects in other Asia-Pacific markets, including Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Japan, using its Indonesian project as a reference for overseas expansion. Beyond data center construction and operation, LG CNS has been expanding into modular data centers, GPU-as-a-Service (GPUaaS) and liquid cooling infrastructure. The company also plans to develop AI factory services that integrate AI platforms and infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Data centers viram pauta eleitoral nos EUA em 2026 Quase US$ 200 bilhões em projetos de data centers foram bloqueados ou atrasados nos EUA no primeiro semestre de 2026. O tema agora influencia disputas eleitorais. A expansão de data centers nos Estados Unidos deixou de ser um assunto restrito a engenheiros de infraestrutura e executivos de big techs. Em 2026, o tema se tornou uma questão eleitoral capaz de influenciar disputas legislativas nas eleições de meio de mandato, marcadas para 3 de novembro. Um relatório do Data Center Watch revelou que quase US$ 200 bilhões em projetos de data centers foram atrasados, paralisados ou bloqueados no primeiro semestre de 2026 por conta de oposição política e comunitária. O número é expressivo e sinaliza uma mudança na dinâmica entre o setor de tecnologia e a sociedade americana. Estados como Pensilvânia, Geórgia, Texas, Nova York e Virgínia já discutem novas regras de transparência e limitações para a construção acelerada dessas estruturas. Só na Virgínia, apelidada de “capital mundial dos data centers”, centenas de novos projetos estão planejados. Por que comunidades estão se opondo aos data centers A resistência não é apenas ambiental, embora preocupações com consumo de energia e recursos hídricos sejam centrais. O que move a oposição é uma sensação mais ampla de perda de controle. Moradores de diversas regiões relatam que grandes empresas de tecnologia fecham acordos com autoridades locais sem consulta pública, construindo instalações bilionárias antes que a comunidade consiga sequer protestar. Em alguns casos, regras de zoneamento tornam difícil identificar o que está sendo construído até que seja tarde demais. Pesquisadores e advogados de direitos humanos apontam que os data centers se tornaram a materialização física do medo e da raiva que parte da população sente em relação à classe tecnológica e ao ritmo acelerado da transformação digital. Como analisamos em nossa cobertura de tecnologia, a tensão entre inovação e impacto social é um tema recorrente, mas raramente atinge o nível de mobilização eleitoral que se observa agora nos EUA. Empregos temporários e promessas questionadas Um dos principais argumentos a favor dos data centers é a geração de empregos. Alguns sindicatos trabalhistas apoiam os projetos por conta das vagas prometidas durante a construção. Dados disponíveis, no entanto, mostram que esses empregos são majoritariamente temporários. Uma vez concluída a obra, a operação de um data center exige uma equipe muito menor. A comparação com o passado industrial americano é inevitável. Comunidades do chamado Cinturão da Ferrugem tinham orgulho de fábricas enormes e esteticamente questionáveis porque elas representavam emprego estável, prosperidade e futuro para as famílias. Data centers, por outro lado, oferecem uma promessa diferente: infraestrutura de ponta que beneficia empresas globais, mas que nem sempre traduz riqueza para a comunidade ao redor. Até figuras políticas alinhadas ao setor de tecnologia enfrentam resistência. Vivek Ramaswamy, por exemplo, foi vaiado ao defender data centers em Ohio, um estado tradicionalmente industrial. A rejeição atravessa linhas partidárias, como destacou a cobertura de analistas políticos americanos. Tanto eleitores republicanos quanto democratas demonstram desconforto com a falta de consentimento no processo. A desconexão entre o Vale do Silício e o restante do país A expansão dos data centers expõe uma fratura cultural que vai além de infraestrutura. Para quem trabalha com tecnologia, a inteligência artificial representa progresso, eficiência e oportunidade. Para uma parcela significativa da população americana, IA e data centers simbolizam ameaças: perda de empregos, concentração de riqueza e degradação ambiental. Essa desconexão não é nova, mas ganhou contornos mais agudos. Enquanto líderes de big techs discutem abertamente a possibilidade de a IA substituir trabalhadores ou até segmentos inteiros da força humana, famílias americanas enfrentam custo de vida crescente e insegurança econômica. Como abordamos em análises anteriores sobre IA e mercado de trabalho, o descompasso entre narrativa corporativa e realidade social tende a gerar reações políticas. Políticos locais já perceberam a oportunidade. Em Nova York, vereadores têm pressionado por maior responsabilização de executivos de tecnologia. A demanda por transparência e tributação mais pesada sobre grandes fortunas do setor tech ganhou tração, especialmente entre políticos que se identificam com pautas progressistas. O que isso significa para o setor de tecnologia O cenário coloca as big techs diante de um dilema operacional concreto. Com quase US$ 200 bilhões em projetos travados, a capacidade de expandir infraestrutura de IA nos EUA está comprometida no curto prazo. Isso pode acelerar a busca por locais alternativos, inclusive fora do país, e pressionar por modelos de negociação mais transparentes com comunidades locais. Para investidores e empresas que dependem dessa infraestrutura, o risco regulatório deixou de ser hipotético. Estados já trabalham em legislações específicas, e o tema promete ganhar ainda mais destaque conforme as eleições de novembro se aproximam. Como discutimos em nossa análise sobre regulação de tecnologia nos EUA, o ambiente político americano está se tornando menos permissivo para expansões sem consulta pública. A questão central não é se os data centers serão construídos, mas em que termos. A era da expansão silenciosa parece estar chegando ao fim. E o mercado de tecnologia precisará aprender a negociar com comunidades que, cada vez mais, exigem assento à mesa. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Rentabilidade passada não é garantia de resultados futuros.

artigo.texto: On the eve of the midterm elections, there may be larger issues but none may approach the convergence of economic development, technology, politics, and local concerns quite like data centers. Certainly, data centers have become a steady rallying cry in advertising and on soapboxes during various campaigns at all levels of government. In fact, some campaigns may have turned based on the stance candidates took on the issue. Some public officials may be ousted by the stance they have already taken. Two well-known political strategists – David Axelrod and Karl Rove – weighed in on data centers at the annual meeting of the American Property Casualty Insurance Association in Boston. “It’s a big issue,” said Axelrod, formerly chief strategist and senior advisor to former President Barack Obama. “It’s been a winning issue for people because they feel a loss of control. They feel that this is being done to them, and not with them.” Axelrod acknowledged data centers are needed to accommodate the massive power demand artificial intelligence has required of critical infrastructure, but people need to feel they are participating in the process. Without a lot of oversight from the federal level, governance of data centers will be done on a state-by-state basis, said Rove, former senior advisor and deputy chief of staff for former President George W. Bush. There will be winners and losers, but the winners will be the friendliest, which can be done while still keeping in mind the concerns and safety of constituents, he said. Rove called out Texas Gov. Greg Abbott for putting a moratorium on data centers until developers demonstrate plans for water usage, power use and sharing capacity, local buy-in on locations, and property-tax obligations without the use of tax incentives. “If you go around to all of the big boys in this business, they’ll say yes to every one of those,” Rove said. “And it is going to be a huge economic driver for the states that figure that out.” “Everyone involved needs to be politically sensitive to why people are so resistant to it,” Axelrod added. The pair of what many may consider unlikely friends also chimed in on AI – another hot-button issue that is not likely to be handcuffed by any regulation at the federal level. “Nothing’s going to happen at the federal level the next two years,” Rove said. “If it doesn’t happen at the federal level, it’s not going to be industry-wide.” AI will evolve at lightning speed during the next two years of the administration so revisiting regulation after that may be difficult, he added. The matter, therefore, will be left up to the states. “I think that issue is so complex that it really cries out for presidents to be conveners of stakeholders to set rules of the road,” Axelrod said. “I think the president has put his thumb on the scale for the industry. I think going state by state is harder, but in the absence of federal leadership – and I don’t know that we’re going to get it for the next two years – I think you’re going to see states intervening in different ways.” Was this article valuable? artigo.texto: Your RAM Has Entered the Chat Your computer probably did not expect to become a supporting character in the AI infrastructure debate. Yet here we are. Sam Altman has questioned whether scarce memory belongs in personal machines when shared servers could put it to work more often. The OpenAI chief made the argument on Cheeky Pint, the podcast hosted by Stripe cofounder John Collison. The episode carries an October 29, 2026 publication date. The Verge subsequently highlighted the remark in its reporting. It is an attention-grabbing position. People buy computer memory to make their own machines useful. AI companies buy memory to serve enormous numbers of customers. Both groups have perfectly understandable reasons to want more. Altman’s statement throws those interests into the same shopping basket. Unfortunately, the basket contains limited silicon, competing priorities, and enough friction to power a small comment section. What Altman Actually Argued The important context is local inference: running an AI model on your own device rather than sending requests to a remote service. Altman challenged the assumption that distributing models across personal computers automatically solves infrastructure constraints. His concern centered on utilization. Memory installed in individual machines may spend much of its life waiting. A shared cloud system can potentially spread work across many customers and keep expensive resources busier. Altman called the allocation “quite terrible” and said people’s memory might be used “5% of the time.” He favored “maximum utilization in the cloud.” Those phrases explain the controversy. However, the exchange supplied no supporting study for that percentage. Readers should treat it as Altman’s assertion, rather than a measured average covering every desktop, laptop, workload, and household. That distinction matters. A memorable number can become accepted fact surprisingly quickly once headlines start passing it around. The Strongest Case for Sharing Consider a hypothetical office with ten employees who each need a powerful tool for a short, different period. Buying ten copies guarantees immediate access. Sharing fewer copies could meet the same demand with less equipment, provided the schedules cooperate. Cloud computing applies a version of that logic to computing resources. Pooling demand can reduce the amount of capacity that sits unused between jobs. This is the strongest interpretation of Altman’s argument. Under tight supply, hardware that serves more useful requests may deliver more benefit per unit of memory. But the conditions do heavy lifting. Requests must fit the available hardware. Customers must tolerate the service’s response time. Peak demand must remain manageable. Sharing works beautifully until everyone wants the office printer at once. Then the elegant allocation strategy becomes a queue, and somebody starts muttering near the paper tray. Efficiency Needs a Clear Definition The analysis gets more interesting when we ask what counts as efficient. Maximum activity is one measure. Useful work completed, money spent, response time, and control over sensitive information are others. Imagine a freelance editor who needs a local tool for one urgent assignment every evening. The hardware might remain idle all afternoon. Its value still depends on being ready when the deadline arrives. That example does not disprove the advantages of pooling. It shows why utilization alone cannot settle every purchasing decision. We do not usually judge a fire extinguisher by how many hours it spends spraying foam. Availability can have value even when a resource waits. Computers are different from emergency equipment, of course. Still, the broader principle holds: a lower activity rate does not automatically establish that an owner bought something wasteful or that centralized access would serve them better. Why the Memory Market Matters This debate has a physical foundation. AI software depends on manufactured components, and chipmakers must decide how to allocate production across different products. Micron has explained that HBM3E, a form of high-bandwidth memory used with AI accelerators, requires roughly three times the wafer supply of DDR5 to produce the same number of bits at the same technology node. That comparison helps explain how AI demand can place pressure on the wider memory industry. Manufacturing more advanced AI memory can require substantial production resources. It does not mean a desktop memory stick can simply move into an AI accelerator. Different memory products have different designs, packaging, and platform requirements. The competition operates partly through manufacturing capacity and investment decisions. Think competing recipes using a constrained kitchen, rather than identical sandwiches being snatched from different lunchboxes. The distinction makes the shortage easier to understand without turning every RAM purchase into a technical misunderstanding. OpenAI Is Already at the Table Altman’s comments also land against the backdrop of OpenAI’s own infrastructure ambitions. This is a major buyer discussing the best destination for a scarce product it wants to purchase. In October 2025, OpenAI announced partnerships with Samsung and SK aimed at expanding advanced memory production and data center capacity. Its announcement identified a target of 900,000 DRAM wafer starts per month. That is a production target, not a count of finished retail memory modules. It also should not become shorthand for a proven amount already delivered. SK’s separate announcement described a memory supply letter of intent and said specific volumes and arrangements would require further discussions. These details matter because infrastructure stories often blur aspiration, agreement, construction, and operation. They represent different stages. A proposed factory cannot fill a shopping cart today, however impressive the announcement sounds. A Business Interest Wort

artigo.texto: CATL Extends Its Lead as North American Slump Weighs on Korean Manufacturers The global electric vehicle battery market continues to post double-digit growth, yet South Korean battery manufacturers are losing ground. With Chinese firms now commanding more than 70% of the global market, the combined share of South Korea’s battery makers has fallen to 12.6%, widening the gap between the two countries. According to SNE Research, an energy-focused market research firm, total battery usage in EVs, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) registered worldwide from January to September 2026 reached approximately 994.5 GWh. This represents a 19.7% increase from the same period a year earlier. Despite the market’s overall growth, the performance of Korean and Chinese firms diverged sharply. The combined market share of seven Chinese battery makers, including CATL, reached 73.0%, rising 3.5 percentage points year-on-year. In contrast, the combined share of South Korea’s three major players — LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI — fell to 12.6%, down 4.1 percentage points from a year earlier. As a result, the market share gap between the two countries’ manufacturers widened from 52.8 percentage points to 60.4 percentage points. On a company-by-company basis, China’s CATL solidified its top position with 389.2 GWh in battery usage, a 24.9% increase year-on-year. As it expanded supply to overseas automakers, its market share rose from 37.5% to 39.1%. China’s BYD, ranked second, grew 7.4% to 150.9 GWh, though its market share declined from 16.9% to 15.2%. The combined market share of CATL and BYD stood at 54.3%, little changed from a year earlier. However, CATL's battery usage grew 17.5 percentage points faster than BYD's. Other Chinese challengers also posted strong growth, with Gotion ranking fourth, CALB fifth and EVE sixth. Among Korean firms, LG Energy Solution maintained its third-place ranking at 81.9 GWh, but its market share slipped from 9.8% to 8.2%. While usage grew in European and Asian markets, a sharp 44.9% drop in North American usage offset those gains. Its total usage increased just 0.7%, well below the overall market growth rate. SK On remained in eighth place as its total usage fell 18.1%, driven by a 46.7% decline in North American usage. Its usage totaled 28.3 GWh, and its market share fell from 4.2% to 2.8%. Regional demand disparities were equally pronounced. China’s domestic market grew 16.2%, while battery usage increased by 33.1% in Europe, 74.1% in Asia excluding China and 176.8% in South America. In contrast, the North American market contracted 24.3% year-on-year to 85.9 GWh. Korean manufacturers, which are heavily dependent on the North American market, were hit particularly hard. By battery type, the share of LFP, or lithium iron phosphate, batteries, supported by their price competitiveness, expanded from 52.5% to 57.7% over the year. South Korea’s battery industry is accelerating business diversification in response to slowing EV demand. SK On is seeking new opportunities by converting part of its Georgia plant to LFP production lines for energy storage systems (ESS) and signing a 9 GWh supply contract with a U.S.-based ESS company. LG Energy Solution and other firms are also rapidly converting their North American EV production lines for ESS use to diversify their customer base. Changes in Chinese tax policy are expected to become a key variable in the competitive landscape. China began imposing a 2% consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries for domestic use in September 2026 and plans to eliminate value-added tax (VAT) export rebates on battery exports starting in January 2027. However, intensifying price competition among Chinese manufacturers is also weighing on profitability. SNE Research noted that CATL’s net profit growth rate in the third quarter of 2026 came in at 14.5%, far below its revenue growth rate of 58.6%. The firm said pricing strategies and the pace of customer diversification through year-end will be decisive in shaping the competitive landscape.

artigo.texto: 30MW-Class Hyperscale Facility Uses Hybrid Air Cooling, Plans Liquid Cooling, Supports 300kW+ Per Rack The first AI data center directly designed and built by a Korean company for an overseas local client has begun operations in Jakarta, Indonesia. LG CNS said on Nov. 2 that it had completed construction of a 30MW-class hyperscale AI data center in Jakarta, Indonesia. The project was ordered by KMG, a joint venture between Indonesia’s Sinar Mas Group and Korea Investment Real Asset Management, last year. The data center was designed as scalable infrastructure capable of stably supporting next-generation GPU-based high-performance computing. A key feature is its hybrid cooling structure, which combines air cooling and liquid cooling in consideration of the high heat generated by AI servers. In the first phase, an air-cooling system using an air-circulation method was applied, and in future follow-up phases the company plans to add a liquid-cooling system, which is efficient for controlling GPU heat, to provide an optimized environment. The power system was also built to withstand a high-density environment of more than 300kW per rack, about 60 times that of a typical data center rack. That level is sufficient to ensure stable power supply even for AI computing resources equipped with multiple GPUs in a single rack. In addition, the power infrastructure was built with redundancy, establishing a system capable of uninterrupted operation 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, even in emergency situations in which the main power supply is cut off. For this project, the group’s “One LG” integrated solution, centered on LG CNS’s design, build and operation (DBO) capabilities, was applied with core technologies from across the group. LG CNS is currently working on the design for a follow-up phase aimed at expanding total receiving power capacity to 400MW. Once construction is completed, the facility is expected to establish itself as one of Indonesia’s representative large-scale AI data centers. Along with this overseas expansion, LG CNS is also accelerating the diversification of its business model. In addition to its existing colocation and DBO businesses, it has been expanding its portfolio to include prefabricated modular data centers, GPUaaS that provides GPUs on a subscription basis, and liquid-cooling infrastructure. Going forward, the company plans to develop these into an “AI Factory” business linked with AI platforms and services. Hyun Shin-gyoon, CEO of LG CNS, said, "This completion is a meaningful achievement that demonstrates competitiveness in the global market by providing overseas customers with the data center capabilities accumulated in Korea," adding, "We will continue to expand our AI data center and AI Factory businesses in the global market, where demand for AI computing is surging."

artigo.texto: South Korea's Mercedes-Benz Korea Ordered to Pay approximately $2,800 per Owner for Concealing Chinese Battery Origin South Korea's Consumer Dispute Mediation Committee has issued a collective dispute mediation decision ordering Mercedes-Benz Korea to pay 4 million won (approximately $2,800) per vehicle owner for failing to properly inform consumers about the manufacturer of its electric vehicle batteries. The committee under the Korea Consumer Agency said on the 4th that it found Mercedes-Benz Korea liable for damages after the company equipped five EQE and EQS models with Chinese-made Farasis battery cells but omitted this from sales guidelines distributed to dealers, presenting the vehicles as being equipped only with CATL batteries. The mediation covers 142 consumers who purchased the EQE 500 4MATIC SUV, EQE 53 4MATIC+, EQE 350+, EQE 350 4MATIC and EQS 350. They filed for collective dispute mediation in May after belatedly learning that Farasis batteries were installed. The compensation amounts to about 4% of the vehicle price, with total payouts estimated at about 560 million won (approximately $420,000). The committee pointed out that Mercedes-Benz Korea produced and distributed sales guidelines containing incorrect information to dealers. It also took issue with the company actively encouraging employees to use those guidelines in sales through staff training. Consumers were deprived of the opportunity to make a rational choice when they purchased vehicles based on explanations from dealer staff, the committee said. In calculating the compensation, the committee considered that batteries are a core component determining vehicle performance and safety. It also reflected differences in market share, brand recognition and technical capability between CATL and Farasis. The possibility that the resale value of Farasis-equipped vehicles declined amid growing negative sentiment toward Farasis batteries after the 2024 electric vehicle fire in Incheon's Cheongna International City was also factored into the calculation. Mercedes-Benz Korea must notify whether it accepts the decision within 15 days of receiving the written decision. Acceptance carries the same effect as a court settlement. If it does not accept, no compensation obligation arises, and consumers may file individual civil lawsuits. The committee plans to proceed with follow-up procedures so that victims who did not participate in the mediation can receive the same compensation. Committee Chairman Han Yong-ho said he hopes Mercedes-Benz Korea will actively engage in resolving the dispute and restore South Korean consumers' trust in German imported cars. The decision dovetails with sanctions previously imposed by the Korea Fair Trade Commission, which investigated Mercedes-Benz's disclosure of battery manufacturer information. In March, the antitrust regulator concluded that Mercedes-Benz had deceived consumers by falsely promoting battery manufacturer information and imposed a corrective order along with a fine of 11.239 billion won (approximately $8.4 million). The consumer committee's mediation is a follow-up decision in a case for which collective dispute mediation proceedings began in July of last year. At the time, 53 applicants sought compensation, alleging that Mercedes-Benz Korea sold EQE vehicles from June 2023 while presenting them as equipped with CATL batteries even though they carried Farasis battery cells. The committee determined that the case met the requirements for initiating collective dispute mediation, as there were more than 50 affected consumers and the core issues of fact and law were common to the case. The controversy began with a Mercedes-Benz electric vehicle fire in the underground parking garage of an apartment complex in Incheon's Cheongna International City in August 2024. After the accident, safety concerns about vehicle batteries came to the fore, and the controversy spread as it became known that the vehicle was equipped with a Farasis product and that the battery had a recall history. With this decision, Mercedes-Benz Korea now faces consumer compensation liability on top of the Fair Trade Commission fine over battery information disclosure. Once the mediation decision is finalized, compensation will be paid to the 142 consumers, and observers say it could influence practices among other imported car brands regarding disclosure of component information. However, it remains undecided whether Mercedes-Benz Korea will accept the mediation, and the possibility remains that the matter could lead to individual lawsuits if it does not.

artigo.texto: South Korea's Big 3 Battery Makers Escape Chasm via ESS, but CATL's 73% Share Keeps Volume Gap Wide South Korea's three major rechargeable battery makers are emerging from the "chasm" of temporary demand stagnation, posting clear earnings improvements in the third quarter on top of gains in the second, driven by surging demand for energy storage systems (ESS). But Chinese competitors are absorbing the market at a faster pace, and the market-share gap is actually widening — prompting South Korean companies to prepare a counterattack on two fronts: the U.S. ESS market and next-generation batteries. According to industry sources on the 3rd, LG Energy Solution posted third-quarter consolidated revenue of 9.6434 trillion won (approximately $7.2 billion) and operating profit of 756 billion won (approximately $562.5 million). Revenue rose 59.0% from a year earlier and operating profit 25.7%, while operating profit jumped 567.3% from the previous quarter. Even excluding 416.9 billion won (approximately $310.2 million) in U.S. government subsidies for North American production, the company still booked a profit of 339.1 billion won (approximately $252.3 million). Samsung SDI, which had remained in the red through the first quarter, completely reversed course with operating profits of 203.8 billion won (approximately $151.6 million) in the second quarter and 407.8 billion won (approximately $303.4 million) in the third. Third-quarter revenue came to 4.6856 trillion won (approximately $3.5 billion), up 52.6% from a year earlier. SK On posted a third-quarter operating loss of 80.5 billion won (approximately $59.9 million), but cut the deficit by 44.3 billion won (approximately $33.0 million) from a year earlier, entering a phase of narrowing losses. Excluding the second quarter, when customer compensation payments were reflected, results are on a gradual improving trend. ESS is at the center of the rebound. LG Energy Solution's ESS shipments rose more than 60% from the previous quarter, and ESS as a share of total revenue climbed from 22.7% in the fourth quarter of last year to the low 30% range in this year's third quarter. Improved utilization at its Polish plant and higher cylindrical battery sales also supported the recovery in profitability. At Samsung SDI, expanded sales of ESS and battery backup units (BBU) for data centers drove the swing to profit. Order backlogs are also building quickly. LG Energy Solution had secured a global ESS order backlog of about 160GWh by the end of the third quarter, and in North America it has locked in most of the volume planned for production through 2028. It recently signed its first direct battery energy storage system (BESS) supply contract with a Big Tech company and was also selected as an "DSX Ready BESS partner" for Nvidia. Samsung SDI has signed supply contracts totaling more than 60GWh from January to October, mainly in the U.S., and plans to raise this year's contract volume to more than 120GWh through additional orders by year-end. SK On has won more than about 10GWh in orders and is negotiating additional contracts with multiple U.S. customers, targeting 20GWh a year. Note: LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI on a consolidated basis; SK On on confirmed third-quarter results The structural growth in ESS demand itself is another tailwind. According to market research firm SNE Research, global lithium-ion ESS battery shipments in the first half of this year totaled 461.3GWh, up 71% from a year earlier. Demand sources are diversifying as investment in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers and power grids expands. "ESS demand is outpacing available production capacity," an LG Energy Solution official said on a conference call. "Supply discussions now cover not only traditional grid and utility customers but also demand from AI data centers and direct purchases by hyperscalers." The problem is China. The global market share of Chinese battery makers led by CATL has climbed to around 73%, and the gap with South Korean companies is widening. Analysts say that while the South Korean Big 3 are climbing out of the chasm, Chinese companies are recovering earnings faster and cementing their market dominance. In response, South Korean companies are using U.S. restrictions on China as a breakthrough. Washington, citing national security, is limiting the use of Chinese batteries in major ESS facilities. Targeting that opening, all three companies have moved to expand North American ESS sales. "South Korean-made batteries are being considered as an alternative in terms of supply-chain diversification, quality reliability and North American market responsiveness," an industry official said. "Companies that previously used Chinese batteries keep inquiring about product specifications, available volumes, pricing terms and the possibility of long-term contracts." Kim Young-kwang, head of SK On's financial management office, said, "Since the Trump administration's tightening of restrictions on China and the push to reorganize supply chains, interest in non-Chinese products has been rising." Capacity expansion is proceeding in parallel. LG Energy Solution plans to raise its North American ESS production capacity from more than 50GWh at the end of this year to 70GWh by the end of next year. "We will strengthen our selection-and-focus strategy to maximize operational efficiency with limited resources," said Lee Chang-sil, chief financial officer of LG Energy Solution. Samsung SDI has begun mass production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for ESS at its StarPlus Energy (SPE) plant in the U.S. and will bring additional lines online in the first half of next year. "Samsung SDI's U.S. operations will also mass-produce LFP for ESS between the second half of 2028 and early 2029," said Cho Yong-hwi, head of Samsung SDI's ESS business team. artigo.texto: PAGE, Ariz. -- Doug Herrera still lives in the house his father built, though his dad died some time ago from cancer. Herrera wonders if that illness could have been linked to pollutants from nearby uranium mining. Now, he worries that a possible new neighbor -- a proposed $10 billion mega data center -- could imperil his health. "I'm a patriot, but I'm highly against the data center," Herrera, 64, said from his front porch near a yard sign that reads "No Data Centers." "There is light pollution, sound pollution. The temperature is going to rise," he said. Page is a gateway to iconic Southwestern landscapes of arid deserts studded with Joshua trees and towering red-rock formations. While the City Council approved the sale of land for a data center, the developer needs zoning and other approvals. Residents concerned about possible health effects have signed petitions and mobilized to oppose construction. The boom in data centers is dividing communities such as Page and turning future construction into a flash point in the midterm elections. The leading candidates in the close race for Arizona's 1st Congressional District are at odds over any new centers there, and the state's attorney general has called for a pause on new approvals and building. Emerging research into data centers' possible health effects is adding grist to the various state fights, giving ammunition to Democrats and some Republicans who've broken party ranks to oppose the sprawling complexes. It has also put some incumbent politicians who have supported data center expansion in unexpectedly vulnerable positions in reliably red states like Ohio and Texas, where the megabuildings now operate by the hundreds. "Two years ago, a lot of these data centers went up and there was not an organized, watchful opposition," said Lee Hannah, PhD, a political science professor at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio. "That opposition has come up in a grassroots way so quickly that decisions made a year ago by local officials or state governments to get behind a data center are suddenly career-ending," Hannah added. The hyperscale centers house infrastructure to power artificial intelligence (AI), with servers that sprawl over tens of thousands of square feet or more. The city of Page approved the sale of 500 acres for the proposed data center, though the location within that acreage hasn't been decided. The area sits on open land studded with blackbrush and native grasses near Horseshoe Bend, an iconic curve of the Colorado River that has long been popular with tourists. Data centers gobble up electricity and rely on backup gas generators during times of peak energy demand. The resulting air pollution has been linked to heart conditions, respiratory issues, and elevated cancer risks, according to a number of environmental studies. Emissions from the centers could cause nearly 1,300 deaths annually by 2030 and an annual public health burden of more than $20 billion in 2028, based on modeling led by researchers at the University of California, Riverside. Cooling components can contain what are called forever chemicals, synthetic substances that accumulate in human tissue, according to advocacy and environmental groups. And the hum and whir of generators and heating and air conditioning systems can exceed 90 decibels, which can harm hearing. Data centers are lit up for operations and security, creating light pollution that can increase the risk of chronic disease, the groups say. The megafacilities also create what are known as data heat islands, which are higher-temperature zones caused by intense energy demands. "We're just starting to see the very early edge of the wave of the research into health impacts of data centers," said Alison Steele, executive director of the Environmental Health Project, a nonprofit public health organization. "By the time we have a substantial volume of research it's going to be too late, because the decisions are being made now." A trade group for the data center industry said a review of the largest data center market -- Virginia -- found that use of backup power sources, including diesel generators, is minimal, and that existing state and federal regulations limit potential emissions or impacts. "Data centers are committed to being responsible partners where they operate," said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs at the Data Center Coalition. It Cuts Across Politics Mounting concerns about data centers are dividing candidates and pitting some GOP contenders against President Donald Trump, who supports the facilities' construction as vital for economic growth. Two in three Americans oppose the construction of new data centers in the U.S., according to an October Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll. Such political standoffs are happening largely in states that Trump won in 2024, where most new data center capacity has been proposed. About 1,400 data centers operate in the U.S., and an additional 2,000-plus are planned. Sixty percent of data center capacity under construction is in states Trump won by five percentage points or more, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company. Excluding Virginia, 92% is in states the president won. Hannah said the uptick in construction has put Trump's coalition at particular risk because data centers are often built in rural areas, where the president has often enjoyed insurmountable margins of support. "This is where most of the data centers go," Hannah said. "They go into red states, because Republicans are less critical of economic opportunity. If it promises jobs and money, they're all in." In Page, signs opposing construction pepper front yards. The opposition to more data centers in the state could pose political risks for GOP House candidate Jay Feely, who won his primary with an endorsement from Trump. artigo.texto: US Data Centers Hit Political Headwinds: Candidates in 21 States Back Moratoriums, Narrowing Room for Industry Expansion The US data center industry is coming under systematic pressure from electoral politics. According to tech media outlet The Information, of the 36 states holding gubernatorial elections on Nov. 3, at least one major-party candidate in 21 states has publicly backed a moratorium on data centers. In five states—Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon and Texas—candidates from both parties hold the same position; in Maine, New Mexico and New York, the pro-moratorium side leads in the latest polls; and in seven other states the races are tight. Together, these 15 states are home to more than one-third of the US population and are also the most concentrated zone of data center construction in the country. That means that regardless of Tuesday's results, the buildable space available to the data center industry will shrink materially, with upward pressure on operating costs. Projects Under Construction Directly Exposed to Policy Risk Looking at project distribution, the footprints of major tech companies overlap heavily with the states backing moratoriums. The Stargate project, a joint venture between OpenAI and Oracle, has large sites in Texas, Michigan and New Mexico; SoftBank-owned SB Energy plans to build an 8-gigawatt campus for OpenAI in Ohio; and Microsoft, Amazon and Nvidia have all established operations in Texas. Data from real estate services firm CBRE shows that metro Atlanta has overtaken Northern Virginia to become the most active data center construction market in the US, and Georgia's gubernatorial race this cycle is also among the closely contested ones. The financial implications of regulatory risk have already made their way into public filings. The IPO prospectus Anthropic released last week lists state moratoriums and other restrictive measures as a major business risk, naming moves in New York and Texas, and says regulatory pressure is one reason it is expanding its international data center footprint. SB Energy and emerging cloud service provider Nscale also list similar risks in their respective filings. Three incumbent governors have already moved first: New York's Kathy Hochul, Texas's Greg Abbott and Oregon's Tina Kotek have all paused approvals for new large data center projects. Hochul's opponent, Bruce Blakeman, has called the moratorium "absurd" but trails badly in the polls; Abbott's opponent, Gina Hinojosa, describes the pause on her campaign website as an "election-year gimmick," suggesting it will lapse after Nov. 4, while advocating a broader, comprehensive moratorium. A Shift in Public Opinion Is the Root Cause The political sensitivity of data centers has risen sharply in a short period, driven by a rapid shift in public opinion. At the start of this year, about 40 towns and counties across the US had imposed bans on data centers; by August the number had surpassed 500, reflecting residents' concerns about rising electricity bills, water consumption, noise pollution and environmental damage. An August poll by the Pew Research Center found that six in ten US adults said they were unwilling to see a new data center built near their community, more than half believed data centers are harmful to the environment, and half said they drive up household electricity bills; fewer than one in four respondents believed data centers benefit local jobs or tax revenue. Association with the data center industry has become a political liability. Nevada Democrat Aaron Ford has branded Republican incumbent Governor Joe Lombardo "Data Center Joe" and set up a dedicated website to promote the label; Wisconsin Republican Tom Tiffany calls his opponent David Crowley "Data Center Dave"; and Oregon Democrats call their opponent Christine Drazan "Data Center Drazan." Alabama's popular candidate Tommy Tuberville, previously a strong industry backer, dismissed such concerns as "nonsense" in July; his campaign ads now strike a different tone: "Politicians grab the headlines, Big Tech takes the tax breaks, and ordinary families foot the bill." Moratoriums Vary Widely in Substance The term "moratorium" is ubiquitous in political discourse, but the substance of policies varies widely by location. On duration, some pauses last just 45 days while others run as long as three years, with most intended to buy time for legislatures to set longer-term standards. On scope, some moratoriums target only facilities above a certain size—New York sets a 50-megawatt threshold, rejecting large campuses used to train frontier AI models but allowing smaller projects to proceed; the "conditional moratorium" backed by Ohio candidate Amy Acton stipulates that data centers meeting certain labor and siting conditions may still be approved. The enforcement mechanism, by contrast, is highly consistent: moratoriums already implemented in the states all rely on halting new environmental permit approvals, with Abbott additionally freezing new grid connection applications and Kotek suspending related transactions on state-owned land. New Hampshire's incumbent governor, Kelly Ayotte, says she cannot act alone and needs to advance the measure through the state budget process next July; her opponent, Cinde Warmington, has pledged to sign an executive order on her first day in office. Not all candidates have chosen the moratorium path. Of the 46 major candidates who have not called for a pause, 38 support at least one restrictive measure targeting data centers, including electricity bill protections, eliminating tax breaks, tougher environmental and water-use requirements, mandatory union labor, and bans on confidentiality agreements in public transactions. Hawaii is the only state where neither party's candidate has proposed data center restrictions. artigo.texto: South Korean AI Data Center Industry Urges Government to Set Up Dedicated Power-Supply Desk With uncertainty over power supply cited as the biggest obstacle to AI data center investment, the industry is calling on the government to establish a dedicated desk and to set clear deadlines for permit processing. Companies say that because they cannot know when or how much electricity they will receive while still reviewing a site, decisions to buy land or commit capital are being held up. The Federation of Korean Industries (FKI) on the 2nd jointly hosted a corporate roundtable on "Revitalizing the AI Data Center Industry Ecosystem" with South Korea's Presidential Committee on AI at the FKI Tower in Yeouido, Seoul. Fifteen companies attended, including Samsung SDS, Hyundai Motor, LG Electronics, FuriosaAI, Rebellions and HyperExcel, to discuss policy improvements needed to boost investment and foster related industries. Power emerged as the most urgent issue. Data center companies asked for a channel through which they can consult relevant agencies on the timing and capacity of power supply even before a site is finalized. The permitting process, split across building, transportation, environment and electrical equipment approvals, was also flagged for improvement, since a delay in any single procedure can push back the entire completion schedule and inflate project costs. The industry recommended that the subordinate regulations of the Special Act on the Promotion of the AI Data Center Industry, set to take effect next March, specify permit processing deadlines and establish a system that coordinates consultations among agencies. Attendees also proposed supplying locally generated renewable energy directly to nearby data centers. Regions with concentrated renewable generation, such as South Korea's southwestern region, often cannot use all the power they produce because of insufficient grid capacity. The industry suggested using microgrids — small-scale power networks combining on-site generation with energy storage systems (ESS) — as an alternative. Companies asked for special provisions and institutional support so that demonstration projects under way at industrial complexes and universities in South Jeolla Province can be expanded into power supply for data centers. South Korean AI chipmakers said they need opportunities to validate their products in actual data centers and build a supply track record. They explained that neural processing units (NPUs) with improved computational efficiency and power consumption have reached the commercialization stage, but compatibility issues with existing software built around foreign graphics processing units (GPUs) are blocking adoption. Public procurement practices were also cited as a problem. Some public AI projects are ordered on the premise of specific GPU products or server configurations, which can narrow the room for South Korean NPUs to participate, according to the companies. They asked that procurement criteria be changed to focus on the performance and capacity needed for actual services such as training and inference. Power and cooling equipment makers said that even when they develop next-generation products, a lack of testing opportunities and data center deployment records makes it hard to enter the market. Operators, for their part, must bear the cost and operational risk of adopting equipment with few proven cases. The industry recommended building large-scale testing facilities, subsidizing the cost of participating in demonstrations, and simplifying the review process for the Korea Certification (KC) integrated national mark. Ha Jung-woo, vice chair of South Korea's Presidential Committee on AI, stressed that AI data centers are an industry that brings together semiconductors, power, cooling and networking technologies, and that South Korean companies' capabilities must be pooled. "Our companies need to connect and advance these technologies well and grow them into high-value 'token factories' that will become a new growth engine for our economy," he said. "Token factory" is a term likening AI data centers to factories that take in power, semiconductors and data and produce everything from text, images and code to the intelligence used to control manufacturing equipment and robots. Kim Chang-beom, senior executive vice chairman of the FKI, said, "It is now important not only how many AI data centers we build but what we fill them with." He added, "We need to create a virtuous cycle in which our companies' semiconductor, power and cooling technologies are used in South Korean data centers, and that experience leads to global orders and exports." The roundtable was organized around the recognition that regulatory uncertainty must be cleared away first if AI infrastructure investment is to translate into South Korean industrial competitiveness. With subordinate regulations being drafted ahead of the special law's implementation, attention is focused on whether the industry's proposals will be reflected in the actual rules. Waiting times for grid connections and permitting delays are cited as common bottlenecks in global data center investment as well. In South Korea too, large-scale private investment could be postponed unless power supply schedules are fixed, which would in turn affect the pace of expanding AI service infrastructure. In semiconductors and equipment, attendees highlighted that South Korean data centers can serve as the first proving ground for South Korean-made products, since companies that secure early references can gain an edge in winning orders abroad. South Korea's Presidential Committee on AI and the FKI plan to flesh out the proposals raised at the meeting and continue consultations so they can be reflected in the government's AI strategy and related policies.

artigo.texto: Chinese Battery Makers Capture 73% Share as South Korea's Big Three Slip to 12.6% The global EV battery market has grown nearly 20% this year, but Chinese companies are monopolizing the gains. While the combined share of seven Chinese makers has climbed to 73%, the share held by South Korea's Big Three — LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On — has been pushed down to the low 12% range. According to figures compiled by energy market research firm SNE Research released on Nov. 2, total battery usage in pure electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrid vehicles (PHEVs) and hybrid vehicles (HEVs) registered worldwide in January-September of this year came to about 994.5 GWh (gigawatt-hours), up 19.7% from 830.7 GWh a year earlier. The market itself kept up double-digit growth, but fortunes diverged sharply among suppliers. The combined share of seven Chinese companies, including CATL and BYD, stood at 73.0%, up 3.5 percentage points from 69.5% a year earlier. Conversely, the combined share of the three South Korean companies fell 4.1 points to 12.6% from 16.7%. The gap between the two camps widened from 52.8 percentage points last year to 60.4 points this year, surpassing 60 points. CATL cemented its No. 1 position with usage of 389.2 GWh, up 24.9% year-on-year. Its share also rose 1.6 points to 39.1% from 37.5%. The growth is attributed to a steady expansion of overseas automaker customers. No. 2 BYD posted 150.9 GWh, up just 7.4%, and its share fell 1.7 points to 15.2% from 16.9%. Because BYD supplies batteries only to its own vehicles, it took a direct hit from a 32.9% drop in EV sales in China. Still, its usage outside China surged 66.8% to 45.9 GWh from 27.5 GWh. CATL and BYD alone account for 54.3% of the total market. South Korean companies were hobbled by the sharp contraction of the North American market. LG Energy Solution held onto third place with 81.9 GWh, up 0.7%, but its share fell 1.6 points to 8.2% from 9.8% as growth lagged far behind the market. It continued supplying Tesla, General Motors (GM), Hyundai Motor Group and Volkswagen, and its usage rose 13.2% in Europe and 49.4% in Asia, but a 44.9% drop in North America — from 29.9 GWh to 16.5 GWh — offset most of those gains. SK On slid to eighth place with 28.3 GWh, a contraction of 18.1%. Its share fell 1.4 points to 2.8% from 4.2%. The blow came from North American usage plunging 46.7%, from 14.2 GWh to 7.6 GWh. Samsung SDI was found to have dropped out of the top 10. Note: Based on SNE Research data Chinese second-tier players also made notable strides. Regional gaps are even more pronounced. Usage in China rose 16.2% to 567.8 GWh, while Europe grew 33.1%, Asia excluding China 74.1% and South America 176.8%. North America, by contrast, was the only region to contract, with usage down 24.3% to 85.9 GWh. Policy factors played a major role in North America's decline. The United States ended its federal EV tax credit of up to $7,500 for new vehicles as of Sept. 30, 2025. After the credit disappeared, North American EV demand slowed and battery usage fell along with it. Note: Based on SNE Research data; absolute usage figures for Europe, Asia and South America were not disclosed Warning bells are also sounding for the battery industry's profitability. artigo.texto: China's Solid-State Battery Race Heats Up: Lithium Sulfide Maker Closes Series A; Dongfeng and Chery Mass-Production Timelines Emerge Capital and industrial activity across the solid-state battery supply chain are accelerating in tandem. Sichuan All-Solid-State New Materials Co., Ltd. (Sichuan All-Solid-State), a Chinese producer of lithium sulfide—a key raw material for all-solid-state batteries—recently closed a Series A round in the tens of millions of yuan (approximately $1.5 million to $7.5 million). The round was led by Hongrong Capital and Mingshi Venture Capital, with Tianhong Investment, Xingxiang Sci-Tech Innovation and existing shareholder Inno Angel Fund participating. According to industry media reports, the proceeds will be directed mainly toward equipment upgrades and capacity expansion on a hundred-ton-class production line, the establishment of a research and development center in Changsha, and team building. Lithium sulfide is regarded as one of the core raw materials in the all-solid-state battery route, and its ability to supply at scale bears directly on the pilot-production and mass-production schedules of downstream cell makers. Progress on the vehicle side is equally brisk. Dongfeng's all-new-generation solid-state battery is nearing the mass-production installation stage, with an energy density of 350 Wh/kg. Vehicles equipped with it are expected to exceed 1,000 km of range and to operate normally at -30°C. The company says it has built a full solid-state battery industrial chain. Chery, for its part, is focused on the Rhino S all-solid-state battery, targeting a cell energy density of 600 Wh/kg and planning in-vehicle validation in 2027. To that end it has assembled a research team of 1,000 highly educated engineers, with R&D spending at the level of 10 billion yuan (approximately $1.5 billion). Huayuan Securities notes that industry developments around solid-state batteries have been密集 since October 2026, with some products already entering pilot production and demonstration installation. As corporate investment continues to rise, related equipment and battery-materials companies stand to benefit. Note: Energy density and range figures are company-disclosed targets or stated metrics. From a supply-chain perspective, solid-state batteries exert a relatively direct pull on equipment and materials. The shift of production lines from liquid to solid-state systems involves equipment upgrades across electrode preparation, solid-electrolyte forming, packaging and inspection, while on the materials side it drives demand across subcategories including lithium sulfide, solid electrolytes, and cathode and anode materials. Among China A-share names, Jinlongyu (002882.SZ) has built a vertically integrated solid-state battery business spanning materials, cells and systems, with main products including solid-state cells, solid electrolytes, lithium manganese iron phosphate cathode materials and silicon-carbon anode materials. Shanghai Xiba (603200.SH) has accumulated comprehensive capabilities across R&D, process scale-up, production-line construction, performance testing, product validation and large-scale manufacturing of advanced materials. For investors, solid-state batteries remain in a transition from demonstration and validation toward large-scale mass production, and the pace of order and capacity realization carries uncertainty. In the near term, marginal changes in equipment tenders and materials procurement are the most direct window into industry progress; over the medium and long term, progress hinges on whether the cost-decline curve for cells and the scale of vehicle adoption can be realized in tandem.

artigo.texto: China's solid-state battery stocks buck market slump with wave of limit-ups; analysts see 2027 as mass-production breakthrough year On Nov. 3, China's A-share solid-state battery sector bucked a weakening broader market. The Shanghai Composite Index widened its afternoon loss to 1.57%, closing at 3,580.79 points, with 717 gainers and 1,577 decliners in Shanghai. The battery index, by contrast, closed up 2.16% at 503.12 points for the full session, outperforming the Shanghai Composite by 3.73 percentage points, with sector turnover reaching 46.858 billion yuan (approximately $7.0 billion). At the stock level, Shangshui Intelligent and Mengguli sealed 20% limit-ups with turnover rates of 27.56% and 11.97%, respectively, both first-board moves. Yema Battery, Fengyuan, Shengyang Power, Shidai Wanheng, Longpan Technology, Baoming Technology and Zhongxin Fluorine Materials all hit their ceilings, Zizhu Gaoke posted a second straight limit-up, and Liwang Shares rose as much as 16.20% intraday. Heavyweight CATL (300750.SZ) gained 4.16% in early trading, logging a fourth consecutive daily advance, and still closed up more than 3%. What is supporting sector sentiment is an increasingly clear timeline for solid-state battery mass production. Southwest Securities believes 2026-2027 will be a period of intensive pilot-line construction, with 2027 likely bringing a window for small-batch production and vehicle validation, before gradual entry into large-scale commercialization in 2028-2030. Guotai Haitong directly defines 2027 as the inaugural year of solid-state battery mass production. Industry progress is confirming that cadence. CATL's Yibin all-solid-state pilot line came online in August this year, with sample energy density exceeding 500Wh/kg, and the company plans small-batch production in 2027. BYD's (002594.SZ) 2GWh automotive-grade sulfide all-solid-state pilot line went into operation in February this year, and the first 20GWh mass-production line in Bishan, Chongqing, is scheduled to break ground in the third quarter of 2026. Gotion High-tech's (002074.SZ) first 0.2GWh pilot line was completed in 2025, and products have already undergone on-vehicle road testing. In addition, Dongfeng's next-generation solid-state battery is nearing the vehicle-installation stage, while Chery has set 2027 as its target for completing validation. Policy backing is equally explicit. The 15th Five-Year Plan for New Battery Industry Development, jointly issued by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and six other departments, proposes that all-solid-state batteries achieve initial large-scale application by 2030, with long-life lithium batteries required to reach 15,000 charge cycles. China's Ministry of Finance and two other departments specified that solid-state batteries will be exempt from consumption tax from Sept. 1, 2026, through Dec. 31, 2028. Shanxi Securities noted that this is a rare case in the battery industry's history of using tax measures to support a frontier technology route in a targeted way; the plan also implements capacity-warning controls and regulates price competition — effectively a battery-sector version of "anti-involution" — providing a five-year institutional lever for industry consolidation. Demand-side data also offer support. Combined power and energy-storage battery output reached 237.8GWh in September, up 57.3% year on year; energy-storage battery sales alone were 73.5GWh for the month, up 104.4% year on year, more than double the growth rate of power batteries. Global energy-storage battery shipments totaled 839.3GWh in the first three quarters, up 96.3% year on year, with Chinese manufacturers accounting for 96.6% of the total. October production schedules for sample battery companies rose 3.8% month on month, with all five core segments hitting year-to-date highs. Several institutions have offered quantitative forecasts for the long-term solid-state battery opportunity. Southwest Securities estimates global all-solid-state battery shipments will rise from 1.87GWh in 2026 to 94.77GWh in 2030 — roughly a 50-fold increase over five years — driven by penetration in high-end new energy vehicles rising from 0.5% to 13%. Precedence Research forecasts the global solid-state battery market will grow from $1.63 billion in 2025 to $7.6 billion in 2030 and further to $31.71 billion in 2035, a compound annual growth rate of 34.56% from 2025 to 2035. Note: Data sources are the public research views and industry forecasts of the institutions above. The sector's deep prior correction also provides elasticity for this rebound. The battery index touched an intraday high of 614.80 points on Oct. 12 and pulled back to 466.93 points on Oct. 23, a maximum drawdown of 24.05% over ten trading days. Meanwhile, CATL disclosed buyback progress on Nov. 2: as of end-October it had repurchased 19.6059 million shares, or 0.4447% of total share capital, for 5.36 billion yuan (approximately $804.8 million), part of a previously proposed 20 billion to 40 billion yuan cancellation-style buyback plan. On valuation, CATL currently trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of about 13.38 times, with a dividend yield of 3.42%, corresponding to earnings per share of 14.13 yuan. Sell-side institutions have recently turned more positive: Soochow Securities assigned a 20x PE for 2027 and a target price of 431 yuan, while Huayuan Securities initiated coverage with a buy rating on Nov. 2. Sinolink Securities said the lithium battery sector's profitability, valuation and institutional positioning are all at low levels in their historical ranges, and it remains firmly bullish on fourth-quarter performance, believing strong third-quarter results could serve as a catalyst for a rebound. artigo.texto: - Blue Vector has selected CATL as its exclusive battery partner. - Skyla V30's first full-scale technology demonstrator rolled out in August, and the model secured its first overseas pre-sales orders in September. CATL (HKEX: 3750) has signed agreements with Blue Vector Intelligent Technology to develop aviation batteries for the Chinese electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft maker based in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province. The companies recently signed strategic and product cooperation agreements, with Blue Vector selecting CATL as its exclusive battery partner, the battery maker said in a statement on Monday. The partnership will focus on the Skyla V30, a product of Skyla Aviation — Blue Vector's eVTOL business — for which CATL will develop custom batteries. The statement did not disclose the deal's value, battery specifications or a supply timeline. The Skyla V30 is a 6-seat, all-electric tiltrotor aircraft designed for intercity passenger travel. Its first full-scale technology demonstrator, A/C01, rolled out on August 31 this year in Harbin, Heilongjiang province, in northeastern China. Under plans disclosed at the time, the demonstrator will undergo systems integration, ground testing and tilt-transition flight tests, marking the project's shift from design and development to full-aircraft engineering validation. Blue Vector said on September 24 that it had signed pre-sales orders for 60 V30 aircraft during the Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou, including 30 from Singapore-based aviation operator Moon Aero. The Moon Aero deal marked the V30's first overseas pre-sales orders. Blue Vector said at the time that cumulative pre-sales orders had exceeded 100 aircraft since the model's global debut in July, and that it planned to continue engineering validation and airworthiness certification work. Blue Vector has also been raising funds to support research and development. On June 30, the company announced the completion of a funding round exceeding 100 million yuan ($14.9 million), jointly led by Shenzhen Capital Group and an unnamed industry-backed US dollar fund. As of that announcement, the company's eVTOL business had completed 5 funding rounds in nearly 6 months, raising more than 400 million yuan in total. For CATL, the agreement extends its push into electric aviation. In August 2024, the company signed a deal with Shanghai-based Autoflight, agreeing to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in the aircraft maker and jointly develop eVTOL batteries. In November 2025, Autoflight unveiled a floating vertiport jointly developed with CATL, integrating an eVTOL takeoff and landing platform, energy storage, charging and other systems into a battery-powered vessel. artigo.texto: Uma análise da Bloomberg com base em dados do Ballotpedia mostra que haverá mais de 40 medidas relacionadas a data centers em votação nas eleições de meio de mandato nesta terça-feira (3). Os eleitores analisarão as propostas em um momento de crescente oposição a novos data centers nos EUA, o que destaca como a IA se tornou uma questão central nas eleições de meio de mandato. Uma pesquisa da Universidade Quinnipiac realizada em setembro mostrou que 72% dos eleitores seriam contrários à instalação de um novo data center em sua comunidade, ante 65% quando a pergunta foi feita em um levantamento de março. Embora os data centers deem suporte a ferramentas de IA amplamente utilizadas, como o ChatGPT e o Claude, pessoas que descobrem que um deles será construído em sua vizinhança frequentemente se preocupam com a poluição do ar, o barulho e o aumento das contas de serviços públicos, como a energia elétrica. Elas também se inquietam com o fato de autoridades locais oferecerem incentivos fiscais às empresas responsáveis pelos projetos e assinarem acordos de confidencialidade para conversar com representantes de interesses privados, deixando os moradores sem informações. Em alguns casos, porém, ativistas conseguiram impedir a construção de data centers. Ao menos 45 projetos, avaliados em US$ 68 bilhões, foram afetados pela oposição local no segundo trimestre, segundo relatório da organização Data Center Watch. Agora, os referendos relacionados à IA concedem aos eleitores uma nova forma de expressar sua oposição. “Medidas submetidas à votação local são uma ferramenta à qual as pessoas podem recorrer e que podem usar em um momento em que se sentem impotentes diante de algumas dessas forças mais amplas que moldam nosso futuro”, disse Megan Mullin, cientista política especializada em meio ambiente da Universidade da Califórnia em Los Angeles, a UCLA. Proibições e destituições Algumas propostas podem proibir completamente os data centers. Isso é possível em Alhambra, cidade da região metropolitana de Los Angeles que pode seguir os passos da vizinha Monterey Park. Em Ohio, cerca de uma dúzia de comunidades votará sobre uma proibição, com a maioria das propostas focada em instalações maiores. Um desses lugares é Piqua, onde a Meta tenta construir um data center. Os eleitores também decidirão se devem destituir o prefeito e dois integrantes da comissão municipal, que apoiaram a construção de infraestrutura de IA na cidade de aproximadamente 20 mil habitantes. Outra iniciativa de destituição ocorre em Yukon, no estado de Oklahoma, onde os moradores decidirão o futuro do prefeito Brian Pillmore. Alguns de seus eleitores querem que ele deixe o cargo porque apoia a proposta de construção de um data center de US$ 1 bilhão da Beltline Energy ao longo da Rota 66. Pillmore disse que vê com bons olhos o envolvimento da população nas questões de desenvolvimento local, mas considera o projeto uma rara fonte de investimento de longo prazo para a pequena cidade. Ele estima que a receita municipal possa aumentar em até 75%. “Cidades como Yukon precisam considerar cada carta que têm na mão”, afirmou. Yukon é uma das muitas pequenas cidades dos EUA em busca de um impulso econômico. Os data centers podem ser a resposta, trazendo investimentos e empregos bem remunerados que não exigem diploma universitário, segundo Dan Diorio, vice-presidente executivo de políticas estaduais e relações governamentais da Data Center Coalition, entidade que representa o setor. As instalações geram uma arrecadação tributária “significativa”, que ajuda a financiar escolas, transporte e segurança pública, disse Diorio. “Medidas submetidas à votação para restringir ou proibir o desenvolvimento de data centers enviariam um sinal de que a região está fechada para negócios” e “privariam as comunidades locais da oportunidade de competir por investimentos e empregos”. Participação da comunidade Algumas comunidades não são necessariamente contra os data centers, mas querem ter mais voz no processo de planejamento. Em Harwood, na Dakota do Norte, a revelação de que um projeto de US$ 3 bilhões estava em andamento levou o morador Michael Swartz a tentar reformular a maneira como a cidade lida com o desenvolvimento industrial. Ele redigiu uma emenda à carta municipal que defende mais transparência e participação da comunidade nas decisões, depois que o prefeito de Harwood assinou um acordo de confidencialidade com a Applied Digital, que está construindo uma instalação nas proximidades. Os moradores levantaram uma série de preocupações quando os planos para o gigantesco projeto de 280 megawatts se tornaram públicos, em setembro de 2025, mas a construção começou menos de um mês depois. “Uma decisão de US$ 3 bilhões que afeta uma comunidade de 800 pessoas não deveria ter sido tomada em três semanas”, disse Swartz em entrevista. O objetivo de seu Artigo X, como a medida é chamada, é exigir a divulgação de informações, uma análise independente e a participação pública em grandes projetos. Medidas semelhantes podem dar mais influência a moradores de outras localidades. O eleitorado de Grove City, em Ohio, poderá alterar a carta municipal para exigir um referendo sobre empreendimentos que ultrapassem determinados limites de tamanho e de uso de água e energia. Se aprovada, uma iniciativa submetida à votação em Janesville, no Wisconsin, dará aos cidadãos o direito de votar sobre projetos com custos superiores a US$ 450 milhões em uma área há muito tempo abandonada onde funcionava uma fábrica da General Motors. A proliferação dessas medidas é “um sinal de que os americanos reconhecem que foram excluídos de negociações que têm um impacto real sobre seu futuro em muitas comunidades”, disse Mullin, da UCLA. Pumped-storage hydropower remains an established technology because it can store large amounts of electricity and release power when demand increases. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), the United States had approximately 23,156 MW of pumped-storage hydropower generation capacity across 18 states in 2025. artigo.texto: As global climate diplomacy shifts from promises to practical implementation, Niger State has an opportunity to position its emerging carbon market initiative as a vehicle for investment, job creation and sustainable development. For Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago, popularly known as the Farmer Governor, the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), scheduled for November 9–20, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, offers a strategic platform to advance the state’s green economy vision. The conference will bring together governments, investors, climate finance institutions, development partners and environmental experts to discuss practical responses to climate change. For Niger State, however, participation should go beyond showcasing its environmental ambitions. The priority should be to secure credible partnerships, develop investment-ready projects and establish a clear pathway for converting its natural resources into measurable climate and economic benefits. Governor Bago’s vision presents an opportunity to connect climate action with Niger State’s agricultural strength, forest resources, renewable energy potential and waste-management needs. If properly developed, these assets could support projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions while creating employment, improving energy access and strengthening rural livelihoods. Niger State’s participation at COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in November 2024 provided an earlier opportunity to promote its green economy agenda, including sustainable agriculture, renewable energy and forest conservation. COP31 should build on that engagement by moving from international advocacy towards practical project development and investment mobilisation. From Green Economy Vision to Carbon Market Investment Carbon markets provide a potential mechanism for financing projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. Under recognised crediting systems, a carbon credit generally represents one metric tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent reduced or removed, subject to the applicable methodology and verification requirements. For Niger State, opportunities could include methane capture at landfills, climate-smart rice cultivation, solar mini-grids and forest restoration. These initiatives could attract investors while supporting the state’s wider development objectives. However, natural resources alone do not guarantee carbon revenue. Projects must demonstrate credible emissions reductions, additionality, appropriate monitoring and independent verification. They must also comply with relevant national regulations and international carbon market requirements. This is particularly important as Niger State seeks to position itself as a pioneer in subnational carbon market development in Nigeria. The ambition to become the country’s first subnational government to open its carbon market to investment, and to advance towards international carbon-credit sales, could be significant. The proposed Niger State Carbon Market Office could play a central role by coordinating project identification, technical assessments, investor engagement, regulatory compliance and stakeholder participation. Its effectiveness will depend on a clear mandate, adequate expertise, transparent procedures and coordination with the relevant federal authorities. International cooperation could accelerate this process. In correspondence to the Niger State team concerning a post-feasibility mission action plan, myclimate’s Article 6 Bilateral Cooperation Team disclosed that a draft memorandum of understanding (MoU) on project development and carbon market activities was undergoing internal legal review, with the intention of finalising it before COP31. The correspondence, signed on behalf of the team by Nsikan-George Emana, Senior Project Manager for Bilateral Cooperation at myclimate, proposed November 12, 2026, for a strategic meeting with the Niger State Government, during which the parties hope to sign the agreement. The proposed engagement offers an opportunity to establish a framework for technical cooperation, project development and potential international market participation. Nevertheless, the MoU remains prospective until formally concluded, and its existence should not be mistaken for evidence that investment has already been secured or carbon credits sold. Niger State should approach the meeting with clearly defined priorities, including project timelines, financing arrangements, responsibilities, community safeguards and measurable implementation targets. Article 6 and the International Opportunity The proposed partnership is particularly relevant to Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which provides frameworks for international cooperation in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. At COP29 in November 2024, countries made significant progress on the rules governing international carbon trading and the UN-supervised carbon crediting mechanism. Under Article 6.2, countries can cooperate through internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, subject to applicable accounting and authorisation requirements. Article 6.4 provides a UN-supervised crediting mechanism, while Article 6.8 addresses non-market approaches. For Niger State, these frameworks could create opportunities to develop projects that attract international finance and contribute to Nigeria’s climate commitments. However, the state must work within Nigeria’s national climate governance arrangements. International transfers under Article 6 cannot be treated as an exclusively state-level transaction where national authorisation and accounting are required.
