artigo.texto: CAMPBELL COUNTY, Va. – A proposed data center development off Cabin Field Road in Campbell County continues to raise questions for county leaders and nearby residents. MESH Capital LLC proposed building three data centers, each approximately 150,000 square feet, on a 57-acre property between Cabin Field Road and U.S. Route 460. More than a year after the proposal first made headlines, construction has not begun. “The developers been radio silent since January. So we really don’t have any indication that they’re going to move forward on the project,” said Matt Cline, the Campbell County Board of Supervisors representative for the Concord District. The proposal first drew significant attention in October 2025, when the Board of Supervisors voted 5–2 against the original rezoning request following opposition from nearby residents. Read more about the original proposal and the October 2025 vote. However, the property’s zoning history has left questions about what could still happen. Cline says the developer applied under the county’s earlier zoning rules before additional restrictions were put in place. “As soon as that happened, they applied for a permit, which locked them into this new zoning before we could add the special use permit process that came on several months later,” Cline said. In December 2025, the county adopted an emergency ordinance removing data centers as a by-right use in heavy industrial zones. For now, county staff says there are no new applications under review. “Nobody has submitted applications for a data center. We’re not currently reviewing plans for a data center, and the property sits as is,” said Brian Stokes, Campbell County’s director of community development. Stokes says if the developer decides to submit plans, the project would need to go through technical reviews and obtain the necessary permits before construction could begin. He estimates that process could take around six months before construction activity starts. Residents concerned about potential impact For people who live near the proposed development, the concerns go beyond whether construction will begin. Members of the Trent family, who live in the neighborhood and asked not to appear on camera, say they are worried about potential noise, water use and the impact a data center could have on their homes and surrounding environment. “We’re not against data centers, but they need to be put where not close to communities and homes and stuff. I mean, you know, like down next to the river, somewhere like that. Not around homes,” members of the family said. The family also worries about what the development could mean for their future in the neighborhood. “It’s just sad. It was all coming to an end. We’re 84 years old,” they said. For now, the property remains undeveloped, and county staff says it has not received new applications for the proposed data center. 10 News will continue following the project and any updates from Campbell County.

artigo.texto: The New Zealand company Lightyears it obtained NZ$174 million in financing to expand its portfolio of solar energy projects and battery energy storage systems (BESS). The resources will allow progress in the development of more than 300 MW of energy infrastructure over the next five years. The deal combines Japanese investment and Australian financing. Obayashi Corporation will contribute NZD 74 million through an equity investment, while Infradebt will provide a NZD 100 million credit facility to support the company’s growth. Based in Auckland, Lightyears seeks to strengthen its capacity to develop and execute several energy projects simultaneously, expanding its presence in different regions of New Zealand. Obayashi and Infradebt back Lightyears expansion The agreement incorporates Obayashi Corporation, a Japanese group with operations in construction and infrastructure, as a strategic partner of Lightyears. For the Japanese company, New Zealand represents a priority market for expanding its investments in renewable energy. As part of the transaction, Lightyears will establish a new company called LYOC1, which will retain the rights to the solar projects included in the agreement. Obayashi will hold a 90% stake in this entity. The investment will be made progressively, as the facilities complete the various stages of development, this mechanism will allow capital outlays to be adjusted to the progress of each project. For its part, Infradebt, an Australian entity specializing in infrastructure financing, will provide a NZD 100 million credit line. The two companies have maintained a financial relationship since 2025. Matt Shanks, managing director and co-founder of Lightyears, noted that the backing of both partners will allow them to develop more projects simultaneously and accelerate the implementation of new energy facilities in the country. Lightyears has a portfolio of 338 MW in solar energy Currently, Lightyears has 65 MW of installed or under-development solar capacity, in addition to a portfolio of 28 projects totaling 338 MW, a base that supports its expansion plans for the next five years. The funding will enable the company to move forward with commercial-scale solar power plants and battery energy storage systems. Both technologies are part of the company’s strategy to expand its presence in the New Zealand electricity market. The combination of photovoltaic generation and BESS storage it will also allow for more flexible electricity management. The batteries store energy during generation periods and supply it later, although Lightyears has not yet detailed the power or energy capacity of the planned systems. Kuratau and Reefton are focusing on solar projects under development Among the company’s facilities, Te Aho o te Rā Solar Farm stands out, a 15 MW photovoltaic park located near Kuratau on the North Island. Its construction began in October 2026 through a collaboration with eight local entities linked to Māori land and investment. The facility will have an estimated annual production of 23.5 GWh, enough to supply approximately 3,300 homes. Its completion is scheduled for July 2027. Another important development is the 14 MW solar park in Reefton, located on the west coast of the South Island. The project is nearing completion and will contribute to the region’s electricity supply. Lightyears is also preparing a 6 MW photovoltaic installation connected to the local Electricity Ashburton grid, with which it will expand its activity in the South Island. The funding opens a new chapter for renewable energy in New Zealand The backing from Obayashi and Infradebt provides Lightyears with financial resources to advance its project portfolio and arrange for the construction of new solar facilities over the next few years. Founded by Matt Shanks and Sean Tobin, the company has been involved in the development of commercial-scale photovoltaic plants in New Zealand. Its new financial structure combines equity investment and specialized financing to support the growth of its operations. With the planned development of more than 300 MW of solar infrastructure and battery storage, Lightyears seeks to expand its stake in the New Zealand renewable energy sector. Achieving this goal will depend on the technical, financial, and construction progress of each facility. Source: Renewables Now Photo: Shutterstock

artigo.texto: O Ministério Público Federal (MPF) ajuizou uma ação civil pública contra a empresa BR Arbo Gestão Florestal e a certificadora internacional Verra, solicitando a suspensão do Projeto Mejuruá, iniciativa de créditos de carbono desenvolvida no município de Carauari, no interior do Amazonas. A ação aponta possíveis violações aos direitos territoriais de povos indígenas e comunidades tradicionais que vivem na região. Entre os problemas apresentados pelo órgão estão a sobreposição do empreendimento com áreas de ocupação histórica dessas populações, a ausência de consulta prévia e relatos de pressão sobre moradores para obter apoio ao projeto. O MPF também pede que as duas empresas sejam condenadas ao pagamento de R$ 6 milhões por danos morais coletivos, com recursos destinados às comunidades atingidas. O Projeto Mejuruá é uma iniciativa privada de manejo florestal e geração de créditos de carbono, na modalidade REDD+. O empreendimento abrange uma área declarada de aproximadamente 678 mil hectares, localizada nas bacias dos rios Juruá, Riozinho e Ipixuna. De acordo com levantamentos técnicos do setor de geoprocessamento do MPF, mais de 50% da área indicada pelo projeto apresenta sobreposição com territórios indígenas e de comunidades tradicionais. Desse total, 179.149 hectares, equivalentes a 26,38% da área, coincidem com o território das comunidades do Riozinho, representadas pela Associação de Moradores Agroextrativistas do Baixo Riozinho (Asmobri). Outros 38.856 hectares, ou 5,72%, correspondem a áreas tradicionais de comunidades do rio Juruá, representadas pela Associação de Moradores Agroextrativistas do Alto Juruá (Amab). A área restante identificada nos levantamentos apresenta sobreposição com territórios de ocupação tradicional do povo indígena Katukina, na região do rio Ipixuna. Segundo o MPF, a existência de registros de propriedade privada não elimina os direitos territoriais das populações tradicionais, que possuem proteção prevista na legislação brasileira e em tratados internacionais. Projeto teria avançado sem consulta às comunidades Outro ponto questionado na ação é a falta de consulta prévia, livre e informada às populações afetadas pelo empreendimento, conforme estabelece a Convenção nº 169 da Organização Internacional do Trabalho (OIT). O Ministério Público afirma que a BR Arbo negou formalmente o direito de consulta às comunidades ribeirinhas e não comunicou à Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas (Funai) a sobreposição do projeto com áreas de ocupação tradicional do povo Katukina. A ação também apresenta relatos de moradores sobre possíveis pressões para conseguir apoio ao empreendimento. Entre as situações mencionadas estão a oferta de benefícios materiais, como caixas d’água, kits de energia solar e antenas de internet via satélite. O MPF relata ainda a circulação de informações falsas sobre a regularização coletiva das terras, incluindo afirmações de que as famílias poderiam perder suas roças e áreas individuais. O documento também menciona áudios com ameaças de desapropriação e medidas judiciais contra moradores que se recusassem a assinar acordos de apoio ao projeto. De acordo com o órgão, os episódios contribuíram para ampliar os conflitos internos nas comunidades e dificultar a mobilização coletiva em defesa dos territórios. Verra também responde à ação A certificadora internacional Verra foi incluída no processo por manter os procedimentos de auditoria e validação do Projeto Mejuruá, mesmo após receber notificações das associações comunitárias e do MPF sobre as irregularidades apontadas. LEIA TAMBÉM: Professor que estuprava enteada desde os oito anos é preso em Parintins O Ministério Público também sustenta que o empreendimento não atende às exigências da Lei nº 15.042/2024, que instituiu o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa, e da Resolução nº 19/2025 da Comissão Nacional para REDD+ (Conaredd+). As normas estabelecem que projetos privados de créditos de carbono com sobreposição a territórios comunitários devem destinar pelo menos 70% dos benefícios financeiros diretamente às populações atingidas. Também estão previstas medidas de acompanhamento pelos órgãos competentes e a oferta de assessoria técnica e jurídica independente às comunidades. Na avaliação apresentada à Justiça, o MPF afirma que essas exigências não foram cumpridas pelo Projeto Mejuruá. MPF pede cancelamento de certificações Além da suspensão integral do empreendimento, o Ministério Público solicita que sejam interrompidas todas as atividades nas áreas de sobreposição com os territórios do povo Katukina e das comunidades tradicionais do Riozinho e do rio Juruá. O órgão também pede que os benefícios materiais já entregues aos moradores sejam mantidos, evitando possíveis retaliações e novos conflitos. Outro pedido é o cancelamento dos registros, auditorias e certificações relacionados ao projeto nas áreas indígenas e comunitárias. A ação ainda questiona uma decisão do Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público (CNMP), que suspendeu e posteriormente invalidou, no fim de 2025, uma recomendação extrajudicial do MPF sobre o caso. O órgão argumenta que a decisão desconsiderou dados técnicos sobre a sobreposição territorial e não ouviu as comunidades atingidas. Em fevereiro de 2026, a Corregedoria do MPF arquivou uma representação disciplinar contra o procurador responsável pela atuação no caso.

Among Korean companies, LG Energy Solution held on to third place with 81.9 GWh, up 0.7% from the same period last year, but its market share fell from 9.8% to 8.2%. artigo.texto: AMD posted a massive Q3 2026. Revenue hit $13.377 billion, up 45% year over year and 16% sequentially. Data Center revenue reached $8.546 billion, up 97% year over year. Embedded Revenue was up big, and client revenue fared better than Intel in many respects. AMD Has Record Quarter Driven By Data Center Here is AMD’s Q3 2026 summary slide. This is an enormous quarter. Embedded revenue was up 29% year over year, and yet that almost feels like a footnote. AMD delivered GAAP operating income of $2.832 billion on revenue of $13.377 billion, with net income of $2.428 billion and diluted earnings per share of $1.46. On a non-GAAP basis, which excludes stock-based compensation, amortization of acquisition-related intangibles and other items, operating income was $3.923 billion, net income was $3.471 billion and EPS came in at $2.09. Even the quarterly numbers were up a lot, with 16% growth on the GAAP side. AMD’s Data Center Is Big Time The Data Center segment generated $8.546 billion in revenue, up 97% year over year and 27% sequentially. AMD attributes this Data Center surge to strong EPYC demand and the launch of Instinct MI450 GPUs. The company says major clients, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, are running workloads on Helios rack-scale solutions powered by these chips. The comparison to Intel’s data center results from last week saw its quarterly revenue of $7.3 billion, up 78% year-over-year. AMD’s Data Center segment at $8.546 billion grew faster at 97%. Both companies are clearly seeing surging demand for AI infrastructure and server processors, but AMD seems to be accelerating. Venice is coming, and we expect AMD to have clear x86 performance leadership, as Intel’s PCIe Gen6 Diamond Rapids platform, we expect, will be later in 2027. On technical merits, we expect AMD to be in a great place, and it seems like AMD is better managing its supply to get chips out. AMD Client and Gaming Segment The combined Client and Gaming segment saw revenue down 8% year-over-year, at $3.722 billion. Client notched up a bit, while gaming went down. Memory and NAND prices are keeping a lid on this market. Of note, AMD said its Ryzen AI Halo Platform with the Ryzen AI Max Pro 400 series is not available, so that means Gorgon Halo? We will have our first Gorgon Halo review soon, as that machine is running benchmarks now. Somewhat notable on the slide is that AMD has three AI-related products highlighted, while Intel’s three summary bullets on its CCPG segment were focused on shortages, demand for future products, and a generic AI PC nod. AMD, with the Strix Halo platform, at least has something it can use to run reasonably large models locally, and you have to wonder if that is a driver here. AMD’s Embedded Grows The Embedded segment delivered $1.109 billion in revenue, up 29% year-over-year. AMD says growth came from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications and industrial end markets. Just as a frame of reference, Xilinx’s annual revenue was something like $3.1-3.2B when AMD completed its acquisition of Xilinx. In most markets, if you grow 29% year over year and see a huge margin increase, it is time to throw a party. This seems to simply offset client’s (gaming) weakness. AMD Q4 Guidance Points To Acceleration AMD expects fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of approximately $17 billion plus or minus 3%. At the midpoint, that represents year-over-year growth of about 66% and sequential growth of roughly 27%. If this quarter seems big, then next quarter seems like it will be significantly bigger. Final Words AMD has its Helios rack-scale infrastructure rolling out, and Venice. Ryan recently went into the Venice architecture. If AMD was ahead in many metrics with its Turin generation, then adding more cores, updated cores, and higher memory bandwidth should be a recipe for clear x86 socket leadership, at least until Intel is able to field Diamond Rapids. It will be interesting to see how much of a price premium AMD can extract for a generational advantage and first-mover status. Socket refresh generations are less exciting than the Turin-to-Venice transition, which is a major platform update (DDR5 channel count and PCIe Gen6). That also means PCIe Gen6 development, like PCIe Gen4, will likely happen more often on AMD than on Intel. Gluing chips together seems to be working out reasonably well.

artigo.texto: Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jumping 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock was up 8% in extended trading. Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter: - Earnings per share: $2.09 adjusted vs. $1.95 expected - Revenue: $13.38 billion vs. $13.09 billion expected Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement. Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius rallied earlier Tuesday and remained higher after AMD reported results. CEO Lisa Su said on the earnings call that she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI growth to accelerate even faster than the company had projected 90 days ago. The company expects data center to drive the majority of its revenue and earnings growth. "We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year," Su said on the earnings call. AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But Intel's stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand. The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago. After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October. "Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts. PC market struggles AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI. AMD is also a major player in the weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm-based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research. AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago. For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount. AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Meta, Microsoft, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering. AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering. During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung. In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications. artigo.texto: Shares of Elon Musk's SpaceX and Tesla fell in premarket trading Wednesday as the Democrats won a significant victory in the midterm elections. SpaceX was last trading down 3.8% and Tesla dropped 3.5% amid big losses for Republican candidates Musk had backed. Artificial intelligence stocks came under pressure overnight as Democrats — seen as proponents of data center moratoriums — won big in midterm elections in key data center hubs. The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk, where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats. SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet. Mixed moves for AI stocks The more direct plays were slightly down. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 2.6% and 2.8%, respectively. Peer Nebius Group was relatively flat and Oracle shed 1.3%. Tech giants Nvidia, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft were all up around 1-2%. AMD shares rose 6.8% after announcing earnings on Tuesday. Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 were flat. The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) was up 0.7%. Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow. Democrat Gina Hinojosa is the projected winner over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, according to the Associated Press. "The one thing that could really end up moving stuff though would be if Abbott were to lose Texas," said Scott Ladner, chief investment officer of Horizon Investments, earlier Tuesday as results rolled in. "Because there is a legitimate question about where do you build these data centers?" "Texas is a fertile ground for that. And if he were to lose, I think that fertile ground is largely barren. So, that's going to be a challenge," Ladner added. Hinojosa has been outspoken in her support of a moratorium on AI data centers. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State. 'Left-tail event' The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing. "We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week. Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo. Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end. "Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

artigo.texto: Data-center fury is a campaign dud See more of our coverage in your search results. Tales of data centers’ impact on this election may have been greatly exaggerated. For months, prominent outlets ran headlines like “Data centers have become political napalm. Election Day will show how far it’s spread,” “Data centers are galvanizing the midterms” and “How data centres became the sleeper issue that could decide the US midterms.” But all that outrage likely will not amount to much. In polls nationwide and in states where data centers have supposedly been a hot topic, such as Texas and Ohio, the issue consistently ranks among the least important to voters. In a CNN Texas poll last month, just 3% named the issue as their top concern; in Ohio, only 2% did. The polling — and guidance from political strategists — suggest that the media coverage and activist frenzy surrounding data centers simply isn’t moving the needle. It is a dramatic shift from earlier this year, when politicians across both parties raced to distance themselves from the industry. Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a pause on new environmental permits for data centers, while Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro removed them from his state’s fast-track permitting program. In Ohio, Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown attacked Republican Sen. Jon Husted for helping bring data centers into the state, while Husted introduced legislation aimed at protecting residents from higher electricity bills. Likewise, in Texas, Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico pushed for tougher restrictions on data-center development. But now? That has largely been forgotten, strategists say. “Candidates who made a data-center moratorium a pillar of their campaigns didn’t get much traction… centering on data centers is going to distract Democrats from the core issues that we know voters are deciding on,” said one Democratic strategist. “Candidates in these ‘data center’ races are primarily putting their ad money into messaging around the economy, corruption and healthcare.” “This is an issue that people are not voting on — nobody’s closing on data centers,” said one longtime Republican strategist who worked on Trump’s 2024 campaign. “For most voters, it’s an imaginary issue. It’s something that they’re just being told about, but it’s not something that is tangibly affecting their lives. The Republicans strategist notes that he advised candidates to stop discussing it and focus on issues that the majority of voters care about. That so much attention was paid to an issue voters actually care little about gives greater credence to the idea that foreign adversaries may have played a role in fomenting data-center anxieties. A Bitcoin Policy Institute report covered by The Post in July claimed that a China-linked network associated with far-left donor Neville Roy Singham Singham and the Party for Socialism and Liberation had inserted itself into local data-center fights across 14 states. The report credited those efforts with helping stall or block at least $23.6 billion in proposed investment through rallies, petitions, door-knocking and packed public hearings. Other data points also suggest foreign interference was a factor — like the fact OpenAI said it had banned accounts likely originating in China that used ChatGPT to generate anti-data-center comments and images. X identified roughly 200 accounts within a much larger Chinese bot network posting content aimed at influencing the American debate over AI and energy policy. To be sure, many Americans still resist these centers in their communities. Some experts caution that politicians have simply kicked the can down the road — and that the fight over data centers could return once the midterms are over. “23% of proposals for new data centers were suspended in competitive congressional districts… versus 13% nationwide,” Paul Renshaw said, based on data that his fact-checking outlet PressAudit compiled. But even he says this isn’t going to be an issue that has to last. In fact, simply rebranding could help dramatically. “People are surprisingly pliable and willing to change their minds… All of the data tells me that people just want a better deal, and they have the power to negotiate for it.” Still others are skeptical that data centers will return as a potent political target — and think the backlash could fade as communities begin to see the benefits. “It was always a fabricated issue… Once they start seeing the effects of [data centers] in their schools and in their local infrastructure, perception is going to change,” said, referring to the tax revenue and jobs that projects could bring. Maybe the answer is to build and bet on the future. If data centers haven’t moved the needle with voters as a threat, perhaps they will as a benefit.

artigo.texto: The Korea Consumer Agency (KCA) on the 4th ordered Mercedes-Benz Korea to pay 4 million won per owner, saying the company failed to properly disclose the manufacturer of its electric vehicle batteries. On this day, the Consumer Dispute Settlement Commission of the agency said that although Chinese Farasis battery cells were installed in five EQE and EQS models, the company explained them as if only CATL batteries were installed, and found it liable for damages. The compensation covers 142 buyers of the EQE 500 4MATIC SUV, EQE 53 4MATIC+, EQE 350+, EQE 350 4MATIC, and EQS 350 who applied for group dispute mediation in May. The panel considered that EV batteries are a core component directly tied not only to driving performance but also to safety, and a key factor that determines an electric vehicle's value. It also acknowledged that Farasis and CATL differ significantly in market share, recognition, and technological prowess. After receiving the decision from the agency, Mercedes-Benz Korea must notify the commission within 15 days whether it accepts the terms. If Mercedes-Benz Korea accepts, the decision takes effect as a judicial settlement. If it does not accept, Mercedes-Benz Korea does not have to compensate. In that case, consumers can file individual civil lawsuits. Han Yong-ho, chair of the agency's dispute mediation commission, said, "We hope Mercedes-Benz Korea will take a more proactive stance in resolving the dispute so that trust in German imports among Korean consumers can be restored."

artigo.texto: Among the nearly 100 pages of risk factors outlined in Anthropic PBC’s landmark initial public offering are the catastrophic threats to humanity that have grabbed headlines. However, it also flagged a more immediate concern that could derail business: mounting backlash against data centers. Public controversy and regulatory scrutiny over the environmental impact, land and water use as well as consumption of limited power resources threaten to delay or prevent data-center development, Anthropic said in the prospectus. That would raise costs and limit its ability to scale, develop and deploy artificial intelligence (AI) models, it says. The company is right to worry. Hatred toward data centers has united people across the political spectrum and around the globe. Warning that the technology could create existential risks probably does not inspire anyone to want to give the AI boom a physical address in their backyards. Illustration: Yusha Opposition to the build-out has surfaced in Australia, the UK and even rural China. Now, it is starting to fester in pockets of Japan, just as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is pushing massive investment. Meanwhile, Anthropic is reportedly in final talks with NTT Data Group to build one of the country’s biggest data centers near Osaka. Yet while anxiety around the technology runs high globally, the Japanese are unusually sanguine about it — robots are seen here more as friendly helpers such as Doraemon than The Terminator. For a smaller, relatively insular economy facing acute labor shortages and demographic pressures, the upsides could be enormous. Many of AI’s strengths neatly address Japan’s acute gaps: translation in a country that has been flooded with foreign tourists, software engineering in a tech industry historically stronger in hardware than coding, boosting efficiency for small and medium-size manufacturers, and easing administrative burdens for the growing cohort of elder caregivers. The list goes on. For now, Japan’s opposition is scattered and local, hardly close to the organized political movement we are seeing in the US. However, there was little excuse anywhere to be so caught off guard. I have been tracking the AI backlash for a while, and the industry’s implicit threat that this might kill us all or take your job has never been an effective way to greet new neighbors. Outside of the Silicon Valley bubble, data centers as the physical manifestation of an abstract tech revolution have become easy targets. It is more than noise, eyesore or water use. It is about having a say. This is partly why the US revolt goes far beyond NIMBYism. Nearly three-quarters of Americans oppose having a data center in their community, while two-thirds are against new ones anywhere. It is already having a material impact: In the first half of this year alone, at least 106 projects, representing about US$198 billion in investment, were blocked or delayed, the Data Center Watch said. It offers lessons for Tokyo to not assume these are just isolated groups of Luddites. Japan has the most favorable environment for data center development among the OECD markets in the Asia-Pacific region, given its established digital infrastructure sector, BloombergNEF assessed. It already has some 2 gigawatts of operating IT capacity, second in the region only to China. Local opposition is a lurking threat, but the more immediate constraint is power. These facilities guzzle enormous amounts of energy to run servers and cooling, and Japan has never been energy rich. Power demand from new data centers and chip fabs is expected to rise from less than 1 percent of the country’s electricity consumption this year to nearly 7 percent by 2035, SMBC Nikko analysts have said. Addressing this challenge could help catalyze a broader shift toward clean energy. The government, for its part, seems aware of the problem. Takaichi has pledged a “sufficient and stable supply of electricity” to meet the growing demands from data centers, doubling down on an earlier promise to “take all possible measures” to do so. The policy direction is right, if ambitious, but increasing investments in green energy would help Japan build resilience in the future, not just power these facilities. Currently, most data center capacity is concentrated in the Greater Tokyo region and Osaka. Mindful of risks in the event of earthquakes or other unexpected shocks, officials have identified potential future sites in Hokkaido, Kyushu and elsewhere. Spreading infrastructure beyond crowded urban areas would also reduce some of the nuisance complaints that have fueled opposition elsewhere. Japan was initially slow to adopt AI, but usage has finally surged. That delay could become a second-mover advantage that the country cannot afford to squander as investors start questioning the payoff from the expensive, hype-fueled AI infrastructure spree. The country has long excelled at developing infrastructure that works for people, from trains that run on time to urban design that fosters community. That could be a major advantage. If Tokyo can construct data centers without neighbors bringing out the pitchforks, it could define what comes next. Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. artigo.texto: BYD India, a subsidiary of BYD, the world’s No. 1 New Energy Vehicle (NEV) manufacturer,today announced that the BYD SEALION 7 has crossed 5,000 customer deliveries in India since its launch in February 2025. The SEALION 7 brings together ocean-inspired design and BYD’s battery and vehicle technologies, including Blade Battery technology and Cell-to-Body architecture. Its Premium variantpairs an 82.56 kWh battery with a claimed NEDC range of 567 km, while the dual-motor Performance variant delivers 390 kW of power and 690 Nm of torque, accelerating from 0–100 km/h in 4.5 seconds. Both variants feature a panoramic glass roof and a 15.6-inchrotating touchscreen. Commenting on the milestone, Mr. Rajeev Chauhan, Head of Electric Passenger Vehicle Business, BYD India, said, “The SEALION 7 has been one of our strongest-performing models in India, and we are proud of the response it has received from customers. This reflects the growing interest in electric SUVs that combine performance, technology and premium comfort.As we look ahead, our focus is on building on this momentum, strengthening the ownership experience and bringing more of BYD’s technology to Indian customers through a product portfolio that responds to their evolving needs.” In August 2026, BYD India introduced the SEALION 7 Dynamic at an introductory ex-showroom price of INR 41.90 lakh. Its 71.8 kWh Blade Battery offers a claimed NEDC range of 520 km, bringing a new entry point to the SEALION 7 range while retaining features such as the panoramic glassroof and rotating touchscreen. The SEALION 7 Festive Edition, launched in October 2026 at INR 50.60 lakh (ex-showroom), adds a Tan and Black interior to the Premium variant. Limited to 150 units, it also features quilted Nappa leather seats, a panoramic glass roof with an electric sunshade and a head-up display. The edition is part of BYD India’s Celebrate Your Dreams with BYD festive campaign. artigo.texto: - The all-electric Denza N9 features a tri-motor all-wheel-drive system with a combined peak output of 890 kW (1,194 hp). - The Denza N9 is currently available only as a PHEV, with a starting price of 409,800 yuan ($61,000). An all-electric version of the N9, the flagship SUV from BYD's (HKEX: 1211) premium brand Denza, has appeared in a Chinese regulatory filing, adding a new powertrain option to a model currently sold as a plug-in hybrid. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology published batch 413 of its new vehicle catalog for public comment on Wednesday, revealing key specifications of the large SUV. The public comment period runs from November 4 to November 10. Inclusion in the catalog is a regulatory step before a vehicle can go on sale and does not mean it has received final approval. The all-electric N9 features a tri-motor all-wheel-drive system with a combined peak output of 890 kW (1,194 hp), exceeding the 680 kW of the N9 plug-in hybrid flash charging edition launched in May. Its front motor has a peak output of 270 kW, while the rear left and rear right motors each deliver 310 kW. The filing lists a top speed of 240 km/h (149 mph). The catalog includes 2 model codes, QCJ6530ABBEV1 and QCJ6530ABBEV2, with identical dimensions, seating options and motor outputs. Both entries list 5- and 6-seat layouts. The vehicle measures 5,270 mm in length, 2,030 mm in width and 1,830 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 3,125 mm. Images in the filings show that the all-electric version retains the N9's overall exterior design and features a roof-mounted LiDAR sensor. A panoramic glass roof and power side steps come standard, while options include a two-tone body. The new vehicle uses a lithium iron phosphate battery with cells produced by FinDreams Battery, BYD's battery division. The filings do not disclose battery capacity, driving range or charging performance. Denza first launched the N9 in March 2025, entering the large luxury SUV market with the flagship model, initially offered as a 6-seat plug-in hybrid. On May 18 this year, Denza launched the N9 flash charging edition with a starting price of 409,800 yuan ($61,000), featuring BYD's second-generation Blade Battery and flash charging technology. The plug-in hybrid has a 75.3 kWh battery that delivers a CLTC electric range of 420 km (261 miles). Denza said at the time that charging from 10% to 97% takes just 9 minutes. ($1 = 6.7180 yuan)

artigo.texto: Dear Editor, As a parent and a teacher, I urge local leaders to demand accountability for data centers. Right now, big polluters are profiting while our families foot the bill. Data centers take up acres of much-needed land that could otherwise be used for affordable housing, education or agriculture. We need our rural landscapes to keep protecting wildlife and providing clean air and water. READ MORE The rush to power data centers is driving new fossil fuel development, threatening climate progress and bringing more toxic pollution to communities. Instead, we could be powering our lives with clean energy that protects our wallets, our climate and our health. The progress we have made in the last 20 years in restricting emissions and reducing pollution will be reversed, especially if data centers are gas powered. This shouldn’t be a difficult choice. Let’s hold data centers accountable with common-sense guardrails now. Anne D’Olivo Manchester, Vt.

artigo.texto: A Chinese green tech company has recently made history with the launch of the world’s first commercially deployed, fully integrated 800-volt direct current (DC) power system at a massive artificial intelligence (AI) data center. Shanghai’s Envision Energy announced the technology on Monday, November 2. It is currently powering live computer workloads at the company’s Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China. The platform combines solid-state transformers, battery energy storage, as well as smart controls to deliver electricity from the grid to computing equipment. As per company representatives, it could cut energy loses, lower infrastructure costs, and support more powerful AI servers within the same space. Kevin Huang, Envision Energy’s senior VP, pointed to the technology’s potential. “AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage, and the grid to meet computing demand,” Huang explained. Powering AI servers As AI data centers expand, they require more electricity to run. Reports show that global data center power demand could surge by 160 percent by 2030. Moreover, research suggests data centers alone could require as much as 68 gigawatts (GW) of capacity worldwide by 2027, roughly equivalent to California’s power grid. More from Energy See All But delivering that power efficiently remains a massive challenge. Traditional data center power systems utilize multiple conversion stages to deliver electricity from the grid to servers. These stages require additional equipment, cables, and space. To address these challenge, Envision came up with a new system that can convert electricity directly from a 10-kilovolt (kV) medium-voltage input to an 800-volt DC power system. It reduces the need for extra equipment and copper cables, leaving more room for computer hardware. To maintain a stable electricity supply, the firm integrated solid-state transformers with battery energy storage. The batteries can also respond to sudden changes in power demand within seconds and provide backup power for several minutes. At the same time, Envision’s Dubhe Controller, coordinates both the transformers and the batteries through its Dubhe Energy Foundation Model. As a result, the system can respond to rapid changes in electricity demand within milliseconds. Targeting more power Envision’s Galaxy AI data center campus began operations in August 2026. It has a planned capacity of three gigawatts (GW). Once fully developed, the facility is expected to support up to one million AI accelerators operating simultaneously. Huang said the system uses renewable energy to power AI workloads. “This is a critical step in turning power-compute coordination from a strategic vision into an operational reality,” he concluded in a press release. In the future, the company aims to source more than 80 percent of the campus’s electricity through direct renewable energy connections. The power architecture could serve as a reference for other data centers as the industry moves toward 800-volt DC infrastructure. “Already operating commercially ahead of wider industry adoption, the system provides a reference for the industry’s transition to 800V DC,” the firm stated. It also aims to expand the technology via its Mission Gobi initiative. It targets five GW of green AI data center capacity across desert regions worldwide by 2030.

artigo.texto: A Google energy executive has told reporters that data centers in orbit can cost up to 100 times more than the same capacity on the ground, according to a report from The Information. We could not open the original paywalled story, so the executive’s name, the exact wording and the method behind the 100x figure remain unconfirmed in this article. What we can verify is the surrounding picture: Google’s own researchers, outside engineers and rival space firms all agree that orbital computing costs more than terrestrial computing today, and they disagree mainly on how much more. The timing matters. Google launched its first Project Suncatcher test satellite on Oct. 1, 2026, and the spacecraft started answering prompts within weeks. We covered that milestone when the first orbital TPU replied with a haiku. Now the company’s own energy leadership is putting a hard price warning on the idea, just as investors weigh a record wave of earthbound data center spending. This analysis lays out what is known about the claim, how it compares with other published estimates, why launch economics dominate the math, and what the number means for cloud buyers who plan capacity over the next five years. It also offers five predictions and a short FAQ. Throughout, we attribute figures to the outlet that published them and label our own arithmetic as arithmetic. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Google’s Energy Chief Reportedly Said About Space Data Centers The headline claim is simple. An energy chief at Google said space data centers can cost up to 100 times more than data centers on Earth, and The Information carried the story. The phrase “up to” matters. It signals a ceiling for the worst case rather than a central estimate, and it likely reflects a spread of scenarios that depend on launch price, satellite lifetime and how much compute each satellite carries. We searched for the underlying text and found no public version of it. Searches for the 100x phrase surfaced only unrelated uses of the number, such as one startup’s plan to give its second spacecraft 100 times the power generation of its first. That absence does not make the claim false. Paywalled scoops often circulate for days before other outlets match the details. It does mean readers should treat the multiplier as reported rather than independently confirmed. One more caution applies. A cost multiplier on its own says little without a baseline. A 100x premium over a cheap grid-connected hall in Iowa is a different statement from a 100x premium over a 2030 gigawatt campus with its own nuclear supply. Until the original report’s assumptions surface, the safest reading is directional: Google’s energy side sees orbital compute as far more expensive than the ground option for now. How 100x Compares With Other Published Estimates The 100x figure sits at the extreme end of a wide range. IEEE Spectrum estimated that designing, building and launching a one-gigawatt orbital data center would cost more than $50 billion, based on a network of about 4,300 satellites and including five years of operating costs. The same analysis put a comparable terrestrial facility at roughly $16 billion. That is a premium of about three times, not one hundred. Skeptics quoted in 2026 coverage land in the same neighborhood. A roundup of the sector reported that critics calculate orbital compute at roughly three times the cost per watt of ground equivalents. Proponents argue the opposite direction. Starcloud, a startup that already flew an Nvidia H100 in orbit, claims unit economics near $0.05 per kilowatt-hour that would make orbital capacity competitive with terrestrial power by the early 2030s. Elon Musk has said space-based solar data centers could beat ground ones within two to three years, a timeline that CNBC’s June 2026 analysis called disputed. Read together, the table shows a spread of two orders of magnitude, from parity to 100x. The spread exists because each party picks a different launch price, hardware life and workload. That makes the 100x figure less a rebuttal of Google’s own research than a different slice of the same model, run with pessimistic inputs. Why Launch Cost Drives the Gap Nearly every serious analysis starts with price per kilogram to low Earth orbit. Google’s researchers argued that orbital computing approaches parity with ground data centers on a cost-per-kilowatt basis once launch falls to about $200 per kilogram. Coverage of the original Suncatcher research put today’s Falcon Heavy price near $1,500 per kilogram, and projected a drop toward $200 by around 2035. Other published ranges run from about $1,000 to $2,900 per kilogram depending on vehicle and customer, and one 2026 sector roundup cited about $2,700 per kilogram for Falcon 9. Simple division shows how sensitive the result is. At $2,700 per kilogram, launch costs run 13.5 times the $200 target. At $1,500 they run 7.5 times. Launch is only one line item, because hardened chips, solar arrays, radiators, inter-satellite links and replacement flights add cost on top. A pessimistic stack of those items is how an analyst could reach a very high multiple. Back-of-envelope arithmetic (ours, not a forecast) Launch price vs. Google's $200/kg parity target $2,700 / $200 = 13.5x $1,500 / $200 = 7.5x Capacity cost for a 1 GW site, using IEEE Spectrum's terrestrial baseline $16B x 3 = $48B (close to IEEE Spectrum's "over $50B") $16B x 100 = $1.6T (what a literal 100x would imply) The $1.6 trillion line is the useful sanity check. No credible developer plans a gigawatt of orbital capacity at that price, so a literal 100x would describe a scenario nobody intends to build. It is a warning about what happens if launch prices stay flat and satellites fail early, not a quote for a project. Launch supply is the second constraint. Quilty Space analysts have warned the industry may fall about 150 launches short

artigo.texto: A Anatel apresentou problemas de solvência para pagar as suas contas básicas o que pode impactar um dos seus projetos mais importantes, o de um data center próprio. De acordo com reportagem da Folha de S. Paulo veiculada nesta terça-feira, 3, a agência precisa de R$ 30 milhões para honrar compromissos. Desde maio deste ano, a entidade está com um contingenciamento de R$ 52 milhões por restrição orçamentária. Essa restrição afeta também outros órgãos do governo que buscam se adaptar aos cortes na máquina pública. Porém, isso gera impacto em suas operações. É o caso do centro de dados, um contrato assinado em dezembro de 2025 e que dura até 2030 por R$ 45 milhões. Esse data center é crucial para o armazenamento e acesso a dados do ecossistema de telecomunicações nacional, com informações de operadoras e usuários, por exemplo. Vale lembrar que grande parte dos dados da Anatel são abertos e podem ser acessados via painéis e outros sistemas na nuvem. Em resposta ao Mobile Time, a Anatel informou que até o momento, “as medidas adotadas têm buscado mitigar os impactos decorrentes de restrição orçamentária imposta à agência”. No entanto, o órgão regulador afirmou que “a persistência das restrições orçamentárias e financeiras poderá exigir novas medidas de reprogramação de despesas”.

artigo.texto: A migração para a inteligência artificial exige uma infraestrutura redesenhada, segundo especialistas que participaram de um painel do Roadshow Embrapii, realizado nesta terça-feira, 4, em Campinas/SP. Um dos pontos que precisam passar por mudança, segundo Gerson Freire, enterprise architect da Dell, é a estrutura de fornecimento de energia elétrica, que precisará ser dimensionada para atender à alta demanda das GPUs. De acordo com Waldir Campos, head de operação da TERRANOVA, houve uma explosão no consumo de energia pelos racks. Atualmente, cada um precisa de algo em torno de 300 Kw. Campos e Freire avaliam que o mercado enfrenta o desafio de manter esses ambientes críticos em pleno funcionamento sem interrupções no fornecimento de energia ou falhas térmicas. O executivo da Dell explicou que, no Brasil, o modelo de refrigeração mais comum é o a ar. No entanto, racks de alta densidade costumam utilizar refrigeração líquida, tecnologia que, segundo ele, tende a se tornar o padrão. Além disso, Freire considera necessário desenvolver redes especializadas para atender às demandas da IA, com altíssima capacidade de transmissão de dados (throughput) e latência mínima. Além dos desafios de infraestrutura, há outro obstáculo: a mão de obra. Para Campos, a escassez de profissionais qualificados pode dificultar a expansão dos data centers na América Latina. Nesse contexto, parcerias com instituições de ensino locais podem ser uma alternativa, já que muitas instalações estão situadas em regiões do interior dos países. “De forma geral, precisamos planejar a infraestrutura de IA como um projeto integrado, que deve entregar resultado”, afirmou Freire.

artigo.texto: Egypt’s Battery Manufacturing Industry Targets EVs and Energy Storage as Investment Plans Advance – Expert View by Spherical Insights RELEASE DATE: Nov 2026 Author: Spherical Insights Request Free Sample Speak to Analyst Egypt has announced a series of battery-manufacturing and energy-storage projects in 2026, led by a BME–CATL plant targeting 1 GWh of annual capacity and a US$200 million Kemet–Cornex storage-battery facility planned at 5 GWh. Together they link electric mobility with renewable-energy storage. Egypt’s battery-manufacturing ambitions moved forward on 13 September 2026, when BME Battery Manufacturing and China’s CATL signed a contract, witnessed by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, to establish an electric-battery plant. The project carries an initial investment above EGP 2 billion, about US$39 million, and a first-phase capacity of 1 GWh a year, with batteries for heavy commercial vehicles as the initial focus. The agreement forms part of a broader series of developments announced in 2026. In January, Kemet Industries agreed to a US$200 million energy-storage battery facility with a Chinese technology partner. In June, AMEA Power and its partners signed contracts covering 1,500 MWh of storage projects and a separate factory designed to produce 3,000 MWh of storage systems annually. Sungrow broke ground on a storage-systems plant with planned annual capacity of 10 GWh in August, while Mansour Group and Tianneng signed a memorandum of understanding in September to explore battery-manufacturing opportunities. These developments connect two markets: batteries for electric mobility and battery systems for renewable-energy storage. The projects remain at different stages, ranging from signed agreements and construction starts to exploratory partnerships. What Is Driving Egypt’s Battery Manufacturing Push? Two policy priorities are supporting Egypt’s battery-manufacturing ambitions. In the automotive sector, the National Automotive Industry Development Programme aims to raise local value-added content to 60 per cent, strengthen domestic component production and attract international manufacturers. Industry Minister Khaled Hashem described the BME–CATL agreement as a step towards developing local battery capabilities as demand grows for electric vehicles and energy-storage technologies. In the power sector, battery storage can help integrate renewable electricity and improve grid flexibility. Egypt commissioned its first utility-scale battery energy-storage system, a 300 MWh facility connected to the 500 MW Abydos solar plant in Aswan, in July 2025. The government subsequently announced a target of 14,320 MWh of battery-storage capacity, with official reports citing both 2028 and 2029 as the deadline. AMEA Power’s two contracted projects total 1,500 MWh, equivalent to approximately 10.5 per cent of that target; the comparison reflects planned project capacity, not completed national progress. How Does the BME–CATL Partnership Support Local Production? BME (Battery Manufacturing Egypt) was established by commercial-vehicle manufacturer MCV and Auto D. The contract was signed by BME chairman Maged Wahib and CATL international investment director Luo Haining. CATL will provide battery technology licensing, production equipment and training, while BME builds and funds the plant and sources battery cells from CATL. The first phase targets 1 GWh a year for heavy commercial vehicles. A second phase would lift capacity to 5 GWh, five times the initial level, and extend into passenger-car batteries and storage systems for solar and wind power. The project targets 40 % local content, covering assembly, battery-management-system integration, thermal management and final system integration in Egypt, and it is planned to serve domestic and international markets. Prime Minister Madbouly said the government wants to accelerate implementation and move quickly to the next executive steps. Ready to lead the Egypt’s Battery Manufacturing Industry Targets EVs ? How Are Battery-Cell Manufacturing and Systems Assembly Developing? Egypt’s planned battery projects cover different stages of the battery value chain, from battery-pack assembly to cell manufacturing and stationary energy-storage systems. The BME–CATL partnership will use CATL-supplied cells for locally assembled battery packs, while Sungrow and AMEA Power are advancing storage-system manufacturing plans. The Kemet–Cornex agreement adds another stage through a proposed US$200 million battery-cell facility targeting an annual capacity of 5,000 MWh (5 GWh). The project also aims to use locally sourced materials and components while transferring manufacturing technology to Egypt. Announced in January 2026 during Electricity Minister Mahmoud Esmat’s visit to China, the Kemet agreement formed part of a broader US$700 million investment package, including a separate US$500 million solar-cell manufacturing complex involving GCL Group. Together, these projects reflect Egypt’s efforts to expand domestic renewable-energy equipment production, attract international investment and develop technical capabilities through technology partnerships. Their eventual contribution will depend on implementation, production timelines and the extent of local manufacturing. Which Projects Are Expanding Renewable-Energy Storage? artigo.texto: A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) alertou o governo federal para o risco de não conseguir pagar todos os seus compromissos até o fim de 2026. A preocupação inclui R$ 30,76 milhões em notas fiscais pendentes relacionadas à aquisição do próprio data center, em Brasília, estrutura que sustenta sistemas digitais usados por cidadãos, operadoras e pela fiscalização do setor. O alerta foi revelado pela Folha de S.Paulo nesta terça-feira (3). O problema está relacionado a um bloqueio de R$ 51,83 milhões no orçamento da agência, que reduziu em aproximadamente 19% os recursos disponíveis para custeio e investimentos. Resposta rápida: a Anatel enfrenta um problema de recursos para honrar despesas, mas não há informação de desligamento do data center ou de interrupção nacional da internet e da telefonia por esse motivo. O risco relatado até agora diz respeito aos compromissos financeiros e à possibilidade de precisar reprogramar atividades e pagamentos. A falta de dinheiro da Anatel pode deixar o Brasil sem internet ou celular? Não há indicação de que isso vá acontecer. A Anatel regula e fiscaliza os serviços de telecomunicações; as redes que levam internet fixa, 4G e 5G ao consumidor são operadas pelas prestadoras. O data center citado na reportagem sustenta sistemas da própria agência, não toda a infraestrutura de conectividade do país. Por isso, é importante não confundir risco orçamentário com uma falha técnica confirmada. Até a divulgação das informações, não foi anunciado um apagão da internet, a paralisação das redes móveis ou o desligamento do centro de dados em decorrência dos pagamentos pendentes. Se as restrições financeiras persistirem, poderão surgir consequências para contratos e atividades administrativas e digitais da agência. Mas afirmar que um serviço específico ficará fora do ar exigiria uma confirmação que ainda não foi apresentada. O que faz o data center da Anatel e por que ele é importante? Um data center reúne equipamentos e sistemas que armazenam, processam e disponibilizam informações. No caso da Anatel, o centro de dados de Brasília dá suporte a serviços públicos digitais, a operações utilizadas pelas empresas de telecomunicações e a ferramentas de fiscalização, segundo a apuração da Folha. Entre as atividades relacionadas à infraestrutura de tecnologia da agência estão: - Atendimento ao consumidor: sistemas para registrar e acompanhar reclamações contra operadoras, como o Anatel Consumidor; - Atividades regulatórias: procedimentos digitais usados pelas prestadoras e no licenciamento de estações; - Fiscalização: ferramentas de trabalho e processamento de informações usadas para acompanhar o cumprimento das regras do setor. A existência de pagamentos pendentes não comprova, por si só, indisponibilidade desses serviços nem comprometimento de dados pessoais. Também não foi relatado um incidente de segurança ou vazamento decorrente do bloqueio de verba. Por que a Anatel tem R$ 30,76 milhões em pagamentos pendentes? O valor está associado à aquisição de um novo data center, contratada em dezembro de 2025 por R$ 44,95 milhões, com vigência até dezembro de 2030. O acordo abrange equipamentos, sistemas de gerenciamento, conectividade, implantação, migração, manutenção, suporte e garantia. Segundo a reportagem, os R$ 30,76 milhões ainda pendentes são classificados como restos a pagar, expressão usada para despesas de exercícios anteriores que continuam sem quitação. Isso não significa que todo o valor contratado tenha vencido de uma só vez, nem comprova que o fornecedor tenha suspendido o serviço. Na semana passada, o presidente da Anatel, Carlos Baigorri, pediu ao Ministério do Planejamento o desbloqueio de R$ 30 milhões. Em agosto, a agência havia solicitado antecipar R$ 23,3 milhões previstos para dezembro, mas o pedido não foi atendido pelo Tesouro Nacional, de acordo com a Folha. Quanto foi cortado do orçamento da Anatel em 2026? A Anatel atribui o aperto financeiro a um bloqueio de R$ 51,83 milhões, definido pelo governo federal em maio. A restrição atingiu o orçamento discricionário, destinado às despesas de funcionamento e a investimentos. Os dados expõem duas situações distintas: a redução do espaço orçamentário para custeio e investimentos e a necessidade de recursos financeiros para cumprir compromissos assumidos. A Anatel publica seu plano orçamentário no portal oficial, enquanto a restrição financeira relatada nesta semana foi detalhada pela Folha. O que dizem a Anatel e o Ministério da Fazenda? Questionada sobre o assunto, a Anatel informou à Folha que revisou contratos, projetos e despesas para reduzir o impacto do bloqueio e evitar custos adicionais, como multas e juros. A agência alertou, porém, que a continuidade das restrições poderá levar a novas mudanças na programação de gastos. O Ministério da Fazenda explicou que os limites de despesas integram a gestão do Orçamento federal e são reavaliados periodicamente. A pasta também afirmou que os pedidos de antecipação de recursos precisam considerar a capacidade de pagamento futura dos órgãos, para não comprometer os meses seguintes. Quando o governo vai decidir se libera mais dinheiro? A próxima avaliação das restrições orçamentárias está prevista para 24 de novembro de 2026, quando a Junta de Execução Orçamentária deverá reexaminar o espaço fiscal para eventual redução dos bloqueios. Isso não é garantia de liberação dos R$ 30 milhões pedidos pela Anatel. A decisão dependerá da avaliação do governo e das condições do Orçamento. Enquanto isso, a agência afirma estar ajustando suas despesas para reduzir impactos. Como reclamar de problemas com internet ou celular na Anatel? Para quem enfrenta um problema real de conexão ou cobrança, o procedimento continua sendo procurar primeiro a operadora, guardar o protocolo de atendimento e, se necessário, recorrer à ouvidoria da empresa. Se a questão não for resolvida adequadamente, o consumidor pode registrar uma reclamação na Anatel. - Entre em contato com a sua

artigo.texto: A lawsuit seeking to reverse the Sangamon County Board’s April 7 approval of zoning to allow for construction of a data center could hinge on the court’s interpretation of the word “shall” within the county’s data center code. Circuit Judge Adam Giganti, at the conclusion of an Oct. 30 hearing on motions to dismiss the suit, said he’s “going to take the matter under advisement and will render a decision as soon as possible.” The July 6 lawsuit was originally filed against Sangamon County and the County Board by residents who live approximately a mile or less from the site. They are seeking to overturn the county’s approval of the project, claiming procedural violations and unchecked environmental concerns. The Sangamon County Board approved a conditional use permit on April 7 that would allow a data center to be constructed on 280 acres of farmland by a vote of 17-10, with one board member abstaining. Amongst other things such as lack of a noise study and pollution concerns, the suit claims the approved zoning petition had insufficient documentation as required by the County Code’s own language stating “(t)he petition for a conditional permitted use for a data center shall include… letters from the serving utility companies indicating the availability and adequacy of utility services.” The County Board approved the zoning petition despite the electricity utility letter submitted referencing a different data center project altogether and the water utility letter stating it was still reviewing CyrusOne’s application. The County Board’s lawyers argue that the Board was “conditionally approving the (conditional use) permit contingent on future submission of these materials.” The Rural Electric Convenience Cooperative will-serve electricity letter, dated Aug. 26, 2025, makes no mention of CyrusOne but it does say the electric co-op will provide electricity to a different, substantially smaller project called the Diamond Core Data Center. The Jan. 29 Apple Creek Water Cooperative letter included in the zoning petition states the water utility is still reviewing CyrusOne’s application. Apple Creek Water Cooperative referred Illinois Times to its attorney from Rammelkamp Bradney but multiple voicemails left for Bradley Wilson were not returned. In court, the county’s lawyers from Champaign law firm Webber & Thies argued the plaintiffs’ “artful pleading” is because the residents are simply upset with the outcome of April’s vote. The lawyers say the county had plenty of reason for approving the data center through the potential for economic incentives, so the lawsuit should be terminated. “The County Board here or the legislature or whatever legislative body it is has policy power. They have the right to legislate. They are making decisions. They are the people’s representatives. The ordinary citizen’s remedy – if they disagree with that decision – is political,” said attorney Daniel Thies during the Oct. 30 hearing. “We don’t want ordinary citizens who have lost in the political process to be able then to hold out the legislators. “The county’s legislative body can decide that it’s going to value economic development more than the potential for a little bit of pollution. That is a prerogative of the people’s representatives through their elected body,” Thies said. The county’s own staff report shows about $71 million of projected property tax revenue would go to three taxing bodies based in Macoupin County, with six Sangamon-based taxing districts expected to split roughly $27 million over a 20-year period, if all assessments go according to plan. Sangamon County itself could expect to see just over $445,000 for 20 years in annual tax revenue, though some large data centers in northern Illinois and other parts of the country have later appealed for property tax reductions. Meanwhile, no state or local sales tax will apply to any of the anticipated $500 million investment since CyrusOne secured a tax break before Gov. JB Pritzker’s executive order to pause a state program providing deals to developers went into effect. As for property value concerns, Thies said the existence of a data center could lead to nearby property value increases with the potential for neighboring data center developments. “There was testimony of a real estate appraiser who studied this question and determined that the surrounding property values, in fact, would not be depressed and very well could rise as they have adjacent other data centers that have been built around the country,” he said. Chloe Russell, a Plainfield lawyer representing members of the Caruthers family, who have farmed land in southwest Sangamon County for close to two centuries, and Cathy Bettis, owner of Joette Kennel, argued Oct. 30 the complaint is not contending issues with the county’s reasoning but “it pleads the county’s violations” of “mandatory petition elements. “On the utility letters, both defendants point to the conditions in the approval order requiring updated and definitive will-serve letters before a building permit is issued. Those conditions prove our point. If the letters had been adequate, no condition would have been needed,” she said, before pointing out how each will-serve letter does not comply with the county’s own code. “The ordinance says the petition ‘shall include,’ before the board acts. artigo.texto: Company leverages expanding residential solar platform and long-duration energy storage capabilities to capitalize on rising demand for reliable, cost-effective power NEW PORT RICHEY, Fla., Nov. 02, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Zeo Energy Corp. (Nasdaq: ZEO) ("Zeo,” "Zeo Energy,” or the "Company”), a provider of residential solar and commercial long-duration energy storage ("LDES”) solutions, today outlined its strategy to drive growth across its two complementary business segments, leveraging continued momentum in residential solar and an expanding pipeline of commercial energy storage opportunities supporting data centers and other energy-intensive applications. Zeo's growth strategy builds on its vertically integrated residential solar platform, which generated 9.2% year-over-year revenue growth during the first half of 2026 despite broader industry headwinds, alongside its commercial energy storage business. Together, these businesses position Zeo to address increasing demand for affordable, reliable and flexible energy solutions across residential and commercial markets. "We see significant opportunities to create value across both sides of our business,” said Tim Bridgewater, Chairman and CEO of Zeo Energy. "Our residential solar platform continues to demonstrate its resilience in a challenging market, supported by a differentiated sales model and disciplined operating approach. At the same time, our commercial energy storage business is positioning us to address growing demand for dependable power solutions, particularly as data center development places increasing pressure on traditional grid infrastructure.” Residential Solar: Driving Growth Through a Differentiated Operating Model Zeo's residential solar business generated $29.4 million in revenue during the first six months of 2026, with second-quarter revenue increasing 23% sequentially. The Company achieved this growth despite a challenging industry environment characterized by elevated financing costs and reduced residential solar activity. The Company's vertically integrated operating model encompasses customer acquisition, system design, permitting, installation and ongoing service, providing greater control over the customer experience and operational execution. Zeo's differentiated direct-sales organization, supported by investments in technology and AI-enabled customer relationship management tools, is designed to improve productivity and enhance operating efficiency. Zeo maintains a disciplined regional growth strategy, concentrating its residential solar operations in select markets, including Virginia, Ohio, Illinois and Pennsylvania, alongside its established presence in Florida. The Company believes this targeted approach enables it to leverage existing infrastructure, optimize customer acquisition costs and expand its presence in attractive markets. The residential solar market also presents a significant long-term growth opportunity. With approximately 8% penetration among an estimated 95 million U.S. homes, compared with approximately 15%-25% penetration in certain international markets, the Company believes substantial runway remains for domestic adoption. Rising utility rates, growing interest in energy independence and the continued development of residential financing solutions are expected to support demand over time. Commercial Energy Storage: Addressing Growing Data Center Power Demand Through its commercial division, Zeo is developing an energy storage business focused on long-duration solutions for data centers, utilities and other commercial and industrial customers. The Company's commercial strategy emphasizes behind-the-meter power infrastructure designed to deliver reliable, continuous electricity while incorporating renewable energy generation and storage technologies. Zeo is particularly focused on opportunities involving smaller and midsized data centers with power requirements of approximately 20 to 50 megawatts, where flexible energy infrastructure can help address grid capacity constraints and accelerate access to power. Zeo's commercial engineering team is evaluating a range of LDES technologies, including molten salt, compressed carbon dioxide and alternative battery chemistries, with an emphasis on applications requiring approximately 10 to 14 hours of energy storage duration. The Company is currently pursuing approximately six commercial projects at various stages of development, reflecting growing demand for distributed power infrastructure and long-duration energy storage solutions. Among these opportunities is Zeo's previously announced non-binding memorandum of understanding with Creekstone Energy to explore the development of approximately 280 megawatts of energy generation and storage capacity for a planned data center campus in Millard County, Utah. The proposed development would incorporate solar photovoltaic generation and storage as part of a subsequent phase of the project's behind-the-meter power infrastructure. Zeo is also evaluating additional opportunities in Utah and other markets where data center expansion is creating demand for reliable, scalable power solutions. Multiple Growth Drivers Supported by a Strengthened Balance Sheet Zeo is pursuing a multifaceted growth strategy designed to capitalize on opportunities across its residential and commercial businesses while maintaining financial discipline. In residential solar, the Company is focused on expanding its sales organization, increasing productivity in existing markets and introducing complementary offerings, including roofing and HVAC services. These additional services are intended to leverage Zeo's established customer relationships and infrastructure to generate incremental revenue opportunities.
