artigo.texto: Brookfield is targeting a massive artificial intelligence data center in the north of England, as Europe scrambles to develop infrastructure to support the rollout of AI amid high energy and land costs. Energy company Drax Group said Tuesday it has signed an agreement with Brookfield and the asset manager's neocloud platform Radiant to jointly develop an AI data center on the Drax Power Station estate in North Yorkshire. London-listed shares of Drax were up 8.8% in early morning trading. The project is initially targeting up to 100 megawatts of capacity to be operational from the first quarter of 2028, with an additional 500 MW of capacity to be brought online between 2028 and 2031. It is then looking to secure more than 1 gigawatt of capacity at the site by an unspecified date. Brookfield estimates total investment, including semiconductors, could exceed £20 billion ($26.8 billion), with an initial £2.5 billion investment in phase 1. "This is a unique opportunity for the UK's AI ecosystem to build at scale," Radiant CEO Mahdi Yahya said in a statement. "By designing, building and operating from the UK, it will give British researchers, startups and enterprises access to frontier compute at home." The first phase of Brookfield's project in North Yorkshire will use power from the grid and target commercial customers from early 2028. The initial phase is subject to planning, regulatory and network approvals from the government and relevant agencies, alongside securing a tenant for the project, Drax said in a statement said. The company added that final investment decisions are yet to be made. Europe's AI data center push While the U.S. has surged ahead on developing the huge data centers needed to power AI, Europe has been slower to break ground on the facilities. The U.K. in particular has struggled with high energy costs and challenges with long waiting times for businesses to connect to the grid. In October, it was reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid. An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC at the time that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site." Unlike the U.K., the Nordics benefit from abundant power and available land. Countries in the region, like Finland, have seen major commitments to develop AI data centers this year. In September, Google said it would invest at least 13 billion euros ($15.1 billion) into AI infrastructure in the country, marking the tech giant's largest single investment in Europe.

In addition, HiNa Battery is partnering with Qingli Special Vehicle Group to develop sodium-battery-based special-purpose sanitation vehicles, including street sweepers and food waste collection trucks. Sodium-ion batteries are noted for their excellent low-temperature performance as a key strength. Tests on large commercial vehicles demonstrated that they maintain over 90% of available capacity even in extreme environments at minus 40 degrees Celsius. artigo.texto: They all spiked: Construction of data centers and power plants; orders for equipment at US manufacturers; and inflation in construction. By Wolf Richter for WOLF STREET. Data center construction spending spiked by another 8.6% in September from August, and by 90% year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $96 billion, according to construction data from the Census Bureau today. Since the beginning of 2021, the annual rate of construction spending on data centers has spiked by 950%. The AI data center construction boom is continuing along a near-exponential curve. Nothing that needs to be funded can grow on an exponential curve for long. But the inflection point imposed by capital constraints hasn’t come yet. The big 12 AI companies are still raising massive amounts of money, more than they’re spending, and have already accumulated an unused war chest of $1.1 trillion in cash and cash equivalents, much of which they can spend even if tanking market make further fund raises too difficult (my analysis). Not even local resistance on the ground by people, municipalities, and state governments have managed to slow the overall growth of data centers though they have delayed or stalled one or the other project. Data centers, their demand on power, their effect on electricity prices, and related issues have entered midterm election rhetoric, but that issue will fade in a couple of days. Construction is the cheap part of data centers. These amounts only reflect the construction costs of the buildings, the improvements around the buildings, and the equipment integrated into the buildings, such as HVAC systems. Not included is the expensive part of a data center: The servers and racks, electronic and optical equipment to connect the servers to the internet, the electrical equipment to supply the servers with power, including in many cases onsite power generators. The construction spending trend – though only a slice of total investments in data centers – is a good indicator about future demand for equipment needed to turn an empty building into an operating data center. Construction spending on power plants and distribution infrastructure rose by 0.9% in September from August and by 11.1% year-over-year to an annual rate of $192 billion. Since the beginning of 2021, the spending rate has increased by 63%. Power plant construction spending includes the costs of the power generation equipment. Factory construction spending has been roughly stable over the past three months at an annual rate of $170 billion, and that was up by 128% from the beginning of 2021. But it has fallen off the construction boom levels a few years ago. This is still a massive amount of factory construction spending, 76% higher than data center spending. And it indicates that expansion of the US manufacturing capacity continues at a breakneck pace. Equipping a modern factory, including semiconductor plants, is by far more expensive than the costs of construction of that factory. Once the factories are built and equipped and production starts, their real contribution to the economy and employment begins and continues for decades. Building a factory is not a one-time shot but a long-term contribution to US production. It’s not the construction spending that matters to the economy, but the future production that will come from these new factories. Shockwaves of demand for US manufacturers. Demand for the equipment that is needed for data centers, power plants, and factories has sent a shockwave of demand through the industrial economy. Orders received by manufacturers in the US of “core capital goods” (durable goods without defense and aircraft) spiked by 10.4% year-over-year in September, to $88 billion, according to separate data from the Census Bureau in October. This category includes manufacturers of factory equipment, construction machinery, computers and electronics, electrical equipment, fabricated metal products, farm implements, appliances, heavy-duty trucks, railroad rolling stock, ships, etc. Orders for machinery spiked by 16.1% year-over-year, to $46.0 billion. This has data centers, power plants, and factories written all over it. Industries in Machinery Manufacturing (North American Industry Classification System, NAICS, code 333) includes manufacturers of: - Engine, Turbine, and Power Transmission Equipment - Ventilation, Heating, Air-Conditioning, and Commercial Refrigeration Equipment - Machinery for Construction, Agriculture, and Mining - Industrial Machinery - Commercial and Service Industry Machinery - Metalworking Machinery - Other General-Purpose Machinery. artigo.texto: The Westbrook City Council voted unanimously Monday night to prohibit standalone data centers . The city updated its land use ordinance to remove the use of data centers from the Rock Row Contract Zone. However, it still allows data centers as an accessory use, like server rooms and IT rooms for hospitals and other large organizations. Previously, the Rock Row Contract Zone was the only place data centers were permitted, and the city’s ordinances didn’t include any additional standards for data centers beyond a usual site plan review. Mayor David Morse said he supported the ordinance amendment and noted substantial concerns about data centers, such as electricity and water demands, noise and infrastructure burdens. “First and foremost our resources and infrastructure need to support the people who live here, our existing businesses, and the housing and economic opportunities our community needs,” Morse said. “Resource-consuming data centers are simply not a good fit for Westbrook.” In June, the Westbrook City Council passed a 180-day data center moratorium on data centers, though the city hadn’t received any applications to build such a facility like some of its neighbors had. During the moratorium, the planning board was tasked with reviewing the city’s ordinances and providing a recommendation. It recommended only permitting data centers as an accessory use and updating the city’s definition of a data center. Westbrook now defines data centers as “one or more buildings or spaces on a property that house networked computer systems and associated equipment, such as servers, network hardware, data storage, power generation or cooling systems, to process and manage data.” Cities and towns across the state have passed temporary moratoriums, and in a handful of others, voters will decide on their ballots Tuesday to temporarily or permanently ban data centers.

artigo.texto: Após a aprovação do Redata gerar uma euforia inicial com uma potencial onda de investimentos em data centers no País, a demora na regulamentação da lei está acendendo um sinal de alerta. Até o momento, nenhum novo projeto foi anunciado – e a consultoria Rystad Energy acaba de reduzir suas projeções para a instalação de data centers no Brasil em dois terços: de 21 gigawatts para 7 gigawatts até 2035, citando a falta de detalhes sobre os critérios para enquadramento no plano de incentivo fiscal. A proposta original do Governo para o Redata beneficiaria apenas data centers que contratassem 100% de sua energia com fontes renováveis. No Congresso, o texto foi alterado para contemplar projetos com fontes “de baixa emissão”. O Ministério de Minas e Energia defendeu publicamente que instalações movidas a gás pudessem ser enquadradas na lei, com essa nova redação. Mas o Ministério da Fazenda tem defendido limitações ou compensações para o uso do combustível fóssil, fontes a par do assunto disseram ao Brazil Journal. Um decreto presidencial detalhando as regras para enquadramento não foi publicado até o momento. "Ainda está pendente uma decisão do Poder Executivo sobre se a geração a gás natural se qualifica como energia de baixa emissão, além de detalhes críticos sobre métricas de eficiência energética, conteúdo local e verificações de compliance", disse a VP e chefe de Novas Energias da Rystad, Marina Domingues, num relatório. Em sua análise sobre o Redata, ela também citou a concorrência por espaço na rede elétrica para conexão dos data centers e potenciais limitações no acesso a energia firme como fatores que aumentam o risco para o desenvolvimento de projetos no País. A Rystad mapeou 20,8 GW em potenciais data centers previstos inicialmente para implantação no Brasil até 2035. Um número que despenca para uma estimativa de 6,7 GW quando ponderados todos os riscos. Nas contas da consultoria, mais de 10 GW em projetos são “de alto risco” e quase uma dezena de GW são de “médio risco”. Se considerados apenas os data centers de baixo risco, a capacidade do País ficaria praticamente estável na próxima década. Além da regulamentação, que depende do decreto presidencial, o Redata ainda deve exigir algumas definições no âmbito de agências reguladoras, de acordo com a Rystad. “Destravar investimentos em hyperscales exige que o Congresso e o Poder Executivo alinhem os prazos dos incentivos fiscais definidos em lei com definições regulatórias que ainda precisam ser escritas,” disse a consultoria.

artigo.texto: Texas Is Becoming A Hotspot For AI Data Centers, And It's Not Just About Cheap Land The Lone Star State, already home to hundreds of AI data centers, is set to open hundreds more in the coming years. Texas currently has over 300 operational data centers and around 250 under-construction or planned ones, for a total of 561 facilities, many of which are concentrated in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. Land availability and cost are certainly important factors, but there are other reasons that explain why Texas is such a desirable market for data center investors. According to commercial real estate and investment firm CBRE, as of April 2026, 78% of investors viewed Dallas-Fort Worth as the "most attractive market" for data center development thanks to power availability and cost, fiber Internet availability, and lower natural disaster risk than other parts of the country. Much of the state, including major cities, has a deregulated energy market that allows homes and businesses to choose their supplier rather than having to rely on a local utility company. It's a system that's intended to provide options to consumers and promote competition, but, in practice, often leads to higher costs. Texas is also known for its lax, business-friendly regulations and has tried to make itself more appealing to data center investors with a state sales tax exemption for data centers. While announcing a $40 billion Google investment intended to boost the state's AI infrastructure, Governor Greg Abbott called Texas "the epicenter of AI development," framing the deal as a job-creating opportunity. While the state might appear an ideal frontier for the AI data center boom, these facilities are facing increasing amounts of backlash from ordinary Texans. Data centers are increasingly unpopular By now, you're probably aware of the multitude of issues that make data centers controversial, such as resource consumption that drives up utility prices (especially in places where resources are already strained) and creating pollution that contributes to climate change. AI data centers have also driven a memory chip shortage that has led to skyrocketing consumer tech prices and come with unexpected consequences like threats to zoo animals and livestock. That's why increasing numbers of people are pushing back against proposed data centers and calling for more regulation on existing ones. Opinions on data centers and their impact are becoming increasingly negative, and elected officials on the local and state level are starting to take note. In July, New York became the first state to put a one-year moratorium on new data centers as the state develops regulations to make them less disruptive and destructive. As of this writing, 16 states have introduced legislation targeting new projects, though several have already failed. Even Gov. Abbott, currently locked in an unexpectedly close gubernatorial race, has changed his tune. In August, the governor mandated a comprehensive audit for all proposed data centers, and in September, he halted all data center permits until the audit is completed. These executive orders are essentially a moratorium on all projects in Texas, which is a major shift in under a year and reflects the public's growing distaste for data centers and their proponents. What other states are seeing data center booms? It's worth mentioning that counting data centers is difficult, as there's no universal definition for what a data center even is. On top of that, they're measured differently; some only count operating data centers, while others go by power consumption or size. Before the moratorium, Texas was on track to become the state with the most data centers by the end of the decade, but it may remain in second place for longer to Virginia. According to the U.S. Data Center Map, which measures active, under-construction, and planned facilities, Virginia has 591 data centers to Texas' 561. In a distant third is California with 343 data centers, followed by Ohio (238) and Georgia (232). The gap between Virginia and Texas could widen depending on how long the audit takes. In the previously mentioned CBRE survey, 72% of investors viewed Northern Virginia as an appealing market for data centers. That said, Virginia is also tightening regulation in response to public outcry. In September, Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced comprehensive data center accountability standards, and a newly introduced state Senate bill that would put a moratorium on new approvals already has bipartisan support. As for power consumption, it's true that everything is bigger in Texas. The state's data centers have a reported power total of 103.7 GW, 10.5 GW of which comes from operational facilities. Virginia is second at 40.6 GW total and 9 GW active. Pennsylvania comes next at 23.4 GW total, though just 328.6 MW of that's from operational data centers. Only counting active ones, Georgia comes in third at 2.5 GW.

artigo.texto: A Melbourne-developed battery that can power a home or be taken on the road is moving towards local production, backed by $6.77 million in funding support from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA). Clutch Industries will establish and operate a scalable manufacturing line in Victoria for its portable PowerNet battery—a modular4 kWh battery made using solid-state battery cells. Related article: Western Australia to lead nation in plug-in solar and batteries The solid-state battery architecture delivers a safer, lighter, and a more compact energy storage system. PowerNet units can be combined to form a household energy storage system or used individually to power caravans, 4WDs, boats and other off-grid applications. Clutch Industries CEO Brad Davis said, “Clutch Industries has a long history of Australian manufacturing, and through our Density battery business, we’re building on that experience to develop next generation energy storage solutions right here in Australia. ARENA’s support will help us take the next major step in scaling up local battery manufacturing. “Our vision for Density goes well beyond a single product. We’re unlocking product innovation, using breakthroughs in battery technology to create solutions that were previously impractical or simply not possible. “With Density products already available through major Australian retailers, we’re excited to continue expanding the brand, growing our manufacturing capabilities and bringing Australian-developed battery technology to more consumers.” The project is expected to help move the technology from product development into scalable Australian manufacturing. Testing will also provide practical evidence about the battery’s real-world performance. Related article: Solar sharing tech wins Good Design Award of the Year The project is being supported through ARENA’s Battery Breakthrough Initiative.

artigo.texto: As a lifetime organizer, my colleagues and I have proven the cliché — “you can’t fight City Hall” — wrong. Whether that City Hall was in New York, Jersey City, Chicago, Baltimore, Philadelphia, D.C., or a dozen other places, we repeatedly won, often over the initial opposition or indifference of mayors and governors. But City Hall is no longer the primary locus of power. Today it is in the unprecedented concentration of money and influence represented by a handful of tech companies based in Silicon Valley. Their dominant role, decades in the making, through Republican and Democratic administrations, has now peaked. So is it time for a new cliché — “you can’t fight Big Tech?” That’s certainly what the tech industry would like people to say. And their wholly owned subsidiary, called the Trump administration, parrots and promotes this line. But, once again, I would take a breath and look at the facts. Here’s one: in 2026, approximately $260 billion in data center construction was stopped in its tracks, according to a study done by Heatmap. For a while, it looked as if projects propelled by trillions in investment dollars, unlimited demand from AI companies, local municipalities desperate for tax revenues, and unions eager for work were unstoppable. But the momentum has already slowed. And the pace of the rejection of new centers has increased because of good, solid local organizing. Everything about this situation is familiar to me. As an organizer with a Metro Industrial Areas Foundation affiliate in Jersey City, Interfaith Community Organization, I was part of an effort that exposed the presence of toxic hexavalent chromium in Jersey City. A team of leaders — the Rev. Willard Ashley, Fr. Geoff Curtiss, the late Myrtle Smith, along with Metro IAF organizers Joe Morris and Stephen Roberson — patiently documented the damage done in Jersey City. Honeywell and PPG each had left tons of toxic chromate waste in the soil and drinking water of Jersey City. Untold numbers of workers and residents had contracted cancer and respiratory conditions. The kids who used the playing fields developed sores on their arms and legs. Fishermen ate fish that sickened them. The state, even under the so-called environmentalist Gov. Jim Florio, either showed no interest or actively cooperated with the polluting companies. The revolving door between state environmental officials and company executives spun constantly. In the long run, none of that worked. Our team sued Honeywell. And a federal court ordered Honeywell to spend $400 million to clean the 100-acre Bayfront site — with the company removing more material, 1.5 million tons, than was taken from the World Trade Center site. A second company, PPG, then settled for $600 million, and is finishing the clean-up of its 100-acre site. The data center cowboys use the same playbook. Avoid accountability. Sign non-disclosure agreements with municipalities. Provide no reasonable estimate of environmental dangers, of increases in water and energy costs, of health risks. Run your diesel generators with impunity, as one Virginia data center just did, forcing residents to flee. New York’ governor, Kathy Hochul and N.J. Gov. Mikie Sherrill have shown that they understand the games played by these companies and are demanding accountability. What the chromium story shows is that endless money and wired relationships only go so far. Nothing is inevitable if elected leaders and organized residents take the initiative and stop data centers in their tracks. It would be far better to halt and properly regulate these centers now, before they inflict the kind of damage the residents and workers of Jersey City endured, than after more harm is done to our kids and grandkids. Gecan is a senior advisor at Metro Industrial Areas Foundation and the author of “Going Public.”

artigo.texto: De acordo com os novos regulamentos, o Presidente do Comitê Popular Provincial tem autoridade para aprovar o registro de projetos, a alteração do registro de projetos, mudanças nos componentes participantes, o cancelamento do registro de projetos e a emissão de créditos de carbono no âmbito do mecanismo nacional de troca e compensação de créditos de carbono. É importante destacar que as organizações e agências participantes do projeto, dentro do escopo especificado, podem submeter suas candidaturas diretamente, via correio, no Centro de Atendimento da Administração Pública Provincial, ou online, através do Portal Nacional de Serviços Públicos e do aplicativo nacional de identificação. Em determinados casos de cadastro no Sistema Nacional de Cadastro, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província receptora é responsável por conceder a abertura da conta e enviar as informações ao órgão ou organização competente, no prazo de 5 dias úteis a partir da data de recebimento da solicitação; em caso de recusa, o motivo deve ser claramente justificado. O decreto também especifica os procedimentos e prazos para o processamento de pedidos de projetos de geração de créditos de carbono. Especificamente, o prazo para notificar a validade do pedido é de 3 dias úteis; o prazo para divulgar o pedido e consultar a opinião pública é de 22 dias úteis. Para projetos implementados em várias províncias, o registro exige o consenso das localidades relevantes. Após a conclusão das etapas de consulta, avaliação e análise, conforme prescrito, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província que receber a solicitação decidirá sobre a aprovação do registro do projeto e sua publicação no Sistema Nacional de Registro. Para procedimentos relacionados à alteração de participantes do projeto, o tempo de processamento não deverá exceder 7 dias úteis a partir da data de recebimento da solicitação; o procedimento para cancelamento do registro do projeto deverá ser concluído em um prazo não superior a 22 dias úteis. Com relação à emissão de créditos de carbono, o Decreto estipula claramente os documentos necessários, a responsabilidade pela obtenção de pareceres dos órgãos competentes e o prazo de processamento. No prazo de 10 dias úteis a partir da data de recebimento dos pareceres dos órgãos e organizações competentes, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província que recebeu a solicitação deverá decidir sobre a emissão dos créditos de carbono e publicá-los no Sistema Nacional de Registro; caso o crédito não seja emitido, os motivos deverão ser claramente justificados. Para projetos de carbono florestal, os procedimentos de registro, ajuste, cancelamento de registro e emissão de créditos são realizados de acordo com o Decreto Governamental nº 180/2026/ND-CP, de 21 de maio de 2026, que regulamenta os serviços de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono florestal. O Decreto nº 396/2026/ND-CP entra em vigor a partir de 12 de dezembro de 2026.

artigo.texto: A single large AI data center can use as much electricity as tens of thousands of homes, and residents in a growing number of communities worry about what that could mean for their utility bills. That concern has carried over from public hearings into tomorrow’s midterm elections. Recent polls show majorities of Democrats and independents, along with a sizable share of Republicans, oppose new data centers in their areas. That leaves candidates in both parties answering questions about projects once courted by state and local leaders. Supporters say the facilities bring jobs, tax revenue and an advantage in AI development. Further, a new poll from ABC News, the Washington Post and Ipsos found that a majority of Americans (57%) believe AI is bad for society, with many more pointing to its dangers than the potential benefits the tech could bring. An even larger number of those polled (66%) are opposed to the construction of new data centers in the US, and more (72%) would be opposed if it were in their community. More from CNET Opposition to AI crosses party lines. The technology has faced a surge in public disapproval this year, putting political candidates on blast and potentially affecting outcomes in key races, political and polling experts told CNET. Ambivalence about AI also feeds into negativity toward data centers, which have, in a short time, become a rare bipartisan issue everyone’s talking about, according to Christopher Lee, partner and senior political strategist for Foresight Strategic Advisors. Lee, who has closely followed election trends in southwestern states such as Nevada and Arizona, said the issue of data centers — massive AI server and compute farms that consume vast electricity and water resources — is going to “hammer” some candidates, especially those who weren’t transparent with constituents in the past about the cost to communities. If a politician voted for the construction of a data center earlier this year, their “political career is going to run into a stone wall,” he said. Reading the room The ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos survey asked a wide range of questions about how Americans will vote in the midterms and what they think of the political parties. Alongside the economy, immigration and the war against Iran, the AI rollout is a critical issue. As noted by CNET reporter Katelyn Chedraoui, AI regulation and data center construction have been the subject of controversy, protests and increased legal action in communities. The poll confirmed as much: 67% of respondents felt the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI, with risks including widespread job losses, psychological dependency, economic inequality and even human extinction. Fears and negativity toward AI also extend to the election process itself, with AI election interference among Americans’ top 10 fears for 2026. A national PR campaign funded by tech leaders and supported by the Trump administration, meant to tout the alleged benefits of data centers, such as job creation and technological advancements, doesn’t seem to be having the intended effect. Some politicians, especially those running for congressional seats, seem to be better at reading the room. According to Lindsey Cormack, an associate professor of political science at Stevens Institute of Technology and co-host of the podcast Government That Doesn’t Suck, many candidates are paying close attention to how they communicate about AI developments, with a particular focus on the problems they present rather than the benefits they provide. “It’s difficult to persuade people with promises of economic development when they’re worried about their electricity bills or water supply,” she said. Cormack, creator of the congressional newsletter archive DCinbox, has tracked a sharp rise in lawmakers linking data centers to consumer energy costs. In an email to CNET, she noted that between January and September 2025, just 5% of Republican newsletters discussing data centers mentioned electricity bills or ratepayers (4 of 76). Over the same period in 2026, that figure surged to 54% (97 of 180). Democrats showed a similar focus, with 40% of their data center newsletters (71 of 176) raising the issue in 2026. The midterms won’t be the end of the battle. AI and data centers are “going to be an issue in 2028 and 2030 and way beyond that,” Lee said.

artigo.texto: OpenAI quer chamar “campus de IA” aos data centers A OpenAI estará a preparar uma campanha para mudar a forma como os americanos veem a inteligência artificial e até o nome dos seus data centers poderá ser alterado. Neste artigo encontras: A empresa estará a ponderar a expressão “AI Compute Campuses”, ou “campus de computação para IA”, numa altura em que cresce a oposição local às enormes instalações necessárias para alimentar os seus modelos. OpenAI quer mudar a imagem dos data centers A proposta, divulgada pelo Axios, faz parte de uma estratégia de comunicação mais ampla. A OpenAI pretende destacar os benefícios económicos dos projetos e responder às críticas relacionadas com o consumo de energia, a utilização de água e o impacto nas comunidades. Segundo a empresa, a nova designação descreve melhor infraestruturas que combinam capacidade de computação, energia e criação de emprego especializado. Na prática, porém, a mudança de nome não altera a dimensão nem o funcionamento dos data centers. Por que motivo existe resistência? Os centros de dados dedicados à inteligência artificial exigem grandes quantidades de eletricidade e água. As comunidades próximas também têm levantado preocupações sobre ruído, poluição, aumento das faturas de energia e falta de transparência nos processos de aprovação. Um inquérito citado pela publicação Redfin indicou que 47% dos americanos questionados se opõem à construção de um novo data center nas suas comunidades. Negociações realizadas através de acordos de confidencialidade têm aumentado ainda mais as dúvidas dos residentes. A oposição já teve consequências concretas. De acordo com o mesmo relatório, pelo menos 19 municípios do Michigan avançaram com restrições a novos projetos. No norte da Virgínia, a Amazon terá abandonado planos para quatro data centers após contestação local. O impacto político da inteligência artificial Chris Lehane, responsável global pelos assuntos públicos da OpenAI, considera que as eleições intercalares norte-americanas serão uma espécie de antevisão do debate presidencial de 2028. A inteligência artificial deverá estar no centro da discussão devido ao seu possível impacto no emprego, na economia e no ambiente. A empresa também quer promover medidas de proteção para sistemas avançados, comparando-as a “limites de velocidade” aplicados à tecnologia. Microsoft e outras empresas seguem caminho semelhante A OpenAI não é a única tecnológica a tentar melhorar a relação com as comunidades onde instala a sua infraestrutura. A Microsoft anunciou uma abordagem centrada nas comunidades, incluindo a promessa de compensar aumentos nos custos de eletricidade associados aos seus data centers e investir em infraestruturas locais. Outras empresas estão igualmente a apostar numa nova linguagem para descrever a corrida à inteligência artificial. Jensen Huang, da Nvidia, já usou a expressão “fábricas de superinteligência” para falar de data centers, enquanto a Meta criou uma unidade dedicada à superinteligência. Um novo nome chega para resolver o problema? A mudança para “campus de IA” poderá tornar a comunicação da OpenAI mais positiva, mas dificilmente eliminará as preocupações das populações. Os residentes continuam a exigir respostas sobre o consumo de recursos, os benefícios locais e os riscos ambientais. Para conquistar apoio, a empresa terá de ir além da publicidade: acordos públicos, dados verificáveis e compromissos claros poderão ser decisivos. Como reconheceu Lehane, as comunidades devem responsabilizar as empresas e garantir que estes projetos trazem benefícios reais. Fonte: Tom's Hardware

Nov 2, 2026 New Mexico Community Center Gains Solar Resilience A building that began as a one-room schoolhouse has grown over the decades into a lifeline for a New Mexico community far from city infrastructure, and a recent solar installation has added resilience to the site. According to Solar Power World, the structure now houses the Ojo Sarco Community Center, which was founded in the early 20th century in an unincorporated community of about 300 people roughly 43 miles northeast of Santa Fe. Carol Miller, a grant writer and board member for the center, described the community as lacking political voice and having lost resources over the years, including its post office. She said residents must commute for nearly everything, with a round trip for basic amenities taking about 40 minutes. The community center has sought to fill those gaps with services including a twice-monthly food bank, summer meal programs for children, safety classes and resident outings such as a night at the opera. The center also recently met all the qualifications to become a state library. PPC Solar, also known as Paradise Power Company, of Taos, built a 7.5-kW solar project paired with 10.6-kWh of LFP energy storage at the center at no cost to the community. The contractor donates a solar array to a regional nonprofit each year, and the Ojo Sarco Community Center was awarded the project after three years of applying. CEO Daniel Weinman said his father founded Paradise Power Company in the 1970s and that the company has installed solar in off-the-grid communities since its start. He said the annual nonprofit donation program has run for more than a decade and has served farming organizations and land conservation groups, among others, with the aim of finding the right fit and making a good impact. For this project, he said resiliency was the best way to do that. Solar Power World spoke with PPC Solar and center organizers about the project's effect since it was built in fall 2025. Larry Miller, project manager and board member, called it a transformative project for the small community and said the solar panels are now part of the center's history and are pointed out to visitors. Carol Miller said the installation has lowered electric costs, which matters for a shoestring operation. She said internet remains available even when the power is out, that children attending library programs are solar oriented, and that the company and its staff have had ripple effects throughout the broader community. Preston Bastardo, who works in sales and design at PPC Solar, said mounting the array on the roof presented challenges that required exploring the attic to land things where needed. He said the building has two large areas and that installation of the batteries faced restrictions, but a mechanical closet was suitable for them. For backup circuits, the project used a partial facility backup with a critical loads panel next to the main panel, and he said everything went smoothly. Weinman traced the effort to the company's roots, noting that in 1972 there was no technology supporting solar and that his father developed his own controls and safety protections, found used panels and batteries, and brought power to places without it. He said his own home started with kerosene lanterns and did not have electricity until a solar power system was installed, which he described as life changing. He said building on that legacy and offering systems to communities that need them adds to it and is profound, and that the company wants to continue participating however it can. Carol Miller said the community is very old and proud of it. Having worked with local businesses and its electrical cooperative, she said owning its power makes the community an exception rather than the rule, and that any technology shared equally in a low-income community has ripple effects beyond what some imagined years ago. artigo.texto: BOTETOURT CO., Va. – Botetourt County, its Board of Supervisors, its Economic Development Authority and a shell company owned by Google are facing a lawsuit over a planned 312-acre Google data center project. The 72-page lawsuit, obtained by 10 News, was filed by a Botetourt County resident who alleges the county violated the Virginia Freedom of Information Act (VFOIA) when it adopted key agreements related to the project without adequately disclosing the actions to the public. The lawsuit argues VFOIA requires local governments to identify the subject matter being discussed during closed meetings. It alleges the Board of Supervisors failed to properly do so before discussing and adopting the Performance Agreement Resolution and the Performance Agreement (two key contacts for the project). The lawsuit asks the Botetourt County Circuit Court to declare the two actions null and void, prevent the Board of Supervisors from taking further action on the performance agreement and related resolution and take back any action take on the Performance Agreement after June 24, 2025. This would include rescinding the expedited permits issued to Google and Google’s eligibility to participate in the Botetourt County Third Party Inspection Program. It would also require the board to follow VFOIA when adopting similar resolutions. Botetourt County officials released the following statement in response to the lawsuit: “As this matter involves pending litigation, Botetourt County will not comment on the specific allegations or discuss legal matters. The County respects the legal process and remains committed to providing accurate and appropriate information to the public as the matter moves forward.”

artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil: país vira válvula de escape dos EUA Com comunidades em todos os Estados Unidos rejeitando data centers, cresce a pressão política para limitar sua construção. Mas, a milhares de quilômetros de distância, o maior país da América do Sul já é um dos principais mercados de IA e está facilitando a chegada de grandes projetos. O Brasil tem sido cortejado pelas gigantes do setor para a construção de grandes projetos de data centers, e pode se tornar uma válvula de escape para a demanda reprimida nos EUA. Por que data centers são importantes? Os data centers são a espinha dorsal da economia digital, abrigando servidores que processam desde transações bancárias até modelos de inteligência artificial. No entanto, essas estruturas consomem enormes quantidades de energia e água, gerando controvérsias em regiões onde a infraestrutura elétrica já está sobrecarregada. Nos EUA, a resistência local tem levado a restrições e atrasos em projetos, o que abre espaço para outros mercados. O Brasil, com sua matriz energética majoritariamente renovável e território vasto, desponta como destino natural para esses investimentos. A fonte não detalhou os números exatos de consumo, mas especialistas apontam que a disponibilidade de energia limpa é um diferencial competitivo. Brasil já é potência em IA Os brasileiros enviam 215 milhões de mensagens ao ChatGPT por dia, segundo a OpenAI, o que torna o país o terceiro maior mercado do criador do chatbot em número de usuários semanais, atrás dos Estados Unidos e da Índia. Esse volume massivo de interações demonstra a familiaridade da população com ferramentas de IA e a demanda crescente por infraestrutura local. O Google disse que planeja dobrar sua infraestrutura de nuvem no país até 2030 em resposta à crescente demanda, e chegou a assinar um acordo de patrocínio com a Confederação Brasileira de Futebol em março para integrar o Gemini às seleções nacionais masculinas, femininas e de base. A iniciativa reforça o interesse estratégico da big tech no mercado brasileiro. Incentivos fiscais impulsionam o setor Uma lei sancionada pelo presidente Lula reduziu impostos de equipamentos para data centers, tornando o ambiente de negócios mais atrativo para investidores estrangeiros. A medida busca equiparar o Brasil a outros países da região que já oferecem condições tributárias mais favoráveis. Com uma população de quase 215 milhões de pessoas distribuídas por uma área maior do que a dos 48 Estados contíguos dos Estados Unidos, o Brasil faz sentido como um país a ser cortejado pelas empresas de hiperescala. A combinação de mercado consumidor robusto e incentivos governamentais cria um cenário promissor. Demanda local versus transferência de operações A demanda local, e não a transferência de operações de empresas americanas para o exterior, impulsionou grande parte do crescimento dos data centers na América Latina. Mas Carlos Barrera, CEO da Atlas Renewable Energy, acredita que isso pode mudar. “De fato, vemos a região como uma válvula de escape atraente para algumas das restrições de capacidade que vocês estão vendo agora nos Estados Unidos”, disse. Essa visão é compartilhada por outros analistas. “A reação negativa nos Estados Unidos não está tanto expulsando as empresas de hiperescala do país, mas direcionando-as para onde a energia estiver disponível primeiro”, disse à Fortune James Mercer, diretor da Metro Colo Advisory, empresa de consultoria em data centers. Ou seja, o Brasil pode captar projetos que seriam inviáveis em solo americano devido à escassez de energia ou à oposição comunitária. Desafios: energia e impostos Mas a eletricidade barata do Brasil também pode ficar mais cara. Barrera disse que o Brasil precisará de mais linhas de transmissão para conectar grandes data centers à rede elétrica, e que autoridades do governo estão divididas sobre a possibilidade de as contas de luz aumentarem ou não. A expansão da infraestrutura de transmissão é um gargalo crítico para viabilizar novos empreendimentos. Outro obstáculo ao crescimento da IA no Brasil é o sistema tributário. Os altos impostos federais de importação tornavam mais caro construir grandes data centers no País em comparação com outros países da região. Embora a recente desoneração de equipamentos represente um avanço, a carga tributária sobre outros insumos e serviços ainda preocupa investidores. Para empresários e comerciantes do noroeste paulista, o desenvolvimento de data centers pode gerar oportunidades indiretas, como demanda por serviços de construção, manutenção, segurança e alimentação. A instalação de grandes estruturas em cidades médias do interior poderia aquecer a economia local, criando empregos formais e movimentando o comércio regional. Perguntas Frequentes Por que o Brasil pode se tornar uma alternativa aos EUA para a construção de data centers? O Brasil é visto como uma válvula de escape para as restrições de capacidade nos EUA, onde comunidades estão rejeitando data centers, e o país já é o terceiro maior mercado do ChatGPT, com 215 milhões de mensagens diárias. Quais empresas de tecnologia estão investindo em data centers no Brasil? O Google planeja dobrar sua infraestrutura de nuvem no país até 2030 e assinou acordo com a CBF para integrar o Gemini às seleções; outras gigantes do setor também têm cortejado o Brasil para grandes projetos. Quais são os principais desafios para a expansão de data centers no Brasil? O Brasil precisa de mais linhas de transmissão para conectar data centers à rede elétrica, e os altos impostos federais de importação encarecem a construção em comparação com outros países da região.

artigo.texto: TL;DR: A Proposta 45, medida de votação na Califórnia que promete acelerar a construção de infraestrutura considerada "essencial", pode abrir uma brecha para que desenvolvedores de data centers evitem a fiscalização pública, segundo alertas de ativistas ambientais. O que aconteceu A iniciativa de votação, conhecida como Proposta 45, foi apresentada como uma solução para agilizar a aprovação de projetos de infraestrutura considerados críticos, incluindo data centers, redes de energia e instalações de telecomunicações. O texto da proposta permite que esses empreendimentos sejam classificados como "essenciais", o que reduz a necessidade de avaliações ambientais detalhadas e de audiências públicas. Organizações de defesa ambiental apontam que a redação vaga da medida pode ser explorada por empresas de tecnologia para construir ou expandir data centers sem a devida transparência. A preocupação central é que, ao serem enquadrados como infraestrutura essencial, esses projetos escapariam de processos de licenciamento que normalmente exigem estudos de impacto ambiental, consultas à comunidade e divulgação de documentos técnicos. Até o momento, a proposta está em fase de campanha, com defensores argumentando que a rapidez na implantação de data centers é vital para a competitividade econômica da Califórnia, enquanto críticos temem que a falta de controle comprometa a qualidade do ar, o consumo de água e a gestão de resíduos eletrônicos. Como chegamos aqui A Califórnia tem sido um dos principais polos de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos, abrigando gigantes como Google, Amazon e Meta, que mantêm enormes fazendas de servidores para atender à demanda global de serviços em nuvem. Nos últimos anos, a pressão por maior capacidade de processamento levou a um aumento significativo na construção de data centers, especialmente em áreas com energia renovável abundante. Entretanto, a expansão acelerada trouxe desafios ambientais. Data centers consomem grandes quantidades de energia elétrica e água para refrigeração, além de gerar calor e ruído. Em resposta, a agência estadual de proteção ambiental (California Environmental Protection Agency) tem exigido avaliações de impacto cada vez mais rigorosas, o que, segundo alguns setores da indústria, retarda projetos e aumenta custos. Foi nesse contexto que a Proposta 45 surgiu, impulsionada por lobby de grandes corporações de tecnologia e grupos de interesse que defendem a desburocratização. A proposta foi incluída na cédula de votação como parte de um pacote de reformas voltadas para a modernização da infraestrutura estadual. Entretanto, organizações não‑governamentais, como a Sierra Club California, alertam que a definição de "infraestrutura essencial" está muito ampla e pode ser interpretada de forma a incluir projetos que, embora tecnicamente críticos, ainda geram impactos ambientais significativos. Elas pedem que a redação da medida seja revisada para garantir que avaliações ambientais não sejam suprimidas. O que vem depois Se aprovada, a Proposta 45 entrará em vigor imediatamente, permitindo que desenvolvedores de data centers solicitem autorizações simplificadas. Isso pode acelerar a construção de novos centros ou a expansão dos existentes, reduzindo o tempo de aprovação de meses para semanas. Por outro lado, a falta de auditoria pública pode dificultar a participação da sociedade civil em decisões que afetam a qualidade de vida nas comunidades vizinhas. A ausência de estudos de impacto pode ocultar riscos como: - Consumo excessivo de água em regiões já vulneráveis à escassez; - Emissão de gases de efeito estufa decorrente de fontes de energia não renováveis; - Poluição sonora e térmica que afeta residências e áreas naturais; - Descarte inadequado de componentes eletrônicos e resíduos de refrigerantes. Os críticos também apontam que a medida pode criar um precedente perigoso para outras categorias de projetos, como usinas de energia ou instalações de mineração, que poderiam ser classificadas como essenciais e, assim, escapar de processos de licenciamento. O futuro da Proposta 45 dependerá da campanha de informação nas próximas semanas. Grupos ambientalistas planejam intensificar a divulgação de documentos que demonstram os potenciais impactos, enquanto representantes da indústria de tecnologia prometem que a medida trará benefícios econômicos e de competitividade global. Para ficar no radar Para os leitores brasileiros interessados em tecnologia e sustentabilidade, a discussão em torno da Proposta 45 oferece alguns pontos de atenção: - Impacto nos serviços de nuvem. Caso a medida seja aprovada, a Califórnia pode acelerar a expansão de data centers, o que pode influenciar preços e disponibilidade de serviços de cloud computing usados por empresas brasileiras. - Precedente regulatório. Uma brecha legislativa nos EUA pode inspirar debates semelhantes em outras regiões, inclusive no Brasil, onde a regulação ambiental de data centers ainda está em fase de consolidação. - Consciência ambiental. O caso destaca a importância de equilibrar desenvolvimento tecnológico com responsabilidade ambiental – um tema que vem ganhando força em conferências como a Campus Party Brasil. Fique atento às próximas edições dos principais jornais californianos e aos comunicados das organizações ambientais. A decisão final será conhecida após a votação, prevista para o próximo ciclo eleitoral estadual. Independentemente do resultado, a Proposta 45 evidencia um dilema recorrente: como conciliar a necessidade de infraestrutura digital avançada com a preservação dos recursos naturais e a transparência pública? O debate está apenas começando, e o desfecho poderá moldar o futuro dos data centers não só nos EUA, mas também em mercados emergentes que buscam atrair investimentos em tecnologia.

artigo.texto: A battery measuring just 2.77 micrometers thick could offer a route to powering wearable electronics, tiny sensors, and medical devices. Developed by a team at Dongguk University in South Korea, the thin-film platform uses tin and carbon layers to control lithium deposition and reduce lithium loss during charging and discharging. Led by Professor Hyun-Suk Kim of the Department of Energy and Materials Engineering, the researchers combined the coating with an added lithium reserve to improve battery stability. The university announced the findings on November 3. Tackling uneven lithium deposition All-solid-state batteries replace liquid electrolytes with solid materials, offering potential safety and energy-density advantages. However, uneven lithium plating and stripping can destabilize their operation. Anode-less designs address part of the manufacturing challenge by allowing lithium from the cathode to deposit onto a current collector during the first charge, forming the anode in place. This architecture can simplify fabrication and increase volumetric energy density, particularly in thin-film batteries. But lithium can become electrically isolated, forming “dead” lithium, or lose contact with the solid electrolyte during stripping. These processes reduce the lithium available for subsequent cycles and compromise capacity. The Dongguk team investigated whether a coating on the current collector could help control that process. “Our interlayer acts as a seed for Li nucleation, promoting uniform Li plating and reducing Li loss and improving the reversibility of repeated charging and discharging,” Kim said. More from Energy See All Tin and carbon guide lithium growth The researchers screened carbon-only, metal-only, and combined metal/carbon coatings. A tin/carbon bilayer on a copper current collector delivered the best overall performance among the configurations tested, showing favorable lithium deposition and interfacial stability. The two layers perform different roles. Tin lowers the energy barrier for lithium nucleation, helping lithium begin forming at the interface. The carbon overlayer regulates subsequent growth, potentially limiting uneven deposition and stabilizing the region where tin and lithium interact. The team also deposited a thin metallic lithium layer onto the coated collector. This prelithiation step created a reserve to compensate for lithium lost during initial cycling. During the first lithium plating, a three-dimensional textured region containing tin and lithium-tin formed within the interlayer. According to the researchers, this structure could accommodate volume and shape changes during later cycles, helping maintain contact and stability. Ultrathin platform shows storage potential The completed battery combined a lithium vanadium oxide cathode, a lithium phosphorus oxynitride solid electrolyte, and the coated copper current collector. It achieved a volumetric energy density of 235.13 Wh/L at its 100th cycle, measured at a reported rate of 0.01 C. Its overall thickness was 2.77 micrometers. “Our approach shows how interface engineering and lithium-inventory management can improve anode-less thin-film batteries,” Kim said. “This approach could support the development of ultrathin batteries for wearable electronics, IoT sensors, and medical devices, as well as scalable anode-less ASSBs for industrial-scale power,” he added. The findings identify a way to manage both lithium deposition and the lithium supply within an ultrathin battery architecture. The study was published in the journal Advanced Energy Materials.

artigo.texto: Exelon utilities could spend $3 billion to $7 billion building 1.5 GW to 3.5 GW of regulated energy storage, not including a $1 billion, 500-MW project already proposed for New Jersey, company officials said Friday during an earnings call. “With regulated storage, we have certainty that projects get built, and control over when and how they're deployed,” Robert Kleczynski, Exelon’s CFO, said during the call. “We view utility-owned storage as one option alongside competitive development, not a replacement for it.” Customers would benefit from the projects through lower capacity prices and the flow-through of investment tax credits, which would ease the assets’ effect on electricity rates, he said. Three states where Exelon utilities operate — New Jersey, Maryland and Delaware — allow them to own energy storage facilities to bolster grid resiliency, Kleczynski noted. Atlantic City Electric’s 500-MW project, developed with Invenergy, would be the largest battery installation in the PJM Interconnection and is expected to provide more than $700 million in net benefits to customers, he said. Exelon expects the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to make a decision on the proposal late in the first quarter next year, according to Kleczynski. PJM isn’t moving fast enough to add generation onto its system, which is the biggest issue facing consumers in the grid operator’s Mid-Atlantic and Midwest footprint, according to Calvin Butler, Exelon president and CEO. Two key PJM initiatives — its backstop capacity procurement plan and its Interim Resource Adequacy Service proposal — have been delayed by only partial approvals by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. “Neither proposal would have solved the reliability and affordability challenges facing our customers, but both represented important steps forward,” Butler said. However, adding energy storage and transmission can help address the issue, according to Butler. Exelon’s current capital expenditure plan calls for investing $16.3 billion on transmission through 2029, and the Chicago-based company sees opportunity for $12 billion to $17 billion in transmission spending beyond that plan, including on infrastructure for large loads. Exelon’s “high-probability” large load additions remained flat at 11 GW — with 9 GW in Commonwealth Edison’s service area in northern Illinois and 2 GW in the Mid-Atlantic region, the company said. Its future pipeline slipped to 23 GW — 14 GW with ComEd and 9 GW in the Mid-Atlantic — from 25 GW last quarter. On the financial front, Exelon’s third-quarter income fell to $729 million, down from $875 million in the same period last year, partly due to higher writeoffs related to a rate case, and higher storm and interest expenses. Third-quarter revenue jumped to $7.3 billion from $6.7 billion in the year-ago period. Not including one-time factors, third-quarter adjusted income increased to 87 cents/share from 86 cents/share in the third quarter in 2025. In a note, Jefferies equity analyst on Friday said the earnings results and the potential spending on storage and transmission, in addition to Exelon’s $41.7 billion capital expenditure plan, were “favorable.” However, the analysts warned that regulatory uncertainty in 2027 dampens the outlook and may offset any incremental earnings from new capital expenditures. Exelon has close to 11 million customers through its six utility subsidiaries — Atlantic City Electric, Baltimore Gas and Electric, ComEd, Delmarva Power & Light, PECO Energy Co. and Potomac Electric Power Co.

artigo.texto: Investing.com -- NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) has instructed its data center partners to reduce their exposure to Chinese customers, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday, citing five people with knowledge of the matter. The chipmaker now requires cloud computing clients to sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies, the FT reported. The company previously had no such restrictions in place. The instructions have been delivered verbally through Nvidia's sales force and regional teams rather than through written documents, the FT report said. The move creates additional obstacles for Chinese technology companies seeking to pursue artificial intelligence development. Many Chinese firms have relied on leasing advanced computing capacity through overseas cloud computing arrangements for AI tasks, including model training. The restrictions come as Washington continues efforts to limit Chinese access to advanced U.S. chips through cloud computing deals. Nvidia chips were seen being smuggled to China in recent years, despite the U.S. imposing strict restrictions on any sales to China since at least 2022. Several high-ranked employees at server maker Super Micro, which assembles Nvidia-based servers, were charged with smuggling about $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI servers to China earlier this year. artigo.texto: Lithium-ion batteries have become the backbone of electric vehicles and energy storage. But a rival chemistry built around one of the world’s most abundant elements is now becoming more and more viable. Sodium-ion batteries are entering commercial production, with major manufacturers betting they could make energy storage cheaper, more resilient, and less dependent on lithium. In February 2026, China’s CATL and automaker Changan unveiled what they described as the world’s first mass-production passenger vehicle equipped with sodium-ion batteries, with sales planned for the middle of the year. In April, CATL also signed a major agreement to supply 60 gigawatt-hours of sodium-ion batteries to energy storage company Beijing HyperStrong Technology over three years. These developments suggest sodium-ion technology is approaching a new stage. But it still faces a fundamental challenge. Lithium-ion batteries have a considerable head start in energy density, cost, and manufacturing scale. Sodium is abundant, but that doesn’t automatically make better batteries Both technologies work on the same basic principle. During charging and discharging, ions move between a positive electrode (cathode) and a negative electrode (anode), with an electrolyte allowing them to travel between the two. The main difference is the element carrying the charge. Lithium-ion batteries use lithium, while sodium-ion batteries use sodium, which is widely available in seawater and common salts. That abundance could reduce dependence on lithium mining and price fluctuations. Sodium-ion cells can also use aluminum current collectors on both electrodes, potentially reducing their reliance on copper. Some designs avoid lithium, cobalt, and graphite altogether. More from Energy See All However, sodium-ion batteries are not automatically free of critical minerals. Certain commercial cathode chemistries still use materials such as nickel and manganese, while their hard-carbon anodes require specialized manufacturing. The supply chain for these components is also much less mature. The International Energy Agency (IEA) notes that sodium-ion battery production remains heavily concentrated in China, despite the potential for more geographically diverse raw-material supplies. Lithium-ion still has the energy-density advantage For electric vehicles, one of the most important measures is energy density. It measures how much energy a battery can store relative to its weight or volume. Here, lithium-ion remains ahead. According to the IEA’s 2026 assessment, the latest sodium-ion cells can reach around 175 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg). By comparison, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells can reach approximately 205 Wh/kg, while nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries can reach around 265 Wh/kg. A less energy-dense battery needs to be larger or heavier to store the same amount of energy. In a vehicle, this can mean less driving range or less space for passengers and cargo. The IEA estimates that an average SUV equipped with sodium-ion batteries could achieve up to 350 kilometers (217 miles) of range, compared with approximately 400-600 kilometers (249–373 miles) for lithium-ion vehicles under average weather conditions. Sodium-ion batteries do have an important advantage in colder environments. The latest cells can retain around 90 percent of their nominal capacity at temperatures as low as -40°C (-40°F), outperforming conventional lithium-ion chemistries, particularly LFP. This could make them useful in cold-weather vehicles and equipment. The competition is shifting toward specific applications Sodium-ion’s strongest near-term opportunity may not be replacing the battery in every electric car. Instead, it could find a place in smaller vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, urban delivery fleets, and stationary energy storage, where weight and volume are sometimes less restrictive. The grid-storage market is particularly interesting. Batteries used to store electricity from solar and wind installations do not need to fit inside a vehicle or maximize driving range. Cost, safety, durability, and reliable performance can matter more than energy density. CATL’s 60 GWh agreement with HyperStrong reflects this opportunity, while its TENER sodium-ion storage system, unveiled in June 2026, points to growing interest in commercial-scale stationary applications. Still, the economics are not settled. Lithium-ion manufacturing has benefited from decades of investment and enormous production volumes. In particular, LFP batteries have become highly cost-competitive, making it difficult for sodium-ion to win simply because sodium is cheaper and more abundant. The IEA says global sodium-ion production in 2025 was less than 1 percent of lithium-ion output. Even announced projects for 2030 represent only a fraction of planned lithium-ion manufacturing capacity. A second battery chemistry, not necessarily a replacement The arrival of sodium-ion batteries is important, but it does not mean lithium-ion is about to lose its dominant position. Lithium-based cells continue to improve, while sodium-ion manufacturers still need to scale production, refine materials, and demonstrate consistent performance. The more likely outcome is a battery industry with multiple chemistries serving different needs. Lithium-ion will remain attractive where range, weight and energy density are priorities. Sodium-ion could become increasingly useful where cold-weather performance, material availability and supply-chain diversification carry greater value. Right now, sodium-ion’s biggest achievement may be giving battery manufacturers another option. And in an industry increasingly shaped by the demand for electric vehicles and grid storage, having more than one viable chemistry could prove just as important as developing a better battery.

artigo.texto: Real estate titans are eagerly watching the upcoming Texas gubernatorial race in anticipation of potential changes to the state's policy on data center development. The asset class dominated discussion on the real estate panel at the Bloomberg Invest conference at the Joule Hotel in Downtown Dallas on Tuesday. When the moderator (former TRDer Joe Lovinger) asked if anything could stymie Texas' growth story, Crow Holdings' Michael Hyun pointed to data center regulation: "If there is a significant slowdown in that development, it affects so many areas of the Texas economy." It's something of a double-edged sword for someone like Hyun, who also noted that the frenzy has drawn real estate's finite resources to the buzzy asset class. "You're competing for many of the same contractors to develop your site and guess who can pay more?" he asked. Still, he characterized a crackdown on data center development as "economic suicide." In the lead up to the midterm elections, Gov. Greg Abbott, facing a viable challenger in Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa, veered from his typical pro-business stance and responded to community outrage over data development. He directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt approvals for data center projects and ordered the Public Utility Commission of Texas to audit pending projects. Even so, at least $9 million or 13 percent of the money he's raised since July 2025 came from data center developers or entities tied to data center development, the Texas Tribune reported. Hinojosa has characterized Abbott's actions as temporary moves in service of attracting voters. She says she supports strict legislative guardrails for data center development to protect water supply and grid capacity and curb tax breaks. Laura Hines-Pierce, the co-CEO of Houston-based Hines, was also on the Bloomberg Invest panel. She said the issue isn't as binary as being for or against data centers. According to Hines-Pierce, part of the gray area is in the domain of developer responsibility. "Data centers don't need to be a Star Wars ship that landed in the middle of a community," Hines-Pearce said. DFW tops real estate markets to watch list … again North Texas topped the list of markets to watch for the third consecutive year in a report from the Urban Land Institute and PricewaterhouseCoopers. The report points to robust industrial development — including data centers — as well as corporate relocations and the rise of Y'all Street.

artigo.texto: Ohio voters rejected the AI buildout almost everywhere it was on the ballot Tuesday, with at least 14 municipalities passing bans or other restrictions on data centers. The Buckeye State is on its way to becoming the prototype for how American voters respond in the face of mass AI infrastructure expansion. Ohio residents across 18 municipalities voted on 21 ballot measures on data centers on Tuesday—more than half of the 41 data center-related ballot measures across the country. With more than 200 operational data centers, Ohio ranks No. 5 among U.S. states in number of data center projects. According to state data, companies plan to invest up to $40 billion in AI infrastructure in the state by 2030. Plans for AI infrastructure expansion across the country face strong national opposition—including in the form of 125 local data center moratoriums already in place in Ohio. Ohio voters’ decisive stance against the buildout could foreshadow not just future election results, but how stakeholders in the private sector and government respond. “With over 100 Ohio townships adopting moratoria or restrictions, strong voter turnout against expansion would signal to statehouses nationwide that ratepayer protections, transparency, and grid safeguards should dominate policy agendas,” Keith Durkin, a sociology professor and director of the Ohio Northern University Institute for Civics and Public Policy (ICAPP), told Fortune. How did Ohio vote? In central Ohio, all five communities with data center measures on the ballot voted against data centers. In Sunbury, residents appear to have passed a charter amendment banning data centers that use 25 megawatts or more, with 100% of the unofficial vote counted. The measure was aimed at a possible hyperscale Amazon project, though the project’s fate remains unclear, NBC4 reported. Pataskala voters also approved a charter ban on large data centers. In Trenton, a ban passed 80% to 20%. Organizers hope it will keep an 18-building Amazon Web Services data center out of the city, though it likely won’t affect a four-building AWS campus already under construction nearby, the Journal-News reported. In Perry, more than 87% of voters approved a measure requiring developers seeking tax breaks to offer the village financial guarantees. In Wilmington, around 80% of voters rejected rezoning across four separate referendums meant to accommodate a data center project. Results in Oregon weren’t yet available as of midnight. Ashville residents voted in favor of entirely blocking a data center campus that is already under construction. The bulk of the ballot measures came from 13 municipalities voting on measures to ban or heavily restrict data centers, including “high impact” campuses using more than 25 megawatts of power. Those measures were on the ballot in the municipalities of Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Grove City, Hubbard, Monroeville, Oregon, Pataskala, Piqua, Sunbury, Trenton, Upper Sandusky, and Urbana. Two measures in Monroe and Sprigg townships, respectively, decided whether zoning restrictions on large data center developments should be implemented as a means to preserve agricultural land. Wilmington voters also decided on four separate referendums on whether to uphold the rezoning of four rural residential sites to light industrial sites to accommodate data center construction. Ashville residents voted on a measure to entirely block a campus that is already under construction, and Perry voters decided on a resolution to require data center developers to implement noise limits and make financial commitments to the village before receiving local tax breaks. What do polls say about Ohio’s sentiment toward AI expansion? A Gallup poll published in May found about 70% of Americans opposed the construction of data centers in their local areas, and Ohio appears to largely mirror the national sentiment. ICAPP, in partnership with SurveyUSA, found in a poll of 1,650 Ohio adults published last month, that 55% opposed data center construction in the state compared to 22% in support, while 65% opposed tax breaks for data center developments compared to 15% in support, and 57% said they would vote in favor of a proposed state constitutional amendment banning new large-scale data centers exceeding 25 megawatts in power demands. About 20% of respondents said they’d vote against the amendment, and 21% were undecided. Durkin attributes the negative sentiment toward data centers to a confluence of factors, primarily fear of the environmental and economic risks associated with the AI boom that has emerged as a result of little knowledge about data centers. “I’ve never seen any pro-data center advertising. I’ve never seen any op-eds from the industry,” he said. “Everything we know is that humans don’t like uncertainty from social behavioral science, and there’s uncertainty around data centers.” This skepticism is bipartisan across both Ohio and the country, and it’s allowed Democrats to make data center construction a wedge issue this election, Tatishe Nteta, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, previously told Fortune. Ben Green, assistant professor of public policy at the University of Michigan’s Ford School, similarly argued data centers have become bipartisan because it has struck ideological chords in both parties. Democrats may oppose the campuses because of climate change concerns, but Republicans similarly value environmentalism through the preservation of land. “Democrats and Republicans might talk about that differently, but massive corporations coming in and forcing a community to deal with some type of project and not really giving a community any voice and operating in secrecy—no one’s really a fan of that,” Green told Fortune. Indeed, in Ohio, the environment was the top reason for negative data center sentiment, with quality of life and the economy representing the second and third most common reason for opposition, respectively,

artigo.texto: Massive AI Data Center Sparks Backlash Despite Clean Energy Promises As more governments put increasing pressure on tech companies to develop more sustainable data centres, to ensure they do not place a further burden on the grid, several tech firms are investing in developing new energy capacity and incorporating other innovative ideas into their facility development. This has led Google to suggest that the development of its new U.S. data centre in Minnesota, and associated energy development, will have a positive benefit on the region's transmission network. Google has proposed an agreement with Xcel Energy to support significant wind, solar and battery storage development alongside its new 780-MW Project Skyway data centre. The tech giant plans to finance Xcel's addition of 1.4 GW of wind, 200 MW of solar power and 300 MW of battery storage to the grid. While the combined capacity of these projects exceeds the data centre's projected electricity demand, wind and solar generation fluctuate depending on weather conditions, and battery storage does not generate additional electricity. Xcel Energy says the new energy resources will serve the wider grid, benefiting other customers as well as the data centre. Google plans to cover the associated costs under the proposed agreement, including payments for capacity it does not fully use. The aim is to get the residents of Pine Island, Minnesota, on board with its development plans, particularly as 71 per cent of Americans surveyed in a Gallup poll earlier this year opposed the construction of a data centre in their local area. Developing such a significant renewable energy project will also help Google meet its target of operating entirely on carbon-free energy by 2030. The proposed agreement includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, meaning that Google will be required to finance the development of the infrastructure even if the demand for AI decreases. Under the proposed agreement, Google would pay minimum monthly charges based on at least 75 per cent of its contracted capacity, even if its electricity consumption falls below that level. If the company terminates the agreement early, it could face exit fees equivalent to as much as eight years of minimum demand charges. Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy, explained, "Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power… That's where these protections come in." The Clean Energy Accelerator Charge (CEAC) agreement model uses the same structure as the Clean Transition Tariff (CTT) Google developed with NV Energy. It is currently pending approval from the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission. In its statement about the agreement, Google's Head of Energy Market Innovation, Briana Kobor, said, "Google's partnership with Xcel Energy reimagines how data centres can be served, enabling us to be a catalyst for electricity innovation and helping to ensure our growth supports a cleaner, more affordable energy future for the communities we call home." The rapid rollout of data centres in the United States is driving up the country's electricity demand to unprecedented levels. The U.S. DOE Office of Science national laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, estimates that data centres could account for 11.8 per cent of total U.S. electricity by 2030. Meanwhile, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) projects that electricity consumed by data centre servers could reach between 446 billion and 818 billion kilowatt-hours (BkWh) annually by 2050, accounting for between 22 per cent and 33 per cent of commercial building electricity consumption. This is driving demand for new clean energy capacity to ensure that data centres are not powered by fossil fuels – although several companies still depend on gas-powered plants. As utilities respond to the growing power demand by rapidly building out the grid, which costs billions of dollars to do, they are ultimately expecting the demand for AI data centres to continue. However, if the demand for AI wanes or the government decides to regulate the sector more strictly, electricity demand could fall, potentially leaving consumers to foot the bill for infrastructure upgrades. In addition, the use of clean power in data centre operations is not the only sustainability concern. In October last year, the Minnesota Centre for Environmental Advocacy filed a lawsuit against the city of Pine Island, claiming that the environmental study for the development was vague, initially omitted Google as the end user, and failed to disclose impacts on energy, water, noise, and generators. The initial Alternative Urban Area Review (AUAR) indicated that the new data centre would use approximately 55.7 million gallons of water per year, thereby increasing the city's total water consumption by approximately 50 per cent. Meanwhile, environmental groups have voiced concerns about the lack of comprehensive groundwater impact analysis. Meanwhile, opponents have questioned whether wastewater discharges may potentially run into the Zumbro River. In a Pine Island survey conducted between 1st and 31st August, 75.8 per cent of participants are against the construction of Project Skyway. While Google has made bold promises to upgrade the grid through clean energy projects, residents and environmental groups have broader concerns about consumer protections and the projects' environmental impact.
