artigo.texto: Why Don't More Data Centers Use Liquid Nitrogen For Cooling? In our technology-oriented world, data centers keep everything running. From cloud storage and websites to AI, both individual users and businesses rely on these facilities. However, all those computers generate a huge amount of heat. As servers get more powerful and packed much tighter together, overheating becomes a pressing issue. Cooling is among the biggest ongoing expenses due to electricity usage. Some estimates say that cooling can eat up to 40% of a data center's total power use. In one of the more innovative ways to fight this, Amazon is using reclaimed water to keep its data centers cool. One solution that might seem like a no-brainer is liquid nitrogen. At -321 °F (-196 °C), liquid nitrogen can pack a huge amount of cooling power into a small space. Despite that, it's not something data centers use, and one of the main reasons is the cost. Any company looking to add liquid nitrogen to its existing data centers would have to change its whole infrastructure. As for new construction, there's still the specialized training needed to work with cryogenic systems safely. Data centers would need special storage and dispensing gear, and that kind of equipment isn't cheap nor easy to use. Anyone operating liquid nitrogen equipment needs proper hands-on knowledge to keep things running smoothly and avoid accidents. Liquid Nitrogen can serve as a backup Still, that doesn't mean liquid nitrogen can't be useful. One place it could come in handy is as a backup for emergency cooling. Namely, when overheating happens or some systems fail, liquid nitrogen could be pumped straight into heat exchangers to cool things down quickly. Even if the power goes out or the main cooling system stops working, liquid nitrogen cooling can still be applied. As such, it can keep temperatures steady long enough to shut things down properly or get systems back online. While it remains far from widespread use, there have been recent developments. In mid-September, Utah-based company Reflect Scientific, which specializes in cryogenic cooling systems, announced that its liquid nitrogen cooling technology is ready for use in AI data centers. Either way, with the ever-growing reliance on data centers, the cooling technology is bound to move forward, and there have already been talks about data centers using nothing except their own heat for cooling.

Kamaya remembers explaining battery data and still being asked, âWhy are we working on solid-state batteries?â Still, they kept going. What kept Maeyama going was the sense that, little by little, they were unquestionably moving forward. âResults were hard to come by, but we knew more about something no one else in the world understood than anyone else did at that moment. Looking back six months or a year, there were always more things we could do. I think thatâs what kept us going.â For Kamaya, the colleagues pursuing the same research mattered just as much. To turn the all-solid-state battery into something real. Because colleagues were working toward the same goal, they could keep at the research for years. That time would later prove enormously valuable. When someone proposed, âLetâs try this approachâ to a new problem, a long-serving member could immediately respond, âWe tried that before. Hereâs what happened.â Instead of repeating the same tests, they could move directly to the next approach no one had tried. artigo.texto: Company withdraws application to build battery storage project in Madison County A company that proposed two battery energy storage facilities in Madison County has withdrawn its application. As IPR’s Thomas Ouellette reports, that’s after it received an unfavorable vote from local officials. Audio Transcript Jupiter Power wanted to build two separate facilities that hold surplus energy from a local power grid. The energy is stored in large lithium batteries until it’s needed in times of peak power use. Before voting unanimously for an unfavorable recommendation, the Madison County Planning Commission raised questions about the safety of the project and any future land sales. The majority of public comment was also firmly against the proposal. Officials from Jupiter Power have not given an exact reason for the withdrawal. In a statement, the company says “Indiana’s need for more power has not changed, and we will continue to evaluate how best to help meet this challenge and support everyone who depends on a reliable grid for their families and businesses.” Jupiter officials had said the completed project would have resulted in a $500 million investment in the county, with no tax abatements requested. The rezoning was proposed in September, but Jupiter Power developers at that meeting requested a continuance to better respond to concerns and questions. At past meetings, Madison County officials, and community members spoke at length about long-term risks of these facilities, including lithium fires that burn hotter and longer than wood fires. Indiana Michigan Power had signed an agreement to purchase one of the finished facilities. Thomas Ouellette is our reporter and producer. Contact him at thomas.ouellette@bsu.edu.

artigo.texto: “People really effing hate data centers,” Abdul El-Sayed said at a campaign event in July, E&E News reported. On Tuesday, he won Michigan’s Senate race, NBC News projected. El-Sayed was one of many winners Tuesday who made the AI buildout part of their argument about the cost of living. Voters named the cost of living a top issue in AP exit polls. In much of the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic, the clearest way that issue showed up was the monthly electric bill, and candidates in both parties blamed data centers for it. The bill The link runs through PJM Interconnection, the grid operator serving 13 states from New Jersey to northern Illinois. Capacity prices on PJM’s grid, which pay power plants to guarantee future supply, rose from $28.92 per megawatt-day in 2024-25 to $329.17 for 2026-27. Monitoring Analytics, PJM’s independent market monitor, estimated that data centers were responsible for 63% of the price increase in the 2025-26 auction, or $9.3 billion recovered from customers through higher rates, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. That adds roughly $16 a month to the average residential bill in Ohio and $18 in western Maryland, IEEFA estimated. The increases may not be over. Consulting firm ICF estimated that residential rates across PJM could climb 30% to 60% by 2030. Consumers have already noticed. In an October Consumer Reports survey, 81% of people who had lived in the same home for at least three years said their electricity bills had risen, and 84% said they’d support their utility creating a separate rate category for large users like data centers. The candidates The candidates who won on this issue made the bill the point. El-Sayed’s plan called for “no rate hikes,” arguing data centers should pay for their own energy demand. Two months after OpenAI and Oracle broke ground on a massive data center campus in Saline Township, he held a rally in front of the site. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted after calling him “the face of data centers,” citing the deals Husted worked on as lieutenant governor. Brown campaigned on eliminating tax breaks for data center companies and requiring them to pay for the utilities their campuses use. Logan Phillips, founder of the election forecasting site Race to the White House, told Fortune that Brown focused on the issue “way before anyone else was focused on it,” while Husted had been “basically at every single ribbon cutting for data centers across the state.” “Boy, did that not age well,” Phillips said. By the end of the cycle, Republicans were moving in the same direction. In Michigan, El-Sayed’s opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, said in August he supported a one-year moratorium on new data centers. In Ohio’s governor’s race, both nominees proposed moratoriums: Democrat Amy Acton, who won, and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds, who won the governor’s race, proposed restrictions on data centers. Voters Where voters could decide the question directly, they mostly said no. At least 14 Ohio municipalities passed bans or other restrictions on data centers Tuesday, including Sunbury, where a ban targets a planned Amazon data center. Nationally, voters in 10 states considered 41 data center measures. The polling matched. More than 70% of Americans said they would oppose a data center planned for their area, according to a Heatmap poll published last week, and rising electricity prices were the top reason for opposition. Not everyone accepts the link. The Ohio Manufacturers’ Association has rejected the claim that data centers are driving up energy costs. “Ohio does not have a data center cost crisis,” the group said. Amazon has declined to say whether Tuesday’s ballot measures will change its expansion plans, and said its commitment to the communities where it operates remains unchanged. The industry also made its case on TV. Build American AI, a nonprofit linked to the AI industry’s Leading the Future super PAC network, spent at least $2.54 million on Ohio ads touting data centers’ economic benefits, according to an investigation by DeSmog. The new Congress could take up the issue. Goldman Sachs strategists believe a Democratic Congress could curb data center tax incentives, though they see a nationwide moratorium as unlikely. The buildout is still accelerating: data center capacity under construction is up 48% nationwide, according to Reuters.

artigo.texto: Shares in Gresham House Energy Storage (GRID) jumped over 6% today after the £540m battery fund unexpectedly put itself up for sale, whilst at the same time saying it would continue to “pursue” its growth plan. Just six weeks after formally rejecting a call from activist investor PrimeStone Capital to sell up and claiming a strong first half showed the potential of its recovery programme, the investment trust’s board u-turned and cited shareholder feedback it could not ignore. Announcing that the company’s financial advisers had been instructed to launch a formal sale process (FSP), chair John Leggate said: “The decision by the board to launch a formal sale process has been taken after careful consideration of a wide range of feedback from our shareholders and has not been taken lightly. It comes against a backdrop in which the board and the manager continue to execute the company’s growth plan which has been reflected in the continued growth in the company’s earnings and a 15.8% uplift in its net asset value during the first six months of the year. “Despite no change in the board’s confidence in the company’s ability to deliver on the growth plan, we recognise some shareholders’ increased desire to accelerate value delivery which has caused the board to commence an FSP process whilst continuing to pursue the growth plan.” GRID shares leaped 6.4% to 101p, a 23% discount to NAV per share of 131.3p at 30 June. Our view Richard Williams, senior analyst at QuotedData, said: “The decision to launch a formal sale process follows growing shareholder pressure to accelerate value realisation, with the 15.8% increase in NAV during the first half of 2026 not being adequately reflected in the share price. The timing is interesting given the substantial value that could still be unlocked through the development pipeline, with three projects totalling 777MW targeting final investment decisions next year that have the potential to generate further meaningful NAV uplifts. This creates something of a dilemma: a sale could provide shareholders with a quicker route to realising value, but potentially at the expense of the considerable upside the board believes remains in the portfolio. Running the sale process alongside the Growth Plan is therefore a pragmatic approach, allowing potential buyers to assess that future value while preserving the option of continuing independently. Much will depend on whether prospective bidders are prepared to recognise the value of GRID’s development pipeline rather than simply its existing operational assets.”

artigo.texto: TerraVolt Holdings, Inc., an infrastructure developer specializing in powered land solutions for data centers, has executed option agreements to purchase 1,077 acres of land outside the town of Declo in Cassia County, Idaho, on which it intends to develop a behind-the-meter digital infrastructure campus. The company said in a press release that the property was zoned for multiple use and was situated near long-haul fiber routes and the Williams Northwest Pipeline. The campus will have an initial 240 MW of dedicated on-site power generation, backed by TerraVolt’s previously announced firm natural gas supply agreement of 55,000 MMBtu per day. “These option agreements secure site control, allowing our team to advance land use plans, environmental due diligence, power plant, electrical distribution, and water treatment system designs, and county and state permitting,” said Joel Stone, TerraVolt Holding Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. “By pairing a strategic, expansive land parcel directly with firm gas supply and pipeline access, we are addressing the single largest bottleneck in the digital economy: the multi-year wait for large-load grid interconnections.” With on-site, islanded power generation, the proposed campus will avoid utility interconnection delays. In states like Texas, data center developments that require grid interconnection face lengthy delays, with w.media reporting in September that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas was tracking 438 GW of large load requests, 89 percent of which were for data centers. TerraVolt said the behind-the-meter deployment will reduce the time-to-power schedule for hyperscale and neocloud deployments and protect existing ratepayers from grid strain or rate increases. TerraVolt plans to sell shovel-ready building sites to data center operators, providing power, fiber, potable and fire-protection water, wastewater treatment, and other site services under long-term infrastructure services agreements.TerraVolt also intends to require low water usage for any data center developments on the property, making it a condition of sale for each site. “We look forward to working closely with Cassia County officials and the local community to deliver responsible, long-term industrial tax base growth without impacting local power rates or the agricultural water the region depends on. That is why every building on this campus will be required to use cooling technologies with low water usage,” said Stone. According to Data Center Map, there are currently 25 data centers under development or operational in Idaho. The state is also home to Meta’s Kuna Data Center, a more than US$ 1.2 billion investment, which became operational on September 3, 2026.

artigo.texto: Por que Data Centers são importantes? E quais os problemas? Guia do Adulto Premium te explica as polêmicas em torno das estruturas que sustentam a inteligência artificial. Crédito: Larissa Burchard/Estadão Gerando resumo Com comunidades em todos os Estados Unidos rejeitando data centers, cresce a pressão política para limitar sua construção. Mas, a milhares de quilômetros de distância, o maior país da América do Sul já é um dos principais mercados de IA e está facilitando sua expansão. Os brasileiros enviam 215 milhões de mensagens ao ChatGPT por dia, segundo a OpenAI, o que torna o país o terceiro maior mercado do criador do chatbot em número de usuários semanais, atrás dos Estados Unidos e da Índia. O Google disse que planeja dobrar sua infraestrutura de nuvem no país até 2030 em resposta à crescente demanda ,e chegou a assinar um acordo de patrocínio com a Confederação Brasileira de Futebol em março para integrar o Gemini às seleções nacionais masculinas, femininas e de base. Outras gigantes da tecnologia também estão investindo. A Amazon Web Services gastou mais de US$ 3,8 bilhões em infraestrutura de data centers no País desde 2011 e se comprometeu a investir outro US$ 1,8 bilhão até 2034, enquanto a Microsoft destinou US$ 2,7 bilhões à infraestrutura de nuvem e IA ao longo de três anos. A demanda local, e não a transferência de operações de empresas americanas para o exterior, impulsionou grande parte do crescimento dos data centers na América Latina. Mas Carlos Barrera, CEO da Atlas Renewable Energy, acredita que isso pode mudar. “De fato, vemos a região como uma válvula de escape atraente para algumas das restrições de capacidade que vocês estão vendo agora nos Estados Unidos”, disse. Com uma população de quase 215 milhões de pessoas distribuídas por uma área maior do que a dos 48 Estados contíguos dos Estados Unidos, o Brasil faz sentido como um país a ser cortejado pelas empresas de hiperescala. Sua oferta de eletricidade também é um grande atrativo e custa menos da metade do que nos Estados Unidos. Segundo um relatório do Ministério de Minas e Energia, o País gera quase 87% de sua eletricidade a partir de fontes renováveis, e o rápido crescimento da energia eólica e solar também levou a um excedente. “A reação negativa nos Estados Unidos não está tanto expulsando as empresas de hiperescala do país, mas direcionando-as para onde a energia estiver disponível primeiro”, disse à Fortune James Mercer, diretor da Metro Colo Advisory, empresa de consultoria em data centers. Leia também - Executivo do setor de chips compara corrida de IA a cassinos e impacta ações tech pelo mundo - IA muda o mapa da Bolsa: software perde espaço e impulsiona chips, energia e data centers Mas a eletricidade barata do Brasil também pode ficar mais cara. Barrera disse que o Brasil precisará de mais linhas de transmissão para conectar grandes data centers à rede elétrica, e que autoridades do governo estão divididas sobre a possibilidade de as contas de luz aumentarem ou não. Outro obstáculo ao crescimento da IA no Brasil é o sistema tributário. Os altos impostos federais de importação tornavam mais caro construir grandes data centers no País em comparação com outros países da região. Para resolver isso, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva sancionou uma lei em 15 de setembro que reduz os impostos sobre equipamentos de data centers que atendam certos requisitos. Isso contrasta com propostas de alguns parlamentares americanos para taxar o consumo de eletricidade e a produção dos data centers. “Se o Brasil quisesse ser um ator relevante no setor de data centers, precisava fazer essa mudança na legislação tributária”, disse à Fortune Christopher Torto, CEO da Ascenty, a maior provedora de serviços de data centers e conectividade da América Latina. Soberania de dados O governo Lula espera que a isenção fiscal, ao trazer mais capacidade computacional para o País, ajude as empresas brasileiras a desenvolver produtos de IA e a depender menos de serviços estrangeiros. Atualmente, 60% dos dados digitais brasileiros são processados no exterior, segundo o Ministério do Desenvolvimento brasileiro. De acordo com a legislação, chamada Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter), as empresas devem oferecer pelo menos 10% de seus serviços computacionais elegíveis a clientes brasileiros e investir 2% do valor dos equipamentos beneficiados pela isenção fiscal em pesquisa e desenvolvimento no Brasil. “O objetivo é melhorar a soberania de dados do Brasil, para que não dependamos tanto de serviços estrangeiros, especialmente nesse momento com Trump”, disse à Fortune Ana Carolina de Assis Nunes, antropóloga brasileira e pesquisadora de data centers no instituto de políticas públicas sem fins lucrativos Data & Society. Nunes destacou que o Brasil quer depender menos da tecnologia estrangeira, mas está concedendo incentivos fiscais às mesmas empresas que dominam o setor. Torto admitiu que é improvável que o Brasil desenvolva seu próprio Google ou Microsoft. Ainda assim, ter data centers locais no país poderia melhorar a latência e manter mais dados no território nacional. “Não se trata apenas dos modelos ou dos próprios data centers; tudo o que gira em torno deles será, de fato, o maior investimento no longo prazo”, disse ele. Potencial de reação negativa Embora o Brasil não tenha visto a mesma escala de reação negativa aos data centers que os Estados Unidos, alguma resistência surgiu. Dias antes de o Redata se tornar lei, procuradores federais brasileiros recorreram à Justiça contra um projeto de data center ligado ao TikTok. Eles queriam um estudo de impacto ambiental e uma consulta ao povo indígena Anacé antes de o data center entrar em operação. Nunes disse que a oposição aos data centers no Brasil não é tão politicamente unida quanto nos Estados Unidos, onde eles têm recebido críticas tanto da esquerda quanto da direita. artigo.texto: Westbrook City Council unanimously approves ban on standalone data centers The new land-use rules allow smaller data operations that support other businesses while removing data centers as a permitted use at Rock Row Westbrook City Council unanimously approves ban on standalone data centers The new land-use rules allow smaller data operations that support other businesses while removing data centers as a permitted use at Rock Row The Westbrook City Council unanimously approved an ordinance Monday night prohibiting standalone data centers in the city. The ordinance allows data centers only as an accessory use, so smaller operations, like server rooms, can continue to support other businesses. The changes also remove data centers as a permitted use in the Rock Row Contract Zone, previously the only area in Westbrook where they were allowed. The vote comes after a 180-day moratorium on new data center projects adopted by the City Council in June. During that time, the Planning Board reviewed the city's existing regulations and considered concerns raised over water usage, energy demands, noise and economic development. The Planning Board unanimously recommended the ordinance following a public hearing on Oct. 6. The City Council held its first reading of the ordinance on October 19 before taking it up for a second and final reading Monday.

artigo.texto: BW ESS has started commercial operations of the first phase of its Hams Hall battery energy storage system (BESS) in the West Midlands, UK. The first phase has a capacity of 350 MW/1,243 MWh, making it the largest BESS in Europe by storage capacity. The project is located next to National Grid’s Hams Hall substation. Furthermore, the second phase will increase the total capacity of Hams Hall to 400 MW/1,424 MWh. BW ESS worked with Sungrow, Energy-IO, National Grid, and NESO during commissioning, testing, and preparation for operations. Earlier, in September 2026, BW ESS acquired two standalone BESS projects from Navacant in Spain. The projects, located in the Valencia region, have storage capacities of 99 MW and 27 MW, respectively. Together, the projects have a combined capacity of 126 MW/up to 675 MWh.

artigo.texto: Regulation Ohio Voters Back Local Data Center Limits in Unofficial Results Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google Voters in Trenton, Pataskala, Granville, Sunbury, Grove City and Ashville backed local data-center restrictions in Ohio’s November 3, 2026 general election, according to unofficial county results that included Delaware County’s election-night summary. Trenton’s Issue 17 drew 79.68% support. Butler County’s unofficial results gave Trenton 3,541 yes votes to 903 no votes, with all eight precincts reporting. Licking County’s results showed Pataskala’s data-center charter amendment passing 5,418 to 1,941, or 73.62% yes, and Granville’s amendment passing 2,015 to 429, or 82.45% yes. Sunbury’s charter amendment passed 2,809 to 763, or 78.64%, with all six precincts reporting. Grove City’s Community Consent Amendment passed 11,317 to 9,411, or 54.60% yes, with all 30 precincts reporting in Franklin County’s summary. Ashville’s referendum drew 1,469 no votes, or 81.61%, against 331 yes votes in Pickaway County’s unofficial results. The Ohio Secretary of State’s ballot catalog identifies the Ashville question as whether to approve a resolution enacting a development-and-supply agreement term summary with EdgeConneX. The totals remain unofficial. The Ohio Secretary of State says certified results will be published approximately three weeks after the election. Construction Bans and Community Consent Pataskala’s official sample ballot shows a direct prohibition on covered data-center construction within city limits, effective immediately. The measure defines covered facilities as buildings, physical facilities or infrastructure used primarily or exclusively for digital information services, with aggregate monthly demand or peak load greater than 25 megawatts. Sunbury’s proposed charter text also uses the greater-than-25-megawatt threshold and defines construction to include related preparations and modifications on single, contiguous, adjacent or otherwise aggregated parcels. Grove City’s Community Consent Amendment applies to heavy industrial development, including data centers, server farms, power generation and large-scale warehousing or logistics facilities. It requires voter approval before city approvals for developments meeting at least one threshold: 50 or more contiguous acres, more than 20 megawatts of electrical power at peak capacity, or more than 500,000 gallons of water per day. Covered approvals include rezoning, conditional-use permits, planned-unit development approvals, annexations and building permits. Applicants must fund an independent impact study but have no control over the selected firm or its findings. The study must address water use, grid demand, noise, traffic, employment, tax revenue against infrastructure costs and environmental effects, and be posted publicly at least 60 days before the referendum. A failed vote blocks city approval and bars the same or a substantially similar application for 24 months. A successful vote permits the normal zoning process but guarantees no permit. Cumulative increases above 10% in acreage, peak electrical demand or daily water consumption trigger another referendum. Trenton’s Court-Ordered Path to the Ballot Trenton’s vote followed a September 1, 2026 Supreme Court of Ohio opinion holding that the city council had a mandatory constitutional duty to certify residents’ data-center amendment petition. The proposed charter change would prohibit data-center construction. Council members had refused certification after concluding that the petition lacked sufficient valid signatures. Trenton Data Center Campus, L.L.C., an entity constructing a data center in the city, intervened as a respondent. The petition contained 336 valid signatures. The council derived its 820-signature requirement from 8,197 registered voters, while the court held that 128 were required based on the 1,277 ballots cast at the preceding municipal election. The court reasoned that the constitutional signature percentage rests on total votes cast, not total registered voters, and that a municipal charter cannot be interpreted inconsistently with the Ohio Constitution. Its limited writ ordered certification for a special election within the constitutional 60-to-120-day period and denied requests for attorney fees and court costs. Statewide Infrastructure Growth and Polling The local votes intersect with Ohio’s broader data-center expansion. The Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel says Ohio has more than 200 data centers, the fifth-highest count among states, with most in Central Ohio, and that companies plan to invest up to $40 billion more by 2030. These facilities support artificial intelligence, cloud storage, streaming and online business operations. A large hyperscale facility can use as much electricity as 100,000 homes, while some data centers use millions of gallons of fresh water daily for cooling. An October 22, 2026 Ohio Northern University release adds statewide polling context. Its Institute for Civics and Public Policy, working with SurveyUSA, surveyed 1,650 Ohio adults between October 8, 2026 and October 14, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. The university reported that 55% of respondents opposed data-center construction in Ohio and 22% supported it; that 57% would vote for a constitutional amendment banning new large-scale data centers with peak demand above 25 megawatts; and that 79% expected higher local water and electricity costs, including 49% anticipating significant increases. For AI infrastructure developers, the practical consequence is a layer of local approval alongside power, water and permitting decisions. Pataskala and Sunbury prohibit covered projects outright, while Grove City requires an independent study and voter approval before city approvals, followed by review of material expansions. Securing land and utility capacity therefore does not settle whether these projects can proceed

artigo.texto: Regulation Data Center Policy Fears Hit AI Stocks After Hinojosa’s Texas Win Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google CNBC reported on November 4, 2026, that AI-linked stocks and Nasdaq-100 futures fell in overnight trading after Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s projected victory in the Texas governor’s race intensified investor concern that state restrictions could delay data-center projects. Nasdaq-100 futures were down 0.8% as election results arrived, more than double the decline in Dow Jones Industrial Average futures. The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF was down 2% on Robinhood. Companies with direct exposure to AI infrastructure posted steeper declines. CoreWeave, which uses borrowed money to build data centers, fell 7% on Robinhood. Texas-headquartered SpaceX dropped 6%, while Nebius Group and Oracle each lost 4%. Hinojosa Campaigned on a Data Center Moratorium Hinojosa was projected by the Associated Press to defeat incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott. In victory remarks published by her campaign on November 4, 2026, she said Abbott had called to congratulate her and offer assistance with the transition. She said the transition would begin the following day and that she would take the oath of office in January. Her campaign platform calls for an immediate moratorium on data centers until the legislature can enact protections and give Texans a role in deciding whether and how facilities enter their communities. It urged Abbott to issue an executive order halting new data centers and to call a special session to address the issue. The platform also criticized a 2015 law signed by Abbott, which the campaign described as providing 20-year tax breaks to hyperscale data centers. It demanded an end to what it called tax giveaways and said passing legislation was the only way to protect Texans. Those positions explain the policy concern, but the election itself did not enact a moratorium or change project rules. Texas Exposure Shaped the Market Reaction The state’s share of planned development helps explain why the result resonated with investors. CNBC cited Wells Fargo estimates that Texas accounts for 27% of planned U.S. data-center gigawatts. Georgia accounts for 7%, while Ohio and Pennsylvania each account for 5%; Democrats were projected to win or retain the governorships in Georgia, Ohio and Pennsylvania. Horizon Investments chief investment officer Scott Ladner said an Abbott loss would raise the question of where to build data centers and warned that Texas could cease to be a favorable location for them. Wells Fargo chief equity strategist Ohsung Kwon had described a Democratic victory in Texas as a potential “left-tail event” for the AI trade. The political result reached a market already under pressure. The Nasdaq-100 entered correction territory at the end of October 2026 amid concern that growth in data-center spending by large hyperscalers and private AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing. The overnight moves therefore added a state-policy risk to existing questions about the pace of AI infrastructure spending. For developers and investors, the immediate issue is implementation rather than a restriction already in force. Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium, community participation and legislative protections, while her victory remarks established a transition timeline. How those proposals affect project approvals, tax treatment and construction schedules will determine the practical consequences for Texas’s planned data-center capacity.

artigo.texto: Next-generation all-solid-state batteries are gaining attention in the electric vehicle battery market, with several battery makers expanding research in the sector. Sunwoda, a Chinese battery manufacturer, has recently announced advances to its polymer-composite approach used for building solid-state batteries. The company claimed that its latest 20 Ah all-solid-state battery, Xin Bixiao, withstood extreme thermal heat without catching fire or exploding. Built with a nanoscale high-entropy silicon anode, a single cell of these polymer batteries showed strong thermal performance, passing the hot-box test with temperatures raised to 400 degrees Fahrenheit (200 degrees Celsius). High-density, long-range The model has previously achieved an energy density exceeding 400 Wh/kg and a cycle life of more than 1200 cycles at a low external pressure of 1 megapascals (MPa). This it stated is a breakthrough for long-range electric vehicles (EVs), offering a range of over 600 miles (1000 km). With over 1,200 cycles and capacity retention above 80 percent, the company claimed the battery could support vehicle use for over a decade, assuming annual driving of more than 12,000 miles (20,000 km). However, the company noted that the thermal and lifespan performance results were not obtained after integrating the entire battery pack in a vehicle. The testing process started earlier this year in May and is still ongoing. More from Energy See All Going forward, the company also plans to build a second-generation sulfide battery by next year at its pre-commercial solid-state battery production line. This manufacturing unit is designed to handle an annual capacity of 0.2 gigawatt-hours (GWh), which is considered small in the battery world, making batteries enough for nearly 2600-2700 electric vehicles per year. Next stop: Aviation batteries Beyond the planned automotive batteries of 400Wh/kg capacity, the Chinese battery maker is also eyeing developing aviation battery cells of at least 450Wh/kg. For this project, the company is working with the Guangdong Engineering Research Center. Another segment that the company is aiming to make its mark in is the electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft batteries. The company is targeting a continuous discharge power density of at least 1,000 W/kg for these aircraft. However, the company has not yet committed to an official deadline for any of these high-energy-density batteries, nor has it defined the scale of production volumes or commercial orders. Meanwhile, Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL), another leading Chinese battery manufacturer, is developing its next-generation solid-state batteries using bisulphide chemistry, a different electrolyte technology. The company announced its 20 Ah solid-state prototype two years ago and has reaffirmed its 2027 target for a small-scale batch production trial. Earlier this year, Sunwoda unveiled its latest fast-charging EV battery technology that can add about 62 miles (100 km) of range per minute and charge from 10 percent to 97 percent state of charge (SOC) in 9 minutes at room temperature. The claims were made for its new 15C lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery. The company said the battery can go from 10 percent to 70 percent in about 5 minutes, then reach 97 percent in another four minutes.

artigo.texto: It appears that BYD Malaysia is gearing up to launch the 2026 refresh of the Denza D9 electric MPV in our market soon. This is based on a new teaser recently published across Denza Malaysia’s social media channels. While the teaser is light on details, the refreshed 2026 Denza D9 is expected to carry major upgrades in charging capability, performance, and equipment. 2026 Denza D9 Malaysia: 2nd-Gen BYD Blade Battery with Flash Charging support? One of the headline upgrades expected on the 2026 Denza D9 is support for BYD’s Flash Charging technology. This aligns with BYD Malaysia’s ongoing rollout of BYD Flash Chargers at key Denza centres, including Balakong, KL North, and Glenmarie. Regional momentum points in the same direction: BYD last month introduced the Flash Charging-capable D9 in Indonesia—where the brand is marketed as Danza due to an ongoing local trademark dispute. On the other hand, the Hong Kong market has recently received the D9 Duo featuring not only Flash Charging capability but also CCS2 and GB/T ports. With Flash Charging enabled, the updated D9 can juice up from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes, while a 10% to 97% top-up takes approximately 9 minutes. To support these speeds, the refreshed model adopts BYD’s 2nd-generation Blade Battery. In Indonesia, the battery pack on the Danza D9 grows to 115.03kWh—a noticeable bump over the 103.36kWh 1st-gen pack fitted to the initial Denza D9 launched in Malaysia in early 2025. That extra capacity extends range considerably: Indonesia’s 2026 Danza D9 FWD claims up to 730km (NEDC), compared to the 600km (NEDC) rated for the existing Malaysian-spec Denza D9 FWD. 2026 Denza D9 Malaysia: More punch and tech additions We are also expecting a healthy bump in performance output as well. The 2026 Danza D9 FWD in Indonesia delivers 340kW (456hp) and 365Nm of torque, far outpacing the 230kW (308hp) and 360Nm produced by Malaysia’s current front-drive model. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s D9 Duo AWD boasts a combined output of 410kW (550hp) and 445Nm. By comparison, the existing AWD variant in Malaysia puts out 275kW (369hp), though it holds a slight edge on peak torque at 470Nm. Other equipment likely bound for our 2026 update includes BYD’s DiSus-C dual-valve intelligent damping suspension, a 16-speaker Devialet audio system, a Child Presence Detection (CPD) sensor, and power-adjustment switches for the third-row seating.

artigo.texto: Southeast ConstructionTech is having a moment, and data centers are the reason. Hypepotamus ran a story under the headline “Data centers, regional growth fuels SE ConstructionTech” that describes a sector gaining momentum after major acquisitions and funding announcements. The piece cites a CBRE report showing Atlanta led North America in data-center capacity under construction during the first half of 2026. That single data point carries more weight than it first appears. Capacity under construction is a leading indicator. It tells you where concrete, steel, electricians, schedulers and software licenses will flow over the next two years. For a region full of general contractors, it also tells software vendors where the buyers are. This analysis walks through what the reporting confirms, what it leaves out, and what it means for cloud buyers, contractors and startup investors. It also sets the story against the wider spending cycle covered in our look at how long the AI capex boom can last. Where the available sources give no figure, we say so instead of guessing. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the Hypepotamus Report Actually Confirms Start with the hard facts, because the available excerpt is short on numbers. Hypepotamus describes the Southeast construction-technology sector as gaining momentum following major acquisitions and funding announcements. It ties that momentum to data-center construction and to broader regional growth. The story names five companies as potential customers for ConstructionTech products: Pulte Group, Holder Construction, Brasfield & Gorrie, Innventure and Cardinal Infrastructure Group. That list spans homebuilding, commercial general contracting and infrastructure work, which matters. It suggests the demand is not confined to one project type. What the excerpt does not provide is equally clear. It gives no acquisition amounts, no funding totals, no product names, no named individuals, no project specifications, no prices and no on-record quotations. We treat all of those as unconfirmed. Any article that fills those gaps with precise figures is guessing, and readers should discount it accordingly. The practical takeaway is simple. The direction of travel is documented. The size of the money is not. Anyone building a business case on this story needs to pull the underlying deal announcements before putting a number in a slide deck. Atlanta Leads North America in Data-Center Construction The headline claim is the CBRE finding. According to the report cited by Hypepotamus, Atlanta led North America in data-center capacity under construction in the first half of 2026. For a metro that many readers associate with logistics and film production rather than hyperscale computing, that is a notable ranking. The story does not supply the megawatt totals, and we will not invent them. What we can say is that leading the continent in active construction puts Atlanta in front of the other large markets that have historically dominated data-center headlines. The ranking reflects pipeline, not completed capacity. Why “Under Construction” Beats “Operating” as a Signal Operating inventory shows what the market built in the past. Capacity under construction shows what developers, utilities and lenders committed to in the recent past and are now paying to deliver. It is a better read on where demand for labor and tooling lands next. A ConstructionTech vendor selling scheduling, document control or field reporting software cares about active sites. Software seats follow crews. A market with a large number of live data-center builds creates a dense cluster of potential customers inside a few hours of driving, which cuts sales costs and speeds up reference selling. The Five Named Customers and What They Signal Hypepotamus lists five organizations as potential customers. The table below summarizes what the story confirms about each. We deliberately avoid adding revenue, headcount or project counts, since the excerpt gives none. The key phrase is potential customer. The story does not say any of these firms signed a contract, rolled out a product or invested in a startup. Readers should not infer purchases from a list of prospects. It is a map of who could buy, not a record of who did. Still, the mix tells a story. A residential builder, large commercial contractors, an innovation-driven company and an infrastructure group all sit on the same prospect list. Vendors that once targeted only commercial general contractors now see a wider addressable market across the region. Why Data Centers Pull ConstructionTech Along Data-center projects are unusually demanding to build. They stack electrical, mechanical and cooling systems into schedules that developers want finished fast, because idle capacity earns nothing and tenants often sign leases well before completion. Every week of delay costs real money. That pressure rewards tools that tighten coordination. Contractors on these jobs juggle long-lead equipment, dozens of trades and heavy documentation. Software that flags a late delivery, a missing submittal or a schedule slip earlier has a direct dollar value. It is the kind of pitch a project executive understands in one meeting. Hypepotamus frames the regional story as a combination of data-center demand and broader growth. We read that as a flywheel. Big builds attract specialist contractors. Specialist contractors attract vendors. Vendors attract investors and acquirers, which funds more product. Each turn makes the next one easier. artigo.texto: Bluebird Solar Private Limited is strengthening its presence in the clean energy sector with the introduction of its Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) portfolio, featuring energy storage solutions based on immersion cooling technology. As battery energy storage adoption expands, thermal management has become an important consideration for system performance, operational reliability, and safety. Maintaining suitable battery temperatures is essential, particularly in installations operating under demanding environmental conditions. Recognising this requirement, Bluebird Solar has introduced two featured energy storage solutions: a 208.99 kWh Immersion Cooling Mobile Energy Storage Vehicle and the ePower T2 Immersion Cooling Containerized Energy Storage System. Immersion cooling is a thermal management approach in which battery components are immersed in a specialised dielectric fluid. The fluid absorbs heat generated during battery operation, helping regulate temperature and support thermal stability. Unlike conventional air-based cooling approaches, immersion cooling brings the cooling medium into direct contact with the battery components. This approach is designed to improve heat transfer and manage thermal conditions within the energy storage system. The company’s new portfolio is intended to address both mobile and stationary energy storage requirements. Its solutions are positioned for applications across commercial and industrial facilities, utility-scale projects, residential energy systems, and telecom infrastructure. This technology-focused expansion forms part of Bluebird Solar 2.0, the company’s broader strategy to move beyond solar module manufacturing and participate in the development of integrated clean energy solutions. With a focus on advanced cooling systems, modular scalability, and operational reliability, Bluebird Solar is expanding its capabilities in India’s growing battery energy storage market.

artigo.texto: Os investimentos do Grupo Schwarz em inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital podem alcançar € 16,6 bilhões em dois projetos de data centers na Alemanha. Controlador das redes Lidl e Kaufland, o conglomerado pretende ampliar a oferta de computação em nuvem e serviços tecnológicos para empresas. A expansão ocorre enquanto sua divisão digital, Schwarz Digits, ainda representa uma pequena parcela do faturamento total. No exercício fiscal de 2025, o grupo registrou € 185,6 bilhões em receitas, crescimento de 5,8%. A Schwarz Digits faturou € 2,2 bilhões, avanço de 15,8%. Com base nesses valores, cálculo do Economic News Brasil aponta participação aproximada de 1,2% da divisão digital na receita agregada do conglomerado. Os números constam dos resultados oficiais, divulgados em junho de 2026. Investimentos do Grupo Schwarz têm prazos e condições diferentes O projeto de Lübbenau prevê € 11 bilhões para ampliar a capacidade de processamento de dados, com a primeira fase programada para 2027. Já o empreendimento de Dummerstorf poderá receber até € 5,6 bilhões até 2033, dependendo de aprovações e decisões futuras. Portanto, o valor agregado reúne iniciativas em estágios distintos. Não representa recursos integralmente desembolsados nem compromissos financeiros com execução definitiva. A infraestrutura integra a estratégia da STACKIT, plataforma de nuvem do conglomerado. O objetivo é atender clientes que procuram alternativas para armazenar e processar informações, especialmente organizações com exigências de segurança e controle de dados. Essa expansão acompanha o aumento dos investimentos em data centers em diferentes mercados, impulsionado pela demanda por capacidade computacional. Cohere amplia a estratégia tecnológica da dona do Lidl Em 29 de outubro de 2026, a canadense Cohere anunciou o fechamento inicial de uma rodada de financiamento liderada por empresas do Grupo Schwarz. A operação pretende captar até 7 bilhões de dólares canadenses, mas o comunicado não informa quanto já foi levantado nem atribui o valor total ao conglomerado alemão. A parceria aproxima a Schwarz Digits de modelos de inteligência artificial destinados ao mercado corporativo. Além disso, pode complementar os serviços da STACKIT e ampliar as oportunidades comerciais fora do varejo. O desafio será converter a capacidade tecnológica em contratos capazes de remunerar o capital aplicado. Embora a receita digital esteja crescendo, o Grupo Schwarz não divulga margem operacional específica da Schwarz Digits nem projeções de retorno dos novos empreendimentos. Sem esses indicadores, a rentabilidade futura da expansão permanece indeterminada.

artigo.texto: O transporte aéreo seguirá regras específicas no mercado regulado de carbono do Brasil, conforme decisão do Ministério da Fazenda. A pasta divulgou, na 5ª feira (29.out.2026), o cronograma de implementação do sistema e os setores que, a partir de 2027, terão de medir, relatar e verificar emissões e remoções de gases de efeito estufa. A implantação será gradual até 2030, e grandes empresas deverão calcular anualmente suas emissões de carbono equivalente. A obrigação de MRV (Mensuração, Relato e Verificação), prevista na lei que criou o SBCE (Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões), valerá para indústrias que emitam a partir de 10 mil tCO₂e (toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente) por ano. Segundo a Fazenda, esse patamar alcança menos de 1% dos CNPJs do país. O setor aéreo, porém, ficará fora do cronograma geral e terá regras sob responsabilidade da Anac (Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil). A Anac também regulamentará o ProBioQAV (Programa Nacional de Combustível Sustentável de Aviação), previsto para entrar em vigor em 2027. As medidas para reduzir as emissões da aviação fazem parte do programa e foram estabelecidas em decreto assinado em agosto pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). A norma atribuiu à Anac e à ANP (Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis) a implementação, a operação e a fiscalização da política. A regulamentação está em consulta pública na ANP e já passou pelo rito na Anac. A orientação será reduzir efetivamente as emissões de gases de efeito estufa. A partir de 2027, companhias aéreas que operam no Brasil terão de diminuir gradualmente suas emissões com o uso de SAF (combustível sustentável de aviação). A separação do setor aéreo do cronograma industrial considera que as agências também levam em conta o Corsia (Esquema de Compensação e Redução de Carbono para a Aviação Internacional), mecanismo global para medir e compensar emissões de dióxido de carbono em voos internacionais. A Fazenda afirma que a integração ao Registro Central do SBCE poderá aproveitar a estrutura em desenvolvimento, seguir práticas internacionais, simplificar a regulação e reduzir custos. As companhias poderão emitir CS-SAF (certificados de sustentabilidade de combustível sustentável de aviação), documentos que comprovam a redução de emissões vinculada ao uso do combustível. Produtores também deverão emitir certificados que mostrem a diminuição das emissões em relação ao querosene convencional. Esses documentos poderão ser vendidos às empresas aéreas, que os usarão para demonstrar o cumprimento das metas climáticas. Para a aviação doméstica, o decreto estabelece metas progressivas. Nos dois primeiros anos, os operadores deverão garantir redução anual de pelo menos 1% nas emissões de dióxido de carbono dos voos nacionais. A partir de 2029, o objetivo aumentará 1 ponto percentual por ano, até chegar a pelo menos 10% em 2037. Os certificados permitirão negociar separadamente o atributo ambiental do SAF e o volume físico do combustível, facilitando seu uso em aeroportos de todo o país e a comprovação das reduções, segundo o Ministério de Minas e Energia. Os certificados também poderão ser comprados por empresas de outros setores no mercado voluntário, para compensação de emissões próprias. Esse modelo, chamado “book & claim”, já é utilizado em outros segmentos. O decreto cria ainda o Programa Nacional de Certificação do Combustível Sustentável de Aviação, que tornará obrigatória a certificação de combustíveis produzidos no Brasil ou importados, com o objetivo de garantir rastreabilidade e integridade ambiental em toda a cadeia. O SAF, anteriormente chamado de bioquerosene, é produzido com matérias-primas renováveis ou de baixo carbono, como óleos vegetais, resíduos agrícolas, lixo orgânico, etanol e gases industriais, em substituição ao petróleo do querosene tradicional.

artigo.texto: A German startup has given old e-scooter batteries a second life by using them to develop a high-performance, affordable, and sustainable 70-kilowatt-hour (kWh) energy storage system for industrial use. The technology was designed by EDENenergy, a Freiburg-based cleantech startup and spin-off of the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (ISE). It relies on modular units and advanced power electronics to connect used batteries into one larger energy storage system. Florian Bierwirth, EDENenergy CEO and co-founder highlighted the importance of repurposing old batteries. “It allows different storage units to be connected and enables communication with various modules without having to disassemble the batteries,” he said. According to the team, the batteries can retain over 90 percent of their original capacity, which makes them suitable for reuse in industrial energy storage. They could also enable businesses to store excess solar power while reducing battery waste. Old batteries reused Reports indicate that about one million batteries from e-bikes and e-scooters are prematurely discarded in Germany each year. However, many of them still have enough capacity to remain useful for several more years. Reusing these batteries has been difficult because they come in different designs, cell types, and battery management systems. To address this, former Fraunhofer ISE researchers developed power electronics that can connect different batteries without dismantling them. More from Energy See All The startup initially focused on batteries from large e-scooter fleet operators to ensure a consistent supply of compatible units. Its first industrial storage system combines 112 used e-scooter batteries, each tested before installation. While the team initially expected the batteries to retain around 80 percent of their original capacity, tests on the first 350 units revealed that some retained well over 90 percent. The firm delivered its first storage system to a customer last month. “In mid-October, we delivered the first storage system to a customer, which was an important milestone for our young company,” Bierwirth highlighted. “With this storage size, we initially aim to target medium-sized companies in the region that have a photovoltaic system but do not yet have a storage solution.” Keeping storage capacity EDENenergy said that the technology is also modular. This means that individual batteries can be replaced without shutting down the entire system. According to the company, municipal utilities could use it to reduce peak electricity demand, increase solar power consumption, or trade electricity. The startup will also remotely monitor the batteries to check their condition and determine when individual modules need to be replaced. Once a battery reaches the end of its useful life, it is removed and sent to recycling partners. Moreover, the system could maintain its full 70 kWh capacity even after 10 years. By comparison, conventional battery storage manufacturers typically guarantee around 80 percent of the original capacity after a decade. At the same time, the batteries could last longer in stationary applications as they experience fewer vibrations and temperature fluctuations. “In stationary storage systems, where – unlike in their first life – they are exposed to fewer vibrations or temperature fluctuations, these batteries can continue to perform well for several more years,” the company concluded in a press statement. Moving forward, the team plans to expand its industrial storage systems to 300 kWh.

artigo.texto: The vote to ban data centers in Trenton has passed, according to unofficial election results on Tuesday, Nov. 3. With 100% of precincts reporting, the measure passed by a landslide 80% to 20%. Trenton resident Barry Blankenship, who led efforts in the city to get the ban on the ballot, said seeing the results was emotional. “Everybody’s just so happy right now that a group of citizens came together, stood up for an issue — Democrats, Republicans alike,” he said. “We stood together and we beat a city.” Looking forward, he hopes the ban will keep an 18-building Amazon Web Services data center from developing within the city and could rein in the electric use of a four-building AWS data center already under construction. Council member Marci Butts told Journal-News she was happy the community got to vote on the measure. “It was very telling to me,” she said. “To see that the number was almost 80% for (the ban), really speaks to what the community actually wants. And I think it’s now our responsibility to respond to that in kind and move forward in the best way.” Butts said she did vote on the measure, but declined to say how she voted. Council member Austin Proffitt congratulated Blankenship and the Woodsdale and Trenton Environmental Resistance group, which “fought hard to have their voice heard.” “I am proud to be a part of a community where residents were unhappy with decisions made by their leaders and chose to get involved and do something about it,” Proffitt said. The Journal-News has reached out to the five other council members and did not receive responses from four of them. Mayor Ryan Perry declined to comment. The measure bans data centers requiring more than 25 megawatts of electricity from developing within city limits. Voters decided on the ban following more than a year of controversy over proposed data center developments, including an annexation fight, contentious council meetings, a citizen-led charter amendment, an Ohio Supreme Court case and Perry’s resignation, effective Jan. 1, 2027. (Perry had said his resignation stems from increasing obligations from both his full-time job and mayorship.) Residents began pushing back after plans surfaced in October 2025 for a data center, citing concerns about noise, light pollution, environmental impacts, rising utility demands and transparency. Path to the ballot In September, the Ohio Supreme Court unanimously ordered the charter amendment onto the ballot, ruling residents had collected enough signatures. The measure would likely not affect the four-building AWS data center already under construction on 141 acres in Trenton. However, it could impact a proposed 18-building AWS project tied to 600 acres in Madison and St. Clair townships. A petition to annex that land into Trenton was withdrawn in September but could be refiled. If annexation eventually succeeds, the ballot measure's outcome could determine whether the project moves forward within the city. Elsewhere, Butler County and other Ohio communities have enacted temporary moratoriums on data centers, though Ohio has no statewide ban. New York remains the only state with a statewide moratorium on large-scale data center development.

artigo.texto: National nonresidential construction spending increased 0.6% in September, mainly on the strength of data center development, according to an Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) analysis of data published on Monday by the U.S. Census Bureau. “Nonresidential construction spending grew for the sixth consecutive month in September,” said ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu on Monday. “As has been the case for several months, data centers accounted for virtually all of that increase. Excluding data centers and the closely related power category, nonresidential spending actually fell in September.” Basu said spending on data center category construction jumped 8.6% in September and has grown at an annualized rate of 217% since May. “Given the recent rise in treasury yields and ongoing materials price escalation, momentum will remain narrowly concentrated in artificial intelligence-related segments over the next several months,” said Basu. “While contractors remain busy in the aggregate, according to ABC’s Construction Backlog Indicator, current market dynamics will continue to favor larger contractors who are far more likely to be involved in data center and power projects.” Meanwhile, residential construction spending declined -5.4% for the month of September and is down -8.8% compared to September of 2025, according to the ABC. On a monthly basis, construction spending increased in half of the 16 nonresidential subcategories, including manufacturing which was up +0.1% between August and September 2026 but still down –17% compared to September 2025. Nonresidential construction spending declined in these sectors during the month of September: Education (-0.1%); Commercial (-0.2%); Healthcare (-0.3%); Highway and Street (-0.4%); Public Safety (-0.6%); Amusement and Recreation (-1.2%) Conservation and Development (-4.5%).

artigo.texto: AI Models & Platforms Envision Deploys SST-Based 800V DC Power at Ulanqab AI Data Center Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google Envision said on Nov. 2, 2026, that an integrated 800-volt direct-current (800V DC) power system is now powering live computing workloads at its Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, China, a deployment the company described in its announcement as the world’s first commercial use of such a system in a large-scale AI data center. The announcement says the system delivers power end to end, from medium-voltage AC input to the server rack, and that it is already operating commercially ahead of wider industry adoption, providing a reference for AI data centers moving to 800V DC power infrastructure. Solid-State Transformers and Real-Time Coordination The newly deployed system integrates three hardware layers: solid-state transformers (SST), battery energy storage (BESS), and equipment that adjusts direct-current voltage for computing hardware. Coordinating them is Envision’s Dubhe Controller, which runs with the company’s Dubhe Energy Foundation Model and adjusts the transformers and batteries in real time so that power supply tracks computing demand, including abrupt swings in load. According to Envision, the deployment is built around three capabilities: stable SST conversion directly from 10-kilovolt medium voltage to an 800V DC bus across operating conditions; battery storage that provides both second-scale power support and minute-scale backup; and millisecond-level coordination between SST and storage that absorbs GPU load fluctuations locally. Envision said the 800V DC architecture simplifies AI data center power systems, citing higher power conversion and watt-to-bit efficiency, a more compact equipment footprint, and reduced cabling and copper requirements. Those advantages, the company said, can lower infrastructure costs and support higher computing density within the same space. Rising Power Demand Per Rack The announcement frames the deployment against a specific operational problem: as AI computing demand accelerates, operators must deliver more power to each rack within constrained space while keeping supply stable as computing loads swing sharply from moment to moment. “AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage, and the grid to meet computing demand,” said Kevin Huang, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of Energy Storage and AIDC Power Systems. Huang said the live system demonstrates an end-to-end architecture connecting renewable supply with computing demand, calling it a critical step in moving power-compute coordination from strategic vision to day-to-day operating practice. Galaxy Campus and Mission Gobi The Galaxy campus, in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, began operations in August 2026, when Envision commissioned the site on Aug. 6 anchored by a 120,000-square-meter AI supercomputing facility, according to the company’s commissioning announcement at the time. That record described the campus as designed to scale to over 2GW of capacity; the Nov. 2 release states a planned capacity of 3GW and says the campus is designed to support up to one million AI accelerators operating in parallel at full build-out, with more than 80% of its power planned to come from direct renewable electricity connections. Envision’s Galaxy campus page markets the site as a net-zero AI data center, advertising long-term fixed electricity pricing at 20% below grid rates under a 10-year price lock, bundled electricity and green certificates, and a 60% green power direct-supply ratio. Envision said it aims to scale the approach through Mission Gobi, an initiative unveiled at VivaTech in Paris in June 2026 with Galaxy as its first flagship project. Mission Gobi targets 5GW of green AI data center capacity in desert regions worldwide by 2030, and the company presents it as a replicable blueprint, arguing that developing even 1% of global desert and Gobi regions could support computing capacity at terawatt scale at highly competitive cost.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media A new report from Georgetown and Duke researchers looks at the advantages of using batteries to meet data center demand — and offers some advice for states. Developers and utilities are building tons of gas generation to power the data center boom. It’s an expansion that could cost them and the rest of us dearly, both in terms of climate change and money that may end up wasted if computing demand fails to materialize. But there’s a cleaner, cheaper, and faster-to-deploy alternative: batteries. That’s the conclusion of a new report from researchers at Georgetown and Duke universities, which lays out the ways states can push utilities and tech firms to opt for energy storage over fossil fuels whenever possible. Fossil fuel power — whether in the form of giant utility-scale plants or generators installed behind the meter at data centers — has become the go-to for many in the AI industry. That’s because gas generation offers round-the-clock power in a single package. Overall, U.S. utilities are planning more than 60 gigawatts of new gas plants to serve data center demand, and around 90 GW of behind-the-meter gas generators for data centers have been proposed nationwide. “At the moment, there’s a lot of inertia and status quo pressure for much of the behind-the-meter resources being natural gas,” said Ian Hitchcock, report co-author and senior program coordinator at the Duke Initiative for Science and Society. Moving ahead with those gas power plans does more than spell climate disaster. If data center proposals fall through or shut down early, other utility customers could be on the hook for the cost of overbuilding gas. That’s called “stranded asset” risk — and states have only begun to tackle it, even amid mounting fears that the AI sector is a bubble about to pop. Batteries “can act as a hedge against that risk,” last week’s report explains. Batteries are much cheaper than round-the-clock gas generation in situations where hours of stored energy can solve near-term needs. They’re also inherently modular and flexible in ways that gas power plants are not, which allows planners to increase or cut back on deployment if data center demand shifts sharply. Plus, batteries can help avoid the need for costly grid buildouts that would otherwise be used to serve increasing electricity demand, and can act as shock absorbers to cushion the grid against data centers’ massive and fast-changing computing loads. While lithium-ion batteries can’t provide round-the-clock power, they can meet large portions of data center electricity needs, said Jackson Ewing, director of energy and climate policy at Duke University’s Nicholas Institute of Energy, Environment & Sustainability. And unlike more future-forward solutions — such as advanced geothermal, next-generation nuclear, and novel long-duration energy storage technologies — “batteries are already showing serious momentum in terms of their deployment trajectory.” In fact, utilities and data center developers are increasingly embracing batteries, even as they pursue gas. A new forecast from BloombergNEF sees U.S. energy storage deployment surpassing 11,000 gigawatt-hours by 2036, a 30% increase from its 10-year forecast from just six months ago. Data center demand is pushing much of that growth. So, what can state decision-makers do to further encourage data centers to opt for batteries? States that directly regulate utility investments can craft “bring your own new clean energy” tariff structures. These regulations can set minimum requirements for data centers to procure or pay for enough carbon-free generation and energy storage to cover some or all of their electricity needs. Certain jurisdictions are already moving ahead with this approach; Google, for example, has signed onto such tariffs with regulators in Nevada and Minnesota. Things get more complicated in states with “restructured” energy markets. In these places, regulators have limited authority over the independent power producers that build big generation and battery projects and sell power into wholesale electricity markets. Still, the report highlights several ways that these states can encourage battery development to serve data centers, including via state energy storage mandates like those launched in Illinois, Maryland and New Jersey, and engaging in state energy planning in conjunction with regional grid operators. “There is not a jurisdiction that has no potential action items if they’re serious about trying to deploy this,” Hitchcock said. Jeff St. John is chief reporter and policy specialist at Canary Media. He covers innovative grid technologies, rooftop solar and batteries, clean hydrogen, EV charging, and more. artigo.texto: Elon Musk, owner of X and head of SpaceX and Tesla, posted two jokes within hours of the 2026 US midterm results, and one of them pushed orbital computing back onto the news agenda. The Times of India ran it under a headline saying Musk sent a “let’s go to Space” message to Google, Amazon, Meta and other data-centre builders. The posts themselves named none of those companies. The first post read “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” The second read “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.” Both were reported on November 4, 2026. They tell us about Musk’s mood and his politics, and they tell us very little about any actual hardware program. Google has been talking publicly about space data centers costing up to 100x more than ground sites, which is a far more concrete data point than a late-night joke. This analysis separates what the record confirms from what headlines imply. It covers the election backdrop, the AI power squeeze that gives the joke its edge, the one orbital project with real reporting behind it, and five predictions for the next year. Where a detail is not on the record, we say so plainly. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Elon Musk Actually Posted on X After the Midterms Two posts anchor the story. Both appeared on X, the platform Musk owns, after the 2026 US midterm elections closed. Outlets including The Economic Times, Rediff and Implicator carried them on November 4. The wording matches across those reports, which is why the quotes above can be treated as accurate. The space-lasers line is a sarcastic reference to accusations that Musk’s political spending or his companies tried to tilt elections. The Economic Times described the posts as Musk mocking his own election spending after what it called a Democratic midterm sweep. The paper also suggested the data-center line could reflect worry about how AI infrastructure might be regulated in the coming years. India Today reported that claims tying Starlink to election manipulation lacked support, and that no credible evidence had surfaced of Starlink being used to hack or sway voting systems. That context matters. The “space lasers” phrase is a punchline built on an internet conspiracy theory, not a confession or a product reference. Nothing in the reported posts mentions a SpaceX program, a launch date, a chip, a satellite count or a budget. Any article that tells you Musk “announced” orbital data centers on election night is stretching the record. He said they looked appealing. He did not say what he would build. The Times of India Headline Versus the Verified Record The Times of India headline is the reason this story trended. It says Musk sent a message to Google, Amazon, Meta and other companies building data centres. The reporting we reviewed says the posts did not directly address Google, Amazon or Meta. Those companies were described as firms expanding data-center capacity for artificial intelligence, which is true, but the link to Musk’s posts is the paper’s reading rather than something Musk wrote. That gap is common in fast news cycles. A joke gets framed as a signal, the signal gets framed as a message, and the message gets an addressee. By the third step the original text has disappeared. The table below keeps score. Readers who want the cleanest takeaway should hold onto the first three rows. Everything below them is interpretation, and some of it is good interpretation, but it is not fact. The Midterm Backdrop: A Democratic Sweep and Its AI Stakes NBC Los Angeles ran live updates under a headline stating that Democrats won control of the House and Senate. The Economic Times used the word “sweep.” For a tech billionaire who spent heavily on the other side, that is the context for a self-mocking post about lasers. The AI industry was already watching the vote closely. Our earlier piece on how investors gamed out congressional control and $1.5T of AI capex laid out the logic. A new majority can hold hearings on power use, tax breaks for data centers and chip export rules. None of those hearings has been scheduled in the reporting we reviewed, so treat them as risks, not events. Business reaction was loud. Yahoo Finance UK collected executive responses under the word “blunami” to describe the election-night result. We did not find a verified statement from Google, Amazon or Meta responding to Musk’s posts, and none of the reports we reviewed claimed one. One point deserves care. Reports conflict on how much Musk spent on the cycle, so we are not repeating any total. A number that varies by outlet is a number we cannot defend. Why Data-Center Politics Gave the Joke Its Edge Implicator tied the posts to a headline about Texas threatening the AI buildout, and Axios linked the remarks to Texas politics and local opposition to data centers. The thread connecting them is simple. Data centers need land, water, transmission lines and enormous electricity, and voters notice when their bills rise. We have tracked that friction for months. A Florida poll found 59% of respondents opposed data centers near them, and the issue landed in a governor’s race. Separate coverage looked at power bills, utilities and nine commission seats on the midterm ballot. Local politics, in short, has become a real constraint on where AI compute can sit. Read that way, “data centers in space looking pretty appealing” is a joke with a logic underneath. If ground sites face permitting fights and angry ratepayers, a site with no neighbors starts to sound attractive. The punchline works because the grievance is real. It is still only a punchline. Moving compute to orbit solves a political problem by creating an engineering one. The sections below show how large that engineering problem is. BYD October EV sales reach a record 300,000+ The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026. BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark. To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates. October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year. BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units. According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America. Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year. By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles. By EI News Network Coal India Ltd. (CIL) has appointed Neopulse Energy Pvt. Ltd. as the Owner’s Engineer for its proposed 80 MW/320 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Odisha. The company will provide technical advisory and engineering oversight during the selection of the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractor and subsequent project execution. As part of the pre-award responsibilities, Neopulse Energy will assist CIL in preparing technical specifications, defining equipment requirements and evaluating technical bids submitted by prospective EPC contractors. Following the award of the EPC contract, Neopulse Energy will review the contractor’s engineering designs, vendor documentation and quality plans. Its scope will also cover technical supervision of equipment manufacturing, construction activities, testing and commissioning. The 80 MW/320 MWh installation will have a four-hour storage duration. The project is expected to provide grid flexibility and support the integration of renewable energy into the electricity network. Battery storage systems can help manage variations in solar and wind power generation and improve the reliability of electricity supply. The appointment places Neopulse Energy in an advisory and technical oversight role, with responsibilities extending from the EPC tendering process through project commissioning. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.
