artigo.texto: Marketing Bago’s carbon market initiative at COP31 By Aliyu Umar Aliyu As global climate diplomacy shifts from promises to practical implementation, Niger State has an opportunity to position its emerging carbon market initiative as a vehicle for investment, job creation and sustainable development. For Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago, popularly known as the Farmer Governor, the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), scheduled for November 9–20, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, offers a strategic platform to advance the state’s green economy vision. The conference will bring together governments, investors, climate finance institutions, development partners and environmental experts to discuss practical responses to climate change. For Niger State, however, participation should go beyond showcasing its environmental ambitions. The priority should be to secure credible partnerships, develop investment-ready projects and establish a clear pathway for converting its natural resources into measurable climate and economic benefits. Governor Bago’s vision presents an opportunity to connect climate action with Niger State’s agricultural strength, forest resources, renewable energy potential and waste-management needs. If properly developed, these assets could support projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions while creating employment, improving energy access and strengthening rural livelihoods. Niger State’s participation at COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in November 2024 provided an earlier opportunity to promote its green economy agenda, including sustainable agriculture, renewable energy and forest conservation. COP31 should build on that engagement by moving from international advocacy towards practical project development and investment mobilisation. From Green Economy Vision to Carbon Market Investment Carbon markets provide a potential mechanism for financing projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. Under recognised crediting systems, a carbon credit generally represents one metric tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent reduced or removed, subject to the applicable methodology and verification requirements. For Niger State, opportunities could include methane capture at landfills, climate-smart rice cultivation, solar mini-grids and forest restoration. These initiatives could attract investors while supporting the state’s wider development objectives. However, natural resources alone do not guarantee carbon revenue. Projects must demonstrate credible emissions reductions, additionality, appropriate monitoring and independent verification. They must also comply with relevant national regulations and international carbon market requirements. This is particularly important as Niger State seeks to position itself as a pioneer in subnational carbon market development in Nigeria. The ambition to become the country’s first subnational government to open its carbon market to investment, and to advance towards international carbon-credit sales, could be significant. The proposed Niger State Carbon Market Office could play a central role by coordinating project identification, technical assessments, investor engagement, regulatory compliance and stakeholder participation. Its effectiveness will depend on a clear mandate, adequate expertise, transparent procedures and coordination with the relevant federal authorities. International cooperation could accelerate this process. In correspondence to the Niger State team concerning a post-feasibility mission action plan, myclimate’s Article 6 Bilateral Cooperation Team disclosed that a draft memorandum of understanding (MoU) on project development and carbon market activities was undergoing internal legal review, with the intention of finalising it before COP31. The correspondence, signed on behalf of the team by Nsikan-George Emana, Senior Project Manager for Bilateral Cooperation at myclimate, proposed November 12, 2026, for a strategic meeting with the Niger State Government, during which the parties hope to sign the agreement. The proposed engagement offers an opportunity to establish a framework for technical cooperation, project development and potential international market participation. Nevertheless, the MoU remains prospective until formally concluded, and its existence should not be mistaken for evidence that investment has already been secured or carbon credits sold. Niger State should approach the meeting with clearly defined priorities, including project timelines, financing arrangements, responsibilities, community safeguards and measurable implementation targets. Article 6 and the International Opportunity The proposed partnership is particularly relevant to Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which provides frameworks for international cooperation in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. At COP29 in November 2024, countries made significant progress on the rules governing international carbon trading and the UN-supervised carbon crediting mechanism. Under Article 6.2, countries can cooperate through internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, subject to applicable accounting and authorisation requirements. Article 6.4 provides a UN-supervised crediting mechanism, while Article 6.8 addresses non-market approaches. For Niger State, these frameworks could create opportunities to develop projects that attract international finance and contribute to Nigeria’s climate commitments. However, the state must work within Nigeria’s national climate governance arrangements. International transfers under Article 6 cannot be treated as an exclusively state-level transaction where national authorisation and accounting are required. Potential projects should therefore be developed with appropriate technical, legal and financial support. artigo.texto: Just a little rain falling all around, The grass lifts its head to the heavenly sound, Just a little rain, just a little rain, What have they done to the rain? . . . Just a little boy standing in the rain, . . . And the grass is gone, The boy disappears . . . By Mary O’Brien When Joan Baez sang “What Have They Done to the Rain” in 1962, she gave voice to a song Malvina Reynolds had recently written as a protest against aboveground nuclear testing. The nuclear fallout from the testing contained radioactive Strontium-90, which can enter the food chain through grass eaten by cows that are eaten by humans. Later the song became identified with acid rain, produced by burning high-sulfur or high-nitrogen fossil fuels, whose sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form sulfuric and nitric acids when mixed with rain. And now, 60 years later? We realize we have done the most un-intelligent thing imaginable to rain: Addicted to fossil fuels, we’ve heated our atmospheric blanket, creating long stretches of no rain, punctuated by storms bringing “historic” floods. The rain’s offspring — streams, rivers, springs, sole source aquifers — are smaller. We bake. We know we need to turn to other sources of energy such as the sun and wind. We are asked to not water our lawns after 10 in the morning. But then enters a juggernaut directed by a few unaccountable billionaires: Artificial intelligence (AI). It’s designed to be smarter than people and to be cheaper than either hourly wages or salaries that humans demand. While humans think about almost anything, AI data centers dutifully undertake intelligence tasks that are assigned to them (or occasionally run loose into other systems). Currently, the AI industry is on the honor system to voluntarily regulate (or not) the digital services it develops. One painfully immediate problem with data centers is that they consume vast amount of fossil-fueled power to be artificially intelligent, and they depend on vast amounts of water to cool their heated, silicon-based thinking. Which leads to a data center question that Grand County (the second driest county in Utah) must answer before Jan. 3, when our 180-day moratorium on data centers expires: Do we write no AI data centers into our land use code, or do we lay out the welcome mat for such data centers in Grand County? A Utah State University poll (and most national polls) indicates that about 75% of Utahns (and Americans) don’t want any more data centers. It is legal for Grand County to say “No.” If the county is going to say “Yes” to permitting data centers, then specifications need to be written into the land use code before Jan. 3 by someone: Where would data centers be allowed? How large could they be in terms of fossil fuel consumption and emissions? How much water would be needed to cool the chips that heat up as they process data? What water source(s) would be used and for which type of cooling processes? What would be the limit on noise at the factory boundary? What light pollution would be allowed? What amount of heat would be permitted for release? What bond requirements would be needed to address failures or shutdown? (For the past 48 years, the public has been paying for cleanup of the abandoned uranium mill tailings site of a private, commercial business.) Grand County Commissioner Brian Martinez has proposed that our county’s land use code permit data centers (and other unnamed industries) that require up to 10 MW continuous power or 20,000 gallons of water a day for evaporative cooling. Ten MW would power all houses in Grand County for a year. (And, a mistake on Brian’s part? A 10 MW data center uses 200,000, not 20,000 gallons of water a day for evaporative cooling. And requires even more water to generate electricity if cooling is by closed loop.) Planning Commissioner Bob O’Brien proposes that the land use code exclude AI data centers. Such a land use code exclusion (1) is responsive to the large majority of the public, (2) requires no water or fossil fuels, and (3) by not requiring extensive, technical data center specifications, can easily be written prior to Jan. 3. If the Utah Legislature, against the wishes of most Utahns and Grand County residents eventually mandates that every county must submit to requests for data centers, then Grand County’s land use code could be revised. But while it’s still legal for Grand County to say no to data centers in the land use code, the county shouldn’t obey in advance. Turn up and speak out. Increase the chance rain will keep falling all around. Mary O’Brien writes from Castle Valley, where she lives with Bob O’Brien.

artigo.texto: A operadora de telecomunicações russa Rostelecom está iniciando a construção de data centers subterrâneos. A primeira instalação deverá ser construída em parceria com a Norilsk Nickel. Essas instalações são consideradas as mais seguras, pois possuem três níveis de segurança. O primeiro nível envolve a criação de um sistema de backup para armazenar cópias de dados que possam ser necessárias caso a infraestrutura principal falhe. O segundo nível envolve a criação de locais geograficamente distribuídos para armazenar poder computacional e serviços. Isso permitirá que a infraestrutura seja distribuída em vez de concentrada em um único local. O terceiro nível envolve a criação de centros de dados subterrâneos, levando em consideração os piores cenários de ameaça. Estão sendo propostas instalações de data centers subterrâneos em minas de carvão abandonadas. Além de garantir a segurança de instalações estratégicas, essa medida também visa apoiar a indústria carbonífera da Rússia. Anteriormente, o presidente da Rostelecom, Mikhail Oseevsky, afirmou no Fórum SOC que o mercado russo de data centers está passando por mudanças devido a diversos fatores, incluindo o fato de os data centers estarem se tornando alvos em conflitos. As mudanças que ele descreveu incluem data centers domésticos consumindo menos energia, distribuídos por vários locais e, possivelmente, até mesmo a transição para energia nuclear. Segundo Oseevsky, dois "fatores" — a segurança física dos centros e a disponibilidade de eletricidade — estão atualmente "mudando drasticamente o paradigma". Ele acredita que esses fatores irão alterar o modelo de construção de centros de dados e sua localização. Especialistas já haviam levantado a ideia de instalar data centers no subsolo. Eles observaram que a construção precisaria levar em consideração as condições locais e uma série de riscos potenciais. Esses riscos incluem não apenas a ameaça de ataques com mísseis ou drones, mas também fenômenos naturais como terremotos ou inundações. Em outubro de 2026, os centros de dados da Yandex e do Sberbank foram danificados por ataques de drones, e a restauração dos serviços online nesses centros ainda está em andamento. Segundo cálculos de especialistas, a construção de uma instalação subterrânea pode ser cerca de 30 a 40% mais cara do que uma instalação comparável construída acima do solo. A estrutura de custos de um centro de dados subterrâneo também é diferente: os custos de refrigeração podem ser reduzidos, mas custos adicionais são incorridos, incluindo suporte e impermeabilização para as estruturas, ventilação da mina e monitoramento de gases, sistemas subterrâneos de supressão e evacuação de incêndio, equipamentos de elevação, cabeamento de energia e fibra óptica a partir do solo e canais de comunicação de backup. O custo também depende se a instalação será construída do zero ou se uma estrutura subterrânea existente será reformada.

artigo.texto: On the edge of Nigeria’s commercial capital Lagos, where the city gives way to the Atlantic, behind walls of concrete and steel are rows of machines designed to store, process and move the digital records of the West African nation. Nigeria’s banks, fintech companies and payment processors have spent years building businesses on computing infrastructure that can sit anywhere in the world. Now, beginning January 1, 2027, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) is requiring financial institutions and participants in the country’s payments system to ensure that payment transaction data generated in Nigeria is stored and managed in Nigeria. Dr Ayotunde Coker, CEO of Pan-African data center operator Open Access Data Centres (OADC), says engagement with companies seeking local infrastructure has increased since the directive. “We’ve got what I call a reasonable level of requests in terms of colocation. We’re ready to really onboard a lot as is required,” Coker discloses to FORBES AFRICA. But the country’s other technology executives, engineers and AI specialists describe a reality bordering on shortage of reliable power, high-density cooling, redundant connectivity, cloud services, cybersecurity, disaster recovery, engineering talent and, perhaps most consequentially, control over the technology that processes Nigerian data. Loading... “Data sovereignty is not achieved simply because the server is physically located in Nigeria. Physical location is only the first layer,” explains Kemisola Adalumo. “Data sovereignty is not achieved simply because the server is physically located in Nigeria. Physical location is only the first layer,” explains Kemisola Adalumo, a Nigerian cybersecurity, governance, risk and compliance and AI-governance specialist, to FORBES AFRICA. That distinction is becoming critical as Nigeria moves from an era of data storage into one dominated by AI. Nigeria’s data-center market has changed in a relatively short period. Industry estimates put the country at roughly 26 data-center facilities, with about 18 operating commercially. The figures vary depending on what qualifies as an operational facility and whether private corporate installations are included, but the country’s infrastructure footprint has expanded substantially. Most of the commercial market is concentrated around Lagos. OADC announced plans in 2025 for a $240 million expansion of its Lagos facility to 24MW by 2027. The project was described as part of a broader $500 million African investment program. Coker says the company is now designing for substantially more AI capacity than previously envisaged. He put the eventual figure at roughly 40MW within the same development shell. Rack Centre commissioned its 12-megawatt (MW) LGS2 facility in 2025, describing it as a Tier III, carrier and cloud-neutral facility serving enterprises, cloud providers and financial institutions. MTN Nigeria has also committed more than $240 million to a 9MW Dabengwa data center in Ikeja. Its first phase was designed as a 4.5MW Tier III facility, with cloud infrastructure developed in partnership with Dell Technologies. And then there is Kasi Cloud. The company broke ground in 2022 on what was initially described as a $250 million data-center campus in the Lekki neighborhood of Lagos. Four years later, the first phase has been commissioned. The broader campus is designed to scale toward 100MW and has been positioned as infrastructure for hyperscale cloud and AI workloads. “We’ve got what I call a reasonable level of requests in terms of colocation. We’re ready to really onboard a lot as is required.” – Ayotunde Coker That matters because conventional data-center infrastructure and AI infrastructure are different businesses. A traditional enterprise workload can be distributed across relatively modest server densities. AI workloads, particularly those involving large numbers of graphics-processing units (GPUs), concentrate enormous amounts of computing power into comparatively small spaces. That changes the engineering equation: power, cooling, rack density and network architecture all become more demanding. A February 2026 analysis by TechCabal noted that Nigeria’s then-operational data centers generally had capacities below 20MW, while hyperscale AI campuses target 50MW to 100MW or more. Engineer Adetola Ibironke, General Manager for Systems Engineering and Projects at PPC Limited, argues that Nigeria remains in a “critical build-out phase”. “Announced capacity must not be confused with operational capacity,” he says to FORBES AFRICA, noting that projects exist at different stages of construction, commissioning and customer onboarding. That gap between announced and usable capacity is one of the least visible features of the boom. A building can be finished while its computing equipment is still being installed. A facility can have power infrastructure without having the required IT load. A data center can have racks without the cloud platform, cybersecurity controls or network redundancy a financial institution needs. The data-center industry uses tiers to describe levels of redundancy and availability. Tier IV represents the highest level in the Uptime Institute’s tier classification system. In Nigeria, Galaxy Backbone’s northern Nigeria city Kano facility holds Uptime Institute certification for both Tier IV design documents and the constructed facility. Uptime’s database also lists numerous Nigerian facilities with Tier III certifications. Galaxy Backbone describes its Kano installation as a Tier IV facility and its Abuja facility as Tier III. But Tier classification answers a narrower question than AI operators now need to answer. It addresses resilience and availability characteristics of the facility. It does not tell a bank whether a particular application can be migrated there without redesign. artigo.texto: China is giving sodium-ion batteries a temporary tax advantage over conventional lithium-ion technology as manufacturers look to bring the alternative chemistry into commercial electric vehicles. One of the country’s leading sodium-ion battery developers, Hina Battery, is planning a 10 GWh production base in Wuhan and has partnered with a vehicle manufacturer to develop electric sanitation trucks. The expansion comes as China introduces a consumption tax on specified lithium-ion batteries while exempting qualifying sodium-ion batteries through 2028. The policy could improve the economics of sodium-ion production, although falling lithium prices have narrowed the cost gap between the two chemistries. The technology is also attracting attention for its performance in extreme cold. FAW Jiefang reported that one of its electric heavy trucks equipped with a sodium-ion battery retained more than 90% of its usable capacity during testing at minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Creating a tax advantage for sodium-ion batteries China’s Ministry of Finance, General Administration of Customs and State Taxation Administration issued Announcement No. 20 (2026) on July 16, revising consumption tax rules for several battery categories. From September 1, 2026, specified lithium-ion batteries became subject to a 2% consumption tax. The rate is scheduled to rise to 4% on September 1, 2027. Qualifying sodium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries and fuel cells are exempt from the tax through December 31, 2028, provided they meet applicable national standards. More from Transportation See All The exemption gives sodium-ion manufacturers a temporary fiscal advantage, but it does not automatically make their products cheaper to produce. Battery-grade lithium carbonate averaged approximately $13,500, per metric ton on October 28. Meanwhile, square lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells for electric vehicles averaged about 5.7 US cents, per watt-hour on October 22. Sodium is more widely distributed geographically than lithium, potentially offering manufacturers a more diversified raw-material supply. However, the downstream sodium-ion supply chain remains concentrated in China, particularly in cell manufacturing, cathode materials and hard-carbon production. Hina targets commercial vehicle production in Wuhan Hina Battery signed an agreement with Wuhan’s Jiangxia District on October 14 to establish a sodium-ion battery production base with planned annual capacity of 10 GWh, with the first phase expected to provide 3 GWh of capacity. Construction is scheduled to begin in early 2027, with initial production targeted before the end of that year. The project was announced during the fourth National Sodium Battery Symposium, showcasing China’s effort to move sodium-ion technology beyond laboratory development and into larger-scale manufacturing. Hina has also signed a separate agreement with Chengli Special Automobile Group to develop sodium-ion-powered sanitation vehicles. The planned lineup includes refuse collection trucks, hook-lift vehicles, dust-suppression trucks and food-waste collection vehicles. Sodium-ion batteries have several potential advantages over lithium-ion alternatives, including access to more widely available raw materials and the possibility of better performance in low temperatures. Their main limitation remains lower energy density, which can translate into heavier or larger battery packs for the same amount of stored energy.

artigo.texto: Share This Article The Connecticut-based company behind a data center planned in Arkansas sued local officials in federal court Thursday over regulations targeting projects like it, claiming the county didn’t have the authority to enact such limits and that the state’s open meetings law was circumvented. The 38-page lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court of Eastern Arkansas, accused Pulaski County of enacting regulations targeting AVAIO Digital’s planned data center that infringe on the federal government’s authority to regulate interstate electrical transmission and commerce. AVAIO asked the court for an injunction preventing the regulations from being applied to its project, monetary damages and for the disclosure of public records it said had been withheld from them. It marks the second lawsuit filed in federal court this year connected to data center projects that have appeared in the state over the last two years. Entergy Arkansas unsuccessfully sued the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, one of its reporters and a local resident in September over the publication of details of the utility’s power agreement for Google’s West Memphis data center that the resident obtained through a public records request. The regulations AVAIO is contesting went into effect earlier this week after the quorum court overrode Democratic Judge Barry Hyde’s veto of them, and were drafted in response to community anger over AVAIO’s project located just off 145th Street. The regulations create uncertainty and threaten AVAIO’s “existing business, financial, and investment arrangements,” the company wrote in the complaint. The lawsuit also accused Democratic nominee for county judge, Wendell Griffen, of having “unlawful control over the Pulaski County Quorum Court,” pointing to his role authoring and advocating for the regulations. Griffen told the Arkansas Advocate that the lawsuit was expected, and said it was the county’s “constitutional power” to regulate data centers within its boundaries. A spokesperson for Pulaski County did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday evening. The company said Griffen and several members of the quorum court engaged in polling and deliberations that violated the Arkansas Freedom of Information Act. The lawsuit also named Democratic Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood, who was the lead legislative sponsor of the regulations. Griffen also disputed AVAIO’s characterizations of his communications with quorum court members. “If they contend that a private citizen exercising his First Amendment right to approach members of the legislative body of the county about a matter of public interest is unlawful authority, then they need to reread the First Amendment to the Constitution of the United States,” Griffen said. The ordinance “is without effect because it is an obstacle to the full exercise of the federal government’s authorities under the Federal Power Act to regulate the transmission of electricity,” AVAIO wrote in its complaint. The alleged polling, the company said, also makes the passed ordinance invalid. Judge Lee Rudofsky, who oversaw Entergy’s lawsuit against the Democrat-Gazette, is the assigned judge on the case. artigo.texto: MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On October 28, HiTHIUM, a leading global energy storage technology company, showcased its ∞Power 6.9MWh 8-hour long-duration battery energy storage system (BESS) at All Energy Australia in Melbourne, alongside its grid compliance capabilities, localized service network and energy storage solutions for C&I and residential applications. Long-duration energy storage is increasingly important for grid flexibility and supply reliability in Australia. The federal government supports dispatchable clean energy projects through the Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS), while New South Wales continues to advance dedicated LDES tenders, creating new opportunities for storage projects of eight hours or longer. At the exhibition, HiTHIUM showcased its ∞Power 6.9MWh 8-hour-native BESS. Australia's high-price events are lengthening, with 4-hour-plus events accounting for over 70% of scarcity revenue in 2025 and shifting storage value toward firm supply duration. CSIRO GenCost analysis shows that two 4-hour systems delivering the same 8-hour output would cost about 23% more than a purpose-built 8-hour system, which offers greater value potential during price peaks. Integrated into a standard 20-foot container, ∞Power 6.9MWh BESS offers up to 96% round-trip efficiency, a 25-year design life, and compatibility with PCS and EMS products from major global suppliers. Compared with a 4-hour configuration, it reduces land use by 15% and can lower LCOS through system optimization. Developed in line with NFPA, IEC and AS standards, the system also delivers a high level of safety. To address Australia's grid connection requirements, HiTHIUM presented its Grid Compliance Simulation and Verification Platform, supporting projects through grid connection, from R0 assessment and R1 capability assessment to commissioning and R2 model validation. By combining grid-code interpretation, plant-level modelling, automated simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing and site measurement validation, the platform helps identify potential compliance risks earlier and reduce late-stage rework. HiTHIUM continues to strengthen its localized service capabilities in Australia. The company has established a localized service network across Australia, covering spare-parts warehousing, training, operations and maintenance (O&M), and compliant battery recycling, with nationwide service coverage. At the exhibition, HiTHIUM signed strategic cooperation agreements with Raystech, Ingeteam and other Australian partners to further strengthen its local workforce, spare-parts infrastructure and safety capabilities. The company also announced that its Brisbane service center is scheduled to open by mid-2027, further expanding its regional service network and bringing efficient, reliable support closer to Australian customers. HiTHIUM also showcased its ∞Power 1022kWh liquid-cooled C&I energy storage cabinet, which combines its proprietary ∞Cell 1175Ah LDES cells with an integrated design for applications including peak shaving and solar self-consumption. For residential applications, the company presented the HeroEE 16 and ARKVOLT F8S series, supporting flexible deployment and integration with solar, heat pumps and EV charging. Through its 8-hour LDES technology, grid compliance expertise and expanding local service network, HiTHIUM is strengthening its ability to support Australian energy storage projects from development and grid connection through long-term operation. These efforts reflect HiTHIUM's commitment to supporting Australia's evolving energy storage needs with integrated solutions and sustained local support.

artigo.texto: The PJM Interconnection on Thursday filed a revised reliability backstop procurement, or RBP, proposal with federal regulators, with a goal of beginning the process on March 1 — about seven months later than originally planned. The revisions come after the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in late September rejected most of PJM’s initial proposal, which was designed to fill a capacity shortfall driven by data center development. FERC said in its decision that the original plan’s provisions for cost allocation, transmission owner exit rules and load-serving entity, or LSE, collateral requirements may have been unjust and unreasonable. The proposed revisions were “carefully tailored” to address the issues identified by FERC while keeping the RBP’s fundamental structure and policy objectives intact, PJM said in its recent filing. Under the new proposal, “PJM is using more current information on large-load growth to improve cost causation, revising the collateral methodology, and, importantly, recognizing that an RBP obligation and its associated collateral can move with the load-serving obligation when a large customer changes LSEs,” Maria Scheller, vice president of energy and planning at the consulting firm ICF International, said in an email to Utility Dive. The proposal sharply reduces risks for providers of last resort and default service providers — utilities that provide power to customers that don’t buy electricity from power marketers, according to Scheller. “If a large load initially relies on default service, the [provider of last resort] may temporarily carry significant RBP collateral and liquidity requirements,” she said. “The key credit question is whether state rules provide timely, certain recovery and adequate customer security, so the utility remains an administrative intermediary rather than taking meaningful balance-sheet or stranded-cost risk.” As a result, the state role is especially important in the process’ outcome, and some state utility regulators may need to craft new rules, according to Scheller. “Regulators may need to determine customer-specific allocation, establish appropriate security and cost-recovery rules, track changes in suppliers, and decide what happens if the underlying large load shrinks, defaults or disappears,” she said. The proposal reduces the direct risk to residential and other existing customers, but it does not eliminate it, according to Scheller. “Administrative costs, collateral and financing costs, regulatory lag, customer default and stranded-cost risk can still create indirect exposure if the state-level mechanisms do not keep the obligation tightly attached to the large load that caused it,” she said. The planned procurement aims to fill a 6.8-GW capacity shortfall from PJM’s 2028/29 base residual auction. However, the procurement may shrink significantly from the initial target after PJM recalculates how much capacity is needed, according to equity analysts with Jefferies. PJM utilities, such as PPL Electric, FirstEnergy and AES Ohio, recently lowered their overall, near-term large load forecasts by 6.5 GW, the analysts said in an Oct. 28 note, citing recent filings to PJM’s Load Analysis Subcommittee. That reduction could reduce PJM’s 2027 load forecast, which would affect the grid operator’s backstop procurement target, they said. With that reduction, the procurement could be for as little as roughly 630 MW, according to the note. The procurement could also shrink if data center developers enter into bilateral contracts with power suppliers. Even so, analysis by Charles River Associates discussed Monday by the subcommittee found that PJM could face a roughly 11.5-GW shortfall by 2030. PJM hired CRA to provide an independent data center demand forecast. Under the proposal, PJM will close the RBP bid window on March 28, with the final procurement target and supply amounts determined on April 28, the grid operator said Thursday. PJM would post the results on May 10.

artigo.texto: Nidec is selling its fan-motor heritage to the data center market, and the pitch now has a video attached. Data Center Frontier lists a video titled “Nidec Brings Decades of Experience to Today’s Data Center Technology Needs.” The confirmed point from that listing is narrow but useful: Nidec is applying thermal-solution design technologies, developed through its fan-motor expertise, to liquid-cooling product development. The story lands in a market that keeps spending. We covered the money side in AI Capex Tops $740B as Markets Doubt the Boom, and the hardware that soaks up those budgets includes cooling loops and backup generators as much as chips. Nidec sits on both of those lines. This analysis separates what Nidec and Data Center Frontier have actually put on the record from what remains open. The fact base is small. No on-record speaker quote was identified in the available results, so this piece paraphrases company statements and names the source each time. Where a number is missing, we say so rather than fill the gap. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Data Center Frontier Published About Nidec The headline is a video title, not a press release. That distinction matters. A video listing on a trade site tells you the vendor has a story it wants told to data center operators, and it tells you which message Nidec chose to lead with: decades of experience. The confirmed content is the link between fan motors and liquid cooling. Nidec built its thermal know-how around moving air with small, efficient motors. It now applies the design thinking behind that work to liquid-cooling products. The listing gives no product price, no launch date, no customer name and no performance claim, and we treat all of those as unconfirmed. Beyond the video, Nidec’s own product pages fill in the portfolio. They list two coolant distribution unit (CDU) formats, In-Rack and In-Row, and they state a shipment count for the In-Rack unit. Nidec Power, a separate arm of the group, describes its generator line for data center backup and prime power. Taken together, the sources describe a vendor that wants to be a one-stop supplier for both heat removal and electrical resilience. The takeaway: this is a positioning story backed by a few hard figures. The figures are worth examining, because they are the only parts a buyer can test. Nidec Data Center Cooling: From Fan Motors to Liquid Loops Nidec is best known as a motor maker. Its corporate site organizes the catalog by application, and the product search by application shows how wide that catalog runs. Fan motors are one thread in it. They are also the thread Data Center Frontier highlights, because fans were the first tool data centers used to throw heat away. Air cooling and liquid cooling look like different trades, yet they share engineering problems. Both need reliable rotating parts. Both need tight control of flow. Both punish designs that waste energy on the pump or fan itself. A company that has spent years tuning fan motors for low noise and steady airflow has real knowledge to carry over, and that is the argument Nidec makes. The argument has limits. A fan moves air through a chassis. A CDU moves coolant between the facility loop and the server loop, with pumps, heat exchangers, filtration and controls in the mix. The motor know-how transfers, but the system design is new ground. Nidec has to prove that the transfer works at the scale operators now demand. Why does this matter to the cloud sector? Cloud operators plan capacity in racks and megawatts. Whatever limits rack density limits how much compute a given building can host. Cooling hardware therefore shapes the cloud cost curve more than most readers assume, even though it rarely makes headlines. The CDU Lineup: In-Rack and In-Row Nidec lists two liquid-cooling products on its product pages: the Coolant Distribution Unit (In-Rack) and the Coolant Distribution Unit (In-Row). The names describe where the unit sits relative to the servers it serves. In-Rack CDU An In-Rack unit lives inside the rack envelope. The appeal is proximity. Short coolant runs keep plumbing simple, and operators can add cooling rack by rack as they add compute. The tradeoff is space. Every slot the cooling unit occupies is a slot the IT gear cannot use, so operators weigh footprint against flexibility. Nidec states that more than 13 kpcs of these In-Rack CDUs have shipped globally. That is the one volume number on the record, and we return to it below. In-Row CDU An In-Row unit sits at the end of, or between, rack rows and serves several racks from one point. The case for it is economy of scale. One larger unit can feed a group of racks, which can cut the number of separate pieces to buy, install and maintain. The case against is concentration. A single unit that serves many racks becomes a bigger failure domain unless the design adds redundancy. Nidec lists the In-Row product alongside the In-Rack one, but the sources available for this report give no shipment figure for it. We do not infer one. 13 kpcs Shipped: Reading the CDU Volume Figure Nidec states that over 13 kpcs In-Rack CDUs have been shipped globally. The abbreviation means thousands of pieces, so the claim reads as more than 13,000 units. Shipment counts of this kind serve as proof of maturity. They tell a buyer the product has left the lab and survived real installations. Still, a shipped count answers only one question. It does not say how many units run in production today, how many sit in warehouses, or how many served pilots. It does not break out customers, regions or rack types. It also covers a period the company does not define in the material we reviewed. Treat it as a floor on credibility, not a performance score. Compare that with how chip vendors report. artigo.texto: Long-Duration Energy Storage Systems Market Size, Share, Trend Report 2026 to 2035 What is Long-Duration Energy Storage Systems Market Size? Global Long-Duration Energy Storage Systems Market is estimated to witness a growth of 10.5% CAGR during the forecast period for 2026 to 2035. Long-Duration Energy Storage Systems Market Size, Share & Trends Analysis Distribution by Technology (Mechanical / Physical Storage: Pumped Hydro Storage, Compressed Air Energy Storage, Liquid Air Energy Storage, Gravity-Based Storage, Electrochemical Storage, Flow Batteries, Metal-Air Batteries, High-Temperature & Liquid-Metal Batteries, Sodium-Ion & Other Long-Duration-Configured Batteries, Thermal Storage, Sensible-Heat Storage, Latent-Heat / Phase-Change Storage, Pumped-Heat / Electrao-Thermal Energy Storage, Chemical Storage, Hydrogen-Based Power-to-Power Storage, Other Power-to-X Storage), by Storage Duration (Inter-Day, Multi-Day, Multi-Day to Seasonal), by Application / Use Case, by end user and Segment Forecasts, 2026 to 2035. Long-duration energy storage systems (LDES) are energy storage technologies designed to retain electricity or energy for extended durations and discharge it when required to maintain a reliable balance between power generation and demand. Unlike conventional short-duration storage systems, LDES technologies can provide sustained energy delivery over several hours and, depending on the technology, for periods extending to multiple days or longer. These systems are increasingly important for integrating variable renewable energy sources, improving grid flexibility, reducing reliance on conventional peaking generation, and strengthening power system resilience. The LDES technology landscape encompasses a diverse range of storage approaches, including mechanical and physical storage technologies such as pumped hydro, compressed air energy storage, liquid air energy storage, and gravity-based systems; electrochemical technologies such as flow batteries, metal-air batteries, and high-temperature or liquid-metal batteries; thermal energy storage; and chemical storage solutions including hydrogen-based power-to-power systems and other Power-to-X technologies. Each technology offers distinct characteristics in terms of storage duration, energy and power capacity, efficiency, response time, geographic requirements, and suitability for different grid and end-use applications. The long-duration energy storage systems Market encompasses the development, manufacturing, system integration, deployment, and commercialization of technologies capable of providing extended-duration energy storage. These systems are utilized for renewable energy integration and firming, grid balancing, ancillary services, energy arbitrage, load shifting, peak demand management, backup power, microgrid resilience, off-grid electricity supply, and industrial decarbonization. Their ability to store surplus electricity and release it during periods of higher demand or reduced renewable generation makes LDES an important component of increasingly flexible and decentralized energy systems. The market ecosystem includes technology developers, equipment and system manufacturers, engineering and infrastructure companies, project developers, utilities, independent power producers, grid operators, and energy service providers. artigo.texto: BYD has reached an important milestone in India, with its Sealion 7 electric SUV recording over 5,000 customer deliveries since February 2025. The milestone comes as the company continues to expand the SUV’s range with new variants and special editions. The Sealion 7 is currently offered in four versions, including the Dynamic, Premium, Performance and the recently launched Festive Edition. The SUV uses BYD’s Blade Battery technology and Cell-to-Body architecture. It also gets an ocean-inspired exterior design, a panoramic glass roof and a rotating touchscreen inside the cabin. BYD Sealion 7: Battery and Performance The Sealion 7 is available with two battery pack options, depending on the variant. The Premium and Performance versions get an 82.56kWh battery pack, while the Dynamic uses a smaller 71.8kWh unit. Here are the key specifications of the electric SUV: The dual-motor Performance variant produces 390kW of power and 690Nm of torque. It can accelerate from 0 to 100km/h in 4.5 seconds. The Premium version gets the larger battery and has a claimed NEDC range of 567km. Both versions come with a panoramic glass roof and a 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen infotainment system. Dynamic Variant Added in August 2026 BYD introduced the Sealion 7 Dynamic in August 2026 at an introductory price of Rs 41.90 lakh (ex-showroom). This version gets a 71.8kWh Blade Battery with a claimed NEDC range of 520km. Despite being the entry-level version, it retains some of the familiar equipment found in the higher variants. - 71.8kWh Blade Battery - Claimed range of 520km - Panoramic glass roof - 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen Sealion 7 Festive Edition Limited to 150 Units In October 2026, BYD launched the Sealion 7 Festive Edition at Rs 50.60 lakh (ex-showroom). Production is limited to 150 units, and the special version is based on the Premium variant. It gets a Tan and Black cabin theme with quilted Nappa leather upholstery. Other additions include an electric sunshade for the panoramic glass roof and a head-up display. The Festive Edition also forms part of BYD India’s ‘Celebrate Your Dreams with BYD’ festive campaign. BYD’s Statement on the Milestone Commenting on the achievement, Rajeev Chauhan, Head of Electric Passenger Vehicle Business at BYD India, said that the Sealion 7 has been one of the company’s strongest-performing models in the country. He also spoke about the growing interest in electric SUVs that offer performance, technology and premium comfort. The company plans to build on the response by improving the ownership experience and expanding its product range for Indian customers. BYD’s Next India Launch: Denza D9 BYD is also preparing to introduce its luxury Denza brand in India on November 13, 2026. The D9 luxury MPV is expected to be among its first offerings in the country. The international-spec electric version gets a 103kWh battery and a front-mounted electric motor producing 313bhp and 360Nm. It has a claimed WLTP range of up to 520km. The D9 gets a three-row cabin with second-row captain seats offering electric adjustment, heating, ventilation and massage functions. It also features premium upholstery, multi-zone climate control and a large touchscreen infotainment system. Its expected price in India is around Rs 90 lakh.

artigo.texto: Oregon approves data center restriction charter amendment OREGON, Ohio (WTVG) — Voters in Oregon, Ohio approved a charter amendment on the November ballot to restrict data center construction. Issue 25 is a charter amendment question on the ballot that caps data centers at 25 megawatts. It passed with 60% of the vote. The push for the ballot question came after weeks of signature gathering by United Neighbors of Oregon over the proposed Vantage Data Centers project near Wynn and Cordurory roads. Supporters of bringing data centers to Oregon argue the multimillion-dollar developments bring tax relief, funding for schools and high-paying jobs. Concerns over strained power grids, water resources and noise have led residents in multiple communities to demand a final say at the ballot box. Oregon’s mayor said the city was the first jurisdiction in the area to bring forward a citizen-led petition aimed at limiting data center development. Citizen-led ballot initiatives in the area are highlighting a tension between local quality of life and economic investment. In Defiance, voters approved a charter amendment that places limits on the size of data centers in the city. The proposed amendment does not ban data centers outright but prohibits data centers that are over 25 megawatts within city limits. Defiance also has a moratorium on data centers that went into effect in September. It will stay in place for six months. Council said it needed the time to study the impact a facility would have on the community. In Huron County, voters in Monroeville overwhelmingly rejected a data center advisory question. The decision does not prohibit the development of data centers, but it helps village council members gauge public sentiment. artigo.texto: CATL Wins Exclusive Battery Deal for Blue Vector Skyla V30 Aircraft In this article (3) CATL has signed strategic and product agreements with Hangzhou-based Blue Vector Intelligent Technology to serve as the exclusive battery partner for its commercial passenger aircraft. Announced by the battery maker on Monday, the tie-up focuses on the Skyla V30, an all-electric tiltrotor model that has secured more than 100 pre-sales orders since its global debut in July. Under the agreement, CATL will develop custom aviation batteries for the six-seat aircraft. The companies did not disclose financial terms, battery specifications or a delivery schedule. Validating the Skyla V30 Platform Engineering work on the airframe is already moving beyond initial digital design. Blue Vector rolled out its first full-scale technology demonstrator, designated A/C01, on August 31 in Harbin in northeastern China. The demonstrator airframe has entered a testing sequence covering systems integration, ground trials and tilt-transition flights. Those trials will test the transition between vertical lift and horizontal forward flight, which forms the core technical challenge for tiltrotor electric craft designed for intercity transit. Commercial demand is building ahead of type certification. Blue Vector booked pre-sales commitments for 60 V30 aircraft at the Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou on September 24. Singapore-based aviation operator Moon Aero accounted for 30 of those aircraft, representing the platform’s first overseas pre-sales customer. That booking brought total advance orders past 100 units as the company conducts airworthiness validation with Chinese civil aviation regulators. Capital Structure and Production Targets Development work relies on fresh venture backing secured over the past two quarters. Blue Vector closed a funding round of more than 100 million yuan ($14.9 million) on June 30, led jointly by Shenzhen Capital Group and an unnamed industrial dollar fund. That transaction marked the company’s fifth capital injection in roughly six months. Across that period, the startup collected more than 400 million yuan to finance aircraft development, prototype construction and test flights. Securing an exclusive battery partnership before airworthiness certification freezes the aircraft’s internal layout. For aircraft manufacturers, battery weight, thermal management and energy density dictate maximum payload and cabin configuration. Swapping pack suppliers later in the certification pipeline resets regulatory approvals, locking airframe designers into their chosen cell platform. For CATL, the deal locks in a captive customer across passenger transit routes in eastern China and regional hubs like Singapore. Operating intercity routes between regional cities demands high cycle life and rapid charging turnaround times at terminal pads, creating recurring replacement demand for specialized aviation-grade cells. Building Out Electric Aviation Across China The Blue Vector contract expands CATL’s ongoing effort to position its battery systems across the electric vertical takeoff and landing sector. In August 2024, the battery maker agreed to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Shanghai-based aircraft manufacturer Autoflight to co-develop aviation packs. That collaboration extended into terminal infrastructure late last year. In November 2025, Autoflight and CATL revealed a floating vertiport vessel that integrates passenger landing pads, battery storage and high-power charging systems onto a marine barge, providing water-based terminal access for coastal cities. Blue Vector must now clear tilt-transition flight trials in Harbin and advance formal airworthiness certification for the Skyla V30 before delivering the first production units to Moon Aero and domestic operators. artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Envision implanta energia de corrente contínua de 800 V baseada em transformadores de estado sólido em centro de dados de IA em Ulanqab Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Em 2 de novembro de 2026, a Envision anunciou que um sistema integrado de energia de corrente contínua de 800 volts (800 V CC) já está alimentando cargas de computação em operação em seu campus de centros de dados de IA Galaxy, em Ulanqab, na China. A empresa descreveu seu anúncio como o primeiro uso comercial desse tipo de sistema em um centro de dados de IA de grande escala no mundo. O sistema fornece energia de ponta a ponta, desde a entrada de corrente alternada de média tensão até o rack de servidores, e já está em operação comercial antes de uma adoção mais ampla pelo setor. Com isso, serve de referência para centros de dados de IA que estão migrando para uma infraestrutura de energia de 800 V CC. Transformadores de estado sólido e coordenação em tempo real O sistema recém-implantado integra três camadas de hardware: transformadores de estado sólido (SST), armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) e equipamentos que ajustam a tensão de corrente contínua para o hardware de computação. A coordenação fica a cargo do Dubhe Controller, da Envision, que opera com o modelo de base de energia Dubhe da empresa e ajusta os transformadores e as baterias em tempo real para que o fornecimento de energia acompanhe a demanda de computação, inclusive diante de mudanças abruptas na carga. A implantação se baseia em três capacidades: conversão estável por SST, diretamente de média tensão de 10 quilovolts para um barramento de 800 V CC em diferentes condições operacionais; armazenamento em baterias que oferece tanto suporte de energia na escala de segundos quanto reserva na escala de minutos; e coordenação, no nível de milissegundos, entre os SST e o armazenamento, que absorve localmente as flutuações de carga das GPUs. A Envision afirmou que a arquitetura de 800 V CC simplifica os sistemas de energia para centros de dados de IA, citando maior eficiência de conversão de energia e de watts em bits, uma área ocupada pelos equipamentos mais compacta e menor necessidade de cabeamento e cobre. Essas vantagens podem reduzir os custos de infraestrutura e permitir maior densidade de computação no mesmo espaço. Aumento da demanda de energia por rack O anúncio situa a implantação diante de um problema operacional específico: à medida que a demanda por computação de IA acelera, os operadores precisam fornecer mais energia a cada rack em um espaço limitado, mantendo a estabilidade do fornecimento mesmo quando as cargas de computação variam bruscamente de um momento para o outro. “Os centros de dados de IA precisam de sistemas de energia que coordenem as fontes renováveis, o armazenamento de energia e a rede elétrica para atender à demanda de computação”, afirmou Kevin Huang, vice-presidente sênior da Envision Energy e presidente das áreas de armazenamento de energia e sistemas de energia para centros de dados de IA. Huang disse que o sistema em operação demonstra uma arquitetura de ponta a ponta que conecta o fornecimento de energia renovável à demanda de computação e a classificou como uma etapa decisiva para transformar a coordenação entre energia e computação de uma visão estratégica em prática operacional cotidiana. Campus Galaxy e Mission Gobi O campus Galaxy, em Ulanqab, na Mongólia Interior, iniciou suas operações em agosto de 2026, quando a Envision comissionou o local, em 6 de agosto, tendo como estrutura central uma instalação de supercomputação de IA de 120.000 metros quadrados, segundo o anúncio de comissionamento da empresa na época. Esse registro descrevia o campus como projetado para atingir mais de 2 GW de capacidade; o comunicado de 2 de novembro informa uma capacidade planejada de 3 GW e afirma que o campus foi projetado para dar suporte a até um milhão de aceleradores de IA operando em paralelo quando estiver totalmente construído, com mais de 80% da energia planejada proveniente de conexões diretas de eletricidade renovável. A página do campus Galaxy da Envision apresenta o local como um centro de dados de IA com emissões líquidas zero e anuncia preços fixos de eletricidade de longo prazo, 20% abaixo das tarifas da rede elétrica, com contrato de preço fixo por 10 anos, eletricidade e certificados verdes incluídos em pacote e uma proporção de 60% de fornecimento direto de energia verde. A Envision pretende ampliar essa abordagem por meio da Mission Gobi, uma iniciativa apresentada na VivaTech, em Paris, em junho de 2026, que tem o campus Galaxy como seu primeiro projeto emblemático. A Mission Gobi tem como meta alcançar 5 GW de capacidade de centros de dados de IA verdes em regiões desérticas do mundo até 2030. A empresa a apresenta como um modelo replicável e argumenta que o desenvolvimento de apenas 1% das regiões desérticas e de Gobi do mundo poderia viabilizar capacidade de computação na escala de terawatts a um custo altamente competitivo.

artigo.texto: Indonesia’s SM+ Data Centers and LG Sinar Mas, together with Korea Investment Real Asset Management (KIRA), have today opened a 21-megawatt (MW) AI-ready data center in Jakarta, the firms’ joint press release said. The facility, known as SMX01, is ready for service with customer onboarding and stabilizing operations being priorities now. The colocation facility has attracted interest from prospective global, regional, and domestic customers. Located in Jakarta’s central business district, SMX01 is designed to accommodate conventional enterprise workloads and higher-density AI computing, with flexibility for modular expansion as demand increases. The facility is owned and managed by SM+ Data Centers, with KIRA as the investment partner and LG Sinar Mas, a joint venture between South Korea’s LG CNS and Sinar Mas-backed SM+, in charge of its design, construction, and technical operations. “Computing requirements are becoming more varied. Some still run conventional systems, while others are beginning to need significantly higher performance capacity for AI. That is why we built SMX01 so it can expand alongside the market and our customers’ needs,” said Herson Suindah, President Director and Group CEO of SM+ Holdings. “SMX01 reaching Ready for Service is an important investment milestone because it turns long-term capital into operating digital infrastructure that can support Indonesia’s next phase of digital growth. We see strong fundamentals in the market, and we are pleased to continue working with SM+ Data Centers and LG Sinar Mas as the facility moves from development into operations,” said Yong Sik Kim, CEO of KIRA. “A data center’s readiness for AI cannot be measured by rack numbers alone. Power, cooling, and structural load capacity must be planned together from the outset. This is the approach we have brought from our experience building and operating data centers in Korea and globally,” said Donghyup Han, CEO of LG Sinar Mas. SM+ owns and manages 31 data centers across 25 Indonesian cities, including 30 edge data centers, with nearly 45 MW of combined IT load capacity in operations.

artigo.texto: Russia is looking for innovative solutions to keep its digital infrastructure functioning amidst the ongoing war with Ukraine in wake of attacks targeting data centers. Rostelecom, a Russian telecommunication company, and Norilsk Nickel, a Russian nickel and palladium mining company, have reportedly started negotiations to build and operate data center facilities underground in order to protect digital services used by government and corporations, as the war continues. The Norilsk Nickel mines would provide safety from Ukraine drone attacks although the financial and technical details have not been disclosed to the public. In late October, Russia’s Digital Development Ministry issued recommendations to protect data centers against aerial attacks. The measures included moving critical infrastructure underground or into bunkers, citing Kommersant. Kemerovo Oblast governor Ilya Seredyuk proposed converting depleted open-pit mines and quarries for this purpose as reported by Russian news publication Meduza. Baxtel reported that Valeriy Ermakov, vice president, Rostelecom, during the RBC Tech forum, said, “A so-called ‘doomsday’ data center is a must-have, because backup is what allows any service provider to recover quickly.” On November 2, Russian President, Vladimir Putin, signed a decree requiring Russian data center operators to reserve 10 percent of their available space and capacity for potential government use. While allowing a special government commission, in consultation with the Federal Security Service, to authorize the use of foreign data centers. This is a notable shift from Russia’s Sovereign Internet Law, which restricted reliance on foreign cloud infrastructure as reported by The Moscow Times. This reflects growing Kremlin concerns about the vulnerability of domestic cloud infrastructure amid the war in Ukraine, as well as the challenges of maintaining Russia’s increasingly centralized and closed Internet, dominated by a handful of domestic technology companies. Rostelecom has outlined three levels of data center protection. The first involves maintaining backup facilities, the second distributes computing capacity across geographically separate sites, and the third places infrastructure underground, according to a company source cited by Vedomosti. Readers would recall that Ukraine and Russia have exchanged numerous attacks on their national digital infrastructure. Ukrainian drone attacks between October 12 and 14 significantly disrupted Russia’s technology sector, damaging three data centers operated by technology giant Yandex and affecting dozens of online services nationwide. Russia’s major technology company VKontakte (VK) also confirmed that its data center in Novosergievka had been struck by a drone, although its services remained operational. A separate attack targeted a data center under construction for Russian state-owned lender Sberbank in Balakovo, Saratov region. The attacks were believed to be retaliatory, following Russian strikes on Ukrainian data center infrastructure in mid-to-late September. These attacks damaged facilities used by internet providers UTELS and Pavutyna, as well as the BeMobile data center, which was hit by a Russian drone strike. The strikes also affected UCloud, a service provider operating from the facility, and De Novo, one of Ukraine’s largest commercial data center operators. Serhiy Petrenko, former head of Yandex Ukraine, has estimated that around 80 percent of Russia’s data centers are concentrated in Moscow and the surrounding region, leaving much of the country’s infrastructure within range of Ukrainian long-range drones as reported by The Kyiv Independent. What Russia is doing now, is similar to what Norway has already done. The Nordic country is home to two notable examples of underground data centers built within former mines. Green Mountain’s facility Rennesøy island and Lefdal Mine Datacenter in western Norway both repurpose underground mine infrastructure to house servers, taking advantage of the natural protection and stable conditions provided by the surrounding rock. Both facilities also use cold seawater from nearby fjords for cooling, reducing reliance on energy-intensive conventional cooling systems. Green Mountain draws water from approximately 100 meters below the surface, where temperatures remain close to 8 °C year-round, while Lefdal pumps cold fjord water directly into its cooling system. These approaches significantly reduce cooling energy consumption and improve overall energy efficiency. Russia also has several geographies that are blessed with a cold climate and thus low ambient temperatures, ideal for data centers.

artigo.texto: SpaceX's construction speed may outpace even Chinese rivals, with some facilities targeting four- to five-month builds. Google and Anthropic's computing agreements carry a combined annual contract value of $26 billion. Power remains a constraint, with SemiAnalysis estimating a possible shortfall exceeding 300MW at Colossus 2. Google spent nearly three decades building the data center infrastructure that supports its cloud and AI ambitions. SpaceX (SPCX) could match that cumulative capacity in just 18 months, according to SemiAnalysis. The Elon Musk-led company could reach 13 GW of data center capacity by 2027, with construction timelines that may outpace even Chinese competitors, the firm said. SPCX stock jumped nearly 4% on Tuesday to $141.31, logging its second straight session of gains. SpaceX's plan to reach 13 gigawatts of data center capacity in 2027 looks achievable, according to SemiAnalysis, which has identified more than 9GW across sites, including 3.6GW already under construction. The company raised its target from 10GW just two months after skeptics questioned whether the earlier plan was possible, the firm said. "We now believe that SpaceX may be the fastest datacenter builder in the world, even more so than Chinese peers," SemiAnalysis said. The projected buildout could match the capacity Google accumulated over nearly three decades in just 18 months. "This would be the largest amount of datacenter capacity ever built by any one company in that timeframe, roughly equivalent to all of Google's datacenter capacity from 1999-2026 in just 1.5 years," the analysts said. In August, SemiAnalysis said SpaceX's 10GW plan could support $300 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027, assuming half its additional computing capacity was rented to outside customers. SpaceX Races To Break Its Own Records SemiAnalysis said MiniHard, an AI data center expansion in SpaceX's Colossus 2 complex, took about five months to build. Gun Range, another facility on a former police training site in Southaven, Mississippi, is targeting four months. "To our knowledge, this would be the fastest greenfield datacenter ever built at scale," the analysts said, referring to a facility built from scratch. "While most are fighting for 8-12-month build times, SpaceX has cut them in half." Project SPAM could move even faster. Construction began last month, with its first computing systems targeted to start running in December, and potentially beating the first Colossus II deployment's 91-day timeline. SpaceX's initial Colossus cluster, a group of connected AI processors, took 122 days to come online. Starbase And Tesla Fuel The Buildout SemiAnalysis said SpaceX is adapting its Starbase rocket campus in Texas for two data centers that could support well over 1GW. Construction progressed from ground clearing in August to building frames and roofs simultaneously by September. "These are multiple construction processes performed simultaneously, a visual representation of speed," the analysts said. The firm also sees a possible data center serving outside customers at Terafab, Musk's proposed Texas chip factory. Meanwhile, Tesla may help speed construction by supplying prefabricated mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems. "If SpaceX and Tesla can manage their global supply chains appropriately, their partnership can easily construct GWs with far fewer constraints than others," the analysts said. "Tesla will likely become more than a BESS merchant to SpaceX soon," they added, referring to battery storage systems. Google And Anthropic Drive Cloud Push SpaceX expanded into AI through its acquisition of xAI in February and its Colossus computing infrastructure. Anthropic agreed in May to use all of Colossus 1's capacity, covering more than 300 megawatts and 220,000 Nvidia GPUs. Google separately agreed to access about 110,000 GPUs, with payments scheduled at $920 million monthly from October 2026 through June 2029. The two agreements carry a combined annual contract value of $26 billion. Power Supply Tests SpaceX's AI Ambitions However, SemiAnalysis flagged a power supply hurdle. The firm tracks more than 8GW of likely generation capacity supplying SpaceX directly, compared with more than 9GW of upcoming data center capacity. "These sites now build so fast that the power supply is often identified mid-flight," the analysts said. At Colossus 2, 5.9 gigawatt-hours of battery storage, gas generation and a planned grid connection could help offset restrictions on turbine capacity. Even then, SemiAnalysis estimates a possible power shortfall exceeding 300MW. More efficient designs, adjustments to computing workloads and battery storage could help close the gap. "If the datacenters are designed right (and our IT MW assumptions are correct), this could work," the analysts said, referring to their estimates of computing equipment's power needs. That's why SpaceX is the most exciting stock to own, not trade" Another user said, "$SPCX Every time Elon says possibility of...in talks with...pursuing...retail starts buying like crazy as the insiders sell their unlocked shares to you." artigo.texto: PSEG Power and Constellation Energy are planning a 200-MW uprate at their jointly owned Salem nuclear power plant in southern New Jersey, according to an earnings presentation by Public Service Enterprise Group, PSEG Power’s parent company. Salem’s current installed capacity is 2,280 MW. PSEG Power would have a 112-MW share of the uprate and Constellation would own the remainder, which would support a recently announced nuclear-focused power purchase agreement with Google. PSEG Power’s roughly 3,760-MW nuclear fleet ran at a 95.5% capacity factor in the third quarter, up from 92.4% in the same period last year, according to the presentation. However, there has been a snag at the Salem plant, PSEG said Monday in its quarterly filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. During a scheduled refueling outage at Salem 1, a visual inspection last month revealed that the thermal shield inside the reactor vessel is degraded, according to the filing. “We have initiated further testing, which is ongoing and is expected to extend the refueling outage,” PSEG said. “The impact of the outage on Salem 1 will depend on the timing and results of the inspection and necessary repairs.” Meanwhile, PSEG continues to explore potential deals with data center developers centered around PSEG Power’s roughly 3.8-GW nuclear fleet, according to Ralph LaRossa, PSEG chair, president and CEO. “PSEG Power is continuing to develop terms with large load entities for contracting arrangements involving existing nuclear production, future nuclear upgrades and other generation opportunities, similar to recently announced power purchase agreements in the PJM region and specifically in New Jersey,” he said during the earnings call. FERC’s recent decision to reject key portions of the PJM Interconnection proposed plan for interconnection data centers and other large loads “reinforces that the focus has shifted to the states to address retail curtailment and cost issues associated with large load customers,” LaRossa said. Public Service Electric and Gas Co., a PSEG utility, is working with the administration of New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, D, and the state’s utility regulators to limit electric cost increases for consumers and consider new utility regulatory models, according to LaRossa. PSE&G, for example, plans to ask the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to approve a plan for recovering the costs for investments made since its last distribution rate case, LaRossa said. “Our filing … is all about staying aligned with the governor's goals to keep rates flat for as long as possible,” he said. The utility expects to file the proposal by the end of the year, PSEG said in its SEC filing. Meanwhile, the BPU’s study on modernizing New Jersey's electric utility business model is now in its second phase, LaRossa noted. “This initiative is focusing on cost discipline, financing modernization, targeted incentives and shared savings and staged performance-based ratemaking,” he said. Those and other options mentioned in the Phase 1 report, such as multi-year rate plans, performance-based rates, performance incentive metrics, earnings sharing mechanisms, decoupling and shared saving mechanisms, provide “constructive paths to strengthen the connection between customer value, cost accountability and timely recovery of prudent investment,” LaRossa said. PSE&G may have opportunities to invest in solar and grid readiness for distributed resources, but the extent of it could hinge on the state allowing utilities to own generating assets, according to LaRossa. “I think the policy is not yet certain here in New Jersey as to whether or not it will move in a regulated direction or stay solely competitive,” he said. On the financial front, PSEG’s third-quarter income fell to $376 million, or 76 cents/share, down from $622 million, or $1.25/share a year ago, mainly on mark-to-market losses at PSEG Power, the Newark, New Jersey-based company said in its SEC filing. Third-quarter revenue slipped to $3 billion from $3.2 billion in the same period last year.

artigo.texto: Econergy Ltd, a leading European renewable energy independent power producer (IPP), has acquired a portfolio of four UK battery energy storage systems (BESS) projects totalling 106 MW. Under the agreement, Econergy has acquired 100% of the shares in the holding company of the four assets, giving it full ownership and control. The acquired 106 MW portfolio is expected to generate approximately £4.7 million in EBITDA in 2027 before undergoing proposed augmentation. The acquisition adds revenue-generating assets to Econergy’s UK portfolio, with scope to build on their value through planned upgrades to long-duration storage. All four standalone BESS assets are in commercial operation, and each site is currently operating as a one-hour battery, with potential to upgrade to three-hour storage. Increasing the duration allows the assets to store more energy and dispatch electricity over a longer period, giving them greater flexibility to respond to changing power prices and market conditions. This could also create additional opportunities to shift electricity from periods of high renewable generation to times when demand is higher, helping to increase the value generated by the assets. The additional 106 MW increases Econergy’s operational UK BESS capacity from 90 MW to 196 MW, taking the company from two to six assets connected to the grid. With a 1.6 GW UK storage pipeline under development, the acquisition builds on Econergy’s wider strategy to diversify its European portfolio across technologies and markets. Storage now accounts for approximately 45% of its total port-folio and 40% of its advanced portfolio. Alongside these four projects, Econergy's operating UK BESS portfolio today comprises West Melton (50 MW/100 MWh, operating since 2024) and Dalmarnock (40 MW/120 MWh, connected to the grid on 1 October 2026). Across Europe, Econergy has a BESS portfolio of 5.9 GW, with 3.3 GW expected to be connected, under construction or pre-construction by 2028. Eyal Podhorzer, CEO and Director, Econergy, said: “We’re pleased to be purchasing these four projects, which represent a business opportunity with clear up-side. The addition of 106 MW of operational storage capacity and the potential to augment the assets to three-hour duration gives us a pathway to build on the portfolio and develop its longer-term value. Alongside our existing assets, and those in development, these projects strengthen our foothold in the UK and a growing platform for further expansion. “This acquisition reflects the way we are evolving our portfolio in response to the changing dynamics of European power markets. The UK has strong storage fundamentals, and its scale and market structure make it an important part of our wider energy storage strategy.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine.
