artigo.texto: Parcerias Drax firma parceria para centro de dados de IA em local de geração de energia no norte de Yorkshire Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A Drax anunciou, em 3 de novembro de 2026, que havia assinado um acordo com a Brookfield e a Radiant para desenvolver, entregar e operar capacidade para centros de dados de IA na central elétrica de Drax, no norte de Yorkshire, com a meta de superar 1 GW em três fases. A Brookfield estima que o investimento potencial total, incluindo chips semicondutores, possa ultrapassar £ 20 bilhões, dos quais £ 2,5 bilhões iniciais farão parte da Fase 1. O capital de investimento e as capacidades operacionais serão fornecidos por meio da joint venture de infraestrutura de IA Brookfield-Qai. A infraestrutura de energia existente é a base do plano A proposta se apoia na infraestrutura já existente na central elétrica. A propriedade ocupa mais de 1.000 acres e dispõe de acesso à rede elétrica de aproximadamente 4 GW, geração despachável ativa de 2,6 GW e sistemas de refrigeração. A proximidade da rede de fibra do Reino Unido acrescenta outro requisito ao desenvolvimento de computação em larga escala, além do terreno e da infraestrutura elétrica. A primeira fase prevê até 100 MW de capacidade computacional e o início das operações comerciais a partir do primeiro trimestre de 2028. Ela utilizaria a infraestrutura existente para importar energia diretamente da rede, com a Drax gerenciando esse fornecimento. O modelo de fornecimento de energia muda na Fase 2, que tem como objetivo acrescentar 500 MW de capacidade entre 2028 e 2031. A geração existente da Drax forneceria energia diretamente ao centro de dados, 24 horas por dia, nos termos de um contrato de compra de energia de longo prazo. Esse arranjo atrás do medidor estaria sujeito às autorizações necessárias. A Fase 3 prevê capacidade adicional após 2031, seguindo a mesma abordagem. Essa estrutura em fases separa o desenvolvimento inicial, conectado à rede, do modelo posterior de fornecimento direto de energia. Também coloca a geração existente da central no centro da expansão proposta, em vez de tratar o projeto simplesmente como um centro de dados construído ao lado de uma usina. A construção depende de clientes e aprovações A Radiant, plataforma de infraestrutura de IA da Brookfield com sede no Reino Unido, liderará o projeto, o relacionamento com clientes e a comercialização. A empresa buscará compromissos de clientes-âncora antes do início da construção, enquanto a Drax ficará à frente das questões relacionadas ao terreno, à integração de energia e ao planejamento. A Fase 1 continua condicionada à aprovação do planejamento, às aprovações regulatórias e de conexão à rede por parte do governo e das agências competentes, à contratação de um inquilino aceitável, à celebração de acordos comerciais e a uma decisão final de investimento de cada parte. Uma solicitação de aprovação de planejamento está sendo preparada, e espera-se que a consulta pública comece em novembro de 2026. Os parceiros esperam criar um fundo voluntário de benefícios para a comunidade, desenvolvido em conjunto com as comunidades do entorno do local. O fundo seria separado das obrigações de planejamento e adicional a elas, bem como às iniciativas comunitárias já existentes da Drax. Mahdi Yahya, diretor-executivo da Radiant, afirmou no comunicado público dos parceiros que o projeto proporcionaria a “pesquisadores, startups e empresas britânicas acesso local a recursos computacionais de ponta”. Contrato de energia e financiamento moldam a expansão As fases posteriores se relacionam com os acordos existentes da Drax para geração de energia a partir de biomassa. Em novembro de 2025, a Drax assinou com o governo do Reino Unido um contrato por diferença que abrange aproximadamente 6 TWh de geração anual de energia a partir de biomassa, de abril de 2027 a março de 2031. Esse acordo inclui um mecanismo que permite à Drax solicitar até 500 MW para uso em centros de dados durante o período do contrato. Esse uso dependeria de um acordo com o governo do Reino Unido e a Low Carbon Contracts Company, levando em conta a relação custo-benefício para os consumidores, a segurança energética e a sustentabilidade. A Drax afirmou que permaneceriam inalteradas as funções da central de apoiar a segurança do abastecimento, fornecer energia despachável de baixo carbono e prestar serviços essenciais ao sistema. O veículo de financiamento foi criado antes do acordo de Yorkshire. A Brookfield e a Qai anunciaram sua joint venture de US$ 20 bilhões em 9 de dezembro de 2025, com o objetivo de investir em infraestrutura de IA no Catar e em mercados internacionais selecionados, e ambos os parceiros contribuiriam com capital e experiência operacional. A Qai é uma subsidiária da Qatar Investment Authority. O acordo conecta, portanto, uma propriedade de geração de energia consolidada a uma plataforma dedicada ao desenvolvimento de IA e a um veículo de investimento já existente. O desafio imediato é executar a primeira fase: garantir o inquilino, obter as aprovações e tomar as decisões finais de investimento necessárias. Qualquer expansão maior também terá de estar alinhada aos compromissos de geração da Drax e obter as autorizações exigidas.

artigo.texto: Via a brief news release on Oct. 26, Anthropic said that it had filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regarding its upcoming initial public offering (IPO). There's not much detail on the release, but the prospectus with the SEC shows that the San Francisco-based company that developed the AI chatbot Claude sees a five-year power bottleneck. The company is moving from a cloud-only, fixed-time compute model to a hybrid setup that includes directly leased chips hosted in data center facilities. In the prospectus, Anthropic discusses launching a new initiative, "Anthropic Direct," to build its own dedicated data centers rather than relying entirely on third-party cloud providers. The company expects this move to lower its long-term costs. Partner companies will buy the land, secure power, build the facilities, and run the daily operations. Anthropic will then lease the computing power directly from those partners. Last month, Anthropic began signing these agreements, committing to $125.2 billion in lease payments over five years, before interest. Anthropic is likely to use behind-the-meter power generation for its data centers to accelerate its development. How Bloom Energy could benefit Bloom Energy (BE -8.61%) provides an alternative to drawing power from a centralized electrical grid through on-site solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) technology. The energy company's SOFCs provide continuous low-emission electrical power. Instead of waiting for a power grid to ramp up to power an Anthropic data center, Anthropic can use Bloom Energy's modular generators to bring data centers online sooner. It isn't far-fetched that Anthropic would turn to Bloom because several of Anthropic cloud-based partners already use Bloom for power needs. Amazon (AMZN -1.41%), through Amazon Web Services, is a major cloud partner for Anthropic. AWS works closely with American Electric Power (AEP +0.67%), which deploys Bloom Energy fuel cells across multiple data center campuses. Specialized cloud provider CoreWeave (CRWV -9.66%), which works with Anthropic, has a partnership to use Bloom Energy power cells at a data center. Bloom is already seeing strong growth The company's financial strength and growing stability are two other reasons Anthropic would turn to it rather than another power provider. Bloom Energy posted record numbers in the third quarter. It reported revenue of $1.26 billion, up 138% year over year. That allowed the company to raise full-year revenue guidance to between $4.4 billion and $4.6 billion, up 122% at the midpoint. BE Bloom Energy NYSE · As of 5:00 PM ET 10/30/26 It's not just revenue that's growing. The company reported earnings per share (EPS) of $0.78, up from an EPS loss of $0.10 in the same period a year ago. Bloom points to a yearly non-GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) EPS range of $3.10 to $3.40, compared to $0.76 in 2025. Bloom has an edge over Oklo Another possibility for Anthropic is to use small modular reactors (SMRs) from Oklo (OKLO -5.82%) to provide behind-the-meter power to its data centers. However, Bloom's SOFCs are already operating at scale. Its systems can be made, delivered, and put into use within months to a year, providing a quick power solution for new data centers. Oklo's SMRs are promising, but its first commercial reactor is not scheduled to come online until 2027 or later, with large-scale multi-gigawatt rollouts pushed out toward 2030 and beyond. On top of that, the regulatory climate for Bloom's power cells is much easier than for any type of nuclear reactor.

artigo.texto: Kingston data center: City leaders approve special use permit KINGSTON, Ga. - Kingston city officials cleared the path Monday night for a massive 350,000-square-foot data center despite fierce community opposition. What we know: Kingston leaders approved a special use permit paving the way for the facility to be built on 560 acres along State Road 293 near Law Road. Thor Equities, a New York City-based developer, expects the campus to generate at least $2 million every year for municipal coffers and deliver 50 or more high-paying jobs. Mayor Michael McFarland called the vote a major financial turning point for local government. "We've been in dire straits as far as financial, and this is kind of a little blessing for us to help us get this city turned around and try to stand on our own," McFarland said. What we don't know: Project timelines and construction start dates for the site remain unannounced by municipal leaders and developer representatives. Local perspective: Furious neighbors packed the meeting room, warning the data center would permanently shatter rural peace. Opponents raised urgent alarms over surging water consumption, power grid strain, noise, pollution and wildlife habitat destruction. Longtime property owners worry their quality of life will vanish forever under industrial development. "I've lived here for 25 years, I love this town. When they leave, it's the lasting footprint we'll have to deal with," resident Cooper Thompson said. RELATED: Bartow County data center: Neighbors raise water, land concerns What they're saying: Frustrated community members described intense personal grief following the council's decision. "I'm just very disappointed, very heart broken," resident Mary Ann Townsend said. Other neighbors stressed the irreversible ecological threats facing local land. "Most people don't want to pay attention to all the species we're losing," resident Paul Muir said. Townsend emphasized that the facility will forever alter views and property lines for generations of local families. "Our grandchildren, as well as us, are going to be looking at this thing every time we come out of our yards. The folks that have lived in that area that have lived there for 50 years or longer have been done an injustice," Townsend said. What's next: Neighbors say their fight against the industrial campus is far from finished. A group of residents has already consulted legal counsel and plans to file a lawsuit attempting to block the data center from breaking ground. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from FOX 5 Atlanta's Denise Dillon, who reported live from Kingston, gathered statements from residents, city officials and Thor Equities representatives, and covered the municipal permit vote.

artigo.texto: Healthy early voter turnout in Mason County attributed to data centers MASON COUNTY, W.Va. (WCHS) — Two data center projects in Mason County, including what could be one of the largest in the world, and an impacted levy extension are driving what some are calling healthy voter turnout there. "Men and women fought for your right to [vote] and it's almost a slap in the face [not to vote] to those patriots that really gave, sacrificed their lives and fortunes for you and I to have the freedom we have and it's really important that we be civic-minded to participate in the process," Mason County Clerk Diana Cromley said. It's the busiest time in the busiest month of the year for Mason County staff, who are spread across the county making sure all the preparations are in place for the thousands of expected voters on Election Day. "People say, 'Oh, I think the election fairy just shows up on Election Day,'" Cromley said. "There's a lot that happens behind the scenes. We touch and test every machine before it goes out of here so we've got over 100 machines that we're touching, making sure that it will give a vote to you and a vote to this person. We check the whole shebang." Nearly 175 poll workers will be at the polls as early as 5 a.m. Tuesday getting 30 precincts ready. "We have a big county," Cromley said. "I don't know if you're familiar with our county but we have two rivers that stretch it. You drive from one end of our county to the other, it's going to take you probably an hour and a half." Cromley said she doesn't want people to accidentally drive an hour away to the wrong precinct and said to call them if a registration card isn't in hand. "Voters who show up and they're at the wrong place and I always advise poll workers – don't send them around the county," she said. "Just call our office and we can tell you what precinct they need to vote at. It makes voters very agitated and upset if you send them all over the county – 'Drive here, I'm not in that book, I'm not in that book.' All of those are because they've moved and they haven't changed their address." Of Mason County's 15,668 registered voters, 2,062 have already cast a ballot. Cromley said the healthy turnout is driven by two planned data centers by Nscale and Starwood Digital Ventures, as well as a levy extension referendum tied to those data centers. The levy could mean tens of millions of dollars for public schools. Opponents of the referendum say a "no" vote could mean money back in the hands of taxpayers. Those for it say a "no" vote also means that data centers would keep their money rather than giving it to local schools. There are four local races. Three of them are contested, including the race for Mason County Commission and the race for West Virginia House of Delegates Districts 17 and 18. The polls are open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. Tuesday in Mason County across 30 precincts.

artigo.texto: Malaysia-based renewable energy firm Northern Solar Holdings Berhad has secured a total of 189 megawatts (MW) for two data center projects in Malaysia, the firm said in two separate exchange filings yesterday. Its wholly-owned subsidiary Northern Solar Assets Sdn. Bhd. had accepted the two letters of award (LOA) to supply the data centers with solar energy under the corporate renewable energy supply scheme (CRESS). Both LOAs include a battery energy storage system (BESS) as well. The first LOA was awarded by a Malaysian property investment and data center infrastructure developer in respect of 100MWac solar capacity coupled with a BESS for a data center with an annual electricity requirement of 262.8 million kilowatt-hours (kWh). The second, awarded by a Malaysian subsidiary of a Singapore-based data center operator, provides 89MWac solar coupled with a BESS for a data center with annual electricity requirement of 233.89 million kWh. The commencement date of both projects has not been finalised and Northern Solar will update once definitive agreements are signed. Both data centers will have a combined annual electricity requirement of almost 500 million kWh. The total value of both projects was not disclosed. In October, Northern Solar had secured a RM34 million contract to develop a 9.5MW large-scale solar photovoltaic plant.

A empresa também lançou o APN Connect, um serviço de rede fotônica que conecta o novo local e o JKT2 ao JKT3. Energia redundante e conectividade no campus A instalação, conhecida como JKT2A, foi projetada para cargas de trabalho de computação em escala hiperescalar, empresarial e de alta densidade. Seu projeto elétrico utiliza duas subestações de energia, uma arquitetura de fonte de alimentação ininterrupta 2N e geradores de reserva N+1. O sistema de refrigeração conta com chillers refrigerados a ar N+1 e unidades de tratamento de ar para salas de computadores N+2. O local também dispõe de um projeto certificado Tier III, operações de segurança 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana, e controles de segurança física em várias camadas. O JKT2A está localizado no campus de Jacarta da NTT Global Data Centers e amplia o ecossistema de conectividade estabelecido pelo JKT2. A NTT DATA contabiliza mais de 240 provedores de serviços de rede no JKT2, além do JKT-IX, de importantes provedores de serviços em nuvem e de conexões essenciais por cabos submarinos. A interconexão direta no campus permite que os clientes expandam a infraestrutura sem perder as conexões com as redes, os parceiros e os ambientes de nuvem existentes. O próprio JKT2A oferece acesso neutro em relação a operadoras e provedores de nuvem, tanto a provedores de rede nacionais e internacionais quanto às principais plataformas de nuvem. APN Connect conecta instalações em Jacarta A NTT DATA descreve o APN Connect como o primeiro serviço da Indonésia a utilizar a tecnologia All-Photonics Network. Desenvolvido com base na tecnologia Innovative Optical and Wireless Network, o serviço oferece conectividade de Camada 1 entre o JKT2/JKT2A e o JKT3, separados por aproximadamente 35 km. Segundo a empresa, o APN Connect oferece alta capacidade e baixa latência, permitindo a sincronização de dados em tempo real entre instalações geograficamente distantes. Entre os usos indicados estão a recuperação de desastres, a replicação de dados e operações resilientes em vários centros de dados. A conexão complementa o projeto de energia e refrigeração da instalação ao viabilizar a sincronização e a recuperação entre locais, ampliando a resiliência para além de um único centro de dados. Desenvolvimento desde 2024 O anúncio da construção feito em 15 de maio de 2024 pela NTT DATA previa a conclusão no início de 2026, o que significa que a inauguração ocorreu depois do cronograma original. Os 12 MW de carga crítica de TI previstos foram mantidos na instalação concluída. O projeto anterior descrevia um edifício de sete andares no centro de Jacarta, a aproximadamente 20 km do Aeroporto Internacional Soekarno-Hatta, com refrigeração a ar, segurança física e várias fontes redundantes de energia. A NTT DATA projetou investir mais de US$ 10 bilhões na expansão de centros de dados entre 2023 e 2027, programa do qual o JKT2A faz parte. O plano de 2024 também previa opções de energia 100% renovável para os clientes do campus, vinculadas à meta da empresa de utilizar 100% de energia renovável em suas próprias operações até 2030. Doug Adams, presidente e CEO da NTT Global Data Centers, afirmou que a economia digital da Indonésia está gerando uma demanda significativa por infraestrutura escalável e altamente conectada, à medida que os clientes desenvolvem projetos de nuvem, IA e transformação digital. A expansão incorpora resiliência ao aumento de capacidade: o JKT2A fornece a redundância elétrica e de refrigeração necessária para a computação de alta densidade, a interconexão no campus preserva as relações existentes dos clientes com suas redes, e o APN Connect amplia a sincronização e a recuperação entre locais geograficamente distantes.

artigo.texto: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) has approved a €30 million loan for a battery energy storage system (BESS) in Tenevo, south-eastern Bulgaria, with the financing part of a wider €60 million package. The project will be delivered by Tenevo Solar Technologies and supported by parallel €30 million funding from Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI). The battery storage facility is expected to deliver 246 MW of power capacity and 512.5 MWh of storage, co-located with an existing 242 MWp solar photovoltaic (PV) plant on the same site. The initiative aims to strengthen grid stability and support the integration of additional renewable energy into Bulgaria’s power system. Background: energy transition and grid flexibility Bulgaria has been accelerating its shift away from fossil fuels and toward renewable energy generation. As more solar and other renewables come online, electricity systems must manage variability and maintain reliability. Battery storage is increasingly used to add flexibility to power grids. By storing electricity and discharging it when needed, BESS can help stabilize the system and improve energy security. The investment: a €60 million package for battery storage in Tenevo EBRD’s financing to Tenevo Solar Technologies covers the development of a major BESS at the Tenevo site. The project forms part of a €60 million financing package, combining the EBRD loan (€30 million) with parallel funding from RBI (€30 million). The BESS will be co-located with an existing solar PV installation of 242 MWp at the Tenevo site. In addition, the site includes a separate 65 MW battery installation with storage of 260 MWh, and the new facility is designed to increase overall storage capacity at the location. Building on earlier solar investment Tenevo Solar Technologies has previously received EBRD support for the Tenevo solar PV plant. The EBRD had provided €50 million to build and operate the fully merchant Tenevo solar PV plant, and the solar project was supported by first loss risk cover under the EBRD’s InvestEU Framework for Sustainable Transition. The new battery project is positioned as an extension of that earlier investment, aiming to enhance the site’s ability to store and dispatch clean electricity. Link to Recovery and Resilience Plan support for renewables and storage The EBRD also worked with Bulgaria’s Ministry of Energy on the design of grant schemes, competitive allocation, and technical verification mechanisms to support renewable energy and electricity storage projects under the country’s Recovery and Resilience Plan. According to the EBRD, September 2026 marked the completion of these schemes. Why the project matters for Bulgaria’s power sector The EBRD described rapid growth in battery storage capacity as a significant energy transition achievement for Bulgaria, supporting renewable energy integration and decarbonisation. In its statement, the bank said the project will help increase system flexibility and integrate more renewables. “By increasing the system’s flexibility and helping to integrate more renewable energy, Tenevo will contribute to a more resilient, secure and sustainable power sector,” EBRD Head of Bulgaria Manuela Naessl said. EBRD’s broader role in Bulgaria The EBRD said it is a leading institutional investor in Bulgaria, having invested almost €5.3 billion across 330 projects to date. The bank’s stated focus includes private sector development, competitiveness, and the green economy transition. Key Details - Initiative or programme: Battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Tenevo - Lead organization: Tenevo Solar Technologies - Partners: Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) - Funding amount: €30 million loan from the EBRD (part of a €60 million financing package) - Geographic focus: Tenevo, south-eastern Bulgaria - Target groups: Not specified in the source - Duration or timeline: Not specified in the source - Expected reach or outcomes: 246 MW battery power capacity and 512.5 MWh electricity storage; improved grid stability and support for integrating additional renewables Why This Matters Battery storage investments are increasingly central to power-sector decarbonisation, because they help grids manage the variability of renewable generation. For NGOs and development professionals, the EBRD and RBI-backed Tenevo project highlights how large-scale clean energy deployment can be paired with grid flexibility measures. The case also reflects a practical intersection between finance and implementation capacity: the EBRD states it worked with Bulgaria’s Ministry of Energy to design grant schemes and verification mechanisms under the national Recovery and Resilience Plan, with completion reported in September 2026. This is relevant to civil society groups monitoring how renewable and storage policies translate into investable pipelines. While the announcement does not provide details on social outcomes or community-level components, it can inform program design and partnership discussions around energy access, workforce transitions, and the governance of energy transition support mechanisms. artigo.texto: RECUPERAÇÃO Um projeto de instalação de centros de dados no fundo do mar pode comprometer o habitat de aproximadamente 300 baleias belugas na Enseada de Cook, no Alasca, nos Estados Unidos. A proposta prevê a instalação de mais de 300 turbinas de maré em uma região essencial à sobrevivência da população, considerada criticamente ameaçada de extinção. O funcionamento dos equipamentos causa ruídos contínuos e alterações na temperatura da água, com consequências para orientação, alimentação e reprodução dos animais. Apresentada pela empresa DeepGreen Holdings LLC, a iniciativa prevê 66 módulos de centros de dados subaquáticos em uma área de aproximadamente 1.650 acres. A região abriga uma das menores populações de belugas do mundo, estimada em 331 indivíduos, segundo o Centro de Mamíferos Marinhos dos Estados Unidos. As baleias dependem intensamente da ecolocalização para encontrar alimento, identificar obstáculos, comunicar-se e navegar. Na Enseada de Cook, o derretimento das geleiras deixa a água turva, reduzindo a visibilidade e tornando esse sistema sensorial ainda mais importante para a sobrevivência dos animais. O funcionamento dos centros de dados pode interferir diretamente nessa capacidade. Bombas, ventiladores e turbinas produzem ruídos persistentes, especialmente em baixas frequências, que se propagam pela água e podem comprometer a percepção dos sons utilizados pelas baleias. A construção das estruturas também representa uma fonte de perturbação. A cravação de estacas no fundo do mar, por exemplo, produz ruídos intensos. “Bombas, ventiladores e, principalmente, conjuntos de turbinas produzem um som contínuo de baixa frequência, e a cravação de estacas durante a construção é ainda mais barulhenta”, explicou Vishal Misra, professor e cientista da computação da Universidade Columbia, à revista Scientific American. Para animais que dependem da ecolocalização para realizar atividades essenciais, a introdução de fontes permanentes de ruído em seu habitat pode representar uma ameaça significativa. A interferência acústica pode dificultar a localização de presas, a comunicação entre indivíduos e os deslocamentos necessários à sobrevivência. O aquecimento da água ameaça a alimentação Os impactos potenciais não se restringem à poluição sonora. A transferência de calor dos servidores para a água do mar pode modificar as condições ambientais da região e afetar outras espécies das quais as belugas dependem para se alimentar. Entre elas está o salmão, importante componente da alimentação das baleias. Esses peixes necessitam de temperaturas adequadas para o desenvolvimento dos ovos, a manutenção do metabolismo e a migração. Alterações térmicas podem comprometer essas etapas e modificar a disponibilidade de alimento no ambiente. A eventual redução dos recursos alimentares acrescentaria outra pressão sobre uma população que já enfrenta dificuldades para sobreviver. Para as belugas da Enseada de Cook, a degradação do habitat significa perder condições necessárias para encontrar alimento, reproduzir-se e manter seus grupos. Outro projeto ameaça habitat de baleias no Maine A DeepGreen também propôs uma instalação subaquática no estado do Maine, onde pretende ocupar 27 acres e utilizar até 50 turbinas de maré nas proximidades de áreas de alimentação da baleia-franca-do-atlântico-norte. A espécie possui menos de 400 indivíduos, segundo estimativas citadas pelo Centro de Mamíferos Marinhos. O aquecimento das águas no início da década de 2010 contribuiu para que essas baleias abandonassem áreas de alimentação que utilizavam anteriormente. A instalação de equipamentos capazes de produzir ruído e liberar calor nas proximidades de regiões importantes para a alimentação pode acrescentar pressões a uma espécie cuja sobrevivência já está ameaçada. As duas propostas integram uma iniciativa que busca aproveitar a energia das marés para alimentar centros de processamento de dados. A água do mar também seria utilizada para dissipar o calor produzido pelos servidores, reduzindo a necessidade de grandes volumes de água doce empregados na refrigeração de instalações terrestres. O projeto está inserido na expansão da infraestrutura computacional, impulsionada também pelo crescimento da inteligência artificial. A demanda por processamento exige instalações cada vez maiores e amplia a pressão sobre os recursos naturais utilizados para sustentar essas operações. Moradores e organizações contestam as instalações As propostas enfrentam resistência nos dois estados. No Maine, a cidade de Eastport aprovou por unanimidade, em agosto, uma moratória sobre o projeto da DeepGreen. No fim de setembro, o município também solicitou à Comissão Federal de Regulamentação de Energia dos Estados Unidos (FERC) que rejeitasse a instalação. Inicialmente, a agência considerou insuficientes os pedidos apresentados para o Alasca e o Maine, apontando falta de informações técnicas e ausência de identificação adequada das comunidades indígenas historicamente ligadas às áreas dos projetos. Posteriormente, as propostas foram reapresentadas e aceitas para análise. A aceitação dos pedidos, entretanto, não representa autorização para iniciar as obras. Celeste Miller, representante da FERC, esclareceu à Scientific American que uma licença preliminar não permite qualquer tipo de construção. Organizações ligadas à conservação da vida marinha e à pesca também apresentaram objeções. A Alaska Commercial Fisheries Conservation Alliance, que contestou o processo referente à Enseada de Cook, manifestou oposição ao projeto no Maine, apontando preocupações semelhantes sobre alterações na temperatura da água e impactos sobre a atividade pesqueira. Louis Wolfson, desenvolvedor do projeto da DeepGreen, afirmou à Scientific American que o licenciamento e a implementação das instalações dependeriam da operação segura dos equipamentos e do cumprimento dos limites federais de proteção aos mamíferos marinhos. A discussão ocorre enquanto mudanças propostas na legislaçã

artigo.texto: The initiatives are being led by Ava Community Energy, a local nonprofit electric service provider serving 2 million residents in two counties and 16 cities in the East Bay, the area east of San Francisco. Eight project sites in four cities — Berkeley, Fremont, Hayward and Livermore — are participating in Ava’s Critical Municipal Facilities (CMF) program which will fund the buildout of solar generation and battery storage at key municipal facilities including fire stations and community centers. “We’ve completely financed the systems, no upfront cost to our cities,” said Howard Chang, CEO for Ava Community Energy. The critical energy program, he said, was a way for Ava to engage with its member jurisdictions to better serve them. “What are your energy needs? Where do you have really critical services that you want to ensure that you have sufficient backup power, both for your own energy needs, but also for broader community resilience?” Chang said, as he went through some of the scenarios the program is designed to address. Ava has installed 500 kilowatts of photovoltaic solar panels and 1.32 megawatt-hours of battery storage across the eight sites, capable of generating 778,000 kilowatt-hours of local renewable energy in just the first year, according to a news release. The program, Chang said, was also crafted as a way to “decarbonize, overall,” noting a number of the member cities have in place climate action plans requiring them to tap renewable sources of energy. “Our Climate Action Plan specifically calls for battery storage in city buildings and critical facilities to help reduce emissions and to allow our staff to serve our community during emergencies and grid outages,” wrote Erik Pearson, environmental services manager for the Public Works and Utilities Department in Hayward, a city of about 156,000 residents south of Oakland. The Hayward Corporation Yard and Fire Station No. 1 were the first of the projects to go online about two weeks ago. The city’s climate action plan, Pearson said in an email, “includes very ambitious goals for reducing greenhouse gas emissions,” and adding more renewables to the energy mix “will play a significant part in [helping] us meet our goals.” Hayward is not new to renewable energy. The city installed its first rooftop solar project in 2005, adding others over the years including, Pearson said, a 1.6-megawatt installation at the city’s wastewater treatment plant. With the two new projects, Hayward will now have 14 city facilities equipped with solar generation, including seven of its nine fire stations. Ava’s next CMF projects will be coming online in the coming months, Chang said. The deployments will also help the utility reduce the demand on its power delivery during high-peak times. “Because these are solar-plus-storage, they can be managed in a way that’s beneficial, both for our own portfolio costs as well as for the grid,” Chang said. Batteries can store up excess solar power during the day and discharge it in the evenings when wholesale power rates climb due to high demand. “That’s generally good. That’s good for us as we manage our wholesale portfolio, and it’s good for our customers,” the CEO said. Ultimately, these efforts are aimed at growing resiliency as California cities and counties are all dealing with risks associated with wildfires, extreme weather and the public service demands these events pose. The sites include fire stations, community and senior centers and more. “So there’s a lot of variety of different types of sites that we’re installing these systems at, and it’s not yet fully known how we’re going to operate these battery systems,” said Chang. “At its core, we’re going to charge and discharge at economically optimal times to try to bring down energy costs for our customers. And that’s important.” It should be noted that the solar energy and battery systems deployed are not seen as a direct “one-for-one” replacement of diesel generators, “but it’s a start to really see how batteries can serve as resilience-oriented backup systems for these really critical sites,” Chang said.

artigo.texto: Digital twins will create a new blueprint for data center design Digital twins enable operators to run 'what if' scenarios Digital twins are not simply tools for simulation. They’re assets that have the potential to reconfigure how data centers are designed, tested and optimized. Many operators have already been quick to catch on to the advantages these tools offer, de-risking critical decisions, accelerating innovation, and optimizing performance. The majority of technology leaders in major corporations are already looking to implement digital twin initiatives. Despite this, only 42% of decision-makers in data centers are currently using digital twins, with many still perceiving them as internal tools. In an industry where downtime is incredibly costly, and infrastructure decisions have long-term consequences, the ability to ‘test drive’ different scenarios in a risk-free environment isn’t just an advantage, it’s a gamechanger. AVP Technology at GlobalLogic (a Hitachi Group company). In fact, according to McKinsey, the implementation of digital twins can accelerate the creation and setup of new projects, including AI-enabled features, by up to 60% and cut costs by around 15%. A 360-degree view of operations The data center industry is facing a perfect storm of complexity. Rapid growth in AI workloads, stringent sustainability requirements, and unprecedented IT infrastructure investment are all converging. Traditional approaches to planning and testing – spreadsheets, static models, and gut instinct – simply can’t keep up. Enter digital twins: precise virtual replicas of physical data centers that enable operators to simulate scenarios, test configurations, and optimize performance before committing resources to real-world deployment. Digital twins aren’t new. Manufacturing, aerospace, and energy sectors have been using them for years. But their application to data centers represents a significant leap forward in how the industry approaches design, operations, and resilience planning. By creating a comprehensive digital replica – from server racks to HVAC systems to power distribution – operators can run “what-if” scenarios that would be impossible or prohibitively expensive to test in production. The value proposition is clear: reduce risk, accelerate time-to-market, and optimize resource allocation. But the devil is in the details. Building an effective digital twin requires more than just 3D modeling software. It demands deep integration across IT and OT systems, sophisticated data analytics, and the right talent to interpret results and translate them into actionable insights. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! AI initiatives face similar hurdles. Just 25% of AI implementations have achieved expected ROI, likely hindered by poor system integration and ineffective strategies for data management. Eradicating IT/OT siloes One of the most transformative capabilities of digital twins is their ability to expose hidden interdependencies between IT and OT systems. In traditional data center planning, these systems are often designed and managed in silos. IT teams focus on compute, storage, and networking. OT teams handle physical infrastructure – power, cooling, and building management. This separation creates blind spots that can lead to catastrophic failures under stress. Let’s look at an example. Imagine that a data center provider simulates a regional power grid failure. Primary power is cut, backup generators take over seamlessly, and failover scripts reroute workloads to a secondary facility. HVAC and building management systems (BMS), which are not integrated with IT systems, continue running in standard operating mode. The HVAC system, functioning separately to the simulated power outage and increased IT load, does not adjust cooling to match the spike in server activity. In a real-life scenario, this could result in server aisles nearing thermal shutdown. When systems are not “in dialogue” with one another, and the physical interdependencies between IT and OT systems are not well understood, operators end up with a false sense of readiness. Another issue is that the industry currently lacks the talent to deploy digital twin technologies. 58% of operators in the UK currently struggle to fill critical roles, whilst 40% state that retaining their core team is particularly difficult. This revolving door of talent can make upskilling a challenge and, as things stand, there aren’t enough experts who understand how to direct simulations. A test-drive – for the data center Just as manufacturers test production line changes in their digital twin before implementing them on the factory floor, data center operators can simulate cooling adjustments, power reconfigurations, or workload migrations in their digital twin before touching production infrastructure. The ability to test failure scenarios such as power outages, cooling failures and equipment malfunctions enables operators to check if their disaster recovery procedures actually work and identify gaps before they become real-world crises. Finally, digital twins are making a real difference in helping operators to draw up Service Level Agreements (SLAs) with customers, providing assurance that they can deliver on certain levels of uptime. As operators look to scale their infrastructure in line with the exponential growth of AI, digital twins have a critical role to play, ensuring performance isn’t comprised even as capacity expands. artigo.texto: With maritime transport now included in the UK Emissions Trading Scheme, ship managers need to understand how the new requirements sit alongside the EU ETS, what this means for SHIPMAN agreements and where potential debt and liability exposures may arise. Since 1st July 2026, maritime transport has been included in the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS). Ship managers must now deal with a second emissions trading scheme to consider alongside the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). The schemes use separate allowances and have different geographical scopes, but the work involved will be familiar to managers already dealing with the EU ETS. Both schemes require emissions to be monitored, reported and verified, followed by the surrender of allowances. The EU ETS covers voyages between EU and EEA ports, part of voyages between EU and non-EU ports, and emissions in EU ports. The UK ETS initially covers domestic UK voyages and emissions in UK ports. Managers will therefore need to identify the emissions falling under each scheme and ensure the correct allowances are surrendered. Does this mean SHIPMAN must be amended again? In most cases, no. The BIMCO ETS clause in SHIPMAN 2024 was not drafted solely for the EU ETS. An Emission Scheme is defined to include the EU ETS and any similar system imposed by an applicable lawful authority. The wording allows the clause to apply to similar schemes introduced elsewhere, including in the UK, the US or China. Where the BIMCO clause has been used without amendments which narrow its scope, the UK ETS should already be covered. Managers should, however, check any bespoke wording. A clause which refers only to the EU ETS or EU Allowances may not extend to the UK scheme. For managers, a more immediate concern may be whether the owner provides the allowances. Where the manager is the responsible entity under SHIPMAN, the owner must provide the allowances needed for compliance. If the owner fails to transfer them, or the manager purchases allowances and is not reimbursed, a substantial debt may arise. ITIC’s new ship managers’ debt collection cover is relevant in this situation. ITIC can fund approved costs incurred in pursuing unpaid management fees and debts relating to emissions liabilities, including EU ETS and FuelEU liabilities. The cover does not insure the credit risk or pay the cost of the allowances. It covers the costs of recovering money due to the manager. In many cases, an initial approach from ITIC may be sufficient to obtain payment. Where it is not, further recovery action can be considered, such as the appointment of lawyers. A manager may also face a claim arising from an error in carrying out its responsibilities. For example, the manager could submit inaccurate emissions data, allocate emissions to the wrong scheme, fail to report within the required period or surrender the incorrect number of allowances. If an error causes the owner a loss and results in a claim against the manager, ITIC’s professional indemnity cover may respond, subject to terms and conditions of the cover. The distinction between these two exposures is clear. If the owner has failed to pay an amount due, it is a debt recovery issue. If the manager has made an error which causes a loss, it may result in a professional indemnity claim. For managers using the BIMCO ETS clause in SHIPMAN 2024, the arrival of the UK ETS should not in itself mean revisiting the contract. The priority is to check that the clause has not been narrowed through bespoke amendments and that responsibility for providing allowances and reimbursing costs is clear. If the owner does not pay, ITIC may be able to assist with the cost of recovery.

artigo.texto: Wildfires in Indonesia have ignited a structural challenge within the voluntary carbon market: the validity of credits derived from forest conservation projects when the underlying asset is destroyed by fire. This is not a speculative risk but an operational mechanism failure that directly impacts the integrity of carbon offset claims. The core issue lies in the divergence between the theoretical reduction of emissions-preventing deforestation-and the physical reality of carbon release when peatlands and vegetation burn. The carbon credit mechanism operates on a specific physical premise: one credit represents one tonne of greenhouse gases either reduced or removed. In the context of forest projects, this value is generated by preserving the carbon stored in trees and soil. Unlike renewable energy projects that displace fossil fuel consumption, forest projects carry a unique operational risk: the carbon asset is biologically active and subject to environmental reversal. When a fire occurs, the carbon previously locked in the biomass and peat is released back into the atmosphere, potentially negating the emissions savings that the project was credited for delivering. The verification of this loss is a multi-stage operational process. It does not rely on visual confirmation alone, such as satellite imagery of burn scars, which can be misleading in peatland areas where fires smoulder underground. Instead, independent verifiers must conduct scientific field measurements to quantify the exact volume of underground peat and biomass consumed. As Bjorn Fonden, Asia-Pacific director at the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), noted, the assessment question is not whether trees remain standing, but whether the project prevented emissions that would otherwise have occurred. If the verified loss reverses previously issued credits, the project may generate fewer new credits in subsequent years, and the specific loss must be compensated to preserve the integrity of the market. The primary operational safeguard against this risk is the buffer pool mechanism. Under this system, a mandatory percentage of credits generated by forest projects-typically around 5 per cent, depending on the project type and risk profile-is withheld from sale and placed into a shared reserve. This reserve acts as a financial and operational insurance policy. When a verified reversal event occurs, credits from the buffer pool are cancelled to offset the loss, ensuring that the total amount of credits in circulation remains accurate. This system is designed to be cross-subsidised; credits from projects in lower-risk regions can cover losses in higher-risk areas, provided the total reserve is sufficient. Ben Rattenbury from carbon ratings firm Sylvera explained that the adequacy of this volume is determined by the crediting standards, which set the rules for how much must be set aside based on historical risk data. However, a significant operational constraint is emerging due to climate change. The buffer pool system was calibrated based on historical fire patterns. As extreme weather events become more frequent and severe, the frequency of large-scale fire events may exceed the rate at which credits are added to the reserve. If multiple large forests burn within a short period, the carbon released could outpace the credits available in the buffer pool, creating a systemic shortfall. This creates a structural mismatch between the pace of environmental degradation and the financial buffering capacity of the market. Some standards are updating their risk calculations to account for these extreme conditions, but the challenge of keeping reserve levels sufficient in the face of accelerating climate risks remains unresolved. Despite these risks, the market has continued to function. Data from carbon market database Allied Offsets indicates that 1,056 new buyers from the Asia-Pacific region entered the market last year. In Singapore, where carbon trading is a significant economic activity, the impact on market depth has been limited. Oi-Yee Choo, CEO of Singapore-based carbon exchange Climate Impact X, stated that trading activity involving Indonesian credits on their platform has remained stable, with no significant shift in demand. This stability suggests that market participants continue to value the offset mechanism, likely because the credit revenue itself serves a critical operational function in fire prevention. The revenue from carbon credits is not merely a financial gain; it is an operational resource for asset maintenance. Funds from these projects are directed toward forest patrols, firefighting teams, early-warning systems, and the maintenance of water levels in peatlands. In peatland areas, preventing the soil from drying out is a critical operational step, as dried peat becomes highly flammable and vulnerable to long-smouldering fires. Zhang Yiwen, co-founder of carbon removal startup CarbonSynk, emphasized that effective projects require due diligence, including the use of satellite images and historical data to identify high-risk zones, and active engagement with local communities to address human activities that contribute to fire risk. The sustainability of the carbon credit market in regions like Indonesia now depends on this operational feedback loop: whether the revenue generated by credits can sufficiently fund the physical measures-patrols, water management, and firefighting-needed to prevent the very events that invalidate the credits. The system is no longer just about protecting a forest for today; it is about ensuring the financial and operational mechanisms can withstand the fires of tomorrow. artigo.texto: Three Kansas communities to decide on data center bans this election WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - Data centers are a big talking point in this midterm election. In Kansas, three communities will decide whether to allow them to built in their cities. El Dorado, Emporia and Ottawa all have data center questions on their ballot. El Dorado In El Dorado, citizens will vote on whether to prohibit “high-impact data centers” with an electrical capacity over 10 megawatts. A ‘yes’ vote supports prohibiting high-impact data centers and battery energy storage systems for 10 years. A ‘no’ vote opposes prohibiting high-impact data centers and battery energy storage systems for 10 years. ‘Protect the Heartland,’ the group opposing data centers in El Dorado, successfully placed the issue on the ballot, saying that residents felt this was their last option. “We felt that we had no other choice but to petition our government for an ordinance,” said Danica Dickson, who opposes data centers. “The ordinance does not ban all data centers. It only bans data centers with a capacity of 10 megawatts and above.” Those who support bringing a data center to El Dorado, like the ‘El Dorado Forward’ organization, say that they believe the city has enough safeguards in place to host one. “We are an economic development-friendly group, not necessarily a data center-friendly group,” said Samuel McVay with El Dorado Forward. “We do believe there are good projects, and we want to regulate the bad ones. We believe our city has systems in place to do that.” The vote serves as a binding mandate, so El Dorado gets to choose between total prohibition or entering the data center market under local government regulation. Related Story: Citizen group wins court fight over El Dorado data center petition Emporia Meanwhile, Emporia is also considering a proposal to ban data centers for several years. The ordinance, if passed, would ban high-impact data centers, including those with a peak electrical load of 10 megawatts or facilities that consume more than 10,000 gallons of water per day. A ‘yes’ vote supports prohibiting high-impact data center construction in the city. A ‘no’ vote opposes prohibiting high-impact data center construction in the city. 12 News asked both supporters and opponents what they think about the fact that three Kansas cities have data center measures on the ballot this election. Opponents say it reflects a lack of trust in local government. “It tells me governments are not representing people at this time,” said Jay Vehige, an opponent. “If they were, we would not have had to go through the petition process. But it also tells me that democracy in Kansas is alive and well.” Supporters of the data center in Emporia, like the spokesperson for Flint Hills Digital Campus, say that the election is about more than data centers and it could affect future development projects. “Residents are not being asked to approve or reject a specific data center development. They are being asked to vote on a proposed prohibition of high-impact data centers for a decade, a decision that could have implications well beyond any single project,” the spokesperson said. “Our vision is simple: The next great chapter of American innovation should not be limited by geography, and communities like Emporia deserve the opportunity to help write it.” Related Content: - Petition protesting Emporia data center deemed invalid - Teacher arrested, carried out of Emporia City Commission meeting - Emporia City Commission hosting special meeting to discuss data center ballot ruling Ottawa In Ottawa, voters are deciding whether they will implement a ban on any utility-intensive data centers. A ‘yes’ vote would adopt the ban, and a ‘no’ vote would reject the ban. The proposal does not include a specified expiration date, differing from El Dorado’s proposed ban of 10 years. Community reaction Regardless of the outcome, both sides say they hope the community can unite again after the elections. “This issue has united people on both sides of the aisle,” Dickson said. “Hopefully the temperature cools down and we can all talk again and remember that we are neighbors,” McVay said. artigo.texto: ClickIP vê risco de bolha com obrigação de investir em data centers Maykon Souza critica proposta de vincular infraestrutura regional a leilões de espectro e defende crédito para o setor. O CEO da ClickIP, Maykon Souza, vê risco de formação de uma bolha de data centers regionais (“edge”) caso a Anatel vincule investimentos em infraestrutura regional a compromissos de aquisição de espectro. Em entrevista ao TV.Síntese que vai ao ar logo mais, às 19h, o executivo afirmou que a obrigação pode estimular a construção de instalações sem demanda correspondente. “Isso vai criar uma bolha e a bolha vai estourar, e vai dar prejuízo para as empresas e prejuízo para o mercado”, afirmou, ao comentar a proposta. Na avaliação de Souza, a demanda por processamento está concentrada nos grandes data centers, os chamados hyperscales, e sua distribuição para estruturas regionais depende das necessidades das empresas clientes. “Acredito que é errado porque a Anatel está querendo criar um mercado que ainda não existe”, declarou. A posição parte de uma operadora que já investiu em um data center em Manaus. Segundo Souza, a ClickIP destinou R$ 21 milhões à infraestrutura e pouco mais de R$ 20 milhões à capacidade computacional. Inaugurada em 2024, a instalação surgiu da necessidade de melhorar a estrutura utilizada pela própria empresa para prestar serviços de conectividade. Demanda interna sustenta ocupação O executivo informou que cerca de oito racks estavam ocupados no momento da entrevista, com predominância do uso interno. A demanda de clientes externos, segundo ele, começa a chegar, com projetos voltados principalmente a empresas da Zona Franca de Manaus. O projeto começou a ser concebido em 2020, e as obras tiveram início em 2021. Durante seu desenvolvimento, os sócios decidiram ampliar o investimento para transformar a infraestrutura em uma unidade de negócios que também atendesse terceiros. Segundo Souza, a contratação do data center não exige que o cliente utilize os serviços de banda larga da ClickIP. A instalação já hospeda servidores de outras empresas e recebe operadoras em regime de colocation. Viabilidade depende das aplicações Para o executivo, a oportunidade para provedores regionais está na interiorização dos data centers, mas a existência de uma cidade sem essa infraestrutura não basta para justificar o investimento. É necessário avaliar a presença de empresas e de aplicações que demandem processamento próximo dos usuários. “Boa parte das aplicações não dependem de baixa latência”, afirmou. Souza defende um modelo no qual o processamento de uma mesma empresa seja distribuído entre sua estrutura interna, data centers regionais e grandes instalações de nuvem. A definição sobre onde executar cada aplicação, segundo ele, precisa ser construída com o cliente. Nesse cenário, o próprio provedor pode funcionar como cliente âncora do empreendimento. Para Souza, o investimento faz sentido quando o uso interno sustenta o modelo de negócios, sem depender exclusivamente de uma expectativa de contratação futura por terceiros. A disponibilidade de profissionais também foi apontada como obstáculo. Segundo o executivo, os fundadores precisaram aprender sobre a operação do setor, e a empresa continua capacitando sua equipe. IA pode exigir outra infraestrutura A ClickIP também avalia que uma eventual expansão para cargas mais intensivas de inteligência artificial exigiria uma estrutura específica. Souza explicou que o data center foi concebido antes dessa demanda e que os desafios envolvem dissipação de calor e balanceamento de carga. Caso a demanda por IA avance para o processamento regional e exija refrigeração líquida, o executivo prevê a construção de um anexo no terreno da empresa. A possibilidade está condicionada à evolução desse mercado. Na discussão sobre políticas de incentivo, Souza apontou o financiamento como uma forma de apoiar os investimentos. “O que o governo de modo geral pode ajudar é com linhas de crédito”, afirmou.

artigo.texto: Data centers are deeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else? Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too. The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “the issue” in the presidential election. So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI “speed limits”; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards — and yes, rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.” Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments) as “good and healthy.” “Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said.

artigo.texto: CATL Wins Exclusive Battery Deal for Blue Vector Skyla V30 Aircraft In this article (8) CATL has signed strategic and product agreements with Hangzhou-based Blue Vector Intelligent Technology to serve as the exclusive battery partner for its commercial passenger aircraft. Announced by the battery maker on Monday, the tie-up focuses on the Skyla V30, an all-electric tiltrotor model that has secured more than 100 pre-sales orders since its global debut in July. Under the agreement, CATL will develop custom aviation batteries for the six-seat aircraft. The companies did not disclose financial terms, battery specifications or a delivery schedule. Validating the Skyla V30 Platform Engineering work on the airframe is already moving beyond initial digital design. Blue Vector rolled out its first full-scale technology demonstrator, designated A/C01, on August 31 in Harbin in northeastern China. The demonstrator airframe has entered a testing sequence covering systems integration, ground trials and tilt-transition flights. Those trials will test the transition between vertical lift and horizontal forward flight, which forms the core technical challenge for tiltrotor electric craft designed for intercity transit. Commercial demand is building ahead of type certification. Blue Vector booked pre-sales commitments for 60 V30 aircraft at the Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou on September 24. Singapore-based aviation operator Moon Aero accounted for 30 of those aircraft, representing the platform’s first overseas pre-sales customer. That booking brought total advance orders past 100 units as the company conducts airworthiness validation with Chinese civil aviation regulators. Capital Structure and Production Targets Development work relies on fresh venture backing secured over the past two quarters. Blue Vector closed a funding round of more than 100 million yuan ($14.9 million) on June 30, led jointly by Shenzhen Capital Group and an unnamed industrial dollar fund. That transaction marked the company’s fifth capital injection in roughly six months. Across that period, the startup collected more than 400 million yuan to finance aircraft development, prototype construction and test flights. Securing an exclusive battery partnership before airworthiness certification freezes the aircraft’s internal layout. For aircraft manufacturers, battery weight, thermal management and energy density dictate maximum payload and cabin configuration. Swapping pack suppliers later in the certification pipeline resets regulatory approvals, locking airframe designers into their chosen cell platform. For CATL, the deal locks in a captive customer across passenger transit routes in eastern China and regional hubs like Singapore. Operating intercity routes between regional cities demands high cycle life and rapid charging turnaround times at terminal pads, creating recurring replacement demand for specialized aviation-grade cells. Building Out Electric Aviation Across China The Blue Vector contract expands CATL’s ongoing effort to position its battery systems across the electric vertical takeoff and landing sector. In August 2024, the battery maker agreed to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Shanghai-based aircraft manufacturer Autoflight to co-develop aviation packs. That collaboration extended into terminal infrastructure late last year. In November 2025, Autoflight and CATL revealed a floating vertiport vessel that integrates passenger landing pads, battery storage and high-power charging systems onto a marine barge, providing water-based terminal access for coastal cities. Blue Vector must now clear tilt-transition flight trials in Harbin and advance formal airworthiness certification for the Skyla V30 before delivering the first production units to Moon Aero and domestic operators. Questions & Answers Q. What is the current development status of the Skyla V30 aircraft? Blue Vector rolled out its full-scale technology demonstrator, designated A/C01, on 31 August in Harbin. The demonstrator has entered testing for systems integration, ground trials and tilt-transition flights between vertical lift and horizontal forward flight ahead of type certification with Chinese regulators. Q. Who has placed pre-orders for the aircraft so far? Blue Vector has secured more than 100 advance orders, including a commitment for 60 units booked in Hangzhou on 24 September. Singapore-based operator Moon Aero agreed to take 30 of those aircraft, becoming the platform's first overseas customer alongside domestic buyers. Q. Why was the battery partnership finalised before regulatory certification? Battery weight, energy density and thermal management determine an aircraft's maximum payload and internal layout. Agreeing on a supplier early avoids costly redesigns, as changing battery packs later in the certification pipeline resets regulatory approvals and disrupts airworthiness validation. Q. How is Blue Vector financing the aircraft's development and testing? The startup gathered more than 400 million yuan across five capital injections in roughly six months. This included a funding round of over 100 million yuan on 30 June, led by Shenzhen Capital Group and an industrial dollar fund, to finance development and test flights. artigo.texto: The American Water Works Association (AWWA), an international, nonprofit scientific and educational society, has released a report outlining how water utilities can assess the potential effects of proposed data center developments on water supplies, infrastructure and wastewater systems. The report titled Cooling the Cloud: Considerations for Water Utilities Evaluating Data Center Development, was developed with Carollo Engineers. It examines the resource, technological, financial and contractual issues utilities should consider before approving or supporting data center projects. These include water supply reliability, infrastructure capacity, wastewater impacts, environmental considerations and the recovery of costs associated with development. According to a press release, the report builds on AWWA’s 2025 publication, Cooling the Cloud: Water Utilities in a Data-Driven World, which examined the relationship between data center development, water utilities and local communities. “Water utilities are foundational to local economic development and industrial growth, making their early involvement in community planning essential for major development projects,” said David LaFrance, CEO, AWWA. “Each community will ultimately consider many factors and viewpoints as it assesses data center proposals, AWWA looks forward to working with our many members to share additional insights on data center development and support informed decision-making.” The report outlines a project-by-project approach, urging utilities to first assess data centers’ cooling technologies, projected average and peak water consumption, wastewater needs and potential future expansion. These factors should be weighed against available water supplies, infrastructure capacity, reuse opportunities and environmental impacts before utilities commit resources. It also calls on utilities to establish clear agreements with developers covering infrastructure investments, project costs and each party’s responsibilities as developments evolve. The aim is to prevent existing customers from bearing additional financial burdens. The report further emphasizes early public engagement, with utilities encouraged to disclose projected water demand, system capacity, potential rate impacts and unresolved concerns. Community benefit agreements are also suggested as a way to improve transparency and ensure accountability. It is noteworthy that the AWWA report does not take a position for or against data center development, but is intended to help utilities evaluate proposals based on their individual circumstances.

artigo.texto: KITCHENER, ON, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Recurrent Energy, a subsidiary of Canadian Solar Inc. ("Canadian Solar") (NASDAQ: CSIQ) and a leading global developer, owner, and operator of solar and energy storage assets, today announced the sale of two standalone BESS projects in France to BW ESS, a global energy storage owner-operator. The portfolio comprises two projects: Baixas, located in the Pyrénées-Orientales department, with a capacity of 100 MW / 400 MWh, and Coquainvilliers, located in Calvados, with a capacity of 100 MW / 400 MWh. Both projects benefit from advanced transmission-level grid connection positions and have been developed around strong grid fundamentals, including very limited expected network constraints. Together, they will provide 200 MW / 800 MWh of flexible capacity to the French electricity system. Recurrent Energy originated and developed both projects, including securing the land, advancing grid connection, and managing permitting and local stakeholder engagement. BW ESS will acquire the projects, marking the first transaction between the two companies and BW ESS' entry into the French energy market. Recurrent Energy will continue to lead the projects through the remaining development phase, drawing on its local market knowledge, technical capabilities, and experience in delivering renewable energy and storage projects. Once the remaining development milestones have been achieved, BW ESS will lead the delivery of the assets through construction and into commercial operation. BW ESS intends to own and operate the assets over the long term. Erik Strømsø, CEO and Co-Founder of BW ESS, commented: "We are excited to work with Recurrent Energy through the next phase and to apply BW ESS' long-term owner-operator expertise as we bring these assets into construction and operation. Entering France is a significant milestone for BW ESS and a natural next step in the expansion of our global energy storage platform. These acquisitions give us an immediate 200 MW / 800 MWh platform in the country and provide a strong foundation for building a sizeable French portfolio. France has a strong nuclear base, but it also has a growing need for flexibility as weather-sensitive demand and an evolving generation mix create more variable system conditions. Batteries can complement France's nuclear backbone by adding the rapid-response flexibility needed to balance the system, absorb surplus power, and make low-carbon generation available when it is most valuable." Dylan Marx, CEO of Recurrent Energy, said: "This transaction with BW ESS showcases our ability to create value through the delivery of high-quality BESS projects, while remaining closely involved in their development through to commercial operation. It is a strong testament to the BESS platform we have built in France and our ability to continue scaling it. Once operational, the projects will provide flexible storage capacity to support grid stability, balance supply and demand, and facilitate the further integration of renewable energy into the French electricity system." artigo.texto: Landover data center project faces new hurdle PRINCE GEORGES COUNTY, Md. (7News) — A proposed data center campus at the former Landover Mall site in Prince George’s County could face a major hurdle after county leaders changed the rules governing data center development. The County Council recently approved legislation closing a loophole in a 2021 law that allowed the Brightseat Park proposal to move forward without another round of council approval. Under the new law, the proposed development must now return before the County Council for additional approval, potentially putting the project in jeopardy as opposition among nearby residents continues to grow. The property, located along Brightseat Road in Landover, has been waiting for redevelopment for more than two decades. Landover Mall opened in 1972 but closed in 2002. The mall was eventually demolished, and its last major store, Sears, closed in 2014. Developers have been pursuing plans for a massive data center campus at the site for the past couple of years. But opponents say the project should not be allowed to move forward under older permitting standards, particularly as Prince George’s County considers tighter restrictions on data center development. “Residents have made it very clear that they do not want the Landover Data center and this development should not be allowed to proceed with building using old permitting standards. But instead should be required to follow any new building standards that are put in place, if and when a moratorium is lifted,” said Beth Landry of the Chesapeake Climate Action Network. SEE ALSO | Amazon is backing out of planned data center project at former GW campus The council’s latest action comes roughly three months after county leaders extended a moratorium on new data center development across Prince George’s County. Council Member Shayla Adams-Stafford has indicated that the new approval requirement could make it extremely difficult for the Brightseat Park proposal to move forward, given the growing opposition. The legislation also signals a tougher approach to future data center proposals, with developers facing additional council oversight, more detailed site review and greater opportunities for public input. The project is not officially dead, but its path forward has become considerably more complicated.

The IEA reports that LFP packs were more than 40% cheaper per kWh than nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) packs in 2025. Part of that gap reflects LFP’s grip on stationary storage, where it accounted for more than 90% of global installations that year. However, while batteries keep getting cheaper to manufacture, the risks from commodity prices, supply-chain constraints and overcapacity cycles can sharply reverse the trend in the short term. artigo.texto: Chinese battery producer CATL unveiled a dual-electric range-extender battery system for heavy-duty electric trucks on 20th October 2026. The pack features a large, swappable battery and an onboard battery that adds driving range. The primary battery is offered with the listed capacities of 432 kWh or 513 kWh, while the further range-extension battery provides an extra 77 kWh. Operators can also simply swap out the main battery at compatible swap stations without having to wait for a charging session to complete. The architecture aims at freight operators, who find vehicle downtime, cost of batteries, and adaptability of routes major issues in running vehicles. The primary swappable battery has been separated from the reserve battery to potentially increase utilisation of batteries and reduce some of the financial hurdles to electrify heavy trucks. CATL is developing the system as part of its QIJI battery swapping ecosystem. The firm is planning to increase the number of sites for electric heavy-duty vehicles. Battery swapping could benefit high-utilisation freight routes with predictable demand, but they have to use standardised batteries and vehicles built to use them, and require significant infrastructure investment and other factors to ensure stations will be viable. Building two batteries also complicates engineering. Automakers need to look at the battery packaging for both battery packs, safety features and the control strategy. Why it matters Swappable batteries and the energy content stored in internal reserves could see battery electric trucks become the norm, entering the realm of the possible for commercial freight hauliers working to a timetable.

artigo.texto: Zefiro Part-Funds Isometric Carbon Protocol for Orphaned Well Plugging Zefiro Methane helped fund and shape Isometric's orphaned well protocol, open for public consultation until November 14, 2026. It would allow the company to resume originating credits. Zefiro Methane Corp., a North American environmental services company specializing in methane abatement and the plugging of orphaned and end-of-life oil and gas wells, says it has supported the upcoming launch of a carbon credit methodology for plugging orphaned wells in the United States and Canada. The Orphaned Well Plugging (OWP) Protocol, developed by the carbon registry Isometric, is nearing completion. Once finalized, it would allow Zefiro to originate carbon credits again from the type of plugging work it performs today, according to the company. In a neighboring area of decarbonization, Cupola and SWCorp Malaysia team up to test low-carbon recycling. Zefiro says these credits would come on top of record fiscal 2026 revenue of $42.5 million. A protocol in consultation until November 14 Isometric released the draft OWP Protocol on October 15, 2026, opening a 30-day public consultation that ends on November 14, 2026. The text sets out requirements for projects that permanently plug leaking orphaned wells to stop methane from escaping into the atmosphere. Credits are based on a direct, on-site measurement of each well's methane leak before plugging. That measurement is projected over a 20-year crediting period using a conservative decline rate. A permanence check takes place 12 to 18 months after plugging, and a portion of credits is withheld until the well is confirmed sealed. To be eligible, a project must show that the well is orphaned, that no public program has scheduled it for plugging and that it would not have been plugged without carbon finance. Zefiro's role as an external contributor The protocol was developed by Isometric's Science Team and reviewed by members of its Science Network, which includes more than 500 academic experts. Zefiro was one of three orphaned well project developers that part-funded its development, and it provided expertise drawn from its field operations and carbon market experience. Isometric notes in its announcement that funding does not influence a protocol's requirements. Credits are issued only where an independent, accredited auditor has confirmed that a project is compliant. Zefiro's input came from Sam Jennings, Director of Carbon Operations, and Tina Reine, Chief Commercial Officer. Mr. Jennings, a second-generation petroleum landman, has two decades of experience at Shell, ConocoPhillips, Marathon and Devon. Ms. Reine, who leads Zefiro's activities in the voluntary carbon markets, has worked in environmental markets since 2007 and holds an MBA from Columbia Business School. Isometric and a growing market London-based Isometric began in carbon removal before expanding into industrial emissions, energy, fuels and materials. Its customers include Microsoft, Boeing, JPMorgan Chase and Anglo American. By its own figures, it serves more than 200 projects worldwide and has been contracted to certify more than 16 million tonnes. In September 2026, Intercontinental Exchange, parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, joined its $50 million Series A financing, and the two companies plan to combine Isometric's certification technology with ICE's market infrastructure and data capabilities. According to MSCI, capital committed to carbon credits hit a record $22 billion in 2025, and the market could be worth between $60 billion and $270 billion by 2050. Zefiro says it completed the first sale of carbon offsets originated under the American Carbon Registry's orphaned well methodology. Mr. Jennings said a framework combining scientific rigor with the practical requirements of financing could help attract the investment needed to plug more leaking orphaned wells.
