artigo.texto: Nearly 15 years worth of hard-won pollution reduction efforts are set to be undone in the United States, as a wave of data centers powered by gas plants enters construction. That’s according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club, first reported by Bloomberg, which notes that the US energy grid is expected to belch out 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, assuming the country’s currently-planned AI developments enter operation as scheduled. That’s a massive rise compared to even 2025 — itself a near-record year for US carbon emissions. If the AI industry and its data center developers get their way, the analysis found, emissions will likely skyrocket by 42 percent over the five-year period, an expected increase of 618 million tons compared to 2025. “The numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds,” the Sierra Club’s principal advisor for climate and energy Jeremy Fisher told Bloomberg. Due to major bottlenecks in the electrical grid, many data center developers have opted for on- or near-site power plants, which are overwhelmingly fueled by noxious fossil fuels. Projects like Elon Musk’s 1.2 gigawatt data center near Memphis are already choking out residents with fleets of methane generators, which legal experts say flaunt all kinds of local permitting and federal environmental regulations. Still, for anybody banking on having clean air to breathe, there is some hope. The number of data center projects at risk of cancellation is rising precipitously as time goes on — driven by grass roots organizing and increasing financial pressures. So if you’re one of the many activists mounting opposition to data centers in your community, just know that the benefits of a cancelled hyperscale facility extend far beyond your backyard. artigo.texto: Liquid Cooling Retrofits: Hard, but Sometimes Worth It Liquid cooling retrofits can boost density and efficiency, but cost, downtime, and infrastructure limits mean they make sense only in select cases. There is little question that liquid cooling is becoming an increasingly attractive way to manage rising heat loads inside data centers, especially as operators deploy denser racks and more AI infrastructure. In many scenarios, liquid cooling can improve thermal efficiency and reduce dependence on large volumes of airflow. It can also help operators curb water use in designs that would otherwise rely heavily on evaporative cooling. The challenge, however, is that most existing data centers were not designed with liquid cooling in mind. Retrofitting an older facility to support liquid cooling can be technically feasible, but it is rarely simple. Here’s a look at why retrofits are difficult – and when the investment may still make sense. Why Liquid Cooling Retrofits Are Difficult From a logistical standpoint, installing liquid cooling is relatively easy when building a new data center. Designers can account for piping, rack loads, redundancy, heat rejection, and maintenance access from the start. It is much harder when an operator wants to retrofit an existing facility, whether to replace or supplement a traditional air-based cooling design. In that case, several challenges tend to stand in the way. Space Constraints Complicate Piping Liquid cooling systems require supply and return lines to run close to servers and other heat-generating IT equipment. In many existing server rooms, however, available space is already constrained, and much of it is occupied by networking and power cabling. Addressing that problem may require repositioning racks, reworking cable pathways, or creating new routes for coolant distribution. In some cases, operators may even need to expand white space or make other physical changes to the facility. All of that is possible, but it can be expensive and disruptive. Heavier Racks Can Strain Raised Floors The structural components of liquid cooling systems, combined with coolant itself and higher-density compute hardware, can significantly increase rack weight. In AI-heavy environments, fully loaded racks can exceed 3,000 pounds. The added weight is especially challenging in facilities with raised floors. Raised-floor designs are common in older data centers because they support airflow management for conventional air cooling. But they may not be able to support heavier liquid-cooled racks without reinforcement or redesign. That can mean extensive structural work before a retrofit can move forward. Downtime Is Hard to Avoid Even for operators willing to make the investments needed to support a retrofit, downtime is often a major concern. Structural modifications, mechanical upgrades, and rack-level changes can take months, especially if servers must be moved or workloads shifted elsewhere during the transition. Even when no major building work is required, some disruption is likely as systems move from an existing cooling model to a liquid-assisted design. That might be manageable for organizations with spare capacity in other facilities or the ability to burst into the cloud, but it is a much harder proposition for sites supporting mission-critical workloads. Mechanical Systems May Need Major Upgrades Adding liquid cooling requires supporting infrastructure to remove heat from the building, which may entail changes to pumps, heat exchangers, water loops, or dry-cooling equipment. Older facilities may not have enough capacity in their mechanical plant to support those changes. Even when they do, integrating new liquid cooling equipment with legacy systems can be complex. Operators must also consider factors such as leak detection, water quality, redundancy, and maintenance procedures. Liquid Cooling Adds Operational Complexity A retrofit can also create ongoing operational challenges. Liquid cooling introduces new equipment, maintenance needs, and failure scenarios that require staff training and updated procedures. When a Liquid Cooling Retrofit Is Worth It Given the cost, complexity, and disruption involved, many operators will conclude that a full liquid cooling retrofit is not the right move for their facilities. Still, there are cases where the economics and the operational logic are compelling. One is a partial deployment. Instead of replacing an entire cooling architecture, an operator may add liquid cooling only for the highest-density racks while leaving the broader air-cooling system in place. That reduces structural changes and the risks of downtime. It is also the approach many colocation providers have taken as they add support for liquid-cooled deployments without converting entire facilities. Another scenario is the single-tenant data center, where one organization directly captures the long-term efficiency and capacity benefits. In those cases, it is often easier to justify the capital expense because the operator and the beneficiary are the same. Retrofits can also make more sense in regions facing water constraints or regulatory pressure around resource consumption. Where water availability is limited or sustainability targets are becoming harder to meet, the case for moving at least some workloads to liquid cooling can grow stronger. Finally, a retrofit may be attractive when the alternative is building new capacity from scratch. If an operator needs to support denser server hardware but does not want to add another facility, liquid cooling may provide a way to increase compute capacity within an existing footprint. In that scenario, retrofitting may be less expensive than expanding the data center portfolio. Retrofitting an existing data center for liquid cooling is difficult, and in many cases the costs will outweigh the benefits. But not always. artigo.texto: OpenAI doesn't want to call them "data centers" anymore. Instead, the ChatGPT maker plans to propose a new, more chic name for the behemoth factories that power your chatbot queries. That new name is "compute campuses," an OpenAI spokesperson confirmed to Business Insider on Sunday. "Compute campuses better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure we're building for AI," the spokesperson said. "These are long-term investments in computing, energy infrastructure and skilled work." Though much has been said about the less-than-stellar reputations of AI data centers (a recent Pew Research poll found that 54% of Americans say AI data centers are bad for the environment), efforts to ameliorate that view have mostly failed. Data centers are now a major issue for voters in the midterms. While major data center builders like Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft have pledged millions of dollars to the communities and schools surrounding their centers, OpenAI is betting that a complete rebrand will also help turn around public opinion. "We want the communities hosting that infrastructure to help shape it and share in the opportunities it creates," the OpenAI spokesperson said. Time will tell, however, if the "compute campus" lingo catches on. Axios earlier reported that OpenAI was also preparing for a blue wave in Tuesday's midterm elections, which could result in a more regulatory-minded government.

artigo.texto: O Brasil deu mais um passo na construção de seu mercado regulado de carbono. A publicação, em 29 de outubro, das primeiras regras para a implementação das obrigações de mensuração, relato e verificação de emissões inaugura etapa importante desse processo. O Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões, criado em 2024, insere o País num movimento internacional de precificação das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. É um instrumento que pode contribuir para o cumprimento dos compromissos climáticos ao valorizar ativos naturais, com efeitos sobre investimentos, custos de produção e competitividade. A nova portaria estabelece um cronograma para que setores passem a mensurar e reportar suas emissões. O País entra, portanto, em uma fase de aprendizado e construção das metodologias que sustentarão o sistema. O processo de regulamentação é marcado por uma interlocução entre poder público e setor produtivo que merece reconhecimento. Aliado ao rigor técnico e à prudência, o diálogo é fundamental para assegurar regras equilibradas que considerem as particularidades da economia brasileira, proporcionem segurança jurídica e estimulem investimentos. O desafio é construir um marco regulatório que concilie integridade ambiental e desenvolvimento econômico, evitando distorções que não se traduzam em benefícios ambientais. Temos uma estrutura produtiva muito particular, com elevada participação de fontes renováveis em segmentos que fizeram investimentos expressivos em eficiência e redução de emissões. Reconhecer essas características e evitar importar modelos concebidos para realidades diferentes é fundamental. Esse cuidado é especialmente relevante quando se olha para setores que já incorporam fontes renováveis, ativos biológicos e ciclos longos de investimento. É o caso da indústria de árvores cultivadas na produção de celulose, em que a dimensão florestal e a industrial são partes indissociáveis de uma mesma cadeia. O setor cultiva 10,7 milhões de hectares de florestas plantadas para fins produtivos e conserva milhões de hectares de vegetação nativa. Todos os dias, planta 2,2 milhões de árvores para fins comerciais. Ao crescerem, elas retiram carbono da atmosfera e o armazenam em sua biomassa. Ao mesmo tempo, fornecem matéria-prima renovável para produtos presentes no cotidiano de bilhões de pessoas e sustentam uma indústria que utiliza 92% de fontes renováveis de energia e investe continuamente na eficiência de seus processos. Uma regulamentação tecnicamente consistente precisa enxergar o ciclo produtivo em sua integralidade, estimular novos avanços e não penalizar quem já investiu. O Brasil tem enorme potencial para retirar CO2 da atmosfera a partir de suas florestas – plantadas ou naturais. A lei que criou o mercado de carbono já prevê o reconhecimento dessas remoções. Agora é fundamental que a regulamentação transforme essa previsão em mecanismos concretos, capazes de valorizar a contribuição das florestas e estimular novos investimentos, gerar empregos e fortalecer nossa competitividade no mercado internacional. Há ainda uma oportunidade que ultrapassa nossas fronteiras. O Acordo de Paris criou mecanismos de transferência internacional de resultados comprovados de redução ou remoção de emissões, os ITMOs (na sigla em inglês). Esse mecanismo pode abrir portas para o financiamento internacional de projetos que contribuam para o enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas, como aqueles ligados à restauração florestal. As regras nacionais para essas operações, ainda em discussão, devem garantir segurança jurídica, transparência e integridade ambiental, criando condições para a atração de investimentos. A discussão ganha mais relevância às vésperas da COP-31, que será realizada de 9 a 20 de novembro, em Antália, na Turquia. A conferência ocorrerá num mundo marcado por guerras, tensões geopolíticas, crise energética e disputas econômicas, no qual a agenda da sustentabilidade perde espaço. Após anos de negociação, as conferências entram no terreno da implementação: como financiar, medir e viabilizar, na economia real, as transformações acordadas. O encontro terá entre seus desafios avançar nas regras para geração de créditos de carbono, conciliando a credibilidade dos créditos às regras viáveis para projetos que exigem investimento e planejamento de longo prazo, como o plantio de florestas. Para o Brasil, essa pauta precisa ser tratada também como agenda de desenvolvimento. Não cabe tratá-la nem com entusiasmo acrítico nem como ameaça ao setor produtivo. É preciso assegurar que o mercado de carbono cumpra seu papel de promover a descarbonização, ao mesmo tempo em que estimule investimentos, valorize iniciativas já desenvolvidas e fortaleça a competitividade. Temos vantagens naturais importantes, uma matriz energética renovável, experiência científica acumulada e setores econômicos que avançaram na agenda de descarbonização. Mas vantagem comparativa não se transforma automaticamente em vantagem econômica. Isso depende de ambiente de negócios, infraestrutura, tecnologia, segurança jurídica e boas escolhas regulatórias.

TOWN HALL NOTES | Smithtown is considering extending its moratorium on battery energy storage systems for another 12 months while the town reviews state fire safety rules and guidance. The Town Board will hold a public hearing on the proposal at 2 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 19, in the Victor T. Liss Board Room at Smithtown Town Hall, 99 W. Main St. The board first adopted the moratorium in September 2024 and most recently extended it in May 2026, according to the town’s public notice. The proposed extension would give Smithtown more time to review recommendations from the state’s Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group, updates to New York’s fire safety code and a battery storage guidebook from the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority. If adopted, the extension would take effect when the law is filed with the New York secretary of state. It would expire 12 months later unless the board extends it again. The town’s existing zoning variance procedures would still apply. Top: An aerial view of Main Street in downtown Smithtown. (GLI/Andrew Theodorakis, file)

artigo.texto: Judge says xAI must face NAACP lawsuit on data center pollution The legal battle revolves around the AI company’s operations in southern Memphis. A federal judge's latest ruling has denied xAI's request to dismiss a lawsuit that alleges its data center campus in Memphis, Tennessee is running turbines without proper permits and violating the Clean Air Act. The decision, from US District Judge Debra M. Brown, allows the lawsuit, which was filed by the NAACP, to move forward. The organization filed its legal action against xAI in April, accusing the company that's now known as SpaceXSI of using unpermitted methane gas turbines to power data centers in the Memphis area. Despite the ongoing lawsuit that also claimed it's violating the Clear Air Act, Elon Musk's company continued to add more gas turbines to another AI data center site in the nearby Southhaven, Mississippi community. In response, xAI requested to dismiss the NAACP lawsuit and even received support from the Justice Department, which claimed that the company's operations are a crucial part of US military operations. xAI said the lawsuit should be dismissed, claiming that its turbines were exempt from permitting requirements since they were mobile. Judge Brown wrote in her decision that the power plant where all the turbines were providing power to xAI's data center wasn't mobile and therefore not exempt from the permitting process. The lawsuit comes at a time when AI companies are ramping up the construction of data centers to fuel their AI needs, while neighbors are becoming increasingly averse to these buildouts.

artigo.texto: Ohio: O Estado concentra o maior número de iniciativas eleitorais relacionadas a data centers: 21. Ohio já é um dos principais mercados para desenvolvedores desse tipo de empreendimento. Atualmente, 154 data centers estão em operação, outros 27 estão em construção e 57 estão em fase de planejamento. - Treze municípios terão propostas de proibição de data centers nas urnas: Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Grove City, Hubbard, Monroeville, Oregon, Pataskala, Piqua, Sunbury, Trenton, Upper Sandusky e Urbana. Algumas dessas iniciativas, porém, restringem apenas instalações classificadas como de “alto impacto” ou empreendimentos que consumam mais de 25 megawatts de energia. - Os distritos rurais de Monroe e Sprigg votarão sobre a adoção de novas regras de zoneamento destinadas a preservar o “caráter rural e agrícola” dessas regiões. Na prática, as medidas impediriam a construção de data centers. As duas pequenas comunidades do sul de Ohio estão entre as possíveis localidades para grandes empreendimentos, incluindo um terreno de aproximadamente 4,05 milhões de metros quadrados que está sendo avaliado para receber um data center da Amazon Web Services. - A cidade de Wilmington votará quatro propostas relacionadas ao zoneamento de quatro terrenos específicos, que permitiriam o avanço de um projeto de data center. A votação ocorre depois que a Suprema Corte de Ohio manteve a decisão do conselho eleitoral do condado de bloquear um referendo que estabeleceria restrições mais abrangentes. - Além disso, os eleitores de Ashville decidirão se querem impedir a construção de um data center cujas obras já começaram. Já os moradores do vilarejo de Perry votarão uma resolução que exigiria que os desenvolvedores oferecessem garantias financeiras ao município e respeitassem limites de ruído nas instalações para ter acesso a incentivos fiscais. - Illinois: Seis municípios do Estado votarão propostas destinadas a orientar seus governos locais sobre a aprovação ou construção de novos data centers: Chouteau, Granite City, Joliet, Morgan, Nameoki e Venice. - Enquanto isso, os eleitores de Bloomington decidirão se aprovam uma moratória integral sobre futuros empreendimentos desse tipo. No início deste ano, a cidade e o município vizinho de Normal estabeleceram uma suspensão de seis meses para instalações com consumo superior a 5 megawatts de energia. - Wisconsin: Os eleitores de Janesville decidirão se futuros projetos com investimentos superiores a US$ 450 milhões (aproximadamente R$ 2,3 bilhões) em uma antiga fábrica de autopeças deverão receber aprovação da maioria da população. Na prática, a votação determinará se o terreno poderá ser utilizado para a construção de um data center. - A proposta se refere especificamente à área de uma antiga fábrica da General Motors, que encerrou suas atividades em 2008, durante a crise da indústria automobilística, deixando um terreno contaminado após o fechamento. - Janesville enfrenta dificuldades para dar uma nova destinação à propriedade desde então. Recentemente, a cidade passou a avaliar a possibilidade de construir um data center no local, proposta que provocou forte reação contrária da população. - Governos locais de outras cidades de Wisconsin também estabeleceram moratórias temporárias para data centers ao longo do ano, incluindo Madison, em janeiro, e Milwaukee, em outubro. - Kansas: As cidades de El Dorado e Emporia votarão sobre a proibição de data centers classificados como de “alto impacto”. Já Ottawa decidirá sobre uma restrição a instalações de “alto consumo de serviços públicos”, definição que abrange empreendimentos com demanda superior a 25 megawatts de energia. - Maine: Quatro municípios do Estado votarão propostas de moratória à construção de data centers, embora a maioria tenha prazo determinado. Peru e Wells decidirão sobre suspensões de 180 dias, enquanto Wiscasset votará uma proibição de seis meses para novos empreendimentos e projetos de expansão de instalações existentes. - A cidade de North Berwick, por sua vez, votará uma proposta própria para proibir data centers com área superior a 2.323 metros quadrados. - Cidades maiores do Maine, incluindo Bangor, já adotaram moratórias locais. Além disso, a Assembleia Legislativa do Estado aprovou uma suspensão válida para todo o território estadual no início deste ano. A medida, porém, foi vetada pela governadora Janet Mills em abril. Esta lista foi elaborada com base em dados de organizações sem fins lucrativos que monitoram iniciativas eleitorais, incluindo o levantamento da Ballotpedia sobre propostas relacionadas a data centers, além de estatísticas sobre consumo de energia e projetos planejados do U.S. Data Center Map. Em quais outros lugares haverá votação sobre data centers? Na Califórnia, a cidade de Alhambra, no condado de Los Angeles, votará uma proposta para proibir data centers. Se aprovada, será a segunda cidade do Estado a adotar esse tipo de restrição por meio de votação popular. Em junho, os eleitores de Monterey Park aprovaram uma moratória. Em Edgewater, na Flórida, a Câmara Municipal já aprovou uma moratória para data centers em setembro. Agora, a medida será submetida aos eleitores para inclusão na carta municipal, documento que estabelece as regras de funcionamento do governo local. Em Nevada, os eleitores de Boulder City decidirão se novos data centers poderão ser construídos em uma área específica que já abriga projetos de geração de energia solar. Em Nova Jersey, os moradores de Downe Township votarão para indicar se apoiam a construção de data centers na pequena comunidade localizada no sul do Estado. A proposta, no entanto, não prevê uma votação sobre a proibição desses empreendimentos. Já os eleitores de Harwood, em Dakota do Norte, decidirão se empreendimentos industriais, incluindo data centers, deverão passar por uma análise adicional e, pelo menos, uma audiência pública antes de serem aprovados. artigo.texto: Warrick Co. holds public meeting on data center zoning ordinance Officials say the proposed ordinance would not rezone any property or approve a data center project WARRICK CO., Ind. (WFIE) - The Warrick County Area Plan Commission held the special forum at Friedman Park Event Center to take public comment on a proposed data center ordinance. Many people in the audience voiced frustration with the draft. First responders: “We still have not had a seat at the table” Christopher Stephens of the Boonville Fire Department was the first speaker. He said fire chiefs across the county have asked to be involved and have not been heard. “We still have not had a seat at the table. There’s been very minimal e-mail communication back and forth, but the requests that have been made multiple times by multiple fire chiefs in the county have apparently fallen on deaf ears,” said Stephens. Residents call for more information Yvon Lauren, a Warrick County resident, told the commission the county should learn more before it passes any ordinance. “I think that we have to make an effort to learn more about it before we pass any kind of ordinance in this county. I have several homes here. I have a large family here and I plan to retire here, stay here. And I really think it’s time we take this very seriously,” said Lauren. Critics say the draft is too vague and that officials still don’t know enough about data centers. “There is some point going to be a glut of data centers” Jim Mauror, also a Warrick County resident, questioned whether the county needs more data centers at all. “There is some point going to be a glut of data centers. We cannot build them continuously and at some point the data centers won’t even be necessary,” said Mauror. Many people at the forum oppose data centers in any form and asked what the benefits would be. Some said there are enough of them already. What the ordinance would do The draft ordinance would create a floating Data Center Overlay District, known as DC-O. Under the proposal, a data center could be built only on land zoned for heavy industrial use (M-2) that also has DC-O zoning. Getting DC-O zoning would require a site-specific rezoning approved by the Board of Commissioners. The ordinance also defines what counts as a data center and lists requirements they would have to follow. Those include: - Operational sound of no more than 55 decibels (dBA) at a neighboring home or residential zoning boundary. - Data center buildings set back at least 300 feet from homes or other residential zoning. - Intensive outdoor equipment, such as generators, transformers and battery storage, set back at least 500 feet. - A landscaped buffer of at least 100 feet near residential property. The draft also asks developers to provide fire and emergency medical services information in their applications. That includes responder training needs and any added staffing or service demands the project would create. Officials say the ordinance does not approve any data center and does not rezone any property. Connection to Project Alloy The forum follows the announcement of “Project Alloy.” It is a proposed data center on roughly 700 acres of Alcoa-owned land near the company’s river-side complex. County officials have said the ordinance is not written around any single project. It is meant to set standards for any data center proposed in the county. What’s next The Warrick County Board of Commissioners will consider the ordinance at a meeting on Nov. 9 at 4 p.m. at Friedman Park Event Center, the same venue as Monday’s forum. artigo.texto: BYD dobra vendas em outubro com alta de 137,6% no Brasil Empresa ampliou participação no mercado nacional de 4,2% para 9,7% e quer liderar o setor até 2030 A BYD emplacou 24.114 veículos no Brasil em outubro de 2026, alta de 137,6% em relação ao mesmo mês de 2025. O resultado representa mais que o dobro das vendas registradas 1 ano antes, quando a fabricante chinesa inaugurou sua fábrica em Camaçari (BA). A participação da empresa no mercado nacional passou de 4,2% para 9,7% no período. No acumulado de janeiro a outubro, a montadora comercializou 193.227 veículos, crescimento superior a 120% na comparação com os 10 primeiros meses de 2025. Os dados foram divulgados pela empresa na 2ª feira (2.nov.2026). As vendas no varejo somaram 14.487 unidades em outubro, o equivalente a 12,7% do segmento e à 2ª posição no ranking nacional. Já as vendas diretas alcançaram 9.627 veículos, avanço de aproximadamente 600% em relação ao mesmo mês do ano passado. A BYD ficou na 5ª colocação nessa modalidade. Entre os modelos da fabricante, o Dolphin Mini foi o carro mais vendido do Brasil no varejo em outubro, com 5.841 emplacamentos. O King, por sua vez, liderou pelo 2º mês consecutivo o segmento de sedãs no varejo, com 1.343 unidades e participação de 32,2% na categoria. A expansão das vendas acompanha o crescimento da operação industrial da BYD na Bahia. Pouco mais de 1 ano depois da inauguração, a fábrica de Camaçari ultrapassou 150 mil veículos produzidos e alcançou mais de 9.500 empregos diretos, segundo a companhia. BYD quer liderança O vice-presidente sênior da BYD no Brasil, Alexandre Baldy, afirmou que a empresa pretende liderar o mercado automotivo brasileiro até 2030. A fabricante também declarou que continuará ampliando a produção na unidade baiana. “Muita gente duvidou da força da BYD e da nossa capacidade de disputar espaço com as fabricantes mais tradicionais do Brasil. Hoje, os resultados mostram que estávamos certos ao acreditar no potencial desse mercado e investir no país. É especialmente simbólico alcançar esses números justamente em outubro, quando completamos 1 ano de operação da nossa fábrica em Camaçari”, afirma Alexandre Baldy.

artigo.texto: Florida utility regulators rejected Duke Energy Florida’s proposal to meet the requirements of a new state law intended to shield ratepayers from the costs of data centers. The Public Service Commission voted against Duke’s proposal to create a new large load tariff designation for data centers in the first test of the law pushed in the spring by Gov. Ron DeSantis intended to ensure customers won’t bear the additional costs brought by new facilities that power artificial intelligence. Commissioner Gabriella Passidomo Smith said the new law “made it clear that large load customers must bear their own full cost of service without shifting those costs to other ratepayers.” Smith added that Duke can serve the large-scale data centers, which require vast amounts of energy to power the burgeoning AI field while still following the new law. Brooke Ward, Florida State Director for Food & Water Watch, called the vote “a victory for affordability and testament to the importance of laws that put people above corporations.” But she added the state needs more affordable energy legislation to “ensure a more equitable energy future for all Floridians.” The new law (SB 484) requires the PSC to develop what are known as “tariffs” and service requirements to “reasonably ensure that each large load customer bears its own full cost of service and that such cost is not shifted to the general body of ratepayers.” That would include costs related to connecting to electric systems and increased power transmission and generation costs. The measure reinforces the ability of local governments to refuse to build data centers in their jurisdictions. But it also allows city and county governments to enter into non-disclosure agreements with tech companies for up to 12 months, which would hide data center proposals from the public during that time. Duke will have to refile a new tariffs proposal. The commission determined Duke’s proposed tariffs excluded certain large load customers who would otherwise qualify under the law’s definition. Commissioners also found Duke failed to provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate that its existing rate schedules, together with the proposed contractual and financial protections, would reasonably ensure that each large load customer bears the full cost of its electric service.

artigo.texto: Data centers were once hailed as the pinnacle of technological innovation, the engines of economic growth, and a determinant of competitive edge. In 2026, however, their high costs, rising electricity demands, and alarming environmental implications have put them at the forefront of national attention. As their name suggests, data centers are buildings that house, run, and cool computers. They can be as small as a room with a single computer or as large as a labyrinth lined with hundreds of thousands of servers. The largest in the United States, Meta’s Prineville data center, covers a vast 4.6 million square feet in the middle of a remote, high-desert region of Oregon. Meta doesn’t disclose just how many servers are inside the facility, but it is estimated that the number is in the hundreds of thousands. While there are already a whopping 3,582 data centers in the United States, the explosive use of AI has triggered an aggressive spike in demand being felt across the country. Current demand is expected to triple by 2030. While these data centers seemingly pop up out of nowhere, the inputs required to run them cannot be underestimated. While reportedly renewable-based, the Prineville data center alone consumes nearly 1.4 million megawatt-hours of electricity annually. In 2023, annual data center energy use in the United States sat at roughly 176 million megawatt-hours. That’s enough electricity to power 16.8 million homes for a year. That is enough electricity to power every home in California and Florida … together … for a year. In addition to electricity, data centers require substantial amounts of water to prevent servers from overheating. In 2014, U.S. data centers “drank” about 5.6 billion gallons of water. In 2023, they consumed 17.4 billion gallons. That’s enough water for one billion showers, three for each American. At first glance, “data center” gives off the notion of being modern and green. After some light research, however, you can find that they account for 0.5 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Half a percentage point seems nearly negligible, but 0.5% translates to 212 million metric tons of CO2, more than what is produced annually by a medium-sized industrialized country like the Netherlands. The Sierra Club, one of the oldest environmental protection organizations in the United States, published a report finding that by 2030, U.S. data centers will be outputting a carbon footprint as large as the entirety of Mexico’s, threatening to set progress on greenhouse gas emissions back by 15 years. While these findings would point to reconsidering the current data center approval process, the White House, prioritizing economic growth, has accelerated approval. A 2025 executive order directs federal agencies to fast-track environmental reviews, open up federal lands, and commit other federal resources to these projects. Unsurprisingly, many Americans would disagree with a data center free-for-all. Fifty-four percent of Americans view data centers as being bad for the environment. More tellingly, Gallup finds that seven in 10 Americans oppose data center construction in their communities. Americans oppose data center development when it comes to their doorstep. While data centers’ rising electricity demands, strong thirst, and behemoth carbon footprint hold their own weight, voters are voicing more concerns about data centers. From higher energy prices in areas in close proximity to data centers and noise pollution concerns to driving up the price of rural farmland and backlash over contaminated wastewater, Americans are tired of being forced to deal with the environmental and fiscal costs of an industry whose benefits are concentrated among big tech investors. Thus, data centers are becoming a hot-button issue in the 2026 midterms, situated among campaign issues such as the “economy,” “immigration,” and “crime.” While there are not clean-cut partisan trends regarding data centers, state-office candidates typically fall into one of two camps: regulation or moratorium. The more conservative approach, moratorium, focuses on a temporary pause or cap on data center development. In Massachusetts, for example, Governor Maura Healey has issued a data center moratorium requiring data center developers to receive local approval. Generally speaking, moratoriums commonly allow state governments to assess options, discuss with community groups, and ultimately make an informed decision. The more growth-oriented approach—regulation—emphasizes the economic competitiveness side of the equation but establishes guardrail regulations that data center developers must satisfy. Both camps acknowledge the various impacts of data centers but address them differently. While data centers have become a major flashpoint in gubernatorial and local elected office positions, they also manifest themselves through ballot measures, questions voters answer at the polls. There are 49 ballot measures regarding data centers this midterm cycle, and voters in 13 states will have the opportunity to influence their state’s data center policy. Measures consist of yes/no questions pertaining to approval, zoning, and prohibition. See if you will have the opportunity to vote directly on data centers here. While artificial intelligence and data centers undeniably bolster the United States’ competitive edge, their infrastructure is not free. There are environmental, financial, and social costs that have become increasingly difficult to ignore. For Boston College, students must consider the entire equation regarding data centers. That means balancing environmental impacts, energy affordability, and AI ambitions. While asking ChatGPT or Claude a question may not have a direct financial cost, it ultimately comes at an environmental cost that some bear more than others.

artigo.texto: Residents in four Madison County townships overwhelmingly said data center development should not be allowed in their communities. Ballot initiatives in Chouteau, Granite City, Nameoki and Venice townships asked voters whether they support future data center development and construction. Residents in all four townships voted no. Chouteau Township had the most decisive result with 83.27% of the vote against data centers. Other townships voted at least 74% against them. In Illinois, townships are subdivisions of local government that operate alongside cities and villages. The township’s elected board may oversee local infrastructure, such as water and sewer services. Each of the townships included in the advisory measure overlaps with Granite City. Because the measures are nonbinding, they do not ban data centers even though residents voted against the projects. Loading... Heather Groetecke is a lifelong Granite City resident and led the effort to collect signatures for the initiatives. She said the initiative will send a strong message to policymakers about the will of the voters despite being a nonbinding measure. “I am so stunned by the numbers,” Groetecke said. “The people actually listened and cared about their neighbors to vote no for that.” Groetecke wanted to put a data center moratorium on the ballot. But she said advisers close to the campaign recommended a nonbinding measure because it would be easier to pass. Madison County data center proposals The developer behind a data center project for Midtown St. Louis recently announced plans to build a 200-megawatt data center at the former Alton Steel site, which closed nine months ago. TerraWatt said it reached a “contingent agreement” to buy the site from Alton Steel Inc. and would close on the property in 2027. That’s if the city agrees to rezone the site, and the plan depends on a study by Ameren Illinois and “TerraWatt’s due diligence.” Granite City officials heard public comment about a proposed data center this spring involving two sites along the Route 3 industrial corridor. The Belleville News-Democrat reported that it received mixed reviews, with some in support of union jobs and others concerned about utility rate hikes, environmental impacts and transparency. Officials in nearby Pontoon Beach heard a similar proposal in May, the Alton Telegraph reported. Some residents accused Granite City Mayor Mike Parkinson and other city officials of misleading the public when they said that they knew little about data center development in public meetings. Residents said in May that officials negotiated a possible land sale for a data center project with special governing district America’s Central Port before alerting the public. Parkinson told the News-Democrat that the documents cited by residents were taken out of context and that the city never collaborated with the port authority to bring in data center projects. Months before the community meetings, Parkinson, Madison County Executive Chris Slusser and Granite City’s economic development director, Cathy Hamilton, were among several St. Louis-area leaders who toured a Google data center on a trip financed by Greater St. Louis Inc. Officials were asked to sign nondisclosure agreements before touring the facility. Granite City officials say the data center project was tabled along with similar proposals in Edwardsville and Troy, Illinois.

artigo.texto: Estherville city council advances data center rules to public hearing ESTHERVILLE, Iowa — A proposed data center in Estherville is moving forward to a public hearing following discussions by city leaders over health and noise concerns. The Estherville City Council agreed to send the Planning and Zoning Commission’s draft rules to a public hearing on Nov. 16. City leaders revealed they are in discussions with two developers, though only one data center would be considered for the community. During the meeting, council members discussed potential noise and low-frequency impacts near an elementary school. Council Member at Large David Hovinga cited his own research on health risks, casting the lone vote against advancing the measure and urging Planning and Zoning to strengthen protections first. “There are issues of sickness, issues of cardiovascular health, mental health issues, low frequency issues, that can’t be mitigated by sound dampening walls and things like that,” Hovinga said. “If the technology is at a place where they can fix those things, then that’s wonderful. But, I would need to see that before I would be comfortable moving forward with a data center in Estherville.” Public input and informational meeting Following the public hearing, the ordinance can still be sent back to the Planning and Zoning Commission for revisions. City officials emphasized the importance of community feedback as the proposal moves forward. “I would encourage everyone to come out to share their thoughts with the other council members,” a council member said during the meeting. “I think all of us want to hear from the public. All of us want to know what the community and citizens of Estherville think about this proposed data center.” Residents will have multiple opportunities to learn more and provide input on the proposal: - On Thursday, Nov. 12, Path-One Data Centers will host an informational meeting at the American Legion in Estherville, where community members can ask questions about small-scale data centers. - On Monday, Nov. 16, at 5 p.m., the Estherville City Council will hold its first official public hearing regarding the potential project. Log in Homeowners could be given a boost with their energy bills, with Octopus Energy teaming up with manufacturers to develop a new generation of home battery storage options. Battery storage typically works by allowing units to siphon in power and store it, chemically or by other means, when the cost of energy is low. Later, when usage price increases, that energy can be reintroduced to the home system to avoid using the higher-billed energy. In theory, as well as lowering bills, it can also reduce strain on the wider grid at key demand times once widely adopted. The ability to integrate home storage batteries with solar panels, for example, can give a home its own source of low-cost energy beyond just when the panels are functioning - like after dark - and the battery’s management system should be able to maximise the efficiency of the home’s energy use overall. Octopus already have plans to release the “Nook”: two battery storage options for bigger or smaller amounts, each of which can store between 2 and 10 kWh of energy. The latter is a little over a medium-sized house’s daily energy use, according to Ofgem figures. Now, through their agreement with zero-carbon new energy technology firm CATL and lithium-ion battery tech firm Ampace, Octopus Energy will look to develop new ranges of cutting-edge options, as they seek to increase the lifecycle of such systems and produce far more affordable home batteries. At its most efficient, a home battery system should be able to offload power back to the grid too, to help further cut household energy bills. As well as the Nook battery options, Octopus already offer other green energy solutions including heat pumps and EV chargers. Jason Zhu, president of energy storage at Ampace said: “The future of energy is not just about generating or storing more power, but about making energy smarter, more connected, and more accessible.” The advance of battery technology and intelligent energy management could “fundamentally reshape how energy is delivered and consumed,” he added. Greg Jackson, CEO of Octopus Energy Group, agreed that the partnership “will transform home energy storage.” “Together, we're building next-generation batteries where hardware and software work in complete harmony to slash energy bills and speed up the green energy transition,” he added. Raymond Ye, president of residential energy storage systems at Ampace, added: “Europe’s energy transition is creating growing demand for smarter and more flexible home energy solutions; with this partnership we see great potential to accelerate innovation and deliver greater value to the market.” Join our commenting forum Join thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their replies Comments

artigo.texto: Novo calendário alcança fornecedores de materiais, energia e combustíveis e prevê entrada do transporte rodoviário; veja os possíveis efeitos para o setor César Tizo - novembro 1, 2026 A produção de materiais usados nos carros, a cadeia de combustíveis e a operação de frotas estão entre as frentes alcançadas pelo novo calendário do mercado regulado de carbono no Brasil. Para o setor automotivo, a mudança começa pelos fornecedores: atividades como produção de aço, alumínio e vidro integram a primeira etapa de preparação, em 2027. O transporte rodoviário de passageiros e cargas terá seu primeiro ano até 2031. O cronograma foi definido pela Portaria SEMC/MF nº 3.199, publicada em 29 de outubro de 2026. A norma organiza a entrada gradual dos setores nas obrigações de mensuração, relato e verificação de emissões de gases de efeito estufa, conhecidas pela sigla MRV. Refino de petróleo e setor elétrico entram na segunda etapa, com preparação até 2029. A relação com o mercado de veículos ocorre tanto nos insumos industriais quanto nos serviços de transporte. O enquadramento dos operadores ainda depende de regulamentação específica: a portaria não inclui automaticamente todas as montadoras, fabricantes de autopeças, concessionárias ou transportadoras, nem permite calcular um aumento no preço dos carros. O cronograma alcança atividades presentes na cadeia de fornecimento de materiais para veículos, como siderurgia integrada, produção de alumínio e fabricação de vidro plano e de segurança. Também inclui determinados produtos químicos, entre eles eteno e negro de carbono, além da produção de petróleo e gás natural. O efeito direto das obrigações recairá sobre os operadores das fontes e instalações que forem efetivamente reguladas. Para as montadoras e fabricantes de componentes que compram esses materiais, o interesse está em acompanhar como seus fornecedores passarão a medir e apresentar as emissões associadas às atividades abrangidas. Como consequência possível, informações de emissões poderão ganhar peso nas decisões de compra de materiais e na avaliação de fornecedores. Essa é uma perspectiva para a cadeia industrial, e não uma exigência de seleção de fornecedores criada pela portaria. O ato não determina a substituição de aço por alumínio ou a adoção de um material específico nos carros. A distinção entre atividades industriais também importa. Usinas siderúrgicas integradas estão na etapa com início em 2027; as semi-integradas integram a fase seguinte, com primeiro ano até 2029. Portanto, nem mesmo todos os produtores de um material entram simultaneamente. A produção de petróleo e gás natural aparece na primeira etapa, enquanto o refino de petróleo fica na segunda. O setor elétrico também integra essa segunda fase, que contempla geração, transmissão e distribuição de energia. São atividades ligadas ao abastecimento dos veículos a combustão e à infraestrutura que atende os elétricos. O objeto da norma é organizar os dados de emissões dessas operações. Ela não altera a composição da gasolina ou do diesel nem estabelece uma nova tarifa de recarga. A repercussão econômica para cada cadeia dependerá das regras finais de cobertura, das metodologias e, posteriormente, do funcionamento do mercado de emissões. Para quem acompanha a descarbonização automotiva, a mudança reforça a importância de observar também a fabricação dos materiais e o fornecimento de energia e combustíveis. Entretanto, o cronograma do SBCE, por si só, não produz uma comparação completa de emissões entre um carro elétrico, um híbrido e um modelo a combustão. O transporte rodoviário de passageiros e de cargas integra a terceira etapa, junto dos transportes ferroviário e aquaviário. O primeiro ano dessa fase deverá começar até 2031. Essa referência marca a preparação do monitoramento, e não a entrega imediata de um inventário verificado por todas as empresas de transporte. Para uma transportadora ou operadora de ônibus, o ponto central será saber quais fontes móveis e operações estarão abrangidas e como suas emissões deverão ser mensuradas. A portaria prevê regulamentação específica para definir fontes, instalações e atividades reguladas, considerando as particularidades de cada setor. O número de caminhões ou ônibus da frota não determina, sozinho, o enquadramento. Também será necessário observar os patamares de emissões previstos em lei e as metodologias aplicáveis. A presença de um código da Classificação Nacional de Atividades Econômicas (CNAE) no anexo não submete automaticamente todas as atividades daquele código às obrigações. Outro detalhe relevante para empresas com operações diversificadas é que o anexo considera a atividade regulada exercida na instalação ou pelo conjunto de fontes móveis, mesmo quando corresponda a um CNAE secundário. Assim, olhar apenas a atividade principal do estabelecimento pode ser insuficiente. Ainda não há base para atribuir um valor de aumento a carros, combustíveis ou fretes em função dessa portaria. O calendário de monitoramento é uma etapa distinta das futuras regras de limitação e conciliação de emissões. Segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, a fase inicial não impõe limites de emissão ou custos de aquisição de cotas. O Plano Nacional de Alocação tem início previsto para 2030, com distribuição gratuita de cotas na largada. Essa previsão geral não antecipa a entrada de todos os setores, que segue escalonada. artigo.texto: The European Investment Bank (EIB) will provide a loan of up to $90 million, guaranteed by the EU through the European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus (EFSD+), to finance the first phase of the Dandara solar photovoltaic (PV) and battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Egypt. Located in Qena Governorate, Phase 1 comprises a 569 MWp solar PV plant and an associated 100 MWh BESS. Dandara Solar Power S.A.E., a project company owned by Norwegian renewable energy developer Scatec ASA and acting as the lead developer, will develop, construct, operate, and maintain the project. The facility will supply renewable electricity to Misr Aluminium Company (EgyptAlum), under a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA). EgyptAlum’s payment obligations are supported by a guarantee from Egypt’s Ministry of Finance. The project is expected to generate around 1,500 GWh of electricity during its first year of operation. The EIB financing, provided through its development arm EIB Global, is backed by the EU, and will be arranged alongside the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and African Development Bank (AfDB) funds. Construction is expected to begin soon, with commercial operations scheduled to commence in April 2028.

artigo.texto: Ohioans overwhelmingly pass data center bans, restrictions on ballot Ohioans made their opinion on data centers clear on Election Day: No. Voters in Ohio municipalities with data center bans on the ballot overwhelmingly supported more restrictions on the controversial developments. Voters in at least 14 Ohio municipalities passed bans or other restrictions on data centers Nov. 3, including in Trenton. Across Ohio, 18 municipalities voted on data center-related measures, the most of any state. Residents in 11 of these municipalities voted on outright bans, while the other seven weighed measures that added new regulations or oversight. How did they vote? The following 10 municipalities passed bans on data center construction: Hubbard, Sunbury, Pataskala, Urbana, Defiance, Upper Sandusky, Piqua, Granville, Conneaut and Trenton. Voters in Oregon also voted on a ban, but the Lucas County Board of Election was not reporting any results as of midnight Nov. 4. The following cities, townships and villages passed other restrictions: - Ashville: Almost 82% of Ashville voters voted to reverse its village council's agreement and negotiations with EdgeConneX to build two data centers. - Grove City: 55% of voters approved a charter amendment that requires voter approval for future large-scale developments, including data center developments that use more than 20 megawatts of electricity or 500,000 gallons of water. - Perry: Over 87% of voters passed an ordinance that requires developers seeking tax abatements or other financial incentives to offer the village financial guarantees. - Wilmington: Through four separate referendums, around 80% of voters rejected rezoning for parcels of land to accommodate a data center project. Monroe and Sprigg Townships in Adams County and Monroeville also had data center related measures on the ballot, but results are not yet available. In Trenton, 80% of voters support ban Almost 80% of Trenton voters passed Issue 17, which bans data centers that use over 25 megawatts of electricity. Debates over two proposed data centers in or bordering Trenton have consumed the Butler County town of around 14,000 for months. Residents with the Woodsdale and Trenton Environmental Resistance, a group that opposed the data centers, collected signatures to get a ban on the ballot earlier this year. After the Trenton City Council voted not to certify the petition in August, the Ohio Supreme Court intervened. The court found the council "disregarded" the law and ordered it to certify the petition. Lacy Roth, 30, voted to support the ban. She told The Enquirer that she wants her 9-month-old son, who she brought with her to the polls, to grow up in a small town without noise and air pollution. "I think Issue 17 is one of the biggest factors to get voters out today," she said. "Because people don't want to see their community change in such a grand way without them actually getting support for it." 40-year-old Lauren Johnson, who stood outside Edgewood Middle School with signs urging people to vote for the ban, said she wants Trenton to remain "a quality place for kids to grow up." "I think our farmland is very important and our greenspace," Johnson said. "I'd like to see it still around for my grandkids." 'We need the data centers' But other residents worry a ban would hurt Trenton economically. "I think we need the data centers," said Daniel Davis, 76. Davis thinks data centers will bring in more jobs and revenue for the city. Two advocates for the Trenton Community Alliance, who sat in lawn chairs outside Edgewood Middle School with signs encouraging people to vote "no," declined to share their names or be photographed. They alleged they've been harassed and that those who disagree with them have been "nasty." One advocate said that data centers are coming to the area, whether people like it or not. "I believe Trenton should get income from the data center, not someone else," she said. The other advocate said she's not for or against data centers, but she's against the Trenton charter changing in a way that could stifle future business. She's also concerned that residents might next try to recall members of the Trenton City Council. Future of Amazon data center in SW Ohio The vote Nov. 3 creates an uncertain future for an Amazon Web Services data center planned for land located just outside Trenton. The city tried to annex land for the project from its two neighboring rural townships, but withdrew its petition in September. Because the ban only applies to land within city limits, the data center could move forward on the land if it remains part of the rural townships. However, the St. Clair Township Zoning Commission passed a resolution Oct. 13 to ban data centers in the township's zoning. That resolution goes to a Butler County hearing Nov. 10 but indicates the AWS data center could face another hurdle. This article originally appeared on Cincinnati Enquirer: Ohioans overwhelmingly pass data center bans, restrictions on ballot

artigo.texto: Daikin has introduced a new Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU) designed for high-density AI data center applications, with orders scheduled to open on November 1, 2027. The unit transfers thermal energy between the Facility Water System (FWS) and Technology Cooling System (TCS), supporting temperature management in environments with high thermal loads. The CDU range offers cooling capacities from 400 kW (approximately 1.36 million BTU/h) to 2.5 MW (approximately 8.53 million BTU/h) per unit. Up to ten CDUs can operate in parallel under centralized temperature and pressure control. Daikin also offers preassembled skid solutions integrating multiple units for larger installations, with configurations suitable for new projects and retrofits. For operational reliability, the CDU incorporates redundant pumps, duplicated temperature and pressure sensors, integrated leak detection and advanced alarm management. The hydraulic circuit uses AISI 316L stainless steel with grooved mechanical couplings instead of welded joints. Front-side service access and sliding rails for pump removal are designed to simplify maintenance and component replacement. Daikin’s proprietary controller coordinates multiple CDUs and adjusts TCS operating parameters using variable-speed pumps and flow, pressure and temperature measurements. A modulating valve with an equal-percentage control characteristic and high-speed actuator regulates heat transfer between the FWS and TCS circuits to control TCS outlet temperature. Alongside the CDU launch, Daikin is expanding its Intelligent Data Center Manager (iDCM) platform beyond chilled water plant control to cover equipment within the data hall. The platform supports centralized monitoring of CDUs, CRAHs, AHUs and Fan Wall systems, including real-time temperatures, equipment status and alarms. It also provides diagnostic functions and integration with existing Building Management Systems (BMS).

artigo.texto: Trump Onsite Power Push Meets AI Data Center Reality Trump’s onsite power push highlights a hard reality: most AI data centers will likely need hybrid energy strategies rather than fully off-grid designs. With data centers dominating industry and policy discussions, it was only a matter of time before President Donald Trump weighed in. In an Oct. 21 Truth Social post, Trump said new, large-scale data centers should generate their own electricity and return excess power to the local community or grid. He also suggested that developers make financial arrangements with host communities, including payments to residents: “As the President of the United States, I have been watching Data Centers very closely, and have come to a very strong conclusion. New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data Centers are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid, and therefore there is electric price increase. In fact, there could be a substantial decrease. Other elements likewise! If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend.’ I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck. MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A. President DJT” The comments are likely to intensify debate across the sector. Many projects already under construction have secured grid connections, signed power purchase agreements (PPAs), or otherwise locked in their energy strategy. If Trump’s position were translated into formal policy, developers would face difficult questions about whether those plans would need to change. Equipment availability would be another major challenge. Many of the components required for gas-fired, nuclear, and battery-backed onsite power systems are already in tight supply, with some turbine models effectively sold out through 2031. That would present a serious challenge for data center designers, engineers, developers, and operators, said Patrick Hughes, senior vice president of strategy, technical, and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA). Hughes was involved in developing the AI Data Center Energy Performance Framework,co-developed by NEMA, the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE), and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL). “It’s possible for a standalone AI data center to provide sufficient onsite power to fuel its own operations – whether it’s a combined-cycle plant or solar plus storage, we have the technology,” Hughes said. “But that doesn’t mean it’s feasible for a single AI data center – let alone the whole fleet of AI data centers – to supply 100% of their own power and operate reliably 24/7; that requires significant operational management and maintenance.” Permitting timelines, fuel and equipment supply chains, interconnection rules, and community considerations vary widely by location, Hughes added. Those factors will shape what is practical at any given site. For many facilities, the most likely outcome may be a hybrid approach that combines onsite generation and storage with a grid connection. Why AI Data Centers Can’t Easily Go Off-Grid There are substantial technical and logistical barriers to any broad requirement that AI data centers supply all of their own power. AI training and inference facilities have power densities and load profiles that differ sharply from those of traditional data centers and from facilities that have historically relied on co-located generation and storage. At the same time, the AI infrastructure buildout is grappling with enormous demand for electrical equipment and skilled labor across utilities, buildings, transportation, and industrial manufacturing. Whether or not developers are pushed toward a bring-your-own-power model, they are already competing with other sectors for turbines, switchgear, transformers, batteries, and specialized labor. Regardless of the onsite resource selected, the AI Data Center Energy Performance Framework offers technical standards and guiding principles for safety, resilience, and grid interaction. Data center designers, engineers, developers, and operators can use it to improve energy and water efficiency while supporting grid reliability and resilience through load flexibility and other grid-interactive operations. Existing Power Deals and Renewable Commitments Complicate the Shift A blanket onsite power requirement would also have to contend with existing clean-energy mandates, corporate sustainability goals, and regional differences in the availability of renewable resources. Many AI data centers already have agreements in place to draw power from solar and wind projects. The Stargate site in Abilene, Texas, offers one example. The project is already using natural gas, fuel cells, and gas engines during the construction phase and to power the first data centers now operating there. Developers are also planning to incorporate solar and wind, and the area’s solar generation potential was one of the reasons the location was selected. Abilene offers strong irradiance, abundant undeveloped land, and no major urban loads nearby. With developers scrambling to find 1.2 GW once all phases are complete, wind and solar are expected to supplement other power sources. Applied Digital’s AI data center project in North Dakota provides another example. The company has arranged for 400 MW of stranded wind power to serve its Ellendale campus and continues to emphasize renewables in its energy strategy. It also recently signed a deal with data center developer Soluna to use output from Soluna’s 150 MW Briscoe wind farm for a new data center in Texas. artigo.texto: Alliant Energy will receive more than $5 billion in federal loans to help the company modernize and build natural gas and energy storage infrastructure. But environmental groups argue the investment’s emphasis on fossil fuel infrastructure will make it harder to reduce emissions and address climate change. U.S. Department of Energy officials announced the low-interest financing last week at an Alliant Energy natural gas plant in Beloit. Federal officials say the funding will help the utility expand power generation, strengthen electric grid reliability and lower costs in Wisconsin and Iowa. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. The Energy Department said the $5.1 billion loan package will help Alliant add more than 2.6 gigawatts of new or upgraded electricity generation capacity. The agency says those projects could add enough electricity to power almost 2 million homes. It comes as peak energy demand in Wisconsin is projected to increase 40 percent by 2032, driven by data centers. One of the three large data center projects under construction in the state is being built in Beaver Dam, inside Alliant’s service territory, by social media giant Meta. Alliant Energy CEO Lisa Barton said the new loans would help the company lower construction costs, which could save customers $1.2 billion over their lifespan. “We’re going to be using these dollars to support upgrades, to invest in new generation facilities, new technologies and so forth,” Barton said in Beloit. “Every dollar that we invest is going to enhance our reliability, our system resiliency and help to drive affordability and economic development in the areas and the communities that we have to serve.” The projects funded by the loan package could also create more than 1,600 jobs during construction, according to the company. With the federal financing, Alliant says the company can pursue 1.6 gigawatts of new natural gas generation, 240 megawatts of increased capacity at existing facilities, 1 gigawatt of energy storage and 2 billion cubic feet of liquefied natural gas storage. The company did not identify any specific projects in the announcement. Gregory Beard, director of the Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing, said the loan package was “common sense” because it supported new electricity generation, storage and expanded liquefied gas storage. “We’re proud to be here to partner with Alliant,” he said. “We’ll be proud to see the projects that come online with all these $5.1 billion of invested capital.” But Jadine Sonoda, campaign coordinator for the environmental nonprofit Sierra Club’s Wisconsin Chapter, said her organization was disappointed to see such a large investment in fossil fuels, though they were grateful for the support for energy storage. She said the investment represents “a massive amount” of new natural gas generation potentially coming onto the grid. “Continual investment in more fossil fuels means more pollution. It means more health impacts and all of the costs that come with it,” Sonoda said. “We are already seeing so many new gas plant proposals. We absolutely do not need more incentives from the Trump administration to expand these options.” Reuters reports that the loan had been initially proposed by the Biden administration as a $3 billion conditional loan tied to clean energy and batteries. But Sonoda said the funding is a “really blatant example” of the Trump administration’s efforts to prop up the data center and fossil fuel industries. “Our electric sector landscape is heavily fossil fuels already. We really need to correct that and turn in the other direction,” she said. “All of these efforts to subsidize and support big tech and the fossil fuel industry are leading us in the completely wrong direction.” Wisconsin Public Radio, © Copyright 2026, Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin System and Wisconsin Educational Communications Board.

artigo.texto: A proposed Senate bill could generate $55 billion in transmission charges from data centers over 10 years if it becomes law. It would require large computing facilities to pay more for access to the electricity grid and the infrastructure needed to serve them. For data center developers, the proposal could raise the cost of grid-connected projects, influence where new campuses are built and change the economics of behind-the-meter generation. It could also make firm transmission service more expensive relative to arrangements in which operators accept power curtailments during grid stress. Developers could face greater pressure to demonstrate load flexibility. But shifting more costs to data centers addresses only part of the ratepayer problem. Utilities also need assurance that the large loads driving infrastructure investments will materialize, arrive on schedule and consume the electricity developers have promised. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to revise its transmission-pricing policy. Under the proposal, utilities would charge data centers for both their share of existing transmission infrastructure and incremental costs associated with serving their loads. Grid Strategies, a consulting firm that specializes in the power sector, estimated in a recently published white paper that the pricing changes would generate approximately $5.5 billion annually in transmission charges, compared with roughly $2 billion that data centers currently pay. The analysis projected a $35 billion increase over current arrangements across the decade. The projected $55 billion includes $35 billion in embedded transmission costs and $20 billion in incremental costs. Both categories support the grid, but the additional revenue could enable transmission construction that otherwise might not happen, said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies. PJM and MISO account for most projected charges Grid Strategies estimated that data centers in PJM's and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator's (MISO's) regions would account for approximately 82% of the projected $5.53 billion in annual charges. The analysis assigned about $2.31 billion in annual charges to PJM and $2.25 billion to MISO. It projects 13.4 gigawatts of new data center capacity in PJM and 16.7 GW in MISO. PJM's higher charges, despite its smaller projected pipeline, reflect the region's higher transmission rates, Gramlich said. Grid Strategies based its incremental transmission cost estimates largely on MISO data. The analysis includes 163 approved transmission projects representing approximately $11.4 billion in investment to connect 43.5 GW of large loads. Researchers calculated an average incremental cost per megawatt and applied it across the regions they studied. Grid Strategies estimated the projected revenue could support nearly 10,000 miles of new 765-kilovolt transmission lines over 10 years. That construction would depend on when and where data centers connect to the grid. The analysis excluded Texas' ERCOT market, where FERC doesn't traditionally regulate transmission service. Grid connections likely to remain attractive Higher transmission charges could make locations with available electrical capacity and predictable power-delivery timelines more attractive. Developers could also turn to behind-the-meter generation to reduce their reliance on utility-supplied electricity. Gramlich said he doesn't expect most data centers to abandon grid connections. Reliable power from an entirely off-grid system generally costs more and presents greater operational challenges, he said. He expects behind-the-meter generation to supplement utility service rather than replace it, potentially reducing the incremental transmission charges associated with a project. The $55 billion estimate assumes new data centers take firm transmission service. Developers that operate entirely off grid wouldn't generate those charges. Gramlich said that scenario is unlikely because data centers still derive substantial value from grid connections. Behind-the-meter generation also brings its own costs and dependencies, including fuel supplies, equipment, permitting and maintenance. Developers may reduce their transmission exposure while taking on other operational and financial risks, said Neil Osnato of Persistence Analytics Group. Utilities need proof demand will materialize Higher transmission charges won't prevent utilities from building infrastructure for data center projects that developers later delay, downsize or abandon. Before committing billions of dollars, utilities should require binding capacity commitments, financial security tied to their actual exposure and contractual protections against early termination, Osnato said. Developers should specify reserved megawatts, expected load ramps, enforceable milestones and consequences for delays or downsizing. Deposits and collateral should cover the costs a utility could fail to recover if a project falls through. Depending on the development, financial backing could include letters of credit, cash collateral or parent-company guarantees. Minimum-billing commitments and early-termination provisions can also protect other customers when actual consumption falls below projections, or a developer abandons a project. Utilities should tie major spending decisions to verified milestones, including site control, permits, financing commitments and executed power arrangements. A material change in a project's load forecast, commissioning schedule or financing should trigger a fresh review of the utility's exposure and remaining construction commitments. Some existing utility tariffs and agreements already contain versions of these protections, Osnato said. artigo.texto: Diante do desafio gigantesco de construir cada vez mais data centers, os EUA estão criando o "Tesla das escavadeiras" Os Estados Unidos estão em uma corrida para erguer centros de dados para os próximos anos, mas precisam de trabalhadores; Uma startup chamada Bedrock Robotics conta com escavadeiras equipadas com IA física para suprir a demanda por mão de obra A startup norte-americana Bedrock Robotics captou US$ 600 milhões em uma rodada Série C com apoio de investidores como a Nvidia. Fundada em 2024, a empresa desenvolve inteligência artificial para operar maquinários pesados de construção de forma autônoma. O aporte visa expandir essa tecnologia para mais veículos e fortalecer suas operações e equipe executiva, buscando suprir a crescente demanda por infraestrutura e data centers em meio aos desafios de escassez de mão de obra. Escavar um terreno para uma rodovia, uma fábrica ou um data center parece um trabalho seguro para um ser humano, já que ainda se depende de uma pessoa no comando do equipamento. No entanto, uma startup de São Francisco quer mudar as regras do jogo: ela pretende colocar uma inteligência artificial no comando desse maquinário pesado. A empresa chama-se Bedrock Robotics, acaba de captar 600 milhões de dólares (cerca de R$ 3,2 bilhões) e sua proposta surge como resposta para um mundo com a pirâmide demográfica invertida. Em resumo No dia 26 de outubro, a Bedrock anunciou uma rodada de financiamento Série C de 600 milhões de dólares. Fundada em 2024 como uma empresa de maquinário de construção autônomo, ela conta com investidores como Valor Equity, 8VC e — como não poderia deixar de ser — a Nvidia. O investimento não veio diretamente da Nvidia, mas sim por meio de seu braço de capital de risco; ainda assim, era previsível que a Nvidia aportasse recursos em uma empresa de IA aplicada ao mundo físico que apresenta um potencial considerável. A ideia da companhia é utilizar o montante captado para expandir sua tecnologia a mais máquinas, fortalecendo tanto o trabalho em campo quanto a estrutura comercial e operacional. Parte desse capital foi destinada à contratação de uma vice-presidente de operações — com passagens anteriores pela Amazon e pela Uber — e de um executivo que liderou a área jurídica da divisão de condução autônoma da Uber. For a look at how much investorsâ jitters are reshaping AI-related debt financing, look to QTS, an investment-grade Blackstone-backed data center operator, that just six months ago was weighing a deal to borrow $800 million at a rate of 1.7 percentage points over Treasurys. That deal never went through. And now, that same debt is being shopped to investors at 2.2 to 2.50 points above comparable Treasury yields for a nearly identical offering, according to people familiar with the matter. Both offerings involve the same company, same blue-chip Wall Street backing, and the same collateral â just for a lot more money. Blackstone declined to comment.Â As debt jitters spread and borrowing gets more expensive, itâs a lesson in just how much sentiment has shifted in such a short amount of time. Know More On Friday, the Financial Times reported that Blackstone told investors it no longer expected Anthropic to get an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its IPO, a reversal of previous guidance about the frontier lab, which is raising billions of dollars to finance its AI buildout. And investment-grade SpaceXâs $40 billion debt launch saw its pricing widen out â reaching an expected 8.75% yield for the riskier portion of its recent debt deal, up from where pricing was discussed just a week earlier, Semafor reported.

artigo.texto: A Anatel alertou o governo federal que pode ficar sem dinheiro até o fim de 2026 para pagar suas próprias contas, incluindo as do data center que mantém em Brasília. A agência reguladora tem R$ 30,76 milhões em faturas pendentes. A Anatel atribui o aperto a um bloqueio orçamentário de R$ 51,83 milhões. A medida foi determinada pelo governo Lula em maio. O presidente da agência, Carlos Baigorri, pediu ao Ministério do Planejamento o desbloqueio de R$ 30 milhões. Sem o desbloqueio, a Anatel corre risco de não fechar as contas do ano. Por que a Anatel ficou sem caixa O aperto nas contas da Anatel vem do contingenciamento geral do Orçamento, usado pelo governo para cumprir a meta fiscal. A agência arca com despesas fixas, como o data center, mesmo com parte do orçamento bloqueada. Em outubro, mesmo sob aperto, a Anatel liberou espectro para a Starlink. O atrito com o governo não é novo: em setembro, a Anatel abriu uma consulta sobre o leilão do 6G sem aval prévio do Planalto. Publicidade A próxima avaliação dos bloqueios está marcada para 24 de novembro. Nessa data, a Junta de Execução Orçamentária deve reexaminar o espaço fiscal para possível redução do contingenciamento. No mesmo dia do alerta sobre o data center, dois deputados apresentaram um projeto para suspender parte da regra da Anatel que torna obrigatória a biometria facial para contratar linha de celular. O PDL 1027/2026 ainda precisa ser votado pela Câmara. O que acontece agora A Anatel aguarda a resposta do Ministério do Planejamento sobre o desbloqueio dos R$ 30 milhões, antes da reavaliação de 24 de novembro.
