Hermiston and Umatilla County will be hit hard. “If an actual moratorium were to take place, we estimate just from data centers operating in Hermiston itself, it would probably end up costing taxpayers in Umatilla County somewhere in the range of a half billion dollars of lost potential revenue over the next 20 years,” Hermiston Assistant City Manager Mark Morgan said. The city of Umatilla has declared an emergency and is in talks with representatives in the governor’s office. Umatilla County is holding a special meeting at 9 a.m. Wednesday to decide about hiring a Portland law firm. The firm, Tonkon Torp LLP, specializes in business law. The agenda does not state specifically it is about the data center moratorium, but both Umatilla and Hermiston officials have said they have support from Umatilla County. “We agree with the city of Umatilla and Umatilla County that the actions taken by the governor are illegal,” Morgan said. “We’ve met with governor’s representatives and we’re working in concert with the city of Umatilla and Umatilla County to examine all of our legal remedies.” The legal contract mentioned in the Umatilla County agenda stated the help from the law firm is not to exceed $250,000. The special meeting is at 9 a.m. Wednesday in Room 130 of the Umatilla County Courthouse in Pendleton. artigo.texto: O Google ligou um chip de inteligência artificial em órbita, enviou uma instrução do solo e recebeu de volta um haicai. Sundar Pichai, presidente-executivo da empresa, anunciou o resultado em 30 de outubro de 2026, segundo o site francês Numerama. A máquina é uma TPU Trillium, o mesmo tipo de processador que o Google instala em seus data centers, e estava a bordo de um satélite do projeto Suncatcher. A resposta saiu do modelo aberto Gemma, rodando na própria placa, em cinco, sete e cinco sílabas no original. O feito é modesto em computação e grande em sinal. O Google ensaia tirar do chão a conta de energia que a inteligência artificial passou a cobrar. O que subiu em 1º de outubro O satélite partiu em 1º de outubro de 2026 numa missão de carona da SpaceX, a Transporter-18, que decolou da base de Vandenberg, na Califórnia. Batizado de MVP, o produto mínimo viável do projeto foi construído com a Planet, operadora de satélites de observação da Terra. O equipamento tem o tamanho de uma geladeira, carrega quatro TPUs Trillium e cerca de um quilowatt de painéis solares. O voo queria saber se chips desenhados para salas climatizadas sobrevivem à vibração do lançamento, ao vácuo, aos extremos de temperatura e à radiação. A resposta veio com sotaque de propaganda. “Bola azul abaixo, os dados correm em graça silenciosa, a luz das estrelas alimenta meu núcleo” (no original em inglês divulgado por Sundar Pichai: “Blue marble below, Data streams in silent grace, Starlight feeds my core”), escreveu o modelo. A conta de energia saiu do chão A ideia do Suncatcher foi revelada em novembro de 2025 e nasceu de um diagnóstico que o setor repete. A inteligência artificial já esbarra menos nos processadores e mais na eletricidade, no resfriamento e no terreno disponível. A Agência Internacional de Energia calculou em abril de 2025 que os data centers consumiram cerca de 415 terawatts-hora em 2024, perto de 1,5% da eletricidade do mundo. A projeção da agência, no relatório sobre energia e inteligência artificial, é mais que o dobro até 2030. No Google, a fatura aparece nos próprios relatórios ambientais. As emissões da empresa cresceram cerca de metade desde 2019, quando ela prometeu zerá-las até 2030, e a companhia atribui boa parte do avanço à expansão da IA. A aposta do Suncatcher é geométrica. Numa órbita heliossíncrona chamada amanhecer-entardecer, a cerca de 650 quilômetros de altitude, o satélite acompanha permanentemente a fronteira entre o dia e a noite, e o Google afirma que ali os painéis rendem até oito vezes mais que no solo. O laser de 2027 e o tamanho real da aposta O estudo técnico do Project Suncatcher publicado pelo Google Research em novembro de 2025 descreve o desenho completo. Grupos de 81 satélites voando a algumas centenas de metros uns dos outros, ligados por laser, com 1,6 terabit por segundo medido em bancada. Num acelerador de partículas, as TPUs Trillium não apresentaram falha dura até 15 krad de dose de prótons, bem acima do previsto para uma missão de cinco anos. O exame decisivo ficou para 2027, quando dois satélites terão de trocar dados por laser em formação cerrada. A concorrência já mostrou que o caminho tem chão. A Starcloud, apoiada pela Nvidia, rodou o Gemma num processador H100 em órbita em dezembro de 2025 e chegou a treinar o nanoGPT, rede aberta criada por Andrej Karpathy, sobre a obra completa de Shakespeare. Pichai disse em entrevista à Fox News em dezembro de 2025 que, dentro de uma década, construir data centers no espaço pareceria mais normal. A pergunta que o anúncio deixa aberta não é técnica. Energia solar captada em órbita e convertida em gigawatts de computação privada transforma uma faixa do espaço próximo em infraestrutura de uma empresa só. O Tratado do Espaço Sideral de 1967, assinado pelo Brasil, proíbe que qualquer país se aproprie de áreas do espaço, mas não define como se reparte o uso comercial de uma órbita. Posições orbitais e faixas de radiofrequência passam pela União Internacional de Telecomunicações, e as conexões por laser não seguem a mesma coordenação. A órbita baixa já é um condomínio disputado. A constelação Starlink, da SpaceX, soma milhares de satélites e é operada pela mesma empresa que levou o equipamento do Google ao espaço, o que deixa o projeto dependente de um concorrente direto. No Brasil, a pressão chega pelo chão. O país atraiu data centers por ter uma das matrizes elétricas mais renováveis entre as grandes economias, e cada novo galpão de servidores disputa energia, água para resfriamento e território com as redes locais e com os usos já instalados. O movimento do Google não reduz essa disputa. Se der certo, ele sobe a demanda e deixa intacta a pergunta sobre quem paga a conta energética aqui embaixo. O teste de formação cerrada em 2027 decide se o Suncatcher vira infraestrutura. Até lá, o haicai prova apenas que um chip de data center acordou no vácuo e respondeu. Se o laser falhar, terá sido o que sempre foi, um poema muito curto.

artigo.texto: As home batteries move from simple wall hardware to fully connected, intelligent energy assets, the partnership will focus on bringing cutting-edge battery innovations directly to everyday households. The partnership brings together two industry heavyweights: CATL and Ampace’s experience in battery chemistry and manufacturing, alongside Octopus Energy’s software platform, smart tariffs, and Virtual Power Plant flexibility capabilities. The collaboration will draw on CATL and Ampace's pioneering research into next-generation battery chemistries – including breakthrough developments in sodium-ion technology, high-density cell designs, and ultra-long lifecycle systems – to build safer, greener, and far more affordable home batteries. Paired with Octopus’s smart tech ecosystem, these systems will automatically charge up when energy is cleanest and cheapest and share power back to the grid during peak times to slash household bills. The collaboration will initially explore opportunities across European markets, where Octopus has retail energy offices. “Combining CATL and Ampace's world-leading battery chemistry with Octopus's smart tech and customer platform will transform home energy storage” said Greg Jackson, Founder and CEO, Octopus Energy Group. “Together, we're building next-generation batteries where hardware and software work in complete harmony to slash energy bills and speed up the green energy transition.” The MoU builds on the relationship between CATL and Octopus, who previously collaborated to roll out 'Swaptopus' battery swapping stations across Europe, demonstrating the strength of their ongoing technical and operational partnership. The partnership improves on Octopus existing suite of offerings in low carbon technology, which currently includes the Octopus Cosy heat pump range, Octopus Charge EV charger range, and Octopus Nook home battery range. Ampace’s battery chemistry technology combined with Octopus’ software will help make existing residential home energy batteries cheaper and better. “The future of energy is not just about generating or storing more power, but about making energy smarter, more connected, and more accessible” added Jason Zhu, President of Energy Storage Systems, Ampace. “We believe the convergence of advanced battery technologies, intelligent energy management, and innovative energy services will fundamentally reshape how energy is delivered and consumed. Through this strategic collaboration with CATL and Octopus Energy, we aim to accelerate this transformation, unlock new possibilities for the global energy ecosystem, and contribute to a more resilient and sustainable energy future.” For additional information:

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The U.S. Department of Energy is launching a new initiative to speed development and deployment of advanced battery technologies, DOE Assistant Secretary Audrey Robertson told Utility Dive. - The Battery Manufacturing Accelerator, or BattMan, aims to strengthen domestic supply chains for battery materials and components, reduce manufacturing costs and shorten commercialization timelines, the department said on Wednesday. - U.S. demand for batteries across transportation and grid management applications is expected to increase from 179 GWh in 2025 to 707 GWh in 2035, according to a June analysis from Bloomberg NEF that DOE cited in a white paper published last month. Dive Insight: A secure, scaled-up domestic battery supply chain is critical for U.S. economic growth and security in the years ahead, DOE said in the white paper, “A National Strategy for American Leadership in Batteries.” For utilities, batteries are increasingly indispensable for improving grid reliability and shifting load, particularly in regions where data center loads threaten to disrupt power flows, DOE said in the paper. Data centers themselves could account for one-quarter of total U.S. battery demand by 2030, according to a Benchmark Mineral Intelligence forecast cited in the paper. The U.S. today is heavily dependent on external trade partners — particularly China — for battery materials and components, which “poses substantial supply chain risks,” DOE said in the paper. Recent investments in U.S. battery cell and pack manufacturing have not been matched by investments in U.S. production of precursor components, creating gaps in the supply chain, DOE said. “We have substantial work to do to secure the materials and manufacturing capabilities [lithium-ion batteries] require,” Robertson said in an email. “China currently controls between 60% and 100% of global production capacity across several critical stages of battery materials and component manufacturing … [which] represents a serious vulnerability for American industry and national security.” China and other Asian countries host nearly all global lithium-ion battery cathode, anode and separator manufacturing and nearly 93% of electrolyte manufacturing, DOE said in 2024. Robertson said the BattMan consortium, which has support from DOE’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, would expand the Trump administration’s efforts to boost domestic sources of battery materials and components. The Pacific Northwest National Laboratory leads the consortium, with participation from Argonne National Laboratory, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the National Laboratory of the Rockies, formerly known as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. BattMan’s research university partners include the University of Alabama, Arizona State University, Binghamton University, the University of Michigan–Dearborn and the University of Washington. DOE says the consortium will advance three strategic objectives: establish a “mine-to-market” domestic supply chain by 2030; develop new battery technologies that are “more affordable, longer lasting, higher performing, and less reliant on critical minerals;” and scale deployment of advanced battery technologies in sectors critical to national security. “We’re excited about technologies that use more abundant domestic materials, reduce dependence on foreign supply chains, and can be manufactured competitively here in the United States,” Robertson said in an email. In August, DOE announced $500 million in funding for seven projects to expand U.S. critical minerals and materials processing, battery manufacturing and recycling projects. Award recipients include a California-based company expanding lithium-ion battery anode manufacturing with U.S.-sourced materials and another firm piloting battery production using ultra‑thin lithium‑metal films and “prelithiated” material. The latter “could enable higher-energy, faster-charging batteries,” Robertson said. According to PNNL, BattMan will work to overcome barriers that have kept promising, U.S.-developed energy storage technologies like these from reaching commercial scale. The consortium will use a “cost-focused” research and development strategy that “[takes] performance, manufacturability and scalability into account up front;” broaden innovation beyond lithium-ion technologies using “platform technologies that are applicable to all energy storage chemistries;” modernize energy storage manufacturing using digital twins and other AI-enabled tools; and develop reliable, data-driven frameworks for validating emerging energy storage technologies, PNNL said.

artigo.texto: SMM, November 4: Entering Q4, the sodium-ion battery industry chain has reached the most critical delivery verification period of the year. SMM data shows that in October, sodium-ion battery cathode material production increased 3% MoM and surged 260% YoY, while hard carbon anode production pulled back slightly by 4% MoM but surged 186% YoY—the high YoY growth confirms the industry is still on a zero-to-one volume ramp-up trajectory, but the mediocre MoM performance reveals another reality: capacity ramp-up pace is generally slower than market expectations, with a clear time lag between order growth and actual delivery. On the price side, cathode NFPP quotes are diverging, precursors are hovering near the cost line, and iron phosphate supply-demand tension remains elevated—the two-way squeeze of cost and order losses is reshaping the industry's competitive landscape. 1. Cathode materials: production up 3% MoM, capacity release below expectations, orders accelerating toward top-tier players 1. Supply side: ramp-up hindered, delivery capacity supplemented by "outsourcing + toll processing" In October, sodium-ion battery cathode material production increased 3% MoM and surged 260% YoY. The overall market operated steadily, but capacity release falling short of expectations was the most prominent contradiction this month. Although 10 kt-scale new lines gradually entered commissioning, compounded by line switchovers and equipment changes, actual output still failed to meet the original ramp-up targets; some enterprises boosted delivery capacity through outsourced processing, and once downstream processes are fully connected after mid-November, monthly capacity is expected to reach the kt level. 2. Demand side: clear divergence, growth concentrated in small power and energy storage The demand side showed significant divergence: in October, some enterprises shipped only a few hundred mt, while November orders have grown to several hundred mt and will be delivered in batches, with growth mainly from small power and some energy storage orders. However, it is worth noting that if lithium carbonate prices continue to weaken, December market conditions may fall short of November—some clients' new orders are already showing loss inversion, and downstream willingness to take orders has clearly declined. From the perspective of enterprise operations, the trend of orders concentrating toward top-tier players is increasingly evident: industry top-tier players already have orders on hand exceeding 1 kt, while their own monthly capacity is only a few hundred mt and cannot fully cover demand, requiring a dual-line approach of "in-house lines + toll processing" to ensure delivery. 3. Price side: NFPP quotes diverging, cost pressure focused on iron phosphate In October, NFPP quotes remained relatively stable, with mainstream transactions concentrated at 24,000-27,000 yuan/mt. In the short term, there is clearly no room for price increases, nor room for cuts—prices have entered a stalemate range. Cost side pressure remains concentrated in the iron phosphate segment. Although phosphoric acid prices have pulled back from 12,000 yuan/mt to around 9,000 yuan/mt, iron phosphate prices remain at around 16,000 yuan/mt due to tight supply-demand conditions, significantly above the reasonable range of 12,000-13,000 yuan/mt. The persistently high raw material costs are driving downstream material enterprises to accelerate the construction of their own iron phosphate production lines or form joint ventures with phosphorus chemical enterprises, advancing industry chain integration. In the precursor segment, mainstream transaction prices are 19,000-20,000 yuan/mt, with large orders as low as 17,000-18,000 yuan/mt, already basically approaching the cost line. Enterprises generally adopt tiered pricing to lock in major clients. 4. Competitive Landscape: Accelerating Tier Differentiation From the competitive landscape perspective, tier differentiation in the industry is accelerating. Top-tier cathode enterprises with planned capacity of 10 kt-level projects are successively coming online, steadily expanding their leading edge. Small and medium-sized startups are under pressure due to tightening financing environments and lagging production line construction, with some enterprises still showing a gap between publicly claimed capacity and actual production. Another noteworthy signal is that NFPP precursor enterprises generally have low willingness to cross over into cathode production, mainly due to concerns about direct competition with downstream clients—this objectively maintains the competitive boundaries of the existing cathode segment. Looking ahead, Q4 cathode shipments may show a "high first, low later" trend, with prices remaining weak under the dual squeeze of cost support and order losses. Top-tier players with scale capacity, integrated costs, and quality client structures will be the first to benefit, with industry consolidation and concentration expected to accelerate. November sodium-ion battery cathode production is expected to increase 9% MoM and surge 162% YoY. II. Hard Carbon Anode: Production Edges Down 4% MoM, Commissioning Window Determines Year-End Output, Stockpiling Willingness Rising 1. Supply Side: Orders at Hundreds of mt Level, Deliveries Yet to Scale Up In October, the hard carbon anode material market operated steadily overall, with production edging down 4% from September and surging 186% YoY. Although most enterprises received orders at the hundreds of mt level in October, actual deliveries have yet to scale up due to capacity constraints—"orders without goods" is the current reality of this segment. 2. Enterprise Operations: October-November Is the Critical Window Before Ramp-Up, Inventory Strategies Diverge From enterprise operations, industry capacity had not yet completed expansion in H1, and new self-owned production lines entered a concentrated commissioning period in H2. artigo.texto: Aramex lança Data Center Logistics para entregas com prazos críticos A Aramex apresentou o Data Center Logistics, serviço voltado à gestão de entregas com prazos críticos para a construção e a operação de data centers, segundo o TradeArabia News Service. A provedora de logística informou que a oferta começa na região do Conselho de Cooperação do Golfo, no Sudeste Asiático, em Taiwan e no Sul dos EUA, abrangendo localidades como Abu Dhabi, Riad, Johor, Texas e Louisiana. A empresa afirmou que a carga destinada a data centers está entre as mais exigentes da logística. Transformadores e chillers podem levar um ano ou mais para ir do pedido ao canteiro e precisam chegar em linha com o cronograma da obra, enquanto cada rack de IA encaixotado pesa cerca de 1,75 tonelada métrica, tem valor de vários milhões de dólares, está sujeito a controles de exportação e pode sofrer danos em trânsito sem deixar marcas visíveis na caixa. A Aramex observou que essas entregas costumam ser divididas entre agentes de carga, despachantes aduaneiros, empresas de transporte pesado e instaladores distintos, sem que uma única parte responda por todo o trajeto. Segundo a empresa, um único embarque atrasado ou danificado pode adiar a data em que um data center entra em operação. O novo serviço foi concebido para assumir a responsabilidade por todo o trajeto. Na construção, abrange transformadores, painéis de manobra, geradores e chillers, incluindo cargas pesadas e fora de medida, acompanhados desde o pedido de compra e entregues em sintonia com o cronograma da obra. Para equipamentos de computação, cuida de racks de IA e equipamentos de rede vindos de fábricas em Taiwan, no Sudeste Asiático, no México, nos EUA e na Europa, por voo fretado ou transporte rodoviário seguro, com conformidade aduaneira e de controles de exportação. Dentro do data center, o serviço inclui manuseio white-glove na doca de carga, desembalagem e posicionamento no salão de dados. O suporte pós-venda cobre peças de reposição, substituições e devoluções depois que a instalação entra em operação. Cada rack de IA é movimentado sob um único processo documentado, com sensores lacrados dentro da caixa que monitoram choque, inclinação, temperatura e umidade desde a fábrica até a entrega assinada no data center. A Aramex afirmou que o serviço se apoia em mais de quatro décadas de experiência em agenciamento de cargas, desembaraço aduaneiro e logística de projetos. No CCG, a Aramex opera o que descreve como a maior rede logística da região, com mais de 7.000 pessoas e estações, armazéns, caminhões e equipes aduaneiras próprios em todos os mercados. Em Taiwan, na Malásia, em Singapura, nos EUA e na Europa, suas equipes trabalham diretamente com as fábricas que produzem os equipamentos, de modo que uma única empresa responde pela carga nas duas pontas do trajeto. O CEO do grupo, Amadou Diallo, disse que um data center é tão rápido quanto sua entrega mais lenta, observando que as empresas que constroem capacidade de IA trabalham com datas fixas e equipamentos fabricados em um continente e instalados em outro. Ele afirmou que transportar esse tipo de carga entre fronteiras no prazo e intacta é a razão de ser da Aramex, acrescentando que o Data Center Logistics aplica essa força a uma expansão exigente e representa um passo importante no crescimento da empresa como provedora de logística global.

artigo.texto: Data centers impulsionam o crescimento dos gastos com construção não residencial nos EUA Os gastos com construção não residencial nos EUA subiram na comparação mensal em 8 das 16 subcategorias, segundo a Associated Builders and Contractors. Os gastos privados com construção não residencial aumentaram 1,1% em setembro, enquanto os gastos públicos com construção não residencial recuaram 0,1%. O economista-chefe da ABC, Anirban Basu, afirmou que os gastos com construção não residencial cresceram pelo sexto mês consecutivo em setembro. Ele observou que os data centers responderam por quase todo o ganho e que, excluindo os data centers e a categoria de energia, estreitamente relacionada, os gastos não residenciais caíram no mês. Basu descreveu o ritmo de expansão dos data centers como cada vez mais difícil de contextualizar. Os gastos nessa categoria subiram mais 8,6% em setembro e cresceram a uma taxa anualizada de 217% desde maio. Para os próximos meses, Basu disse que o impulso permanecerá estreitamente concentrado nos segmentos ligados à inteligência artificial, citando os recentes aumentos no rendimento dos títulos do Tesouro e a escalada contínua dos preços de materiais. Ele acrescentou que, embora os empreiteiros sigam ocupados no agregado, segundo o Indicador de Carteira de Obras da ABC, as condições atuais de mercado continuarão a favorecer os empreiteiros de maior porte, que têm probabilidade muito maior de estar envolvidos em projetos de data centers e de energia.

artigo.texto: The nationwide crunch for power — mostly driven by massive data centers — is so severe, even the board members of a local utility company are weighing the benefits of a temporary pause on their development. Members of Salt River Project’s district board consulted utility staff Monday about their options for curtailing new data center interconnection agreements, amid concerns that residential customers may end up subsidizing the AI data center boom’s growing energy bill. Data centers’ forecasted energy demands are unprecedented. In an exchange between two SRP board members and the utility’s chief legal executive, Michael O’Connor, it was revealed that more than half of SRP’s planned capacity could go directly to new data centers. “I’ve heard these figures in separate presentations,” said Krista O’Brien, a director-at-large, “that we’re planning to grow by 4,700 megawatts by 2035, and then I’ve also heard that 3,000 of those megawatts are data centers.” SRP’s chief legal executive Michael O’Connor said that estimation seemed plausible. Another board member responded, saying those figures match what they heard at a September Power Committee meeting. That added capacity will add millions in new infrastructure, operations and maintenance costs for SRP. Ken Clark, who represents SRP’s sixth division, says that’s a concern, because the utility has dealt with relatively flat energy growth for the last 20 years. “I find it very hard to believe that we are not shifting costs to other customer classes just by the fact that we have to build new plants that we would not otherwise have had to build, right?” said Clark. But O’Connor says it’s unlikely SRP can pass a data center moratorium, because state law says the utility must serve any eligible customer. That law is provided as a check on SRP’s legal monopoly on much of the Phoenix metro, including parts of Mesa, Tempe and Chandler. “You have this service territory,” O’Connor said. “No one else can come in and serve here. In exchange, you actually have to serve those people coming in.” O’Connor says exceptions can be made if there are safety concerns, to which director at-large Kathy L. Mohr-Almeida asked, “there’s reports that data centers — you know, it’s likely that artificial intelligence has a 10% to 25% opportunity to eliminate humanity. Is that not something that is a safety concern?” O’Connor said he didn’t disagree that reports like that exist, but he says, SRP has a specific role it must fulfill within state law. “And as you’re going to see, because we have exclusive service territory and an obligation to serve, some of those questions are really left for the legislature, or the communities themselves — not SRP,” O’Connor said. John Tucker, SRP’s director of financial strategy, addressed concerns from Kennedy and other board members that SRP is shifting the costs of serving new data centers onto other customers. Tucker explained two new tariffs board members approved for large energy customers last year. He says SRP collects the estimated costs associated with meeting 80% of a data center’s peak energy demand up front, an industry-leading level for developer collateral. Collaterals are collected by utility companies in large energy agreements, usually at much lower rates, to ensure operational costs can still be met if the business shuts down and the utility loses that customer. Tucker says SRP also collects collateral on data centers’ associated transmission costs. “We’ve been sending out some very large bills to some of these data centers in terms of the infrastructure costs,” Tucker said. “These are nine-figure bills that we’re sending to people.” Between these two cost streams, Tucker says data centers are paying more than it costs the utility to serve them. There was little public discussion on the impact to SRP’s water supplies before leaders went into executive session on the item. - An Arizona Court of Appeals panel still won’t let Arizona Public Service levy an extra fee on customers who have solar panels on their homes. - Outside groups from across the political spectrum have poured nearly $2 million into Arizona’s Corporation Commission race, which will decide which two candidates secure seats on the state’s top utility regulator next year. - AI data centers in the Phoenix area use relatively little water on site, but they use lots of electricity, which takes a lot of water to generate. - The agency, which delivers water to the Phoenix and Tucson areas, joins Nevada and Arizona in its legal claims against the harms of water cutbacks from the shrinking river. - Amid ongoing rate cases for two of the state’s largest electric providers, Arizona’s top utility regulators have spent time embroiled in an internal employment dispute that has spilled into public view.

artigo.texto: Localizado em Golmud, província de Qinghai, no noroeste da China, o projeto foi investido e construído pelo China Green Development Investment Group (CGDG). Segundo a empresa, trata-se atualmente da maior instalação de LAES (energia eletroquímica de ar frio) do mundo . A China alcança um avanço significativo no armazenamento de energia utilizando ar liquefeito. Segundo a mídia chinesa, um projeto de armazenamento de energia em ar liquefeito (LAES) de 60 megawatts (MW) no noroeste da China foi oficialmente conectado à rede elétrica e começou a gerar eletricidade. Isso é considerado um avanço significativo na engenharia e comercialização da tecnologia LAES. O projeto representa um marco significativo nos esforços da China para desenvolver tecnologias de armazenamento de energia que apoiem seu sistema elétrico em meio à crescente proporção de energia renovável. Segundo a CGDG, a instalação tem uma capacidade instalada total de 60 MW, com previsão de absorver aproximadamente 600.000 kWh de energia limpa por dia. Espera-se que o projeto gere cerca de 180 milhões de kWh de eletricidade anualmente, o suficiente para atender às necessidades de consumo anual de aproximadamente 30.000 residências. O LAES é uma tecnologia emergente de armazenamento de energia a longo prazo. Ele utiliza eletricidade para comprimir e resfriar o ar até que ele se liquefique durante períodos de baixa demanda de eletricidade. Quando a eletricidade é necessária, o ar liquefeito é aquecido e expandido para acionar uma turbina, gerando assim eletricidade. Essa tecnologia é considerada superior ao armazenamento de energia em baterias tradicionais em termos de escala, tempo de armazenamento e vida útil. A CGDG afirmou que o projeto Golmud utiliza um processo de liquefação criogênica a -194 graus Celsius. Os equipamentos utilizados no projeto são totalmente nacionais, com 100% de seus componentes fabricados na China. A empresa também afirmou que o projeto aplica tecnologias para as quais detém direitos de propriedade intelectual independentes. Segundo a CGDG, este projeto é atualmente líder mundial em capacidade e volume de armazenamento no setor de armazenamento de energia de baixa agregação (LAES). Espera-se que o projeto apoie a absorção de energia renovável, alivie a demanda de pico das usinas termelétricas e utilize a energia de resfriamento do gás natural liquefeito (GNL). Especialistas acreditam que a operação do projeto representa um avanço significativo para a China na construção de um novo tipo de sistema de energia, onde a energia renovável desempenha um papel fundamental no fornecimento. Este projeto preenche muitas lacunas em aplicações de armazenamento de energia de longa duração em larga escala globalmente e fornece um modelo escalável para aplicações de tecnologia de armazenamento de energia de longo prazo em larga escala, contribuindo para a formação de uma cadeia industrial completa – um passo crucial para alcançar as metas de carbono da China. artigo.texto: R$ 31 milhões: Anatel fica sem dinheiro para pagar o próprio data center Agência pediu, mas não recebeu recurso do Tesouro Nacional em outras ocasiões. A Anatel estaria sem dinheiro para custear o próprio data center em Brasília, segundo informações do jornal Folha de São Paulo nesta terça-feira (03/11). A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações alertou o Governo Federal de que precisa de R$ 30,76 milhões para arcar com as notas fiscais referentes ao projeto. Além disso, a agência também estaria sem recursos para pagar contas básicas. O presidente Carlos Baigorri buscou o Ministério do Planejamento na semana passada para solicitar o desbloqueio de R$ 30 milhões. Em ocasiões anteriores, ainda segundo a Folha, o pedido não foi atendido pelo Tesouro Nacional. A Anatel atribui a falta de recursos ao bloqueio de R$ 51,83 milhões, determinado em maio. Houve uma redução de 19% no orçamento discricionário, aquele destinado a custeio e investimentos. Já o data center foi contratado em dezembro de 2025, ao custo de R$ 44,95 milhões em produtos e serviços. De acordo com a Folha, o contrato inclui desde equipamentos até a manutenção e garantia. Nós buscamos a Anatel. Embora a agência não tenha comentado os valores citados na apuração da Folha, ela alertou que “a persistência das restrições orçamentárias e financeiras poderá exigir novas medidas de reprogramação de despesas”. {{ excerpt | truncatewords: 35 }} {% endif %}

artigo.texto: NTPC Green Energy Limited (NGEL) has issued a Supply of Battery Containers and Grid-Forming PCS tender for 10 GW/ 40 GWh BESS across its project portfolio. The proposed 10 GW/40 GWh BESS capacity represents a significant addition to India's planned energy storage infrastructure, as the country looks to address the intermittency of renewable power generation and improve grid reliability. Key Components Of The 10 GW BESS Plan The scope of work includes the supply of LFP-based containerised battery systems along with grid-forming PCS. The selected bidders will also supervise the erection, installation and commissioning of the systems at project sites, up to the PCS output terminals. The procurement is expected to support the deployment of large-scale energy storage capacity across NGEL's project portfolio, helping improve the integration of renewable energy into the power grid. The scope also includes comprehensive servicing and maintenance for 15 years from the commissioning date of each project. The long-term service support will be provided through a Long Term Service Agreement (LTSA), covering the battery storage systems and associated equipment as specified in the tender. NGEL's Earlier BESS Tender For Bikaner Solar Park This is not the first large-scale battery storage initiative undertaken by NTPC Green Energy Limited (NGEL). The company had earlier floated an engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) tender for a 7,800 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at the NTPC REL Bikaner Solar Park in Rajasthan. The project was divided into five blocks, with individual storage capacities ranging from 1,200 MWh to 2,200 MWh. The tender covered turnkey execution, including design, engineering, equipment supply, installation and commissioning, along with 15 years of operation and maintenance support. What are battery containers and grid format PCS? Battery containers and grid-forming Power Conversion Systems (PCS) are two key components of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). Together, they enable electricity to be stored, converted and supplied to the grid when required. Grid-forming PCS, meanwhile, converts the direct current (DC) electricity stored in batteries into alternating current (AC) for grid use, and vice versa during charging. Unlike conventional grid-following systems, grid-forming technology can help establish and regulate grid voltage and frequency, supporting grid stability even when renewable energy generation fluctuates. Together, these technologies can improve renewable energy integration, provide flexibility in electricity supply, support grid stability and help ensure reliable power delivery. They are particularly important as India increases its dependence on solar and wind energy, which are variable in nature.

artigo.texto: Marvell Technology's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday. "You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here." Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release. Marvell shares slumped 13% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank nearly 19%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch. Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models. "We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said. Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending. This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology. Marvell's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies. In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers. "This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them." Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone. CORRECTION: This story has been updated to reflect that Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston described the deal as an 'enormous' opportunity. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

(TSXV: ETL) (FSE: OW3) (OTCQX: EEMMF), “E3”, “E3 Lithium” or the “Company,” a leader in Canadian lithium development has entered into a collaborative research agreement (the “Project”) between E3, the National Research Council of Canada (“NRC”), and major South Korean battery manufacturer POSCO through its subsidiary POSCO AMERICA CORPORATION (“POSCO”), among other input contributors, whereby E3 will be the exclusive lithium carbonate provider to the Project to support the development of a “made in Canada” lithium-manganese-rich (LMR) cathode. E3 Lithium is receiving CA$98,798 in funding from the NRC’s Critical Battery Materials Initiative, for this Project. E3’s lithium carbonate contributions will support the Project in producing lithium-manganese-rich (LMR) cathode active materials (CAM) from Canadian feedstocks. E3, along with Manganese X Energy Corp. and NiVolt Technologies Inc., will produce the necessary chemical precursors, while the NRC will carry out downstream synthesis into cathode material and testing in coin cells. POSCO will provide industrial validation of the CAM material, according to their internal benchmark metrics. POSCO is one of the world’s leading battery materials producers, with integrated capabilities targeting one million tonnes of cathode capacity by 2030, currently supplying major global automakers and battery manufacturers. “E3 Lithium is working alongside a group of Canadian peers developing cathode for the future of North American batteries," said Chris Doornbos, President and CEO of E3 Lithium. "LMR batteries offer increased energy density and safety with significant cost savings, with LG, Ford, and GM currently pursuing this cathode as an option. artigo.texto: It is the largest BESS by storage capacity (MWh) in Europe and a significant step forward in the delivery of infrastructure supporting the UK’s transition to a cleaner, more resilient energy system. Located adjacent to National Grid’s Hams Hall substation, the project will help balance variable electricity demand and intermittent renewable generation, supporting greater integration of renewable energy while strengthening grid resilience and energy security. The project reached commercial operation just 20 days after energisation. From commissioning and testing to operational readiness, BW ESS worked closely with partners including Sungrow, Energy-IO, National Grid and NESO. Achieving this milestone safely and efficiently reflects the engineering expertise, rigorous preparation and close coordination behind Hams Hall, as well as the technical capability and commitment of everyone involved. Hams Hall’s capacity will increase to 400 MW/1,424 MWh following completion of its second phase. At full capacity, the project will be capable of supporting the electricity needs of around 1.3 million homes for up to 3.5 hours, which is approximately equivalent to the number of households across Greater Manchester. “The start of commercial operations at Hams Hall is a landmark moment for BW ESS and a significant addition to Europe’s energy infrastructure” said Erik Strømsø, CEO and Co-Founder of BW ESS. “The project was built and commissioned on budget and ahead of schedule, which is a remarkable achievement for a system of this scale and complexity and a testament to the dedication and expertise of our team, and the commitment and collaboration of our partners.” Long-term revenues for the project are underpinned by a 10-year floor and optimisation agreement with EDF and financing was recently secured from lenders OCBC, Rabobank and Societe Generale. Hams Hall forms part of BW ESS’ 2.6 GWh Ardenham portfolio, co-owned with leading energy and decarbonisation investor AIP Management. Its entry into commercial operations expands BW ESS’ operating presence in the UK, alongside the 331 MWh Bramley BESS in Hampshire. artigo.texto: Blackstone, one of the largest private equity firms in the world, officially changed the name of its dedicated energy investment fund to include the phrase “energy transition” in 2022, having already ceased investing in oil and gas production five years earlier. The pivot toward a new energy future has not diminished interest in the fund. In mid-October, Blackstone announced that the fund pulled in $8.7 billion in investor money this year, reportedly turning away an additional $3 billion to stay under its maximum investment cap. Blackstone’s is one of several energy transition funds at private equity firms that have consistently grown over the past decade. That growth has continued even as general climate-oriented investment has fallen over the last few years. Colloquially, “energy transition” refers to the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy that is necessary to limit the worst impacts of climate change. But on Wall Street, the term can mean something a bit different. Some transition funds — including Blackstone’s — see opportunities for profit in natural gas, data centers, and rising electricity costs. “I know a lot of the investors out there do consider gas a transition fuel,” said Ryan Loughead, a senior associate and former climate solutions analyst for BloombergNEF, an energy research firm. Private equity funds take new investor money every few years, and then use it to buy existing companies, maximize their profits, and then sell them, returning the money from the sale to investors. Unlike publicly traded companies, whose stocks are available for anyone to buy, private equity firms typically only take investments from large organizations, like pension funds, or very wealthy individuals, and they have faced criticism for prioritizing returns at the expense of workers and the environment. The transition to renewable energy has been a booming business for private equity firms. “Transition funds” in private equity have raked in $178 billion between 2021 and the beginning of 2026, triple the amount raised by comparable funds dedicated to fossil fuels and general energy, according to Loughead’s research. They’ve maintained their popularity even as other forms of climate-related investments have flagged in the United States, with climate-related venture capital on track to suffer its worst year this decade. (While private equity funds buy out established companies, venture capital funds make smaller investments in startups.) These shifts have coincided with changes in federal policy, as well as the overall economy. The Biden administration’s signature climate law once spurred innovation in new technologies, but Republicans in Congress repealed most of that legislation last year. Meanwhile, the tech industry’s data center buildout is creating surging demand for electricity and drawing trillions of dollars from investors. In the financial industry, the energy transition has grown into a sophisticated economic trend with established players and markets, said Dan Cohn, an energy finance analyst with the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a think tank focused on the energy transition. Private equity funds don’t typically demonstrate investor interest in a budding industry so much as a view that the industry is becoming economically important. “Investors are sensing oncoming scarcity [of electricity] and are positioning themselves accordingly,” Cohn said. “That speaks to both the moment of rising electricity demand, but also the maturity of clean energy technologies.” But while these funds seek to capitalize on high demand for electricity, they don’t all show a clear commitment to reducing emissions. Blackstone’s fund is explicit in its view that methane gas, a fossil fuel, is an essential component of the energy transition. The fund no longer invests in oil and gas fields, but it does invest in natural gas plants. When Blackstone rebranded the fund in 2022, the fund’s director, David Foley, explained why natural gas plants were still on the table. “A lot of the capital invested in the energy transition is going into simple renewable power generation assets like solar and wind,” he told an industry publication. “While this is important, just adding renewables to the grid doesn’t necessarily mean you can shut down and remove existing sources of power, such as coal and gas.” This year, the fund announced investments in six companies, including a natural gas plant operator and a data center cooling technology company, alongside a company focused on renewable energy development and some transmission and grid technology companies. Blackstone did not reply to a request for comment. Meanwhile, the private equity firm Brookfield governs its transition funds partly through an explicit commitment to decarbonization and emissions reductions. The company has said it can invest in natural gas in cases where it replaces dirtier fossil fuels, but Brookfield has also drawn criticism for describing gas expansion as part of the energy transition. Similar funds in Europe, like Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ Energy Transition Fund, are far more focused on clean energy sources like green hydrogen, with little emphasis on natural gas. “‘Energy transition’ is a flexible term,” Cohn said. “And I’m unsurprised to see either the gas or electrical equipment and data center-related companies in some of these funds. That is perfectly consistent with how I know some investors think about the energy transition.” BlackRock, another private equity giant unrelated to Blackstone, explicitly defines “transition” investing as something different from “sustainable” investing: “not all sustainable strategies are transition, and not all transition strategies are sustainable,” its website reads. That partial overlap could complicate investors’ claims about how sustainable their portfolios are. artigo.texto: Recently, the groundbreaking ceremony for the industrialisation base project of hydrogen energy application for new-type power and energy storage battery systems in plateau and extreme cold conditions was held in the Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone, marking the project’s entry into the substantive construction phase. This project is a key demonstration initiative within the regional new energy layout, focused on addressing the practical challenges of deploying energy storage and hydrogen technologies in extreme cold environments. Total floor area: 31,523 m². Yuedong Steel Structure is responsible for the general construction contracting. The project is located in the Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone.Total floor area: 31,523.12 m².The plan includes the construction of Plant 1, Plant 2, and auxiliary guardhouse facilities. The project has a clear positioning, specifically targeting special operating conditions such as plateaus and extreme cold, to advance the industrialisation of ESS battery systems and hydrogen-related technologies. Such scenarios have long been plagued by equipment performance degradation and operational stability challenges caused by low temperatures, representing an area where China’s new energy industry has yet to achieve a breakthrough. Jilin Province Yuedong Steel Structure Group Co., Ltd. is undertaking the general construction contracting for this project, responsible for the overall implementation of civil works and supporting facilities. On the day of the groundbreaking, representatives from the construction, design, supervision, and contracting parties attended the event to witness the project’s commencement period. Building a technology transfer platform for cold-region applications and addressing supply gaps in new energy equipment Industrial projects in extreme cold regions impose higher requirements on construction techniques, material selection, and scheduling. The project team will advance each construction period in accordance with regulatory standards, with particular attention to structural details, pipeline reservations, and equipment foundations suited to extreme cold conditions, striving to deliver a safe, stable, quality-compliant engineering platform with demonstrative impact. Northeast China and extensive plateau regions across the country are rich in wind and solar power resources, but low temperatures constrain the large-scale deployment of energy storage and hydrogen equipment. Many energy storage and hydrogen products perform well under normal temperature conditions, yet their reliability and service life are significantly affected after prolonged exposure to low temperatures. Once this industrialisation base is completed, it will establish a corresponding technology transfer platform, facilitating the transition of energy storage and hydrogen technologies adapted to extreme cold conditions from the laboratory to mass production. After the base becomes operational, it will be capable of undertaking trial production, pilot testing, and batch manufacturing of related products, thereby addressing the supply gap in new energy equipment for cold regions. Leveraging Changchun’s industrial supporting advantages, the base can also integrate with provincial wind and solar power development and hydrogen demonstration application projects, forming a closed loop encompassing technology R&D, equipment manufacturing, and scenario validation. The maturation of energy storage and hydrogen technologies for cold regions can also extend outward, providing product support for new energy projects in other plateau and extreme cold areas across China.

artigo.texto: This story was originally published by Canary Media. It has been edited to conform with Corporate Knights style. Developers and utilities are building tons of gas generation to power the data centre boom. It’s an expansion that could cost them and the rest of us dearly, both in terms of climate change and money that may end up wasted if computing demand fails to materialize. But there’s a cleaner, cheaper and faster-to-deploy alternative: batteries. That’s the conclusion of a new report from researchers at Georgetown and Duke universities, which lays out the ways states can push utilities and tech firms to opt for energy storage over fossil fuels whenever possible. Fossil fuel power – whether in the form of giant utility-scale plants or generators installed behind the meter at data centres – has become the go-to for many in the AI industry. That’s because gas generation offers round-the-clock power in a single package. Overall, U.S. utilities are planning more than 60 gigawatts of new gas plants to serve data centre demand, and around 90 GW of behind-the-meter gas generators for data centres have been proposed nationwide. “At the moment, there’s a lot of inertia and status quo pressure for much of the behind-the-meter resources being natural gas,” said Ian Hitchcock, report co-author and senior program coordinator at the Duke Initiative for Science and Society. A safer alternative Moving ahead with those gas power plans does more than spell climate disaster. If data centre proposals fall through or shut down early, other utility customers could be on the hook for the cost of overbuilding gas. That’s called “stranded asset” risk – and states have only begun to tackle it, even amid mounting fears that the AI sector is a bubble about to pop. Batteries “can act as a hedge against that risk,” last week’s report explains. Batteries are much cheaper than round-the-clock gas generation in situations where hours of stored energy can solve near-term needs. They’re also inherently modular and flexible in ways that gas power plants are not, which allows planners to increase or cut back on deployment if data centre demand shifts sharply. Plus, batteries can help avoid the need for costly grid buildouts that would otherwise be used to serve increasing electricity demand, and can act as shock absorbers to cushion the grid against data centres’ massive and fast-changing computing loads. While lithium-ion batteries can’t provide round-the-clock power, they can meet large portions of data centre electricity needs, said Jackson Ewing, director of energy and climate policy at Duke University’s Nicholas Institute of Energy, Environment & Sustainability. And unlike more future-forward solutions – such as advanced geothermal, next-generation nuclear, and novel long-duration energy storage technologies – “batteries are already showing serious momentum in terms of their deployment trajectory.” Developers like it In fact, utilities and data centre developers are increasingly embracing batteries, even as they pursue gas. A new forecast from BloombergNEF sees U.S. energy storage deployment surpassing 11,000 gigawatt-hours by 2036, a 30% increase from its 10-year forecast from just six months ago. Data centre demand is pushing much of that growth. So, what can state decision-makers do to further encourage data centres to opt for batteries? States that directly regulate utility investments can craft “bring your own new clean energy” tariff structures. These regulations can set minimum requirements for data centres to procure or pay for enough carbon-free generation and energy storage to cover some or all of their electricity needs. Certain jurisdictions are already moving ahead with this approach; Google, for example, has signed onto such tariffs with regulators in Nevada and Minnesota. Things get more complicated in states with “restructured” energy markets. In these places, regulators have limited authority over the independent power producers that build big generation and battery projects and sell power into wholesale electricity markets. Still, the report highlights several ways that these states can encourage battery development to serve data centres, including via state energy storage mandates like those launched in Illinois, Maryland and New Jersey, and engaging in state energy planning in conjunction with regional grid operators. “There is not a jurisdiction that has no potential action items if they’re serious about trying to deploy this,” Hitchcock said. Jeff St. John is chief reporter and policy specialist at Canary Media. The Weekly Roundup Get all our stories in one place, every Wednesday at noon EST.

artigo.texto: The American Shore and Beach Preservation Association selected five projects nationwide for its 2026 Best Restored Shore Award, which recognizes outstanding natural infrastructure restoration projects that restore natural resources, enhance habitat, increase shoreline resilience, and provide long-term benefits to coastal communities. They noted that the Queen Bess project exceeded its habitat restoration and bird-nesting goals, with monitoring demonstrating significant benefits to avian communities most impacted by the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. “This award is a testament to what Louisiana can accomplish when we put restoration dollars to work with a clear vision and a commitment to our coastal resources,” said Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority Chairman Gordon “Gordy” Dove. “Queen Bess Island is an important part of Louisiana’s coastal ecosystem, and its restoration is helping protect critical habitat for generations of birds while strengthening the resilience of our coast. We are proud to see this Louisiana project recognized on the national stage.” Located near Grand Isle in Jefferson Parish, Queen Bess Island is an important nesting site for brown pelicans and other colonial waterbirds. Years of erosion and subsidence had significantly reduced the island’s available nesting habitat in active use by a brown pelican colony. The Queen Bess Island Restoration Project increased the abundance and quality of nesting habitat on the island by placing material to expand nesting habitat and elevate the island. The project also improved the existing protective rock ring, added breakwaters and bird ramp features, and initiated vegetative plantings, all designed to improve the island’s long-term stability and ecological function. The project was funded through the Louisiana Trustee Implementation Group’s Deepwater Horizon Natural Resource Damage Assessment funds and implemented through a partnership among the Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority, the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries, federal trustees, and other partners.

artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Liquid Cooling Is Changing What Data Centers Need to Measure Liquid cooling changes data center operations by making precise, real-time measurement across both liquid and air environments essential. For high-density AI environments, the data center industry has made its decision on liquid cooling. Facilities running dense AI workloads have led the way, and direct-to-chip cooling, in which liquid is routed through cold plates directly onto the processors, is becoming increasingly important in AI-optimized environments. The question is no longer whether liquid cooling will become more widely deployed. The more important operational question is what accurate, reliable measurement looks like in this new scenario. Liquid cooling solves a thermal problem. But operating these systems reliably over time introduces a different set of requirements, and the measurement infrastructure that supports reliable operation is part of that shift. From One Domain to Two Running a liquid-cooled facility is not a straightforward extension of running an air-cooled one. It is a categorically different operational environment, demanding new expertise across power, structural and mechanical engineering, fluid dynamics and chemistry, and instrumentation. And across all of these disciplines, measurement is the layer that makes the environment controllable. In a traditional air-cooled facility, the management of controlled environments is well understood. Temperature, relative humidity, and differential pressure have decades of industry practice behind them, supported by mature sensor technology and standardized guidance such as that published by ASHRAE, the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers. Operators know what they are measuring, why they are measuring it, how the information feeds into controls, and what the numbers mean. Liquid cooling extends that domain significantly. Pipes carrying cold water have always been part of data center infrastructure. What changes when cooling is brought all the way to the chips through CDUs and cold plates is the scope and criticality of liquid-side measurement. The parameters that now require dedicated instrumentation include liquid temperature, pressure, flow rate, and level, as well as leak detection and coolant health indicators such as pH, turbidity, conductivity, and refractive index. Each carries its own failure modes and must be understood in the context of cooling-loop performance and liquid quality. Liquid cooling takes over where air-side cooling runs out of headroom, but air-side management remains essential for everything else. Direct-to-chip cooling removes heat from the hottest components, but residual heat still needs to be managed with air. That is why operators need to understand both environments together. Measurements in a Liquid-Cooled Environment Alongside the liquid-side parameters, ambient conditions in the data hall and in the critical parts of the cooling system must be actively managed. Dew point is one area where the risk concentrates. Liquid cooling improves efficiency by circulating cold liquid over the cold plates. However, colder piping in an air-conditioned space also poses a risk of condensation. When pipe surface temperature drops below the ambient dew point, water can form near equipment, where the consequences of a failure event can far exceed any maintenance budget. A common practice is to maintain coolant supply temperatures at least 2°C above the measured ambient dew point. The coolant distribution unit is responsible for maintaining that margin, but only if it has a continuous and accurate picture of the actual dew point. The measurement challenge across all these parameters is not exotic. It draws on well-established sensor physics. The greater challenge is applying that physics correctly by understanding where to measure and how sensor data should feed into control decisions. Dynamic Facilities Demand Dynamic Measurements AI workloads fundamentally differ from traditional data center workloads in ways that matter for cooling. AI training jobs are intensive, and AI inferencing is intermittent. A cluster can move from idle to full load in minutes, generating a sharp change in thermal output that the cooling system must respond to in real time. The CDU managing that cluster needs to continuously control the cooling loop, ensuring supply and return temperatures stay within limits, pressure and flow rates remain within tolerance, and the ambient dew point near the cold manifolds stays within tolerance as conditions change. Reliable measurement is what makes that dynamic control possible. Without accurate, real-time data on critical parameters across the facility, control systems may be operating on delayed or inaccurate information. The consequences can cascade. Inefficient cooling wastes energy. Inadequate cooling puts hardware at risk. Overcorrection can waste energy and reduce operational efficiency. What the Next Generation Will Require Rack densities will continue to increase, and each step in that progression adds measurement requirements that do not yet benefit from decades of established industry practice. Reliable measurements give operators confidence that both the cooling infrastructure and the compute hardware it supports are operating within safe parameters. They enable more precise control, help facilities pursue efficiency targets, and provide early warning when conditions begin to drift. Without trustworthy measurements, a liquid-cooled data center is operating on assumptions. As cooling architectures become more complex and air-side and liquid-side environments increasingly need to work together, understanding what rigorous measurement looks like in this environment is where the hard work of the next phase begins.

artigo.texto: At about 6 a.m. on Sept. 18, 2026, workers at the Moss Landing Power Plant in California spotted a flare-up along the north wall of the Moss 300 battery building. The building had burned in January 2025, and the new flare-up came more than 20 months later. Vistra, the plant’s owner, said it believes about 1,200 of the roughly 2,500 battery modules still inside the structure ignited. Those modules had not been de-energized because they sat in a section of the building that was unsafe to enter after structural damage from the first fire. Monterey County issued a shelter-in-place order, and the natural gas plant on the site was temporarily shut down. By late afternoon, county officials reported the fire was inactive. The episode arrived as the industry can point to a very different set of numbers. The Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) reports that the battery energy storage system (BESS) failure rate, measured against cumulative deployed capacity, fell 99% between 2018 and 2025. Both facts are true at once, and together they define the challenge for utilities that are leaning harder on storage every year. The technology is getting safer, but reliability is being decided by specific engineering choices: how old a design is, how hard it is operated, what protects the cells from one another, and how well the equipment that ties the system to the grid is built to last. Storage Becomes a Grid Fixture The scale of the buildout explains why those details matter. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), utility-scale battery storage capacity in the U.S. grew at an average annual rate of 70% over the last three years, reaching 43.6 GW at the end of 2025. Operators added another 8.3 GW in the first half of 2026, bringing nameplate capacity to nearly 52 GW. Furthermore, they have reported plans to add 54 GW more over the next two and a half years: 14 GW in the second half of this year, 26 GW in 2027, and 14 GW in 2028. On those figures, the fleet would roughly double. Much of that capacity is paired with solar (Figure 1). The EIA notes that solar photovoltaic plants host the largest battery storage units. The Bellefield Solar and Energy Storage Farm, which serves the California Independent System Operator (CAISO) and began operating in December 2025, couples 500 MW of solar with 500 MW of storage, and plans call for doubling both by November 2026. If that happens, the EIA says, Bellefield will become the largest storage facility in the country. In Florida, the Manatee Solar Energy Center pairs 75 MW of solar with 409 MW of batteries, while Nevada’s Gemini Solar Hybrid combines 690 MW of photovoltaics with 380 MW of storage. 1. Battery storage units are regularly being paired with solar plants and sometimes even wind farms. This rendering shows a renewable generation site with solar arrays, wind turbines, and battery storage cabinets. Courtesy: nVent The reliability case is easiest to see in the West. The Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC), in a December 2025 report prepared with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), the North American Electric Reliability Corp. (NERC), and CAISO, noted that roughly 27 GW of BESS capacity was installed in the Western Interconnection when the report was published. Storage, it said, helps meet system demand “particularly during evening hours when solar generation is ramping down and the demand on the system is still high,” and it contributes to ancillary services that support grid stability. Data centers are adding a new dimension. Vince Sprenkle, director of the Grid Storage Launchpad at the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL), said in a lab feature last year: “We are seeing a dramatic shift in the energy sector due to things like the scaling of data centers. It is changing the dynamic of where we need energy storage.” PNNL said in a January news release that artificial intelligence (AI) data centers can cause sudden spikes and drops in demand, which stored energy can be called on to absorb. What the Failure Data Shows EPRI’s BESS Failure Incident Database, which the institute started in 2021 after a cluster of lithium-ion fires in South Korea and an incident in Surprise, Arizona, tracks failures worldwide. The 99% figure includes 33 non-public incidents that EPRI is aware of. The institute attributes the improvement to lessons from early failures being built into newer designs and best practices. The database has limits that matter to anyone reading it as a reliability measure. EPRI says its focus is on incidents with wider public health and safety impact rather than operational failures, so it is not a measure of everyday availability. It is compiled from media reports and other public documents, and EPRI acknowledges it cannot guarantee that every incident is captured. As of Oct. 11, 2026, the stationary-storage table listed 165 incidents worldwide. EPRI, working with TWAICE and PNNL, has also classified incidents by root cause (design, manufacturing, integration and construction, operation, or a combination) and by the physical location of the failure, including cells and modules, controls, and balance-of-system equipment. The framework is a reminder that cells are only one place a system can fail. Moss Landing: Lessons From a Legacy Design WECC’s report on the January 2025 fire is the clearest public look at how an early large-scale system differs from what is being built today. WECC stressed that the report is not a root cause analysis, and Vistra says the cause of the fire is still unknown. What the report does document is the design and operating context. Phase 1 of Moss Landing, which reached operation at the end of 2020, was housed in a repurposed turbine building, with racks of nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) cells stacked two high across two stories. artigo.texto: O primeiro teste de inteligência artificial do Google em órbita terminou de um jeito inesperado: com um poema enviado do espaço para a Terra. A empresa anunciou em 30 de outubro de 2026 que o satélite experimental do Project Suncatcher executou o modelo Gemma 4 em um de seus chips de IA e transmitiu a resposta para uma estação terrestre. É um passo importante para a ideia de construir data centers no espaço, alimentados por energia solar. Mas há uma diferença entre a demonstração e essa ambição: por enquanto, o Google tem um protótipo que realiza tarefas curtas de processamento, não um serviço comercial capaz de substituir os enormes centros de dados em funcionamento na Terra. O que a inteligência artificial do Google escreveu no espaço? Depois de semanas verificando os sistemas do satélite, os engenheiros enviaram uma instrução da Terra pedindo ao Gemma 4 que produzisse um haicai, forma curta de poema de origem japonesa, sobre estar no espaço. O texto foi gerado pelo computador a bordo e recebido durante a passagem da nave pela região de Svalbard, na Noruega. Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ O poema descreve a Terra como uma esfera azul abaixo do satélite, imagina fluxos de dados em silêncio e associa a luz das estrelas à energia que alimenta o computador. A resposta pode parecer simples, mas é a prova de que o equipamento recebeu uma instrução, executou um modelo de linguagem em órbita e devolveu o resultado. O Google chama esse resultado de seu primeiro marco de “Hello World”, expressão usada em programação para indicar que um sistema conseguiu realizar uma operação inicial. Segundo a empresa, foi a primeira resposta de IA obtida a partir de uma TPU de classe data center em órbita. Isso não equivale a dizer que foi a primeira IA da história a funcionar no espaço. Depois do haicai, os pesquisadores fizeram novos testes com poemas de outro formato e solicitações sobre o estado dos equipamentos do satélite. A confirmação foi publicada no blog oficial do Google em 30 de outubro. Como funciona o satélite do Project Suncatcher? O protótipo foi desenvolvido em parceria com a Planet Labs e lançado em 1º de outubro de 2026 a bordo de um foguete Falcon 9, da SpaceX, na missão Transporter-18. O equipamento leva quatro TPUs, sigla para Tensor Processing Units, os processadores especializados que o Google também utiliza para acelerar modelos de inteligência artificial em seus servidores terrestres. O modelo usado no teste foi o Gemma 4, da família de modelos abertos do Google DeepMind. Ele não deve ser confundido com o Gemini, serviço de IA oferecido aos usuários. A demonstração foi de inferência: o sistema utilizou um modelo já preparado para produzir uma resposta, em vez de treinar um novo modelo do zero. Segundo informações publicadas pelo TechCrunch, o satélite gera até cerca de 1 kW de potência elétrica, mas dispõe de energia e capacidade de dissipar calor suficientes para acionar apenas uma TPU por vez, durante aproximadamente 20 minutos. Portanto, ter quatro chips a bordo não significa que todos possam trabalhar simultaneamente. Essa restrição explica parte da complexidade da missão. Um computador potente produz calor mesmo no espaço, e o vácuo não permite resfriá-lo por circulação de ar como acontece na Terra. O calor precisa ser conduzido para superfícies capazes de irradiá-lo. A nave também está sujeita à radiação espacial, que pode alterar informações armazenadas e comprometer os cálculos. Por que o Google quer construir data centers no espaço? A ideia do Project Suncatcher é investigar se conjuntos de satélites, abastecidos por painéis solares e conectados entre si, poderão executar trabalhos de IA em grande escala. Em determinadas órbitas, o acesso frequente à luz solar poderia oferecer uma fonte de energia atraente para uma indústria que precisa de cada vez mais eletricidade. O desafio é transformar essa vantagem potencial em uma infraestrutura confiável. Não basta colocar chips em órbita. Será necessário demonstrar resfriamento eficiente, resistência a anos de radiação, comunicação rápida entre satélites, manutenção viável e custos de lançamento competitivos. Isso também ajuda a entender o debate sobre os gastos bilionários da indústria com servidores e aceleradores de IA. O Overdrive já explicou por que os investimentos em inteligência artificial levantam preocupações financeiras. Levar parte desse processamento ao espaço seria uma aposta ainda mais longa, não uma solução imediata para o preço da computação. Qual é o próximo passo do Google? Com a primeira resposta recebida, a equipe continuará avaliando como as TPUs se comportam sob estresse térmico e exposição à radiação em condições reais de voo. Esses resultados são fundamentais para descobrir se componentes utilizados em data centers podem operar de forma confiável fora da Terra. O próximo objetivo anunciado é colocar dois satélites interconectados em órbita em 2027. A missão deverá explorar a comunicação por enlaces ópticos, que utilizam luz para transmitir dados entre naves. Essa conexão é essencial para a proposta de fazer diversos computadores espaciais trabalharem de maneira coordenada. Até lá, o poema é um resultado técnico, não a inauguração de uma nuvem de IA espacial para consumidores. Para quem quer experimentar modelos semelhantes sem depender integralmente da nuvem, o Overdrive reúne opções de inteligência artificial que podem rodar no computador e um guia para executar IA local sem internet. Perguntas rápidas O Google já tem um data center funcionando no espaço? O Google tem um protótipo em órbita que executou uma tarefa de inteligência artificial e enviou o resultado à Terra. Ainda não existe, nessa missão, um data center comercial operando continuamente como os servidores terrestres. Qual IA escreveu o poema enviado pelo satélite? artigo.texto: SECI, OHPC Plan 3 GW Floating Solar, BESS Projects in Odisha by 2030 Solar Energy Corporation of India and Odisha Hydro Power Corporation have signed a binding term sheet to jointly develop 3 GW of floating solar and battery energy storage projects across Odisha's reservoirs by 2030 through a 50:50 joint venture, with power offtake envisaged through GRIDCO. The term sheet was signed at the BRE Summit and Expo 2026. November 04, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) and Odisha Hydro Power Corporation (OHPC) have signed a Binding Term Sheet for jointly developing large-scale floating solar photovoltaic (PV) projects integrated with battery energy storage systems (BESS) across various reservoirs in Odisha. The projects will be developed through a 50:50 joint venture (JV), with power offtake envisaged through GRIDCO Ltd. The term sheet was signed by Sivakumar V Vepakomma, Director (Power Systems), SECI, and Amiya Kumar Mohanty, Director (Operations), OHPC, in the presence of Odisha Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi, Deputy Chief Minister Kanak Vardhan Singh Deo, Akash Tripathi, Managing Director, SECI, and Vishal Kumar Dev, Additional Chief Secretary, Energy Department, Government of Odisha. With an estimated floating solar potential of around 12 GW, Odisha offers significant opportunities for harnessing reservoir resources for renewable energy development. Under the proposed partnership, SECI and OHPC are targeting approximately 3 GW of renewable energy capacity under the capital expenditure (CAPEX) mode by 2030. The initiative also represents an important milestone towards SECI's target of adding 10 GW of capacity through its own projects by 2030, strengthening its portfolio of owned renewable energy assets. The proposed integration of floating solar PV and battery storage is expected to support the supply of reliable, clean and dispatchable renewable power, particularly during peak demand hours. The collaboration is also aimed at strengthening Odisha's energy security while facilitating greater renewable energy integration into the power system.
