artigo.texto: O mercado de geração distribuída (GD) de energia solar no Brasil começou 2026 em ritmo mais lento, com retração nas novas conexões, queda nas importações de módulos fotovoltaicos e dificuldades para transformar propostas comerciais em vendas. Ao mesmo tempo, sistemas de armazenamento com baterias e infraestrutura de recarga de veículos elétricos ampliam sua participação nos negócios dos integradores, indicando uma diversificação das soluções oferecidas pelo setor. Os dados fazem parte do Estudo Estratégico de Soluções Energéticas Distribuídas (SED), elaborado pela Greener, com resultados referentes ao primeiro semestre de 2026. O levantamento mostra que o Brasil chegou a 53 GW de potência instalada em geração distribuída até junho, com a adição de 3,97 GW no período, volume 23% inferior aos 5,2 GW registrados no primeiro semestre de 2025. A desaceleração foi mais expressiva na minigeração distribuída, com queda de 33,7% na potência adicionada em comparação com o mesmo período do ano anterior. Já a microgeração permaneceu praticamente estável, com retração de 0,8%. Na quantidade de novas conexões, o recuo foi de 16%, passando de 488 mil no primeiro semestre de 2025 para 411 mil nos seis primeiros meses de 2026. O número de novas unidades consumidoras que passaram a receber créditos de energia de forma remota também diminuiu, com queda de 43%, de 951 mil para 541 mil. A distribuição da potência adicionada por classe de consumo também revela mudanças no perfil da geração distribuída brasileira. O segmento residencial passou a concentrar 65% da potência instalada no primeiro semestre de 2026, ante 57% em 2025 e 39% em 2019. Em sentido contrário, a participação comercial caiu de 30% em 2023 para 19% no período mais recente. A expansão da GD continua distribuída pelo território nacional. Os 3,97 GW adicionados no semestre foram registrados em 5.192 municípios. São Paulo liderou a lista de cidades com maior potência adicionada, com 43 MW, seguido por Brasília, com 36 MW, e Cuiabá, com 32 MW. Importação de módulos fotovoltaicos recua 48% O movimento de desaceleração também aparece na cadeia de fornecimento de equipamentos. As importações de módulos fotovoltaicos nacionalizadas no Brasil somaram 5,5 GWp no primeiro semestre de 2026, retração de 48% em relação aos 10,6 GWp do mesmo intervalo de 2025. A maior queda ocorreu na geração centralizada (GC), cujo volume importado diminuiu 82%, passando de 2,3 GWp para 0,43 GWp. Na geração distribuída, a redução foi de 39%, de 8,2 GWp para 5 GWp. Com isso, a GD respondeu por aproximadamente 90% do volume nacionalizado no período. Apesar da retração, os custos de nacionalização continuam representando uma parcela relevante do valor dos equipamentos. Segundo o levantamento, esses custos correspondem a 44% do valor CIF, com o Imposto de Importação, de 25%, como principal componente. Dificuldade de integradores na conversão de proposta O cenário de desaceleração também se reflete na atividade comercial das empresas integradoras de energia solar. A média mensal de orçamentos avançou de 20 no primeiro semestre de 2025 para 25 no mesmo período de 2026, crescimento de 25%. Entretanto, a taxa de conversão das propostas em vendas ficou em apenas 18%. Na prática, aproximadamente oito em cada dez orçamentos não se transformaram em negócios. A média mensal de sistemas vendidos passou de quatro para cinco por empresa, acompanhando a recuperação na quantidade de propostas. O financiamento também perdeu participação nas vendas. No primeiro semestre de 2026, 33% das vendas contaram com crédito, oito pontos percentuais abaixo do registrado em 2025. Os juros elevados e as dificuldades de aprovação bancária continuam entre os principais obstáculos para o fechamento de negócios. A concorrência baseada em preços aparece como a maior pressão sobre os integradores, citada por 63% das empresas entrevistadas. Na sequência estão os juros elevados no financiamento, mencionados por 52%, e as dificuldades de aprovação de crédito, apontadas por 40%. Outro desafio é a inversão de fluxo de potência, que passou a atingir 38% dos integradores, ante 28% no primeiro semestre de 2025. Embora a taxa de resolução dos casos tenha avançado de 39% para 50%, metade das ocorrências ainda não havia sido solucionada, segundo o levantamento. Baterias ampliam participação no mercado solar Em meio à desaceleração dos sistemas fotovoltaicos convencionais, o armazenamento de energia começa a ganhar espaço no portfólio das empresas. O estudo aponta que 86% dos integradores já oferecem sistemas híbridos, percentual 15 pontos percentuais superior ao registrado no primeiro semestre de 2025. A participação dessas soluções nas vendas também aumentou, passando de 2% para 5% em um ano. Além disso, 38% dos integradores realizaram pelo menos uma venda de sistemas com baterias no primeiro semestre de 2026. A principal motivação dos consumidores para procurar soluções de armazenamento é a confiabilidade do fornecimento de energia e a continuidade das atividades, responsável por 51% da demanda identificada. Outros fatores incluem consumidores sem acesso à rede elétrica, interesse em novas tecnologias e redução de custos em horários de ponta. O segmento residencial concentra 65% das vendas de sistemas com baterias, com destaque para residências de alto padrão, que representam 40% do mercado. Já os segmentos comercial e industrial somam 25%, com oportunidades relacionadas à proteção de cargas críticas, ao perfil tarifário e aos impactos financeiros de interrupções no fornecimento. Apesar do avanço, a ampliação das vendas ainda depende da capacitação técnica e comercial dos integradores. O levantamento destaca a necessidade de desenvolver competências para diagnosticar o perfil de consumo dos clientes, dimensionar os equipamentos e avaliar a viabilidade econômica das soluções. artigo.texto: IT Home, November 2 news: Today, CATL announced the simultaneous signing of a strategic cooperation agreement and a product cooperation agreement with Blue Vector. CATL has custom-developed an aviation power battery for Blue Vector’s SKYLA V30 aircraft. Blue Vector has selected CATL as its exclusive battery partner, and both parties are jointly advancing innovation and application in electric aviation technology. Blue Vector notes that for eVTOLs, the power battery system directly impacts the aircraft's overall weight, range, flight performance, and operational safety. Compared to ground vehicles, electric aviation demands higher standards for the safety, reliability, and lightweight design of power systems, and related technologies must undergo continuous validation through system integration, engineering verification, and airworthiness certification processes. CATL has deep expertise in battery technology research and development, system safety design, manufacturing processes, and quality management. Blue Vector specializes in the research, development, production, sales, and operational services of eVTOLs. Its SKYLA V30 is a fully electric tiltrotor eVTOL aircraft, continuously advancing key technologies such as full-aircraft design, power system integration, flight control, and software-defined aircraft architecture through research and engineering validation. In addition to the collaboration on the SKYLA V30 model, both parties will cooperate in areas such as technological innovation, scientific research synergy, standard setting, market expansion, and scenario operations. IT Home notes that the SKYLA V30 is a 2.5-ton, six-seat all-electric passenger eVTOL featuring a tiltrotor design, combining vertical takeoff and landing capability with the efficient cruise performance of a fixed-wing aircraft, offering a range of 260 kilometers and a maximum speed of 320 km/h.

artigo.texto: A new survey by the University of Houston’s Hobby School of Public Affairs shows that 65% of likely voters in Texas believe artificial intelligence will do more harm to society than good. This comes from the Hobby School’s newly released report “Texas Votes 2026 Data Centers and Artificial Intelligence,” which explores the views of the state’s likely voters on data centers and AI. Among Texas voters’ top concerns are the potential effects of data centers on electricity prices and water supplies, along with the possibility that they could increase the frequency of power outages. More than two-thirds of those surveyed said they are extremely or very concerned about the massive computing centers’ resource consumption. According to the survey, 79% of Texas voters support limiting the number of data centers that can be built in the state. A total of 99% say proposed data centers should cover the cost of electric-grid expansions needed to power the facilities. The report also found a disconnect between Texas’ public officials, who have tended to rally around data center expansion, and voters, who are highly skeptical of AI expansion. In response to the growing backlash and a tightening race against Democratic rival Gina Hinojosa, Gov. Greg Abbott has issued decrees pausing data center grid-connection approvals and directed the Texas Water Development Board to compel data centers to report their water usage until an audit of the projects is conducted. That’s a departure from Abbott’s November 2025 declaration that Texas is “the epicenter of AI development.” What’s more, the governor has declined to call a special legislative session to address growing concerns about the expansion of data centers statewide. artigo.texto: Mercado de carbono brasileiro terá regras próprias para aviação Portaria coloca setor sob regras da Anac, que regulamentará o uso do SAF, o combustível sustentável de aviação O setor de transporte aéreo terá de cumprir regras próprias no mercado regulado de carbono do Brasil, definiu nesta semana o Ministério da Fazenda. O cronograma de implementação foi divulgado na 5ª feira (29.out.2026) pela pasta em uma portaria que definiu as datas e os setores que serão obrigados a medir, relatar e verificar emissões e remoções de gases de efeito estufa a partir de 2027. Leia a íntegra (PDF – 190 kB). O novo sistema, que será gradualmente implementado até 2030, determina que grandes empresas comecem a medir anualmente suas emissões de carbono equivalente. A obrigação de MRV (Mensuração, Relato e Verificação), prevista na lei que criou o SBCE (Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões), será aplicada a indústrias com emissões a partir de 10 mil tCO₂e (tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente) ao ano, o equivalente a menos de 1% dos CNPJs do país, segundo a Fazenda. O setor aéreo, no entanto, ficará submetido a regras distintas, sob regulação da Anac (Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil). O órgão é responsável pela regulamentação do também recém-lançado ProBioQAV (Programa Nacional de Combustível Sustentável de Aviação), que deve entrar em vigor em 2027. As regras para a redução de emissões no setor aéreo estão dentro do programa e foram definidas em decreto baixado em agosto pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). A resolução deu à Anac e à ANP (Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis) a competência para implementar, operacionalizar e fiscalizar o nova política. A regulamentação, que está em consulta pública na ANP e já passou pelo rito na Anac, será guiada pela redução efetiva de emissões de gases de efeito estufa. A partir de 2027, companhias aéreas que atuam no Brasil precisarão reduzir gradualmente as suas emissões por meio do uso do SAF (combustível sustentável de aviação, na sigla em português). Ao separar o setor aéreo do cronograma das demais indústrias, o Ministério da Fazenda levou em conta que o processo regulatório das agências considera o Corsia (Esquema de Compensação e Redução de Carbono para a Aviação Internacional, na sigla em português), um mecanismo global criado pela usado para medir e compensar as emissões de dióxido de carbono em voos internacionais. “Essa abordagem permitirá aproveitar a infraestrutura em desenvolvimento para o Registro Central do SBCE, com alinhamento às melhores práticas internacionais, simplificação regulatória e redução de custos para o setor”, disse a Fazenda. CERTIFICADOS DE SAF As regras para o setor de aviação permitirão que as companhias emitam um documento chamado CS-SAF (certificados de sustentabilidade de combustível sustentável de aviação), que comprova a redução de emissões associada ao uso de combustíveis sustentáveis. O decreto também determina que os produtores de combustível sustentável emitam certificados que indiquem a redução de emissões em comparação ao querosene tradicional. O documento poderá ser vendido às companhias aéreas, que precisarão utilizá-lo para comprovar cumprimento de metas climáticas. A regulamentação institui metas graduais de redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa na aviação doméstica. Nos primeiros 2 anos, operadores aéreos devem garantir uma redução de pelo menos 1% ao ano nas emissões de dióxido de carbono em voos domésticos. A partir de 2029, a meta de corte cresce 1 ponto percentual até 2037, quando deverá atingir pelo menos 10%. O CS-SAF permitirá que empresas negociem separadamente o atributo ambiental do combustível sustentável de aviação do seu volume físico. “O mecanismo amplia a viabilidade logística do SAF, facilita sua utilização em aeroportos de todo o país e estabelece um sistema seguro para registro, rastreabilidade e comprovação das reduções de emissões”, afirma o Ministério de Minas e Energia. O combustível também poderá ser utilizado por outra empresa de qualquer setor no chamado mercado voluntário, por meio da venda de certificados para compensar emissões próprias. O modelo proposto é conhecido como “book & claim” e já é adotado em outros segmentos. O decreto cria também o Programa Nacional de Certificação do Combustível Sustentável de Aviação, que estabelece regras para certificação obrigatória do combustível produzido no Brasil ou importado. O objetivo é assegurar a rastreabilidade e a integridade ambiental do produto ao longo de toda a cadeia. O SAF, antes chamado de bioquerosene, é um biocombustível feito a partir de matérias-primas renováveis ou de baixo carbono, como óleos vegetais, resíduos agrícolas, lixo orgânico, etanol ou gases industriais, em vez do petróleo usado no querosene tradicional.

artigo.texto: As data center developments expand across Iowa, lawmakers are looking for ways to increase transparency around the industry’s resource use and the public incentives companies receive. Rep. Cindy Golding, R-Cedar Rapids, introduced House File 2690 during the 2026 Legislative Session, which would have required data centers to submit quarterly reports on their energy and water consumption, with information made publicly available within 30 days. Seven bills related to data center policies were introduced in the Iowa legislature in 2026, but none of them were passed into law. Golding said her proposal was prompted by constituents who felt they were being left out of conversations about large-scale data center development, including projects in the Cedar Rapids area. “I am not opposed to data centers. I’m not even opposed to hyper centers,” Golding said. “I’m opposed to the lack of transparency with constituents, especially when tax dollars are involved.” Cedar Rapids has been a recent hub for data center development in the state, attracting developments including Google’s Hyperscale Campus, which is a project included in Google’s multi-billion dollar investment in Iowa. Golding distinguished traditional data centers, which can range from server rooms in commercial buildings to smaller offsite facilities, from hyperscale data centers, which require significantly more electricity and water, and generate more concentrated heat. RELATED: Advocacy groups focus on abortion, tax relief, and education ahead of midterm elections She said concerns grew as residents began noticing increased construction activity and traffic without understanding the scope of the projects. “Our economic development initiatives should be focused on growing Iowa, not importing large corporations who then export our resources and our revenues,” she said. Iowa data centers become platforms on the campaign trail Data centers have become a large issue for Iowa candidates running for office, with candidates raising questions about the tax incentives, resources use and transparency surrounding the industry. According to the Iowa Department of Revenue, eligible data center businesses that invest more than $200 million within their first six years of operation receive a full exemption on Iowa Sales and Use tax on qualifying items. Items include computers, servers, cooling systems, and power infrastructure. In August, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand introduced his policy plan for data centers if elected to office. The policy included ending tax breaks for data centers, and requiring transparency from centers surrounding building size and acreage, number of jobs, overview of water usage and energy use. “These major corporations should be paying full freight and carrying their own weight, not raising Iowans’ costs for anything, and must respect the communities they move to,” Sand said in a statement. Similarly, his Republican opponent Zach Lahn said he wants to raise taxes on data centers, and in a gubernatorial debate on Oct. 14, said data centers should not receive any tax incentives and proposed a moratorium if residents feel development is moving too quickly. A moratorium would require a pause on the construction of a center, until laws are enacted to regulate data center development. “The number one thing with data centers is that we need to be negotiating properly,” Lahn said in the Oct. 14 debate. “I believe the state has a role to play to make sure they’re setting the rules of the game.” U.S. Senate candidates Democratic nominee Josh Turek and Republican nominee Ashley Hinson clashed on the topic of data centers in their last debate on Oct. 13, according to previous reporting by The Daily Iowan. The candidates both opposed a federal moratorium on new data centers, but disagreed on the implementation of data centers in the state. Turek opposed continuing tax breaks for centers, and suggested closed-loop water circuits that reuse water to reduce data centers’ consumption of local water supplies. Hinson said data center regulation should happen at the local level, and supported re-opening Duane Arnold nuclear plant to help meet rising electricity demands in the area. The plant is located in Palo, and was shut down in 2020. UI data center tool provides resources to Iowans Beyond the potential economic benefits of data centers, questions about their environmental impacts, infrastructure needs and tax incentives have also become an important part of broader policy discussion. The University of Iowa’s Hubbell Environmental Law Initiative, or HELI, developed its Iowa Data Center Decision Tool to help local governments and community leaders navigate these questions. Jennifer Terry, director of HELI, said the tool was created after communities across Iowa expressed difficulty finding the information and resources necessary to make informed decisions about data center development. The initiative worked with city and county planners, utility providers, economic development organizations, and other community stakeholders to develop a resource that addresses the different considerations involved in approving data center projects. “The decision tool is not pro data center or anti data center,” Terry said. “It doesn’t tell communities whether they should or shouldn’t do data center development.” Instead, Terry described the resource as a risk management tool that encourages communities to consider questions about water availability, energy capacity, land use and resident input before entering into agreements with developers. Mae McDonough, who worked on the tools development, said the project began less than a year and was released in August. HELI plans to continue updating the resource as the industry and policy landscape changes. artigo.texto: O Brasil pode atrair US$ 60 bilhões por ano em investimentos em data centers até 2050, o dobro dos cerca de US$ 30 bilhões anuais de hoje. É o que projeta o estudo "Global Data Centre Outlook 2026-2050", da PwC com a Oxford Economics. O levantamento cobre 46 países e territórios e modela como a corrida por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial deve se espalhar pelo mundo até a metade do século. No cenário central do estudo, o gasto global com data centers sobe de cerca de US$ 800 bilhões em 2026 para US$ 1,1 trilhão em 2030 e US$ 1,8 trilhão em 2050. Somado ao longo de todo o período, o total projetado é de US$ 31,6 trilhões. Em um cenário de aceleração ainda maior da adoção de inteligência artificial, o investimento acumulado pode chegar perto de US$ 50 trilhões, segundo a PwC. "O Brasil reúne características importantes para atrair esta nova onda de investimentos. Somos um país com um grande mercado consumidor", disse Daniel Martins, sócio da PwC Brasil que lidera o setor de energia e utilidades, ao comentar o estudo. Por que o Brasil pesa nessa conta O país aparece entre as economias das Américas com maior potencial de ampliar participação no setor, ao lado do Chile e do Canadá. É hoje o maior mercado de data centers da América Latina. Publicidade Segundo a PwC, três fatores decidem como esse dinheiro se divide entre os países: a disponibilidade de energia, as regras de soberania de dados e a cadeia de suprimento de semicondutores. É justamente nesses três pontos que o Brasil tenta se posicionar, com energia relativamente barata e a promessa de dados processados dentro do próprio país. O movimento já havia sido descrito em outros números no país. Em setembro, um estudo setorial avaliou que um único data center de IA pode movimentar R$ 25 bilhões e gerar 37 mil empregos. O governo também aposta na área: o presidente Lula já disse que o programa Redata pode trazer R$ 500 bilhões em investimentos ligados à inteligência artificial em português. O boom tem um custo que já aparece nos números: data centers de IA em São Paulo consomem 16,1 bilhões de litros de água por ano, segundo outro estudo. É o lado da conta que o otimismo do investimento não resolve sozinho.

artigo.texto: O rápido desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial ( IA ), da computação em nuvem e da economia digital está transformando os centros de dados de uma infraestrutura tecnológica em um alicerce essencial da economia digital. À medida que a IA se desenvolve, a demanda por poder computacional, armazenamento, conectividade e processamento de dados aumenta, exigindo que a infraestrutura dos centros de dados seja moderna, flexível e escalável. Segundo as previsões, o mercado de IA do Vietnã poderá atingir US$ 1,52 bilhão até 2030, enquanto a IA deverá contribuir com até US$ 130 bilhões para a economia até 2040; somente a infraestrutura de IA poderá representar aproximadamente US$ 25 bilhões. Esses números mostram que a necessidade de construir infraestrutura capaz de suportar o desenvolvimento da IA não é mais uma preocupação de longo prazo. No entanto, construir data centers de última geração não se resume simplesmente a aumentar a escala. A infraestrutura deve atender às demandas de alta densidade de computação, GPUs, redes de alta velocidade, armazenamento de alta capacidade e tecnologia de refrigeração avançada, garantindo, ao mesmo tempo, a continuidade, a segurança e a escalabilidade dos dados à medida que a tecnologia evolui. Em particular, o rápido aumento da demanda por computação também exerce maior pressão sobre o consumo de eletricidade, água de refrigeração, custos operacionais e controle de emissões. Portanto, a questão não é apenas quantos centros de dados adicionais o Vietnã precisa, mas, mais importante, como construir e operar essa infraestrutura para que ela possa acompanhar o rápido desenvolvimento da IA, sendo também eficiente em termos energéticos, segura, sustentável e não se tornando obsoleta rapidamente. Com base nesses requisitos, em 3 de novembro de 2026, o jornal Indústria e Comércio organizou um seminário com o tema: “Data Centers do Vietnã: Infraestrutura Estratégica para a Era da IA”. Participaram do seminário especialistas como: Sr. Ha Dang Son - especialista em energia e Diretor do Centro de Pesquisa em Energia e Crescimento Verde; Sr. Nguyen Tien Long - Vice-Diretor de Negócios daFPT International Telecommunications Company Limited (FTI), subsidiária da FPT Telecom; e Sr. Do Thanh Thang, Diretor de Otimização de Operações para o Leste Asiático da Schneider Electric.

artigo.texto: A sprawling data center and energy complex proposal east of Casper is not dead, according to the property owner, despite Prometheus Hyperscale pulling out of the project last Wednesday. Falls Ranch, a limited partnership owned by Texas billionaire Russell Gordy, announced last week that “work will continue without delay.” “The work by the community and local leaders has helped lay the foundation for a project with the potential to position Natrona County as a leader in the growing data center industry, building on Wyoming’s energy resources, skilled workforce and experience supporting major industrial development, and should not be wasted,” Falls Ranch stated in a press release after Prometheus’ announcement. Though it was not involved in initial development plans, according to the company, the groundwork has been laid for it to see the project to fruition. “We anticipate that with this change, the project should continue forward on a more efficient track, including community and business collaborations,” Falls Ranch representative Robert Hand said. “This has always been a Wyoming project, but today it represents something even greater: an opportunity for Natrona County to shape its own economic future.” More details will be revealed in the near future, Hand added. Prometheus announced its departure from the project Wednesday. Originally, the $500 million, 1,250-megawatt complex was to be sited on Falls Ranch property spanning Natrona and Converse counties north of Interstate 25. In its latest configuration, it would sit entirely in Natrona County, south of the interstate. The move opened the door for developers to bypass a state-level Industrial Siting Council review and permitting process to instead empower Natrona County commissioners to vet the project. If green lit locally, however, the endeavor would still be subject to review from several state and federal agencies. That process had not advanced beyond initial discussions before Prometheus exited the project. artigo.texto: Wave of BESS augmentation financing expected in a few years The topic of battery energy storage systems (BESS) augmentation was a key one at the Battery Asset Management Summit UK & Ireland 2026 last month, held in London by our publisher Solar Media, part of Informa Connect. There may be a wave of BESS augmentation-linked financings in a few years’ time in the UK, a speaker at a recent Solar Media event said. The topic of battery energy storage systems (BESS) augmentation was a key one at the Battery Asset Management Summit UK & Ireland 2026 last month, held in London by our publisher Solar Media, part of Informa Connect. Speakers from various UK BESS owner-operators discussed the topic on stage at the two-day event. Here are the key takeaways, in a shortened write-up of a piece that originally appeared on our sister site Energy-Storage.news as part of its subscription-based ESN Premium offering. Build assumptions, track the market Javier Arrue, investment director at BW ESS, said you need some assumptions around augmentation built into your model from the start, that you need to track the market but also that BESS supply developments were making life a bit easier for augmentation planning. “It’s also interesting to see battery manufacturers now defaulting to 4-hour systems. That supports delaying augmentation as you’re adding extra capacity to your batteries, which is a benefit,” he said. Expect a wave of augmentation financings in the medium term Pablo Zalvide, structured finance and M&A lead for UK BESS at Fotowatio Renewable Ventures (FRV), expects a wave of financings for augmentation in a few years’ time. “In a few years, there will be a wave of projects needing refinancing. Even where debt sizing was based on a 15-year warranty duration, most financing in place today is structured as mini-perm, around seven years. That means a wave of projects will come up for refinancing, potentially with outdated duration assumptions by that point. I’d expect a good portion of those projects to pursue augmentation at the point of refinancing,” he said. LTSAs Ricardo Folgado, managing partner for owner-operator TagEnergy, essentially said that factoring augmentation into long-term service agreements (LTSAs) is a challenge and so, for multiple reasons, the company tends to stay away from such contracts. Folgado said: “You want to sell the assets, you want to recontract, you want to augment, you want to do something, and you’re locked in, so they’re not ideal. That’s probably an obvious thing to say, but my advice would probably be to not enter into a long-term contract.” Have a good energy management system Gore Street Capital’s senior asset manager, David Harris, said having a good EMS is key. “I think when it comes to state of health (SOH), the point where it really matters is when you start to augment your sites because then you have a site that’s in two halves where you might be able to dispatch at full power one half of your site for a full hour, but then your more degraded older part of the site might only last 50 minutes,” he explained. “So that’s where you really need to have a good EMS in place that can telemeter the right values and discharge each unit at different rates, perhaps, but maintain a declared level for that full hour, or where it can.” Augmentation risk is under-priced currently Harris’ colleague, project development manager Michael Darzi, highlighted augmentation and repowering as a key risk that is currently being under-priced. “Let’s say we might go with one technology provider when we build our system, but as technology evolves, maybe that supplier will no longer be relevant in the market, or maybe we like someone else’s technology. How does that play with the existing technology? How do the EMS and the PPC controller also have an impact?” he asked. Read more about:

artigo.texto: MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sungrow, a globally leading PV inverter and energy storage system provider, announced the Australian debut of its all-in-one residential energy storage system, PowerHarbour, at All-Energy Australia 2026. The platform responds to Australia's booming home battery market, with accelerating uptake driven by the federal government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program. Built around Sungrow's "Triple W" value proposition — Win More, Waste Less, Work Faster — PowerHarbour combines intelligent energy management, flexible storage and simplified installation in an integrated solution. It aims to simplify energy management for Australian households, whether installing a new solar-plus-storage system or upgrading an existing setup. Integrated EV Charging: Empowering the EV and V2X Era Australia's growing EV market is also reshaping household energy needs. According to the Electric Vehicle Council, battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles accounted for 34.5% of new vehicle sales in September 2026, highlighting the increasing relevance of home charging. Responding to this shift, the PowerHarbour Pro range introduces integrated EV charging in selected configurations*, bringing the inverter, energy management system and charging hardware together within a compact power core. Designed with future V2X applications in mind, it reflects Sungrow's approach to connecting home energy management with electric mobility. High Flexibility & Scalability: Tailored for Australia's Large Residential Loads For many Australian households, solar generation peaks during the day, with Solar Sharer offering free midday electricity in some regions; household electricity demand often surges in the evening. To address this mismatch, PowerHarbour incorporates AI-driven energy management that analyses weather forecasts, solar predictions, consumption patterns, and electricity pricing to optimize energy scheduling—helping homeowners, especially those in larger properties with higher electricity demands, make the most of the energy they generate. Heavy-Duty Protection: Built for Extreme Australian Climates From coastal salt mist to harsh inland conditions, PowerHarbour is engineered for high durability across Australia's environmental extremes: Optimized Installation: Streamlined for Local Clean Energy Contractors For Australian installers, PowerHarbour's integrated architecture streamlines new installations and existing system upgrades. Its stackable battery modules and plug-and-play design help reduce installation complexity and additional wiring requirements. "Australia's transition towards more connected home energy systems presents a significant opportunity for the industry. We believe the next step is not simply adding more features, but making solar, storage and energy management work together more effectively. With PowerHarbour, our focus is on bringing these technologies together in a practical, flexible solution that can support different household needs as the market evolves." said Scott Su, Technical Service Director, Sungrow Australia. As Australia's residential energy landscape evolves, Sungrow aims to support smarter home energy systems through PowerHarbour and close collaboration with local distributors and installers, helping households meet changing energy needs and move toward a more sustainable energy future.

artigo.texto: AI, energy storage, and more: ISO-NE staff share expertise at October events Collaboration, expertise, and innovation are three of ISO New England’s core values. Staff embody these values by presenting their work at electricity industry conferences and events around the region, the country, and the world. Here’s a selection of their October speaking engagements. Chris Geissler, director of Economic Analysis, Market Development, discussed the Capacity Auction Reforms key project at the Northeast Energy and Commerce Association Fuels Conference in Boston on Oct. 1. He highlighted efforts to modernize the capacity market through seasonal resource accreditation and incentives that support resource performance and winter reliability. Xiaochuan Luo, director of Power System Technology, Advanced Technology Solutions, took part in the Integration of Artificial Intelligence in the Electricity System workshop hosted by the National Academies in Washington on Oct. 26. He was part of a panel titled “AI in Markets, Operations and Data Centers through a Cyber-Physical Security Lens.” Parviz Alivand, principal economist and manager of Market Design, Market Development, took part in the Nodal Trader Conference in Washington on Oct. 22. He was part of a panel titled “Changing Market Dynamics and New Nodal Models,” where he discussed Capacity Auction Reforms, the Day-Ahead Ancillary Services market, and strategies for relieving congestion on the transmission system. Steven Judd, manager of Long-Term Planning, System Planning, and Melissa Winne, lead state policy advisor, External Affairs, led a webinar on Oct. 1 to provide an overview of ISO New England’s longer-term transmission planning (LTTP) process and 2025 LTTP request for proposals. Winne also presented on LTTP topics at the E2Tech Forum in South Portland, Maine, on Oct. 13. Matt Kakley, manager of Media Relations and Strategic Communications, Corporate Communications, spoke at the Connecticut Power and Energy Society’s Future of Energy conference on Oct. 29 in Fairfield. He was part of a panel titled “The Business of Communicating Energy in 2026.” Kakley discussed the ISO’s unique role in New England and how it communicates technical information to help the public understand the challenges facing our future energy landscape. Steven Otto, manager of Economic Analysis, Market Development, spoke on Oct. 26 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, at an event titled “Launching Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES) in Massachusetts: Storing Energy Today for a More Resilient Tomorrow.” He was part of a panel focused on the role of LDES in advancing the affordability and reliability of electricity. Two members of the External Affairs team, Kerry Schlichting, manager of State Policy, and Sarah Adams, senior state policy advisor, External Affairs, hosted virtual office hours on Oct. 23. The event was designed for a non-technical audience to learn about ISO New England. Adams presented on the region’s transition to a new generator interconnection framework at the REV Conference in South Burlington, Vermont, on Oct. 14. She discussed reforms that streamline the interconnection process, improve project readiness requirements, and support the efficient integration of new energy resources onto the grid. On Oct. 28, Adams provided a regional update at the Vermont System Planning Committee quarterly meeting in Killington. She covered market conditions, the ISO’s 2027 priorities, transmission planning initiatives, large load integration, and generator interconnection reforms. Adams and Ruben Flores-Marzan, policy advisor for environmental and community affairs, External Affairs, presented at the Southern New England American Planning Association Conference in Mashantucket, Connecticut, on Oct. 8. They discussed how local land-use decisions shape the region’s electricity future, highlighting the connection between community planning decisions, electricity demand growth, and the region’s evolving grid and transmission needs. Graham Jesmer, senior regulatory counsel, Legal and Compliance, presented on ISO-NE’s approach to dispatching distributed energy resource aggregations during the “Curtailment Problems and Solutions” panel at the Special Institute on Meeting the Demand conference in Denver, Colorado, on Oct. 8. - Categories - Events - Tags - ISO leadership

artigo.texto: The hotbed issue striking statewide for local communities and Tennessee state leaders is AI data centers. On Oct. 27, Gubernatorial candidates faced off at the Tennessee Press Association’s hosted forum. Democratic nominee and Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green and Independent candidates David Hatley and Lauren Pinkston attended the event. Candidates discussed their response to local communities imposing moratoriums on future data center expansions — an issue that currently faces MTSU’s own Rutherford County. Rutherford County Commission unanimously recommended a 12-month moratorium Oct. 12 for a new Rutherford County data center development, pausing its advances and moving the proposal closer to county officials’ consideration. Set for Nov. 3, the Rutherford County Public Works and Planning Committee will discuss “a resolution establishing a one-year moratorium on the acceptance and processing of any land use applications for data centers,” per their meeting agenda. Whichever candidate secures Governor in this election will decide how this issue will be carried out in Tennessee communities. Candidate response Memphis journalist and co-forum moderator Otis Stanford asked candidates, “What specifically would be your policies, as valid, for state government oversight of these data centers?” Given two minutes each for a response, all three candidates agreed to placing limitations on data center advancements but with differing approaches. Hatley said state leaders owe it to citizens to protect them and make sure the data centers are the ones paying for property taxes, power, water and other utilities. The Independent also echoed data centers should have limitations on where they can be placed and how loud they can be. “If they want to come to Tennessee, they’re gonna play by our rules. We have to have these guardrails,” Hatley said. Once data centers can abide by legislation, Hatley said, then counties have the opportunity to vote if they want moratoriums or allow advancements. Green said she’s been against data centers for years and is currently fighting for a moratorium on the Memphis City Council. Green said the next step is to take this statewide before there is “human harm.” “We’re talking about our air and our water. There is nothing more vital to our life, much less the livelihoods of the people whose jobs will be taken by AI,” Green said. Pinkston also calls for a statewide moratorium on data centers, due to technology “outpacing our ability to legislate it.” “The last thing that I want to see is someone in the middle class, in the working class, have to foot the bill for the expansion of the utility systems, and of the water systems that are going to be required to actually keep these businesses up and running in Tennessee,” Pinkston said. Republican candidate and current Sen. Marsha Blackburn did not accept the invitation to TPA’s forum, but she has shared publicly that communities should be able to decide if they want data centers. Blackburn said communities have the right to decline center advancements while some other county mayors are actively recruiting data centers, according to WSMV 4. “There are county mayors that are saying we’ve got excess capacity when it comes to water and utilities and yes, we want them. We’ve got space for them. And they are actively trying to recruit them because they want the jobs,” Blackburn said to WSMV 4. Instead, Blackburn proposes her support for a rate payer protection plan that would let citizens know their water utility and electric power rates are “not going to go up with the advent of any kind of data center” and that the “data center is going to pay for that cost.” Other moratoriums placed this year and public outcry In August, Metro Nashville voted to impose a moratorium on data center advancements at its location next to the Nashville Zoo. The temporary moratorium pauses permit approvals until after Dec. 1, after Nashville Zoo claimed that the data center would cause detrimental harm to its animals, conservation efforts and community. “While this is meaningful progress, our work isn’t over. We remain committed to ensuring the proposed data center is not built adjacent to Nashville Zoo,” according to the zoo’s website. Memphis’ one-year moratorium recently failed to pass Oct. 20, but instead city council members reached for a substitute ordinance that halts data center construction for 135 days. After Tennessee elects its new governor, Tennesseans will have a clear path on how state government oversight will tackle data center advancements and public discourse. Election Day is Nov. 3. For more news, visit www.mtsusidelines.com, and follow us on Facebook at MTSU Sidelines and on X and Instagram at @mtsusidelines. Also, sign up for our weekly newsletter here.

artigo.texto: Alhambra’s Measure DB, a city-wide data center ban by public vote, is leading with 81.8% voting yes, and 18.8% voting no. Results from the Los Angeles County Registrar’s Office included vote-by-mail ballots received before election day, vote center ballots cast before election day and election day ballots transported and counted after vote centers closed. Should voters approve Measure DB with the simple majority needed to win, Alhambra would become the second California city – following in the footsteps of Monterey Park earlier this June – to pass a city-wide data center ban by public vote. The ballot title reads: “Data Centers Prohibited. Shall an ordinance be adopted affirming the Council adopted ban on “Data Centers” by amending the Alhambra Municipal Code to again define ‘Data Centers’ and prohibit them in all zones of the City?” “Measure DB is at 82% support, showing that Alhambra, like Monterey Park and many communities across the SGV, is united against data centers,” SGV Progressive Action co-founder Andrew Yip said. “Even with little to no campaigning, Measure DB has received overwhelming support from voters.” Throughout Los Angeles County, specifically across the San Gabriel Valley, officials have considered various actions to protect residents’ health and utilities amid the data center sprawl. According to the Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning, “developers have expressed preferences for jurisdictions with municipal power utilities, such as the City of Vernon, instead of the County’s unincorporated communities.” Yip and other organizers based in the region under the coalition No Data Center San Gabriel Valley have campaigned for stronger protections like a public vote banning the technology, with Baldwin Park, Montebello and El Monte on their watchlist. Monterey Park voters in June banned the technology outright, passing Measure NDC with 88% of the vote, after a monthslong campaign by community members to prevent data center developer HMC StratCap from building a hyperscale data center at Saturn Park, a site in Monterey Park. Speaking about council’s unanimous approval to place Measure DB on the November ballot, then-Mayor Jeff Maloney said the city had “other pressing land use needs.” “The demand on the space we do have is not going down,” Maloney said in July. “Housing, recreational opportunities, business opportunities – and when you dedicate a big area of land to something, that is essentially low intensity, low economic growth.” Speaking about the poll results, Council member Maloney said he’s “not surprised.” “There was a big push against these types of projects in our community, and I think that the community was really anxious and yearning for an opportunity to have a say on it,” Maloney said. “I’m really pleased that we went through and put this on the ballot, and I’m really pleased with the results so far … these types of passive projects could have a negative impact on our environments.” Results from the Los Angeles County Registrar’s Office are still being tallied.

artigo.texto: Anatel fica sem dinheiro para arcar com o próprio data center Agência precisa de R$ 31 milhões para a estrutura Kleber Pizão - 03/11/2026 22h19 A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) informou ao Governo Federal a possibilidade de suspensão do pagamento de despesas básicas. A instituição acumula R$ 30,7 milhões em faturas pendentes relativas à implantação do seu próprio Data Center localizado no Distrito Federal. A infraestrutura dá suporte para o funcionamento de plataformas digitais voltadas ao público e às operadoras de telecomunicações. O espaço também é responsável pela manutenção dos sistemas internos que viabilizam fiscalizações e rotinas administrativas do órgão. Diante do cenário, o presidente da agência, Carlos Baigorri, solicitou ao Ministério do Planejamento o desbloqueio de R$ 30 milhões. O pedido não é novo e já havia sido negado pelo Ministério da Fazenda, de acordo com a apuração da Folha de S. Paulo. — As projeções apontam risco de insuficiência de limite financeiro para o pagamento integral dos compromissos previstos, especialmente no último trimestre de 2026 — afirmou o presidente da agência. A agência atribui o quadro ao bloqueio governamental de R$ 51,8 milhões determinado em maio, que reduziu sua verba discricionária de R$ 275,3 milhões para R$ 223,5 milhões, um corte de 19%. No final do ano passado a Anatel firmou um contrato de R$ 44,9 milhões com empresas de tecnologia para realizar serviços e fornecer equipamentos. A vigência do acordo vai até dezembro de 2030. Para conter os efeitos do contingenciamento, a agência reguladora adequou contratos, projetos e despesas operacionais no intuito de evitar multas e juros. O órgão relata contenções orçamentárias desde agosto, quando pediu a antecipação de R$ 23,3 milhões previstos para dezembro. — Até o momento, as medidas adotadas têm buscado mitigar os impactos decorrentes da restrição orçamentária imposta à agência. Contudo, a persistência das restrições orçamentárias e financeiras poderá exigir novas medidas de reprogramação de despesas — declarou a agência. O Ministério da Fazenda justificou que as limitações decorrem da necessidade de contingenciamento reavaliada a cada dois meses pela Junta de Execução Orçamentária, com revisão em 24 de novembro. O Tesouro analisa os pedidos para preservar a capacidade mensal de pagamento. Em reação aos cortes, cerca de 40 entidades empresariais divulgaram na terça-feira (27) um documento intitulado “Regulação não é gasto, é investimento”. A iniciativa defende a autonomia orçamentária das agências para assegurar o funcionamento pleno no Orçamento de 2027.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Daily presents a selection of the latest developments from China's automotive industry. Here are the key stories in this edition. BYD Sales Hit 2026 High in October BYD sold 490,168 vehicles in October, coming close to the 500,000 mark. Passenger vehicles accounted for 483,125 units, while exports of passenger cars and pickups reached 169,564 units, up 103% year on year. The Dynasty and Ocean series remained the group's main volume drivers, with combined sales of 423,843 units. Its premium and specialty brands also contributed, with Fangchengbao selling 43,872 vehicles, Denza 15,152 and Yangwang 258. From January to October, BYD's total sales reached 3.62 million vehicles. Overseas exports surpassed 1.5 million units over the same period, underscoring the growing importance of international markets to the automaker's business. CATL Partners with Blue Vector on eVTOL Batteries CATL has partnered with Chinese eVTOL developer Blue Vector Intelligent Technology to develop a customized aviation battery for the company's SKYLA V30 electric aircraft. Under agreements signed on November 2, CATL will become the aircraft's exclusive battery supplier, extending its battery business into the emerging electric aviation sector. The SKYLA V30 is a six-seat, two-ton-class, all-electric tiltrotor aircraft designed for low-altitude intercity passenger transport. The battery system will be tailored to meet the aircraft's range and safety requirements. Beyond battery development, the two companies will also work together on technology development, research, industry standards, market expansion and operational applications. Blue Vector has raised approximately RMB 200 million over the past two months as it advances its eVTOL development. ECARX, Arm to Explore Next-Gen AI Computing Platforms Chinese automotive technology supplier ECARX has signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with Arm to explore next-generation high-performance AI computing platforms for mobility and other industries. The planned collaboration will cover both automotive applications and emerging fields such as physical AI. The two companies intend to work on advanced computing architectures, performance optimization, software adaptation, functional safety and cybersecurity. Their goal is to develop customized solutions for China and global markets, addressing the growing demand for computing power and energy efficiency in complex AI applications. The agreement builds on their existing collaboration through SiEngine, ECARX's automotive semiconductor joint venture. SiEngine's 7nm SE1000 smart cockpit chip is already in mass production, with cumulative shipments exceeding one million units. It is also developing a 5nm automotive-grade AI chip integrating cockpit and driving functions.

artigo.texto: Relative to the size of its electricity system, peak loads, population and economy, Bulgaria has by far the highest battery energy storage penetration rate in the entire world. Moreover, it crushed its own records by almost doubling total capability to 6.23 GW in less than six months. Battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Bulgaria have been growing even faster than the country’s already stellar photovoltaics rate. Operating power online has reached 6.23 GW altogether late last month, compared to 5.41 GW in mid-August and 3.43 GW before the end of May, Capital reported, citing an update from the Electricity System Operator (ESO). The facilities in operation can store more than 19 GWh, translating to an average durability of more than three hours. It is likely another in a string of records, at least among the more developed markets in the segment. Notably, it means four-hour BESS are dominantly being installed, and even one five-hour project has been reported. Battery capability covers 85% of PV capacity Bulgaria is at the top of the world chart relative to the size of its electricity system, peak loads, population and economy. It is in the first league even in absolute terms. Solar power capacity has reached 7.3 GW, the article adds, so the battery coverage in the category is a whopping 85%! Batteries have turned to intensive charging during the night as winter approaches While photovoltaic output has become much more erratic as winter has approached, batteries have turned to intensive charging during the night. After the state support programs have passed, new projects are commercially based and entering a now more saturated market. Between October 1 and 25, batteries supplied 18 GWh per day, against 19.9 GWh absorbed, the news outlet calculated. Prominent role for regional stability ahead of pan-European acceleration As an early mover, Bulgaria’s BESS facilities had a prominent role during this year’s heat waves and droughts in maintaining the stability of the electricity system in the entire region. Neighboring Greece and Romania are accelerating deployment, with high ambitions, as do countries throughout Europe. Nevertheless, wholesale electricity in Bulgaria remains expensive, as well as in most of Southeastern Europe and Hungary, except tangibly milder peaks and daily spreads. Importantly, net power exports have surged. Battery storage still has much room to grow in the wider market. Another factor, besides the energy crisis looming again due to the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, is that Romania’s only nuclear power plant Cernavodă has been offline since August, and one of the two reactors in Bulgaria’s Kozloduy is inactive for maintenance between October 8 and late November. In addition, at the end of October, just two years after its first battery systems came on stream, Bulgaria had 85% of its overall peak electricity load covered with battery power. Some of the most developed markets were much weaker: Texas (17%), Great Britain (17%), Australia (23%) and California (33%).

artigo.texto: Alpena County approves data center moratorium resolution Encourages local governments to enact ordinances Trending ALPENA -- Alpena County Board of Commissioners approved a resolution encouraging local units of government to enact ordinances, restricting the development of data centers in Northeast Michigan. According to County Administrator Jesse Osmer, the commissioners had been approached by community members regarding a data center moratorium. Osmer said that the county doesn't have much say in a moratorium, rather the City of Alpena and townships have to set their own ordinances. "Speaking with the majority of you I found that most of you were opposed (to data centers)," he said. Osmer added that the county can only encourage local units of government to take certain stances when it comes to data centers and moratoriums. "We ourselves cannot put much into place as far as any type of ordinances or anything like that," he said. Osmer explained that the resolution encourages local units of government, townships and the City of Alpena, to create systems that would allow for full transparency in the event that a data center approaches a municipality in the area. "I don't know of any data centers coming to the area, but basically putting on a pause and putting that framework into place in the coming months," Osmer said. In September, Osmer explained that townships enforce their own ordinances, planning development, zoning, et cetera. In the case of a data center, it would be up to the local unit of government to set procedures. If a data center company was looking at county land to develop, the county and company would have to comply with whichever municipality it falls under. He added that in the case of county owned property or in a situation where county property would have to be rezoned, then the county would have an advisory role only though the coordinating zoning committee. “Local cities, villages, and townships actually have the jurisdiction over planning zoning, site plan reviews, approvals, code enforcement related to data centers and their affiliated uses,” Osmer said. “In accordance with their adopted plans, ordinances and procedures, the county does not have jurisdiction over planning development or approval for those data centers.” He explained that the county can draft a “nice letter” making recommendations to local municipalities. “Because it's not really an ordinance or anything. It's a nice letter, basically, to the municipality, it asks, ‘Please refrain from any action that would bring those facilities into our area anytime soon,'" he said. The Alpena County resolution states that local units of government should adopt a moratorium on the planning, construction, permitting, or expansion of any data center. It also states that in the event that a proposed data center comes to the area, a comprehensive study is done to ensure the local ecosystem is protected from potential pollution and/or damage. "It is in the best interest of Alpena County residents that any data center development occur within a clear and comprehensive regulatory framework that protects public resources, ensures transparency, and prevents unintended financial or environmental consequences," the resolution stated. The adopted resolution defines a data center as a specialized facility that houses computing systems and stores large volumes of data. The resolution also notes the rapid growth of cloud storage and artificial intelligence (AI) across the country which places an increased demand on data centers real estate. The resolution also encourages transparency and public disclosure regarding data center projects, including the following considerations: - The source of electrical power for the facility; - The anticipated water usage of the facility and protective measures; - How electric utilities will meet the increased energy demands; - Contractual protections, minimum usage requirements, or exit provisions; - Measures to ensure environmental compliance, equitable cost allocation, and meaningful community benefit. Kayla Wikaryasz can be reached at 989-358-5688 or kwikaryasz@TheAlpenaNews.com.

artigo.texto: Com a previsão de que o mercado brasileiro de data centers dobre de tamanho até 2030, a Powersafe mostra suas soluções para garantir energia segura, incluindo um serviço de logística reversa para baterias. Com avanço dos data centers no Brasil, Powersafe aposta em baterias de alta performance para garantir continuidade das operações Empresa, que já fornece tecnologia para dois dos maiores operadores do País, apresenta no DCD Connect Brasil 2026 soluções Getpower para sistemas de energia de emergência, com engenharia, instalação, comissionamento e logística reversa Novembro de 2026 Com a previsão de que o mercado brasileiro de data centers dobre de tamanho até 2030, a Powersafe, empresa nacionaispecializada em soluções de armazenamento e fornecimento de energia, aposta na ampliação dos negócios com baterias de alta performance para atender à crescente demanda por segurança e continuidade operacional dessas instalações. A companhia, que já fornece tecnologia para dois dos maiores operadores de data centers do País, apresentará suas soluções durante o DCD Connect Brasil 2026, nos dias 4 e 5 de novembro, em São Paulo. Segundo levantamento da consultoria JLL, o Brasil precisa cerca de 660 megawatts (MW) de capacidade de data centers em construção, associados a aproximadamente US$ 17,4 bilhões em investimentos. O crescimento do setor, impulsionado pela computação em nuvem, digitalização das empresas e inteligência artificial, amplia a necessidade de infraestrutura elétrica capaz de assegurar o funcionamento ininterrupto de servidores, equipamentos de processamento e sistemas de comunicação. Tecnologia de alta performance para operações críticas Nesse cenário, a Powersafe destaca as baterias estacionárias Getpower das linhas GP-PLX e GP-XP, desenvolvidas para aplicações de alta taxa de descarga, especialmente em sistemas UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply), conhecidos como nobreaks. Esses equipamentos fornecem energia imediatamente após uma falha da rede elétrica, mantendo as operações até a entrada dos geradores de emergência ou o restabelecimento do fornecimento. Diferentemente de sistemas de armazenamento projetados para fornecer energia durante várias horas, as baterias de alta taxa de descarga são dimensionadas para entregar grandes quantidades de potência em intervalos curtos, geralmente de cinco a 15 minutos, conforme as características da instalação. O crescimento da infraestrutura digital exige sistemas de energia cada vez mais confiáveis. Nos data centers, mesmo interrupções de poucos segundos podem comprometer operações críticas. Por isso, a escolha das baterias precisa considerar não apenas a capacidade de armazenamento, mas principalmente a potência disponível, a confiabilidade e as características de cada instalação, afirma Leandro Alvares, diretor-executivo da Powersafe. As soluções Getpower comercializadas pela Powersafe já estão presentes em instalações de dois dos maiores operadores de data centers do Brasil, reforçando a atuação da empresa no segmento de infraestrutura crítica. Solução completa e logística reversa As linhas Getpower GP-PLX e GP-XP utilizam tecnologia chumbo-ácido regulada por válvula (VRLA), com eletrólito absorvido em manta de microfibra de vidro (AGM), e são desenvolvidas para aplicações que exigem alta potência, confiabilidade e desempenho em descargas de curta duração. A linha GP-PLX incorpora placas finas de chumbo puro (TPPL, do inglês Thin Plate Pure Lead), construção que favorece baixa resistência interna e a entrega de alta potência em descargas de curta duração. Já a GP-XP é apresentada como Ultra High Rate, voltada a aplicações que exigem taxas de descarga muito elevadas, especialmente em sistemas UPS. A escolha entre diferentes tecnologias de baterias, incluindo chumbo-ácido e íons de lítio, depende de fatores como autonomia necessária, espaço disponível, investimento inicial, vida útil, manutenção e requisitos de segurança. Embora as baterias de íons de lítio apresentem vantagens relacionadas à densidade energética e à menor ocupação de espaço, as soluções de chumbo-ácido de alta performance continuam sendo alternativas competitivas para aplicações que exigem elevada potência durante curtos períodos. Não existe uma solução única para todos os data centers. Cada instalação possui requisitos específicos de potência, autonomia e disponibilidade. Nosso trabalho é avaliar essas condições e oferecer a tecnologia mais adequada, considerando desempenho, segurança operacional e custo total ao longo da vida útil dos equipamentos, explica Alvares. A estratégia da Powersafe para o segmento de data centers contempla o fornecimento das baterias e os serviços associados ao ciclo de vida dos equipamentos, incluindo estudos de dimensionamento, engenharia, instalação, testes, comissionamento e suporte técnico. Outro diferencial é a logística reversa das baterias ao final da vida útil. Por meio do programa Ecosafe, a companhia realiza a retirada e o encaminhamento de equipamentos inservíveis para processos de reaproveitamento, requalificação ou reciclagem por empresas homologadas, com rastreabilidade e atendimento às exigências ambientais. A iniciativa está alinhada à Política Nacional de Resíduos Sólidos e à Resolução CONAMA nº 401/2008, que estabelece critérios para o gerenciamento ambientalmente adequado de pilhas e baterias. Além da confiabilidade energética, os operadores de data centers precisam considerar o custo total de seus sistemas e a destinação dos equipamentos ao final da vida útil. Nossa proposta é acompanhar o cliente desde a especificação da tecnologia até a substituição e a logística reversa, contribuindo para uma operação mais eficiente, segura e ambientalmente responsável, acrescenta Alvares. A empresa avalia que a ampliação dos investimentos em infraestrutura digital deverá impulsionar a procura por soluções de armazenamento e fornecimento de energia nos próximos anos, tanto em novos empreendimentos quanto na modernização de instalações existent

artigo.texto: Nvidia in Talks to Guarantee Debt for Nscale’s $44.6B Anthropic Data Center Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions of dollars in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s planned Anthropic data center in West Virginia, The Information reported, with Bloomberg later confirming. Anthropic has signed a $44.6 billion contract for the campus’s first 460-megawatt building, which will use Nvidia’s Vera Rubin chips, and the two are discussing a second deal of roughly $45 billion. Under the proposed residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, temporarily take over the site and help find a new buyer and tenant. Nvidia’s past support for cloud providers has mostly covered leases and chip purchases rather than construction. It has extended around $170 billion in investments and credit support to neoclouds and major customers, including $1 billion to Nscale in September. The stakes are high for Nscale, which is seeking a public listing at up to $35 billion. It had about 25,000 advanced AI chips running in August against plans for nearly 500,000, its West Virginia site has caused flooding of nearby homes, and Microsoft recently withdrew from a planned site in England. The talks come as neocloud shares slide and Anthropic faces questions over financing its expansion, with Blackstone reportedly warning it may receive a junk credit rating after its IPO.

artigo.texto: Newswise — Binghamton University is a member of a new national consortium to accelerate the transition of energy storage innovations from discovery to domestic manufacturing. The new Battery Manufacturing (BattMan) Accelerator, led by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL), will bring together national laboratories, universities, and industry partners to address critical barriers in scaling next-generation battery technologies. Jie Xiao, a Binghamton University alumna, serves as accelerator director. “Breakthroughs in battery science must be matched by our ability to manufacture them at scale,” said Jie, the Boeing Martin Professor of Mechanical Engineering at the University of Washington and a Battelle Fellow at PNNL. “This effort brings together the tools, data, and partnerships needed to design manufacturable solutions from the start and accelerate their transition into industry.” The BattMan Accelerator will bridge the gap between discovery and manufacturing while establishing comprehensive manufacturing systems with super intelligence that integrate materials development, process design, and production in a seamless manner. Nobel laureate M. Stanley Whittingham, SUNY distinguished professor of chemistry, will serve as the lead investigator from Binghamton. He noted that the accelerator’s goals align closely with efforts of the Binghamton-led battery ecosystem that includes New Energy New York and the NSF Energy Storage Engine in Upstate New York. “Incorporating super intelligence into both research and manufacturing allows us to move from trial-and-error to predictive design,” Whittngham said. “This capability is key to accelerating innovation while ensuring technologies can be produced reliably and affordably at scale.” Whittingham said he expects close interactions between the New York efforts and BattMan. Binghamton is one of five university partners; the others are the University of Washington, University of Alabama, Arizona State University, and the University of Michigan. Argonne and Oak Ridge National Laboratories are also partners. The BattMan Accelerator aligns with the DOE’s Genesis vision to integrate super intelligence, materials science, and advanced manufacturing into a coordinated, data-driven innovation ecosystem. The initiative seeks to lower manufacturing costs, speed up development from lab to scale, and boost U.S. leadership in energy storage manufacturing through scientific innovation. About Binghamton University Binghamton University is a nationally ranked public research university and one of four university centers in the State University of New York (SUNY) system. Founded in 1946 and located in Vestal, N.Y., Binghamton is an R1 research institution, tackling complex challenges and driving innovation in areas that shape our world – from next-generation energy storage to responsible AI. Binghamton enrolls more than 18,000 students in 130+ majors across six schools, providing clear pathways for undergraduate students to future careers, supporting graduate students as they advance boundaries of innovation and discovery, and building partnerships that serve the public good from Binghamton to the rest of the world. artigo.texto: Tech billionaires poured hundreds of millions into the midterms, but it didn’t buy them much. Tuesday’s election results were a repudiation of the Trump administration, but also of another power center across the country: Silicon Valley. Tech billionaires like Elon Musk and venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz poured historic amounts of money into this year’s midterms, only to see their chosen candidates bulldozed by a blue wave. And AI safety candidates and critics of data center construction saw major wins, despite millions of dollars in spending from industry PACs. By Tuesday night, Democratic advisers were declaring victory — and delivering a warning to Big Tech. “The biggest names in tech decided two years ago to stand behind a president who had sold out and screwed over every person he has ever done business with and thought they would get the better of him,” said Cooper Teboe, a Silicon Valley donor adviser and chief strategist to Rep. Ro Khanna. “They lost out, made terrible political investments across the country, and I suspect will spend the next two years paying the price.” Musk was the biggest loser of the night. The richest man in the world poured nearly half a billion dollars into efforts to elect Republicans across the country — including nearly $216 million to his self-funded America PAC — but Democrats still won control of the House and Senate, as well as key gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio. An especially painful race was the Texas Senate contest, where Republican Ken Paxton lost to Democrat James Talarico — whom Musk had spent more than $200 million trying to defeat. Voters also handed a stinging rebuke to the AI and crypto industries, and to billionaires like Andreessen and Horowitz who funded their political operations. Sherrod Brown, whom the crypto industry helped oust from Congress in 2024, won his Ohio Senate race Tuesday, despite $55 million in spending against him from cryptocurrency PACs. Brown made fighting the rising energy costs associated with AI data centers central to his populist campaign and promised to “stand up to Big Tech” if elected. Indeed, despite debate about whether issues related to data centers and AI were important to voters this cycle, they appeared to be surprisingly relevant in exit polling. An NBC poll (opens in new tab) Tuesday night found that 56% of voters said AI or data centers were a “crucial or major factor” in their congressional vote. And as of that evening, it appeared that at least 35 local ballot measures banning or limiting data center construction across the country were set to pass. In another shocking loss for the AI industry, Darline Graham — who replaced her brother Lindsey Graham in Congress after his death — lost her bid for Senate in South Carolina to Democrat Annie Andrews. Graham had drawn millions from pro-AI PACs, including American Mission and Building the Future. Andrews capitalized on the donations, dubbing Graham “Data Center Darline,” and called for a two-year moratorium on data center construction in the state. Meanwhile, a number of AI regulation proponents won close congressional races. In Colorado, Manny Rutinel, the sponsor of early state legislation targeting AI companies, ousted the Republican incumbent; in Kansas, regulatory proponent and Democrat Adam Hamilton did the same. Rutinel, in particular, was a favorite of donors working in and around frontier AI labs who are concerned about the risks of the technology — a burgeoning group who contributed millions of dollars to pro-regulation candidates this cycle. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff spoke to AI safety concerns in his victory speech Tuesday night, specifically calling out the “titans of Silicon Valley [who] dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.” And Rep. Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, was already calling on Democrats to make AI a top priority going forward, saying in a statement that Congress should “investigate how these companies are putting the jobs, freedom, and lives of Americans at risk.” In one twist, Republican Byron Donalds — who has repeatedly expressed support for building data centers in the U.S. — won his race for Florida governor, riding on millions in contributions from pro-AI PAC Leading the Future and developers of data centers. And in Florida’s 25th District, the Leading the Future-backed Democrat Jared Moskowitz defeated Republican Scott Singer, who was supported by pro-regulation PAC Public First Action. Silicon Valley also seemed poised for victory closer to home in California, where a coalition of tech titans came together to fight Prop 40 — an effort to levy 5% tax on the wealth of the state’s billionaires. Prominent figures including Sergey Brin, Eric Schmidt, venture capitalist John Doerr and Stripe CEO Patrick Collison donated more than $340 million to oppose the measure, which was trailing in the polls Tuesday night. Still, opponents of the AI industry seemed to be reading the election results as a clear-cut victory. On Tuesday night, Shaunna Thomas — director of the Guardrails Alliance, a PAC that fights AI money in politics — posted on X (opens in new tab) that Democratic leaders should “absorb this remarkably clear lesson: Aligning with Big Tech is a political catastrophe.” More about the author

artigo.texto: O sul da Malásia, em áreas que antes abrigavam plantações de óleo de palma e abacaxi, testemunha a rápida expansão das ambições tecnológicas globais da China. Guindastes e canteiros de obras se multiplicam em dezenas de hectares onde empresas constroem enormes complexos para atender companhias de tecnologia. A estratégia da neutralidade Nesses novos centros de dados, operam alguns dos chips de inteligência artificial mais avançados fabricados pela Nvidia. Embora essas peças tenham exportação proibida para o território chinês pelas regras dos Estados Unidos, as restrições geralmente não impedem que empresas como a ByteDance acessem os mesmos semicondutores em instalações situadas fora da China. Essa distinção impulsionou o país de 35 milhões de habitantes no boom tecnológico global. Motivadas por terrenos baratos, eletricidade acessível e conexão com cabos submarinos, corporações estrangeiras despejam bilhões de dólares na região. O estado de Johor tornou-se o epicentro desse movimento, acumulando dezenas de projetos aprovados ou em construção. “É algo impressionante e difícil até de imaginar”, afirmou Steven Tan, CEO da Pro3c, empresa taiwanesa que fabrica componentes ópticos usados nos chips da Nvidia. “Todo mundo está vindo para cá.” Gigantes dos Estados Unidos, a exemplo de Microsoft, Google e Oracle, investem pesado no território malaio para atender clientes asiáticos. Simultaneamente, o local virou um centro de processamento para marcas chinesas como Tencent e Alibaba, posicionando infraestruturas rivais praticamente lado a lado. “Este é o único lugar do mundo onde estamos vendo isso acontecer”, afirmou Lee Ting Han, integrante do governo de Johor envolvido na aprovação dos projetos. “O que torna a Malásia tão especial para essa onda da IA é justamente sua posição neutra e não alinhada.” O avanço chinês e as brechas regulatórias O movimento começou em 2021, impulsionado por restrições energéticas em Singapura. A DayOne, ligada a uma das maiores operadoras de data centers chinesas, liderou a chegada de companhias daquele país à região, transformando até mesmo campos de golfe em complexos tecnológicos. A expansão coincidiu com o endurecimento dos controles comerciais americanos, mas a captação de recursos internacionais permitiu que a empresa mantivesse fortes laços com Pequim. Autoridades dos Estados Unidos monitoram de perto o papel do Sudeste Asiático nessa dinâmica. Relatórios internos apontam que a capacidade computacional disponível para empresas chinesas em países da região rivaliza com a da China continental. Críticos apontam que as políticas americanas deixaram lacunas significativas. “Nada disso é ilegal”, disse Jimmy Goodrich, pesquisador da Universidade da Califórnia em San Diego e ex-executivo do setor de semicondutores. “É uma enorme lacuna nos controles de exportação que ninguém corrigiu. Essas brechas dão à China acesso a capacidade computacional gigantesca e espaço para alcançar os concorrentes na corrida pela IA.” Desafios locais e regulação O ritmo acelerado gerou alertas internos. O governo malaio passou a adotar exigências mais rígidas, dificultando novas aprovações ao cobrar fontes independentes de água e energia. Apesar disso, os empreendimentos já licenciados seguem transformando a economia e a paisagem local, alimentados pelas próprias rivalidades internacionais que marcam a tecnologia moderna. “Só quando a situação fica complicada é que temos trabalho para fazer”, afirmou Eric Yong, corretor imobiliário e desenvolvedor do setor na região.
