artigo.texto: Mercado global de umidificadores industriais: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de umidificadores industriais até 2035, impulsionada pela demanda de data centers e do setor farmacêutico Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Umidificadores Industriais, o setor inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de umidificadores industriais entra em uma fase de expansão constante, com projeções que apontam para um CAGR de 4,2% até 2035. Em 2026, o mercado é avaliado em aproximadamente US$ 2,1 bilhões, sustentado pelo papel decisivo do controle preciso de umidade na manufatura avançada, na operação de data centers e na conformidade sanitária. Diferentemente dos umidificadores de uso doméstico, os sistemas industriais são projetados para alta capacidade, confiabilidade e integração com sistemas de gestão predial, o que os torna indispensáveis em setores nos quais os parâmetros ambientais afetam diretamente a qualidade do produto, a continuidade operacional e o cumprimento de normas. A trajetória da demanda vem sendo remodelada pela rápida expansão de data centers de hiperescala e de colocation, onde a regulação da umidade é essencial para evitar descargas eletrostáticas e corrosão, bem como pelo aumento da capacidade de produção biofarmacêutica, que exige salas limpas rigorosamente compatíveis com as normas de BPF. Ao mesmo tempo, eficiência energética e conservação de água se tornam critérios de compra decisivos, levando os fabricantes a adotar tecnologias adiabáticas e ultrassônicas que reduzem os custos operacionais. O cenário competitivo segue fragmentado, reunindo conglomerados globais de engenharia e empresas especializadas de nicho que disputam espaço com base em inovação, redes de serviços e custo total de propriedade. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico deve permanecer como o maior e mais dinâmico mercado, apoiada pela expansão industrial na China, na Índia e no Sudeste Asiático, enquanto América do Norte e Europa concentram-se na demanda de reposição e na modernização para sistemas de umidificação inteligentes e conectados. Este relatório oferece uma visão orientada por dados sobre tamanho de mercado, segmentação, dinâmica da cadeia de suprimentos e estratégias competitivas, capacitando os agentes do setor a navegar pelas oportunidades e pelos riscos inerentes a esse mercado de base tecnológica até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado de umidificadores industriais projeta um CAGR de 4,2% entre 2026 e 2035, com o índice de mercado subindo para 142 (2025=100). Essa perspectiva pressupõe a continuidade dos investimentos de capital nos principais setores usuários, sobretudo data centers e produção farmacêutica, além de crescimento moderado da produção industrial nas economias emergentes. Espera-se que o mercado se beneficie da migração para soluções integradas de controle de umidade que combinam sensores, automação e monitoramento remoto, permitindo aos operadores otimizar o uso de energia e água. No entanto, o ritmo de crescimento será contido pelo alto custo inicial dos sistemas avançados e pela natureza cíclica de alguns segmentos industriais, como têxtil e gráfico, nos quais as expansões de capacidade são irregulares. Geograficamente, a Ásia-Pacífico responderá pela maior parcela da demanda incremental, impulsionada pela construção de novas instalações e por regulamentações ambientais mais rígidas na China e na Índia. América do Norte e Europa registrarão atividade constante de reposição e modernização, com foco em tecnologias energeticamente eficientes e no cumprimento de normas de segurança no trabalho. O segmento de pós-venda, que inclui peças de reposição e contratos de serviço, deve crescer mais rápido que as vendas de equipamentos, abrindo oportunidades de receita recorrente para fabricantes e distribuidores. No conjunto, o mercado está preparado para um crescimento moderado, porém resiliente, com a diferenciação tecnológica e a capacidade de prestação de serviços se consolidando como os principais campos de disputa competitiva. Vetores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Vetores de Demanda - Rápida expansão da capacidade de data centers, onde o controle preciso de umidade evita descargas eletrostáticas e a corrosão de equipamentos - Exigências rigorosas de BPF e de salas limpas na produção farmacêutica, que impulsionam a demanda por umidificadores a vapor e ultrassônicos - Crescimento do processamento de alimentos e da logística de cadeia fria, em que a gestão da umidade garante a integridade e a validade dos produtos - Adoção crescente de sistemas de automação predial e industrial inteligentes que integram a umidificação ao sistema de gestão predial para otimizar energia - Aumento da conscientização sobre segurança no trabalho e normas de qualidade do ar em ambientes industriais - Expansão de instalações de preservação em museus e arquivos, que exigem controle especializado de umidade Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Altos custos de capital e de instalação dos sistemas industriais avançados de umidificação, sobretudo em projetos de modernização - Retrações cíclicas em setores usuários importantes, como têxtil e gráfico, que levam ao adiamento de investimentos - Requisitos complexos de manutenção e problemas de qualidade da água, que podem desestimular a adoção em algumas regiões - Concorrência de soluções alternativas de controle climático e de fabricantes locais de baixo custo em mercados sensíveis a preço Estrutura da Demanda por Setor Usuário Produção Farmacêutica (participação estimada: 24%) A produção farmacêutica depen

artigo.texto: The Tamil Nadu government has released a three-year Tamil Nadu Battery Energy Storage Systems Policy 2026, envisaging deployment of 2.5 GW/10 GWh of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) during this period. Existing solar and wind renewable energy projects of one MW and above will be encouraged to install BESS for renewable energy integration, peak management or grid support. It will be mandatory for new solar or solar-hybrid renewable energy projects of one MW and above applied on or after the date of notification of the policy or commissioned on or after April 1, 2027 to install BESS capacity of at least 10% of the solar project’s installed capacity. Co-located and standalone BESS will be eligible for 100% waiver of applicable transmission and wheeling charges attributable to the eligible BESS, according to the policy. This Policy will apply to all the BESS projects applied on or after the date of notification of this Policy or commissioned on or after April 1 next year and will encourage standalone and co-located projects. The Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation (TNPDC) will procure BESS capacity aggregating to 2,500 MW/10,000 MWh from eligible BESS projects availing benefits under this policy in the first phase. The Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation Limited will be the State Nodal Agency to co-ordinate, facilitate, and monitor the implementation of BESS Projects and it will operate a single window system for BESS projects. With the State having an installed renewable energy capacity of 29.8 GW, including 14.5 GW of solar power and 11.6 GW of wind power, the policy will aim to support grid stability and renewable energy integration and energy security. Tamil Nadu is currently developing four BESS projects, comprising a 500 MW/1,000 MWh project under Viability Gap Funding for Development of Battery Energy Storage System scheme, a 375 MW/1,500 MWh project under Viability Gap Funding Scheme for development of BESS supported through Power System Development Fund scheme, and two solar with BESS projects of 15 MW/45 MWh each. artigo.texto: In India, a minimum storage duration for BESS projects has been set by CTUIL, an India-based transmission utility, through an advisory of 20 October 2026. A project that seeks ISTS connectivity must offer 4 hours of discharge, unless its applicant falls in the right of first refusal (RoFR) category. An applicant in that category must offer 2 hours, provided that it was eligible and that it applied by 21 February 2026. The 4-hour minimum also applies to a standalone BESS at a pooling station or substation, and such a project must apply for co-located renewable generation. A pending applicant below 4 hours has been given a way to comply, as it may raise its MWh without changing its MW. It must then furnish the eligibility documents within 2 months. CTUIL sets 4-hour storage minimum for BESS seeking ISTS access The minimum storage for BESS projects that seek ISTS connectivity in India has been set by CTUIL at 4 hours, whereas applicants in the RoFR category must offer 2 hours. artigo.texto: Holly Ridge residents weigh leaving homes as Meta Data Center construction disrupts community Neighbors report frequent water outages, rising utility bills and heavy traffic, while Meta says it enforces strict site rules and dust controls. HOLLY RIDGE, La. — Ongoing construction of the Meta data center is creating severe growing pains for Holly Ridge neighbors, driving some longtime residents to consider leaving the area entirely. Residents living directly across from the site say construction crews frequently strike underground utility lines, cutting off running water to nearby homes. Neighbors also report surging utility bills, relentless dust and heavy construction traffic that blocks residential driveways. “It’s just way more traffic and everything — more traffic, more dust,” said Kevin Dove, a Holly Ridge resident living near the project. “It’s just a whole totally different country. I mean, this is not country anymore. It’s like turning into town.” Randy Dove, who has lived on his property for more than five decades, said the heavy congestion directly interferes with his daily routine. “They don’t give no respect to let you out of your own driveway that we’ve been using our driveway for 50-something years,” he said, adding that he now plans to move. Meta stated that all project drivers must follow strict traffic regulations or face removal from the job site. The company also said crews actively manage dust levels and maintain close communication with local leaders. However, several neighbors say those measures fall short of addressing their day-to-day disruption. “We haven’t been expecting anything because they haven’t seemed to show any concern on what they’ve done,” resident Lisa Hopkins said. “Yeah, they’re giving the school scholarships and stuff and that’s great, but what have they done for the residents right here dealing with this traffic and noise every day?” Hopkins and Randy Dove both noted that the ongoing disruption is forcing an outcome they never anticipated: abandoning their roots. “We’ve done a lot here and we’ve made it home,” Hopkins said. “And the thought of having to move and start over, it’s sad. Of course we want to get out of here now because it’s not going to get any better.” “Who wants to live amongst all this here?” Dove added. “It ain’t even got started yet because it’s going to get worse as it goes throughout time. So we’re not looking forward to that, having to leave our home place, the place that we’ve known all our life.” Copyright 2026 KNOE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Questions remain after city council tightens oversight of data centers with 9-2 vote SAN ANTONIO - The city has adopted new rules that tighten oversight of data centers, a move supporters say will give residents more say in projects that can affect neighborhoods, while critics warn the changes could push jobs and investment elsewhere. City Council voted 9-2 to require public review and council approval for new data center projects. The rules took effect immediately and apply to the industry’s footprint in San Antonio, where there are 75 data centers operating or planned for operation. The changes also add restrictions on where data centers can be built and the rules they must follow. A key piece of the new policy requires projects to go before City Council for public approval before moving forward in the process. “We’re able to deliver today as the largest city in Texas to push on the best regulations possible here in the state of Texas,” Ric Galvan said after the vote. Supporters say the new rules give residents a voice amid concerns about water use, electricity demand and noise. But critics of the tighter regulations say the restrictions could drive jobs and investment out of the city. Officials with District 6 and the city’s zoning and policy staff said projects with existing permits can move forward. Councilman Marc Whyte said he understands why some residents are worried about data centers near their homes. “We know that there’s a lot of fear out there about these data centers. People don’t want them placed right in the middle of their neighborhoods, and I understand that,” Whyte said. Questions remain about whether the new rules will protect communities from issues other parts of the country have faced, whether the regulations could discourage businesses from building in San Antonio, and how the new process will work for projects already in the planning stages.

artigo.texto: A new USC Annenberg survey finds broad concern about the expansion of artificial intelligence and the infrastructure powering it, with large majorities calling for greater regulation and questioning whether technology companies and government will act in the public interest. As Americans prepare to vote in the 2026 midterm elections, these issues have emerged as a significant national concern, crossing partisan, generational and geographic lines. Nearly one-third of Americans rank AI and data centers among the three most important issues facing the country, according to a new probability-based national survey from the USC Annenberg Center for Climate Journalism and Communication utilizing the Understanding America Study. That places the issue behind only inflation and the cost of living, selected by 86% of respondents, and political polarization, selected by 35%. It ranks ahead of immigration, financial well-being, climate change, crime and unemployment. The findings suggest that as AI becomes more deeply embedded in the economy and daily life, voters are thinking not only about what the technology can do, but also about who will oversee its growth, who will benefit, and which communities will bear its costs. Seventy-six percent of respondents say the government is doing too little to regulate AI, and 77% say it is doing too little to regulate data centers. At the same time, 71% do not trust Big Tech companies at all to act in society’s best interest when it comes to data center development. Fifty-nine percent say the same of the federal government. “Our research has focused on the origins of community pushback against the expansion of data centers since the summer of 2025,” said Allison Agsten, director of USC’s Center for Climate Journalism and Communication, scholar at the Leonard D. Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy and Government Service, and executive producer of the podcast, Electric Futures. “With the midterms around the corner, the timeliness of these issues requires understanding the public’s opinions today.” Concern Extends Across Party Lines The survey reveals political differences, but it also finds a notable degree of concern across party affiliations. Democrats express the greatest skepticism: 86% say the government is doing too little to regulate AI, compared with 72% of independents and others and 68% of Republicans. Similarly, 88% of Democrats, 73% of independents and others, and 69% of Republicans say data centers are underregulated. Distrust of Big Tech is also widespread. Seventy-nine percent of Democrats, 72% of independents and others, and 61% of Republicans say they do not trust technology companies at all to act in society’s best interest when developing data centers. “Although we find that Republicans and daily users of AI are slightly less negative about AI and data centers, they are still mostly negative,” said Wändi Bruine de Bruin, Provost Professor of Public Policy, Psychology and Behavioral Science and senior scholar at the USC Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy and Government Service. The pattern extends across the country. The survey found little to no regional variation in most attitudes toward AI and data centers, indicating that the concerns are not confined to communities where new facilities have received the greatest public attention. Americans Question Who Benefits Most respondents have either negative or mixed feelings about AI: 32% describe their feelings as somewhat or very negative, while another 40% report mixed feelings. Just 20% feel somewhat or very positive. They are also skeptical about the effects of the data centers needed to support AI. Sixty percent believe data centers are somewhat or very bad for nearby communities, while 67% say they are bad for the environment. Only 13% see data centers as beneficial to nearby communities, and 7% consider them beneficial to the environment. Looking a decade ahead, 36% expect AI to have a mostly negative effect on their own lives, compared with 24% who anticipate a mostly positive effect. Nearly half expect AI to negatively affect Americans’ financial well-being, while only 16% foresee a positive effect. Opposition to data center construction is strongest close to home, with 62% opposing development in their area. But the findings suggest that this sentiment is not simply a case of residents wanting facilities built somewhere else. Forty-six percent oppose data center construction in the United States more broadly, and among those who oppose local construction, most also oppose it nationally. That distinction could become increasingly important to candidates and policymakers as data center proposals raise questions about electricity demand, water use, land development, economic growth and local control. Even Frequent AI Users Express Reservations The survey also complicates the idea that familiarity with AI necessarily translates into confidence about its broader effects. Twenty-seven percent of Americans report using AI tools daily. Daily users are more positive than people who use the technology less often, but significant concerns remain within this group. Nearly three-quarters of daily users say the government is doing too little to regulate AI, and three-quarters say the same about data centers. Among respondents who use AI at any frequency, 44% say they use it more often than they would like. Only 7% would like to increase their use. Age differences are similarly modest. Adults 45 and younger are somewhat more likely than older Americans to identify AI and data centers as a leading national concern and to oppose data center construction. Yet the two groups report nearly identical levels of distrust toward Big Tech and the federal government. A New Approach to Sharing Timely Research The findings are part of Electric Futures: AI, Data Centers, and Trust, an October 2026 survey of 2,980 Americans developed by Agsten and Charles Zukoski, former USC provost and host of the Electric Future

artigo.texto: The One-Way Street Runs the Other Way: Clinton’s WTO Forecast and the BYD Reality On March 8, 2000, President Bill Clinton went to the Paul H. Nitze School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins to make his closing argument for granting China Permanent Normal Trade Relations and supporting its entry into the World Trade Organization (Johns Hopkins Gazette). I reprinted that speech in full in The Biden Administration Confronts Global Change, and concluded there that it is hard to find any foreign policy forecast as wrong as this one. That judgment can now be tested against a single company. When China became the 143rd member of the WTO on December 11, 2001 (WTO), BYD did not build cars. It was a Shenzhen battery maker, founded in 1995 by the chemist Wang Chuanfu, that made rechargeable cells for mobile phones (CNBC). It entered the automobile business only in January 2003, when it bought a struggling carmaker, Xi’an Qinchuan Automobile, from the state-owned defense conglomerate Norinco (Wikipedia, BYD Auto). In April 2026 alone, BYD exported 135,098 vehicles, every one of them fully electric or plug-in hybrid (Yahoo Finance). BYD is, in other words, a company whose entire life as an automaker falls inside the WTO era. It is as clean a test case as one could design for the claims Clinton made in 2000. Taking those claims one at a time shows how thoroughly reality reversed them. Forecast One: “A One-Way Street” Clinton’s central economic claim was blunt: “Economically, this agreement is the equivalent of a one-way street.” China would open its markets; the United States would merely maintain the access China already enjoyed. American firms would be able to sell into China “without being forced to relocate manufacturing to China.” In his words, “We’ll be able to export products without exporting jobs” (IATP full text). The street did turn out to be one-way. It simply ran in the opposite direction. As Ross Babbage has laid out, China’s manufacturing output was half that of the United States in 2004. Twenty years later it is double, and China’s trade surplus has reached $1.2 trillion, the largest ever recorded by any country. BYD is that reversal in automotive form. SNE Research put BYD’s non-China deliveries at roughly 497,000 units in the first half of 2026, up 81 percent year on year (BYD Today). The company is targeting 1.6 million overseas sales this year, supported by new or expanding plants in Hungary, Brazil, Thailand, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Turkey (Boston Brand Media). Clinton imagined American workers building products for Chinese consumers. What emerged is a Chinese firm building factories inside other countries’ borders, with assembly jobs going to the host nation while the battery cell, the chemistry, and the software stay anchored in China. The jobs were exported. So, increasingly, is the factory. Forecast Two: No More Forced Technology Transfer Clinton told his audience that, “for the first time,” American companies would be able to sell in China without being forced to “transfer valuable technology.” The automobile sector shows how hollow that promise was. From 1994, China required foreign automakers to enter the market through joint ventures with Chinese partners and capped foreign ownership at 50 percent. The rule was designed to protect domestic players and give them access to foreign automakers’ technology (Caixin Global). WTO accession did not end it. Ten years after China joined, foreign carmakers were still “forced to team up with local partners” and could own at most half of those ventures (Reuters factbox). The cap was not lifted for passenger-car manufacturing until January 1, 2022 (International Trade Administration). The U.S. Trade Representative had long criticized the joint-venture regime as a means of forced technology transfer (HKTDC Research). The timing tells the story. Beijing opened the door to full foreign ownership only once its own electric-vehicle champions were strong enough not to need the protection. The two decades in which foreign automakers trained China’s automotive ecosystem were the same two decades in which BYD learned how to build cars. Forecast Three: The State Would Recede The most revolutionary claim in the speech was that WTO membership would push the Chinese state out of economic life. Clinton described the state-owned enterprises as “dinosaurs that are least likely to survive in the global economy.” By lowering the barriers that protected them, he said, China would be “removing government from vast areas of people’s lives,” leaving the Party with “fewer instruments” of control. The state did not recede. It changed instruments. BYD’s entry into the car business was itself a product of state and local politics. When Wang bought Qinchuan, local authorities wanted to keep the ailing factory open and preserve employment, and BYD reportedly received a large piece of land for free along with loans at marginal interest rates (CarNewsChina). That pattern then scaled up nationally. The Center for Strategic and International Studies calculates that Chinese government support for the EV sector totaled $230.9 billion from 2009 to 2023 (CSIS). CSIS calls this a highly conservative estimate, because it excludes local-government rebates, cheap land and utilities, and subsidies to the battery supply chain (Quartz). Babbage identifies four structural levers behind China’s export machine: a protected home market of 1.4 billion consumers, state subsidies the OECD estimates at three to five times those of other major economies, a currency the IMF assesses as undervalued by 20 to 40 percent, and a state apparatus of commercial intelligence, IP theft, cyber operations, and influence that works alongside Chinese firms abroad. Clinton saw a state trying to shovel coal into the furnaces of a sinking Titanic. What Beijing actually built was a state that picks the industries of the future and funds them at a scale no market competitor can match. Forec

artigo.texto: Data centers have become one of the nation’s defining political issues ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. As tech giants invest hundreds of billions of dollars to build behemoth facilities and use vast amounts of power to support their artificial intelligence race, communities have pushed back. Candidates on the federal, state and local levels have responded to data center opposition by proposing stringent regulations on the industry — and by painting their opponents as data center supporters. This contentious issue could influence the control of Congress and reshape statehouses across the country. But for all the focus on data centers on the campaign trail, industry experts say the election’s actual impact on the development boom may be less widespread than the rhetoric would suggest. In Congress, even if a wave of anti-data center Democrats take control of both chambers, they would still struggle to pass significant legislation that could receive the signature of President Donald Trump, a vocal supporter of the industry. In many states, candidates on both sides of the aisle are supporting stricter data center rules — meaning the industry is in for a tougher road no matter who wins. But there are state-level races in the key digital infrastructure markets of Texas, Pennsylvania and Georgia where candidates have staked out different positions, and the election could determine how much data center development will be allowed to move forward. Just in those three states, Morgan Stanley estimates the planned development of 284 data centers totaling more than 33 gigawatts of capacity are at risk pending the results of these races. “I don't think at the federal level the policy is going to shift much,” MOCA Economics Chief Economist Brandon Michalski told Bisnow. “If we go to the state level, that shifts dramatically and could change the trajectory significantly.” The Battle For Capitol Hill From Ohio and Michigan to Wisconsin, Texas and Maine, data centers have emerged as a major campaign issue in high-profile House and Senate races ahead of this week’s midterms. Data centers are deeply unpopular, and congressional candidates from both parties have made proposals to rein in development or limit its impacts a core element of their campaigns as voters voice growing concerns over electricity costs, environmental impacts and the broader consequences of the AI data center boom. The trend is especially visible in political advertising. As of the beginning of October, House and Senate campaigns had spent more than $29M on ads mentioning data centers, almost always negatively, according to AdImpact data analyzed by Bisnow. Although opposition to data centers cuts across party lines, Democrats have more aggressively nationalized the issue, contrasting calls for oversight of the sector with the Trump administration’s support for accelerating AI infrastructure development. Prominent congressional Democrats have already proposed measures like a national data center moratorium and released an investigation arguing that hyperscalers aren’t paying their fair share of grid costs. Now, party leaders are signaling their intent to make more aggressive oversight of the industry a prominent part of their policy agenda following the midterms, particularly if the party gains control of one or both houses of Congress. Last week, the Senate’s top Democratic tax writer announced plans to pursue an additional excise tax on data centers while eliminating the industry’s ability to tap a range of existing tax benefits tied to depreciation, research spending, opportunity zones and REIT structures. Although Republicans have also pursued measures aimed at addressing voter concerns over data centers driving up electricity prices, GOP leaders have privately acknowledged that data centers have become a winning issue for Democrats. The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned major technology and AI firms in August that Democrats were successfully making data centers the “centerpiece” of the Senate race in Ohio and that deteriorating public sentiment toward the industry was becoming a broader risk to Republican candidates specifically. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle,” the letter warned. The data center industry has taken notice of this partisan dynamic. AI infrastructure super PAC Leading the Future and connected groups have spent significantly more supporting Republicans than Democrats, according to Forbes, while hyperscalers and AI giants like OpenAI have reportedly ramped up lobbying in anticipation of more aggressive Democratic oversight of data center development and the AI trade. Investors and analysts focused on the data center industry have similarly warned that the potential for Democratic victories in the House and Senate poses a threat to the industry’s growth and would bring greater regulatory and political risk. “There will be congressional hearings. There will be investigations,” said Brian Gardner, chief Washington policy strategist at Stifel, according to Reuters. “You never know where that stuff leads, and there can be negative headlines.” Yet despite the rhetoric and the flood of money pouring into congressional races, not everyone is convinced that even a Democratic sweep would materially change the federal regulatory environment for data centers. A report published this week by MOCA Economics examining data center construction spending projected that Democratic control of at least one chamber would be a “nothingburger for policy.” Michalski, who authored the report, said Democrats could introduce more restrictive bills, but Trump’s veto power would make measures such as a national moratorium, sweeping new grid cost requirements or additional tax burdens extremely difficult to enact. artigo.texto: MILTON, Del. - The town of Milton is taking steps toward potentially banning data centers, with the Town Council voting to schedule a public hearing for Jan. 4 to consider a proposed moratorium on the facilities. Although Milton has not received any applications from data centers looking to move into town, Mayor John Collier said town leaders want to explore the potential effects before making a decision. The proposed ordinance cites concerns about noise levels and the potential impact data centers could have on the power grid. Some people in Milton have expressed opposition to the facilities, citing concerns about their effects on the community. "I don't think anybody wants them because we're finding out more and more about the problems that they will create in a community," said Margie Pease Collier said the town must weigh those concerns against the potential economic benefits of bringing new businesses to Milton. "First of all, whether we want one or not. And then what would be the benefit of having one? You know, Milton right now doesn't have any significant employers other than the school district and the brewery. And if you really want to build a great community, you've got to have employers." Collier also emphasized that data centers can vary significantly in size, meaning some facilities could potentially be more suitable for Milton than others. "There's a lot of misinformation out there. What I've learned is data centers can be as small as 10,000ft², or they can occupy 100 acres. Well, there's got to be something in between that spectrum that would fit here." The proposed ordinance will go before Milton's Planning and Zoning Commission before the public hearing. Town leaders want the commission to examine what data centers could mean for Milton and what such developments might look like if they were proposed. The discussion also comes as Milton looks ahead to updating its comprehensive plan in 2028. Town leaders want to determine how data centers might fit into the community's long-term development. The public hearing on the proposed data center moratorium is scheduled for Jan. 4, 2027.

artigo.texto: MISSOULA — Data centers are a hot and controversial topic across the country right now. Much of the controversy centers around the impacts of data centers on both human and ecological health. The University of Montana’s Bureau of Business and Economic Research (BBER) has now published a study on the economic impacts of data centers. WATCH THE VIDEO BELOW: It is solely focused on impacts to jobs, tax revenue and energy for hyperscale data centers - centers 500 Megawatts (MW) and above. Jeff Michaels, director of the BBER, says the study was largely conducted through economic modeling (through the use of REMI modeling) of what Montana may look like with differently sized hyperscale data centers. “That's the kind of facility we don't have right now in Montana. We got nothing like it. So we sort of created some models of what that could look like here and estimated, you know, job creation, income creation and a lot of work on property taxes because that's a big part of what Data centers could bring to the state,” said Jeff Michael. “The findings overall were that, we looked at data centers and in terms of their capacity,” said Michael. Michael says that depending on the size of the data center, the number of jobs created and taxes generated vary. The study looked at 500 MW increments, examining both what each increment could bring in terms of direct and construction jobs. It also had estimates for personal income growth and tax revenue generation. The study found that impacts from a 1,000 MW data center that takes four years to build could directly result in 500 construction jobs and up to 1,500 statewide jobs. Those jobs may result in up to a total personal income increase of $93 million. Once the 1,000 MW data center is fully built and furnished with several billion dollars worth of Nvidia chips, the study estimates that the data center could have 250 direct jobs at the facility and a total of 452 jobs statewide. That would result in a total personal income increase of an estimated $34.2 million. “Still a big employment generator, but maybe not in terms of thousands, but in hundreds of jobs,” said Michaels. The potential tax revenue increases would also be significant, with a 1,000 MW data center projected to generate $47 million in annual property taxes. The property tax payments could also increase with co-developed new power generation, with the potential result of $54 million. “The biggest benefit of Montana, all these jobs would be a benefit, but the biggest potential benefit in the long run would just be a huge expansion in the property tax base,” said Michaels. With that benefit to the tax base, individuals’ property taxes could see a decrease, depending on how much their county decides to mill. “A certain amount of it is sort of in statute, and that's we follow the statute, which generally results in this sort of 50-50 split of new revenue and some reduction in the mills. So that's sort of how we follow it. I mean, it would be at the discretion of the county; they could go beyond that if they wanted to,” said Michaels. He also says, however, that the increases in property taxes could vary over the years. He says this is because the billions of dollars worth of chips contained within a data center depreciate rapidly, ultimately decreasing the overall value of the property. With all of the potential monetary benefits data centers could bring, it is important to note that all the findings were under the guidance of current state law, which could change in the upcoming legislative session.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de placas de resfriamento líquido: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de placas de resfriamento líquido até 2035: demanda por servidores de data center impulsiona expansão Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de placas de resfriamento líquido, o setor entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimento mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de placas de resfriamento líquido atravessa um ponto de inflexão crítico, à medida que as exigências de gestão térmica se intensificam nas indústrias de alta tecnologia. Em 2026, o segmento já superou o nicho da computação de alto desempenho e alcançou a adoção mainstream, impulsionado pelo crescimento exponencial da intensidade de dados e pela eletrificação dos transportes. As placas de resfriamento líquido, ou cold plates, são trocadores de calor especializados que fazem circular o fluido refrigerante por canais internos para absorver e transferir o calor residual de componentes com alta densidade térmica. Sua eficiência afeta diretamente o desempenho e a confiabilidade dos sistemas, o que as torna indispensáveis em servidores de data centers, baterias de veículos elétricos, eletrônica de potência e computação de alto desempenho. O período até 2035 será marcado por mudanças estruturais: o aumento da densidade de potência dos servidores, a proliferação de aceleradores de IA e a transição para arquiteturas de veículos elétricos de 800 volts exigirão projetos de placas mais avançados, incluindo variantes de microcanais e de duas fases. Os avanços em ciência dos materiais com ligas de alumínio e cobre, a usinagem de precisão e a vedação à prova de vazamentos moldarão a dinâmica competitiva. Este relatório oferece uma visão orientada por dados sobre tamanho de mercado, segmentação, cadeia de suprimentos e perspectivas regionais, proporcionando às partes interessadas um arcabouço analítico transparente para navegar por um cenário em evolução. O cenário-base para o mercado mundial de placas de resfriamento líquido projeta expansão robusta entre 2026 e 2035, com taxa de crescimento anual composta (CAGR) de 8,2%, elevando o índice de mercado a 220 em 2035 (2025=100). Essa perspectiva se apoia na aceleração da transição do resfriamento a ar para o resfriamento líquido nos data centers, onde a densidade de potência por rack ultrapassa 20 kW e torna necessário o resfriamento líquido direto no chip. O setor de veículos elétricos também dará contribuição relevante, à medida que os sistemas de gestão térmica de baterias adotam cada vez mais placas de resfriamento líquido para ampliar a capacidade de recarga rápida e prolongar a vida útil das baterias. Geograficamente, a Ásia-Pacífico manterá sua liderança, sustentada pela base industrial chinesa de veículos elétricos e eletrônicos, enquanto América do Norte e Europa registrarão crescimento acima da média, graças aos investimentos em data centers e a regulamentações rigorosas de eficiência. Restrições de oferta, incluindo a volatilidade do preço do cobre e a capacidade de usinagem de precisão, podem conter o crescimento, mas devem ser mitigadas por inovações de projeto e substituição de materiais. O mercado permanecerá moderadamente consolidado, com especialistas em gestão térmica e novos entrantes de setores adjacentes competindo com base em projeto personalizado e integração de sistemas. No conjunto, a perspectiva é positiva: os vetores de demanda superam as restrições e o mercado está posicionado para gerar valor significativo até 2035. Vetores e restrições da demanda Principais vetores de demanda - Aumento da densidade de potência dos servidores de data centers, impulsionado por IA e computação em nuvem, o que exige placas de resfriamento líquido para dissipação eficiente do calor. - Necessidades de gestão térmica das baterias de veículos elétricos, já que a recarga rápida e a maior densidade energética demandam placas de resfriamento líquido para manter a temperatura ideal. - Crescimento da computação de alto desempenho e dos aceleradores de IA, contextos em que o resfriamento a ar é insuficiente e que impulsionam a adoção de cold plates avançadas. - Confiabilidade e densidade de potência da eletrônica de potência em aplicações de energia renovável e industriais, que exigem resfriamento líquido para sistemas compactos de alta potência. - Sistemas de aviônica aeroespacial e de diagnóstico por imagem demandam estabilidade térmica precisa, viabilizada por placas de resfriamento líquido diante de restrições de tamanho, peso e potência. - Equipamentos de telecomunicações, incluindo estações-base 5G, requerem placas de resfriamento líquido para controlar o calor em ambientes externos e de alta densidade. Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - Custos iniciais elevados e maior complexidade dos sistemas de resfriamento líquido em comparação com o resfriamento a ar, o que limita a adoção em segmentos sensíveis a custo. - Riscos potenciais de vazamento e preocupações com confiabilidade, que exigem vedação e testes robustos e podem afastar usuários finais avessos a risco. - Volatilidade dos preços de matérias-primas, sobretudo cobre e alumínio, com impacto nos custos de fabricação e nas margens de lucro. - Falta de projetos padronizados e de interoperabilidade entre unidades de distribuição de refrigerante (CDUs) e placas, o que retarda a implantação. - Restrições na cadeia de suprimentos de usinagem de precisão e fabricação de microcanais, especialmente para projetos avançados de placas. artigo.texto: Michigan trails neighboring states in data center power as governor candidates discuss moratorium SAGINAW, Mich. (WNEM) - Data centers are a flashpoint in the race for Michigan’s next governor. They could affect electric bills and water and take up acres of property. A review of data from several data center research groups shows Michigan has 2.5 gigawatts of power planned, approved or running for data centers. Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Texas and Virginia each have more. One researcher said the trend is like a gold rush. Companies are proposing hyperscale data centers across the country, but builders will finish only a fraction of them. What hyperscale data centers are Each hyperscale data center covers hundreds of acres, uses a large amount of water, and pulls a large amount of energy. Erik Nordman, director of the Institute of Public Utilities at Michigan State University, said this new generation of hyperscale data centers is causing the controversy. He said they are built specifically for artificial intelligence computing. Nordman said his institute has received interest over the past year from people in Michigan and across the country about how data centers might affect electric and water utilities. Two projects approved in Michigan Michigan has cleared two hyperscale projects. In Washtenaw County, crews are building “The Barn” for Oracle and OpenAI. Nordman said the site in Southeast Michigan will use about as much electricity as the city of Detroit, about 25% of DTE’s current load. Google plans a project called “Project Cannoli” in Wayne County. Nordman said it is based on a template Google has developed and implemented in other states. He said the template is considered one of the best practices among industry leaders. Together, the two projects will use 2.4 gigawatts of power. Both are in DTE Energy’s territory. Nordman said Michigan’s investor-owned utilities, including Consumers Energy and DTE, say they have enough electricity and resources for the initial hyperscale data center in Southeast Michigan. If more growth happens, he said, more resources would need to be built. How Michigan compares with other states The U.S. Data Center Map tracks the gigawatts powering data centers that are planned, approved or running in each state. Michigan has 2.5 gigawatts, according to the map. Michigan’s neighbors have more: - Illinois: almost 12 gigawatts - Indiana: about 10 gigawatts - Ohio: almost 19 gigawatts Nationwide, Texas leads with almost 104 gigawatts. Virginia ranks second with more than 40 gigawatts. Nordman said several factors can affect where data centers are sited. He listed the cost of electricity, access to transmission lines, available land near transmission lines, the business environment, and tax breaks. He said Michigan has community resistance to data centers, which he called a headwind for developers. He said Michigan has abundant clean water that is useful for cooling, but residents are protective of the resource. Nordman said the state’s sales and use tax incentives are meant to attract data center owners, but it is unclear whether they will be enough. Nordman said Texas has a “very liberal approach to permitting and facilities.” He said a data center can build and connect to the electric grid more easily there than in a place like Michigan. Nordman said Virginia has a lot of data centers because it is the national hub where the internet started and is connected to the Pentagon and government agencies. He said AI data centers are appearing in other places. Nordman said Michigan is lagging, but more developers could still come. Governor candidates on moratorium Nordman said people are probably in a wait-and-see period, and decisions will follow the election. He said it is hard to tell which direction those decisions will go. He said both candidates are trying to walk a fine line. He said there is grassroots dissatisfaction with how data center development has progressed in Michigan and elsewhere, but the candidates also see an economic development opportunity they don’t want Michigan to miss. Both candidates for governor, John James and Jocelyn Benson, have talked about a moratorium on data centers, which would pause new projects. Both said they want to protect utility bills and water. Benson said, “I think data centers threaten the fabric of many of our communities, particularly our rural communities, and do threaten the possibility of driving up water rates, energy rates, and using or abusing our natural resources like our water.” She said she has called for a moratorium “until we put guardrails in place.” James said, “No new data centers until we have a plan to protect our people.” He said he has said this for a long time and on the debate stage in the primary. “Local control comes first,” James said. “And then we need to make sure our electricity bills don’t go up, that we protect our water.” Consumers Energy response Consumers Energy said earlier this year that a hyperscale data center is coming to its service area. The company declined an interview request. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call, someone asked Garrick Rochow about the candidates’ stances. Rochow is president of CMS Energy Corporation and Consumers Energy. The question was how to think about the data center opportunity window. “Politics do not equal policy,” Rochow said. “And some of the spin that you see leading up to the election does not equal reality.” Rochow said there is common ground on affordability and data centers. He said both candidates support those investments in Michigan and the jobs and property tax value that come with them. “No one said no data centers,” Rochow said. “In fact, they’ve talked about responsible data centers. And we’re for that as well.” Rochow said he expects data centers to continue to move forward after the election. He said he sees a strong environment for data center growth across Michigan. artigo.texto: SPRINGFIELD, Ga. — The Effingham County Board of Commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday night to table a vote on the OpenAI data center site plan until Nov. 17. District 2 Commissioner Roger Burdette made the motion to table the site plan vote after an extended back-and-forth with Rich Modliszewski, the Octans GA LLC representative presenting the Project Camellia site plan. Burdette said Modliszewski’s presentation lacked clarity and conflicted with conversations he had had with OpenAI representatives, particularly regarding berms intended to mitigate noise. “I’ve been talking about a berm since day one,” Burdette said. “I was told we were going to have a 20-foot berm, that if we needed to add something extra like a concave acoustic wall that we would do that. If I can’t get approval on some dirt tonight then I can’t stand behind this site plan.” District 4 Commissioner Beth Helmly also announced that the Board of Commissioners would discuss a data center moratorium at its next meeting. Commissioners also voted to approve the Effingham County Zoning Ordinance and adopt the county's official zoning map, completing unfinished business from their previous meeting. Site plan discussion The site plan for the proposed Project Camellia campus at the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub covers approximately 1,347 acres and includes six data center buildings, a warehouse, an operations building, two electrical substations, cooling infrastructure, electrical yards and approximately 1,600 parking spaces. However, it contained no written commitment to construct a 20-foot dirt berm along Hodgeville Road, which borders high-density residential neighborhoods. Commissioners raised questions about water and sewer service, wetland impacts and the generators that would be used after construction. OpenAI had previously committed to using battery storage as backup power for the data centers. Modliszewski clarified that generators would be used for “life safety and security systems,” not to power the data center buildings. He deferred many of the questions to engineers from Thomas & Hutton, calling them forward to respond or saying he could provide answers later. “I’m not an engineer,” he told commissioners. “I was here to talk about the merits of the site plan and its conformity to the ordinance. Most of the questions tonight had absolutely nothing to do with conforming to the zoning ordinance. A lot of that needs to be settled during the development plan application when the engineering is actually complete. This is a preliminary site plan.” When Burdette pressed him about the promised 20-foot berm, Modliszewski initially could not confirm it. He said some form of noise mitigation would be provided in accordance with zoning requirements. After a brief recess requested by Burdette, during which Modliszewski took a phone call in a corner of the commission chamber, the Octans GA representative returned and said he could promise a 20-foot berm. That did not satisfy Burdette, who stood by his motion to table the vote. “I expected tonight to have somebody with the capabilities of coming here and telling people about this project and we haven't had that,” Burdette said. “I really appreciate what all of OpenAI has done for us so far, but safety's got to be number one, and we have to have reassurance of that, and I don’t have that assurance.” He said he hoped to have more questions answered by Nov. 17. Residents voice concerns Effingham County residents filled the commission chamber to capacity despite the election-night meeting. Some wore “No Data Center” stickers alongside their “I Voted” stickers on their T-shirts. Members of the Protect Effingham Alliance distributed instructions for a silent protest in anticipation of what many expected would be approval of the OpenAI site plan. Alexis Lane and Anna Lee HeidtHarris, co-founders of Protect Effingham, joined other residents in celebrating the decision to table the site plan but said significant concerns remain. “Obviously we’re appreciative of the tabling,” HeidtHarris said. “We definitely need more time.” However, she said the presentation made clear that OpenAI was focused on meeting requirements rather than honoring verbal commitments. “I wish that they would put this much passion into worrying about other aspects of the project as they are for these berms,” Lane said. “There are a tremendous amount of concerns other than that that they don’t seem to be worried about.” She cited the revised site plan's increase in proposed data center building heights to 42 feet as one of those concerns. County resident Jerri Howell distributed petitions seeking amendments to the Effingham County Code of Ordinances that would revise data center definitions and prohibit data centers in all zoning districts. The petition drive began about a month ago, and Howell said it had already collected more than 1,500 signatures. Even if OpenAI's site plan is eventually approved, she said, the petition's goal is to establish more safeguards for future development proposals. As for a potential moratorium, Howell said it was too little, too late. “We've already given access to what is arguably one of the largest if not the largest hyperscale data center in the country,” she said. “I feel like we're doing a moratorium to save face as opposed to pressing pause and actively thinking through this.”

artigo.texto: Neopulse Energy Private Limited has been appointed as the Owner’s Engineer by Coal India Limited (CIL) for its 80 MW / 320 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project in Odisha. The appointment marks another step towards strengthening energy storage infrastructure and supporting renewable energy integration in India. Under the engagement, Neopulse Energy will provide independent technical support to Coal India throughout the pre-award and post-award stages of the Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contract. During the pre-award stage, the company will assist with preparing technical specifications, defining equipment requirements and evaluating technical bids received for the EPC tender. Following the award of the EPC contract, Neopulse Energy will review the contractor’s engineering designs, vendor documentation and quality plans. Its responsibilities will also include technical supervision and oversight during equipment manufacturing, project construction, testing and commissioning. The 80 MW / 320 MWh BESS project is expected to support grid flexibility and improve the integration of renewable energy into India’s electricity network. Battery storage plays an important role in managing the intermittent nature of solar and wind power while supporting reliable electricity supply. Through this appointment, Neopulse Energy will contribute its technical expertise to CIL’s expanding renewable energy and energy storage portfolio. artigo.texto: [SMM ESS Flash] CATL Opens Argentina Office and Supplies 1,025 MWh to Central Puerto CATL has opened a commercial and technical office in Buenos Aires staffed for sales, engineering and project management, and is already supplying batteries to two Central Puerto projects totalling 205 MW and 1,025 MWh of storage capacity. The projects are Nuevo Puerto at 150 MW/750 MWh and Central Costanera at 55 MW/275 MWh, both using CATL lithium iron phosphate batteries with five-hour duration and both awarded under the AlmaGBA storage programme, with Nuevo Puerto holding a 15-year supply contract with distributor Edenor and Central Costanera serving Edesur. Nuevo Puerto is close to 80% complete, and Central Puerto plans to energise one project before the end of 2026 and the other in January 2027, with batteries installed but commissioning dependent on transformers from China delayed in transit. Argentina has awarded 713 MW under AlmaGBA and a further 700.5 MW across 20 projects under AlmaSADI at an estimated investment of US$700 million, while CATL says it has more than 15 GWh of awarded storage projects in Latin America and has shipped over 330 GWh of energy storage batteries globally to June 2026.

artigo.texto: Solid-state battery race: Sunwoda tests polymer cells with automakers as CATL targets 2027 Sunwoda is advancing a polymer-composite approach to solid-state batteries as CATL pursues sulfide chemistry. The two Chinese suppliers are developing different electrolyte technologies and production timelines. Sunwoda’s latest disclosure confirms that its battery has completed design and process verification and remains under customer evaluation, while CATL continues to target small-batch production in 2027. Sunwoda Electric Vehicle Battery Co., Ltd. (SEVB), the automotive battery subsidiary of Sunwoda Electronic Co., Ltd., disclosed the update on October 30 through the Shenzhen Stock Exchange’s investor interaction platform. The company did not identify the automakers evaluating its cells or disclose sample volumes. It had already reported customer testing in May 2026, making the latest response an update on ongoing work rather than the start of a new testing programme. CATL reaffirmed its 2027 small-batch production target in an October 27 investor response. CATL previously reported its 20 Ah solid-state prototype in 2024. While CATL is developing sulfide-based cells, Sunwoda’s Xin Bixiao programme uses a polymer-composite electrolyte. Polymer cells operate at pressures below 1 MPa Sunwoda’s 20 Ah Xin Bixiao cell has a reported energy density of 400 Wh/kg and a cycle life exceeding 1,200 cycles under external pressure below 1 MPa. Its disclosed design includes a 12-micron polymer-composite membrane and a nanoscale high-entropy silicon anode. The company has also reported that the cell passed a 200°C hot-box test. The low-pressure requirement relates to maintaining contact between electrodes and the solid electrolyte as materials expand and contract during charging and discharging. Some sulfide-based designs require sustained external pressure to limit interface deterioration. Sulfide materials also require moisture-controlled manufacturing because reactions with water can release toxic hydrogen sulfide (H₂S). Sunwoda says its polymer-composite design can accommodate electrode movement while maintaining contact between cell components. Operating below 1 MPa could reduce a battery pack’s structural requirements, but the cell-level results do not show that additional support can be eliminated. The reported cycle life and thermal results also do not demonstrate equivalent performance in a complete vehicle battery. For illustration, increasing a hypothetical battery from 55 kWh to 80 kWh could raise range from 550 km CLTC (approximately 450 km WLTP) to 800 km CLTC (approximately 660 km WLTP), assuming unchanged vehicle efficiency. This is an illustrative calculation, not a Sunwoda vehicle projection. Pilot production and aviation applications SEVB has connected a solid-state battery pilot line with an annual design capacity of 0.2 GWh. Its roadmap includes a second-generation sulfide battery targeted for 2027 and a future cell exceeding 500 Wh/kg targeted for 2030. Both remain development targets, not confirmed commercial production dates. Sulfide electrolytes also cost more. Shanghai Metals Market has assessed lithium phosphorus sulfur chloride (Li₆PS₅Cl), a sulfide electrolyte, at approximately 3,500 to 4,500 yuan per kilogram, compared with around 30 to 50 yuan per kilogram for conventional liquid electrolytes. The materials are not direct substitutes, but the difference illustrates the price gap between the two materials. Sunwoda is also involved in the Guangdong Engineering Research Centre for Aviation Power Batteries, which has set a target of at least 450 Wh/kg for aviation battery cells. Its eVTOL development targets include continuous discharge power density of at least 1,000 W/kg. Aviation is one potential application for high-energy-density batteries, although the disclosed targets do not establish commercial orders or production volumes. Li Auto and Xiaomi’s battery plans The October 30 investor exchange also raised questions about Li Auto and Xiaomi developing in-house battery packs for selected models. Sunwoda said it respected customers’ decisions and would seek to expand its business through product development and service. Both automakers are also significant SEVB shareholders. Li Auto agreed to invest 2.65 billion yuan (approximately 395 million USD) for an initial 8.79% stake. Xiaomi subsequently proposed a 1.7 billion yuan (approximately 253 million USD) investment for a 5.34% stake, subject to shareholder approval. After the proposed transaction, Li Auto’s stake would fall to about 8.32%, making it the second-largest shareholder, with Xiaomi third. Neither company has been identified as an evaluator of the current solid-state samples. Their in-house battery plans provide commercial context, but do not establish lost orders or a direct connection to Sunwoda’s solid-state development. Next steps include vehicle-level validation and repeatable production. Sunwoda’s polymer approach offers an alternative to sulfide chemistry, but manufacturing yield, cost, durability and pack integration will determine its commercial prospects.

artigo.texto: ENGIE is adding 150 MW/300 MWh to its Hazelwood BESS in Australia and has engaged Sungrow, a China-based maker of PV inverters and energy storage systems, as the technology provider. Sungrow will supply 66 ST5015-UX battery units from its PowerTitan 2.0 series, along with 33 SC6900UD-MV power conversion system (PCS) inverters and an EMS3000 smart controller. Elecnor will serve as the balance of plant (BOP) contractor on the expansion. Grid-forming technology will be a part of the plant, so that it can support voltage and frequency stability and can respond rapidly to changing conditions on the network. Commercial operations are targeted for 2028, and the plant will then store and deliver electricity for Victoria and the National Electricity Market (NEM). Sungrow to supply 300 MWh grid-forming BESS for ENGIE in Australia The 150 MW/300 MWh expansion of the Hazelwood BESS in Australia is to be fitted with 66 battery units and 33 PCS inverters that Sungrow will supply to ENGIE. artigo.texto: Coal India Limited (CIL) has appointed Neopulse Energy Pvt. Ltd. as the Owner’s Engineer for its 80 MW / 320 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project in Odisha. CIL awarded the contract a month after issuing the BESS tender for the project in Odisha. With this, CIL continues the trend of PSU's counting on external expertise when it comes to renewable energy projects. Other than NTPC through NTPC Green, most PSU's have usually struggled to execute green projects on their own. As CIL expands its renewable energy and energy storage portfolio, Neopulse will provide independent technical support across both stages of the Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contract. Under the pre-award scope, Neopulse will undertake technical specifications, define equipment requirements, and provide technical bid evaluation support for EPC tendering. As part of the post-award scope, Neopulse Energy will review the EPC contractor’s engineering designs, vendor documents, and quality plans. It will also provide technical oversight during manufacturing, construction, testing, and commissioning of the energy storage system. These activities are central to ensuring the project's technical compliance and supporting the integration of more renewable energy into India's grid. About The Tender The BESS tender issued for this project is spread across four locations in Odisha—Bhatli, Basta, Padampur, and New Bolangir. It also provides for 15 years of comprehensive Operation and Maintenance (O&M). For developing the BESS system and its associated power evacuation infrastructure, the EPC contractor is required to undertake the entire scope of work. Under the contract, the contractor will be responsible for setting up the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and making the energy storage facility available to GRIDCO on an 'on-demand' basis. Earlier this year, SECI, on behalf of GRIDCO, had initiated and awarded a tender for a 500 MWh (125 MW x 4 hours) grid-connected Battery Energy Storage System project. Subsequently, GRIDCO issued a Letter of Award (LoA) to Coal India Limited on April 30, 2026, for developing a 40 MW / 160 MWh BESS project across two locations in Odisha. The project comprises a 20 MW / 80 MWh BESS connected to the 132/33 kV GSS Padampur and another 20 MW / 80 MWh BESS at OPTCL's 220/132/33 kV GSS New Bolangir.

artigo.texto: HIZENERGY, a China-based supplier of commercial and industrial (C&I) BESS solutions, has presented its C&I BESS portfolio in a keynote presentation at Frankfurt, Germany. The portfolio is led by the ENERBOX series, which is an all-in-one AC-coupled cabinet with 125 kW of power and 261 kWh or 313 kWh of energy capacity. That capacity can be expanded by connecting the cabinets in parallel, and each unit can be operated on the grid, off the grid or with a seamless switch between them. The units have passed UL 9540A safety testing, and they can be fully commissioned on site within two hours. They are intended for factories, industrial parks and commercial premises, where they can be used for PV self-consumption, peak shaving, energy arbitrage and critical-load backup. These sites are being supported from a central hub in the Netherlands and through 12 after-sales service points in Europe, where the company has live deployments. HIZENERGY presents 125 kW ENERBOX C&I BESS in Frankfurt, Germany The ENERBOX cabinet of 125 kW and up to 313 kWh has been presented by HIZENERGY in Frankfurt, Germany, as the lead product in its C&I BESS portfolio for Europe. artigo.texto: Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Dominion executives expect their upcoming merger with NextEra will create a nuclear-energy powerhouse and position the combined company to better develop its energy-storage solutions amid growing demand for both technologies. Nuclear Titan in the Making? As Dominion Energy Incorporated prepares to be acquired by NextEra Energy Incorporated, following shareholder approval in September, executives are optimistic the company's slate of projects will continue to develop under new leadership. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $95 billion worth of active and proposed projects owned by Dominion. According to Industrial Info Resources data, nearly half of the $95 billion total is attributed to active and proposed developments at Dominion's four operational nuclear plants, which will double NextEra's number of nuclear plants following the acquisition. NextEra's total operational nuclear capacity would double to more than 10 gigawatts (GW), making the combined company the second-largest nuclear power generator in the U.S., behind Constellation Energy. In a recent earnings-related conference call, Bob Blue, the chief executive officer of Dominion, offered details on the company's latest Integrated Resource Plan (IRP). He said Dominion has "some limited opportunities" to perform upgrades at its nuclear facilities, which would focus on "investments necessary for subsequent license renewal." Among the upgrades underway are a condenser replacement and a control-system upgrade on Unit 1 at Dominion's North Anna Nuclear Power Station in Mineral, Virginia. Both are part of a broader plan to allow Unit 1 to operate through 2058, an extension from the previous 2038 that was approved in August 2024 by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). Industrial Info Resources offers more information on the North Anna developments in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Plant and Project databases, where readers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in a plant profile and detailed reports on the condenser replacement and control-system upgrade. The merger is expected to close in the second half of 2027. By the Numbers - More than $95 billion: Total investment value of active and proposed projects owned by Dominion - About $47 billion: Total attributed to active and proposed developments at Dominion's four operational nuclear plants - More than 10 GW: Total operational nuclear power from a combined NextEra-Dominion company Quadruple the Storage? Blue said in the earnings call that battery energy-storage system (BESS) projects would be a priority for the newly formed company following the merger. He pointed to energy-storage legislation that Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) signed into law in April, which he said "establishes substantially higher targets for both short- and long-duration storage." "Looking longer term, the proposed combination with NextEra Energy would bring together significant capabilities and experience in energy storage," Blue said. "We believe that positions the combined company exceptionally well to deploy storage at scale, as the technology matures and system needs evolve." Dominion's projects under development include a 50-MW BESS unit at the Dulles Solar Energy Center, which is designed to generate 100 MW from PV panels. It's stand-alone BESS projects include a proposed Drake Battery Storage Plant in Topping, Virginia, which would store up to 80 MW for the power grid. Subscribers can read detailed reports on the Dulles and Drake projects. Steven Ridge, the chief financial officer of Dominion, said the latest IRP "increases battery [storage capacity] on the system by about four times. For instance, in the 2025 IRP, for 2030 through 2034 battery [capacity] was 850 MW. In the 2026 update, it is 3.3 GW." He also noted that "some of the IRP would be under a PPA [power-purchase agreement] structure." Dominion, like many other utilities, grows its generation portfolio through a mixture of plants that it owns and operates, plus additional power procured by independent power producers (IPPs). The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed projects owned by Dominion. Key Takeaways - Dominion is set to be acquired by NextEra in the second half of 2027. - The combined company would be the second-largest nuclear power generator in the U.S. - Recently enacted energy-storage legislation in Virginia could prove fruitful for the new company. artigo.texto: ‘Big techs’ operam com gargalo de chip, energia e prédio de data center Analistas e investidores pararam de se preocupar se há de fato demanda para os altos investimentos, mas querem saber como estes serão financiados Queima de caixa, diluição de ações e endividamento com infraestrutura para a demanda de inteligência artificial estão sob o olhar atento de analistas e investidores, após a divulgação de balanços trimestrais de Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta e Microsoft, que operam com gargalo de oferta. “O gargalo hoje é chip, energia e prédio, não cliente”, diz a analista da gestora São Pedro Capital, Gabriela Moraes. “O Google começou a alugar capacidade de terceiros por não conseguir construir [data centers] rápido o suficiente”, ilustra. Juntas, as cinco “big techs” reportaram gasto de capital (capex) de US$ 209,5 bilhões no terceiro trimestre, um salto anual de 81,1%, segundo o Valor Data. A queda de ações de Alphabet, Amazon e Meta logo após a publicação de seus resultados mostra a preocupação sobre “como” estas empresas estão financiando o capex elevado, observam analistas consultados pelo Valor. As três ‘big techs’ encerraram o trimestre com fluxo de caixa negativo. Foi a primeira queima de caixa da Meta desde 2012. “A diferença está sendo coberta com dívida e ações”, diz a analista da São Pedro Capital. O mercado, afirma, passou a cobrar “de onde vem o dinheiro” e quanto isso vai diluir o acionista. A queda de 7% das ações da Meta, logo após a divulgação do balanço, foi mais impulsionada pelo anúncio de uma nova classe de ações sem voto, criada justamente para financiar o crescimento, do que por um caixa negativo. “O anúncio foi lido pelo mercado como ‘follow-on’ à vista”, diz Moraes. Ela lembra que o custo de proteção da dívida da Meta - swap de inadimplência de crédito (CDS, na sigla em inglês) - foi à máxima histórica. Desde junho, a Alphabet, controladora do Google, captou US$ 40 bilhões em emissão de ações junto a investidores, incluindo US$ 10 bilhões em papéis para a Berkshire Hathaway. Já a Microsoft anunciou uma emissão histórica de US$ 25 bilhões em títulos de dívida (bonds) no dia seguinte à divulgação do balanço. Empresas de nuvem e centros de dados emitiram US$ 368 bi em dívidas neste ano, mais de seis vezes o valor de 2025 As gigantes de computação em nuvem e empresas de centros de dados emitiram quase US$ 368 bilhões em dívidas no acumulado do ano até o dia 28 de outubro, mais de seis vezes a soma de 2025, apontam dados compilados pela Bloomberg. “O mercado de crédito pode ter dificuldade em absorver esse montante”, diz o analista do Itaú BBA, Stephano Gabriel. Ele cita os exemplos do custo de proteção da dívida da Meta (CDS, na sigla em inglês), alcançado a máxima histórica em 26 de outubro e a derrocada das ações da CoreWeave, empresa de nuvem computacional especializada em IA (“neocloud”, no jargão do setor). Desde o início de outubro, as ações da empresa recuaram 39% após a disparada do risco de sua dívida de US$ 50 bilhões. O avanço na receita de computação em nuvem das “big techs” sinaliza que a demanda por IA justifica o endividamento para acelerar a infraestrutura computacional de IA. No terceiro trimestre, as três líderes do mercado global de nuvem geraram crescimentos em linha ou acima do esperado pelo mercado, na comparação com igual período do ano anterior: a receita da Amazon Web Services (AWS), divisão de nuvem da Amazon, cresceu 39,3%; as vendas de Microsoft Azure avançaram 48%; e a divisão Google Cloud teve um salto de 102,6% na receita. As “big techs”, em especial as que vendem serviço de nuvem computacional, afirmam que há uma demanda reprimida de IA, parada por falta de infraestrutura - há falta de chips, energia e prédios para data centers. Somando a carteira de pedidos (“backlog”) de nuvem, “Amazon, Microsoft e Google somam US$ 1,8 trilhão em receita contratada esperando capacidade para ser entregue; e as três repetiram que a demanda excede a oferta”, completa Moraes. Na temporada de balanços do quarto trimestre, as “big techs”’ devem manter o ritmo elevado de capex e de queima de caixa, afirma a estrategista global da XP, Maria Irene Jordão. O foco do investidor será a projeção de capex de 2027, que não veio nas conferências desta temporada de balanços. Necessidade de mais endividamento e emissão de novas ações “dependerá bastante das condições de mercado”, observa Jordão. “As companhias, de modo geral, seguem nessa toada enquanto o mercado estiver receptivo.”
